News.title: Anyone moving money between ISAs warned over simple mistake that could affect tax-free savings
News.content:
Anyone moving money between ISAs warned over simple mistake that could affect tax-free savings

If you want to move your ISA money, the safest approach is generally to start the process with the new ISA provider

View Image Be careful when moving ISA funds (Image: Getty Images/Image Source)

Savers looking for a better return on their money are being warned about a surprisingly easy mistake to make when switching ISAs.

‌



With savings rates changing regularly, moving your money to a better-paying account can make perfect sense.

‌



But if the money is already sitting inside an ISA, simply withdrawing it yourself and paying it into your new account may not be the clever shortcut it appears to be.

‌



That's because HMRC distinguishes between transferring an ISA and taking money out of an ISA before subsequently paying money into another one.

And with an annual ISA allowance of £20,000 for the 2026/27 tax year, getting that distinction wrong could potentially cause problems with your allowance.

We also treat our community members to special offers, promotions, and adverts from us and our partners. If you don’t like our community, you can check out any time you like. If you’re curious, you can read our Privacy Notice. NEWSLETTER: Or sign up to the Mirror's Money newsletter here for all the best advice and shopping deals straight to your inbox.

‌



The ISA switching mistake to avoid

ISAs allow you to save or invest without paying UK tax on income or capital gains generated within the ISA. You can currently save up to £20,000 across ISAs during the tax year.

However, you might have considerably more than £20,000 sitting in ISAs because money saved during previous tax years remains within its tax-free wrapper.

Imagine, for example, that you have built up £35,000 in a Cash ISA over several years. You find another Cash ISA offering a better rate and want to move the whole £35,000.

‌



The important thing is how you move it. If the new account accepts ISA transfers, you can ask the new provider to transfer your existing ISA.

The historic ISA savings being transferred don't suddenly become £35,000 of new ISA subscriptions for the current tax year. But withdrawing £35,000 yourself is different.

Once you've taken the money out of its ISA wrapper, you shouldn't simply assume that you can deposit the whole £35,000 into another ISA as a new contribution.

‌



That could be particularly important if you've already paid money into ISAs during this tax year.

Don't close your old ISA yourself

If your aim is to switch provider, the safest approach is generally to start the process with the new ISA provider.

Check that the new account accepts ISA transfers and ask the provider to arrange the move. Don't withdraw the money first unless you understand exactly how the rules of your particular ISA work.

‌



It is also worth checking whether there are penalties for leaving your existing account. A fixed-rate Cash ISA, for example, may impose an interest penalty for accessing the money before the end of the fixed term.

There are also different Cash ISA rules around access and withdrawals depending on the type of account you have, so it pays to check the small print before moving anything.

There's an important exception

This is where ISA rules become slightly more complicated. Some ISAs are flexible . A flexible ISA can allow you to withdraw money and replace it during the same tax year without the replacement counting again towards your annual allowance, subject to the relevant rules.

‌



But flexibility isn't automatically included with every ISA. So seeing the words "easy access" doesn't necessarily mean you have a flexible ISA for tax purposes.

Before withdrawing money that you intend to put back, check the terms of your account or speak to your provider.

What does an ISA expert say?

Investment and ISA expert Ruby Layram says the problem is that withdrawing the money yourself feels like the obvious thing to do.

‌



She said: “If you find a better ISA rate, it can be tempting to simply withdraw your savings and pay the money into the new account yourself. But that isn't necessarily the same as making an ISA transfer, and that distinction really matters.

“Money built up inside an ISA over previous tax years can normally be transferred without using your current year's ISA allowance, provided you follow the proper ISA transfer process.

“There are exceptions, particularly with flexible ISAs, but not every ISA is flexible. You should never assume you can take money out and put it back without checking first.

‌



“If you're moving ISA savings because you've found a better deal, my advice is simple: don't touch the money until you've checked the transfer rules. Ask the new provider to arrange the ISA transfer and check whether there are penalties for leaving your existing account.”

What if you have a Stocks and Shares ISA?

The same principle of using the proper transfer procedure is important for investment ISAs too. If you're switching investment platforms, don't automatically sell everything, withdraw the cash into your bank account and start again elsewhere.

Depending on the providers and investments involved, it may be possible to transfer the ISA while maintaining its tax wrapper.

‌



It is also worth remembering that Stocks and Shares ISAs work differently from Cash ISAs . Your money is invested rather than simply held as cash, which means its value can fall as well as rise.

Charges matter too. If you are moving an investment ISA, check platform fees, dealing charges and any costs involved in leaving or transferring.

Remember that investments can fall as well as rise and you could get back less than you invest.

‌



ISA rules are changing

There is another reason to start paying closer attention to where your ISA money is held. From April 2027, the Government plans to limit Cash ISA subscriptions to £12,000 a year for people under 65 , while retaining the £20,000 overall annual ISA allowance.

Other changes are also planned as part of the ISA reforms. That doesn't mean savers need to make rushed decisions now. But it does make understanding whether you're contributing, withdrawing or transferring money increasingly important.

First-time buyers are facing a separate ISA shake-up. The Government is developing a replacement for the Lifetime ISA for new savers, meaning anyone currently building a house deposit may need to weigh up whether to open a Lifetime ISA now or wait .

‌



Five things to check before moving an ISA

Before doing anything with your ISA savings:

Check whether the new ISA accepts transfers. Ask the new provider to initiate the ISA transfer rather than withdrawing the money yourself. Find out whether your existing ISA is flexible. Check for exit charges or lost interest before switching. Keep track of how much new money you have subscribed to ISAs during the current tax year.

Shopping around for a better return on your savings is sensible. But with an ISA, how you move the money can be every bit as important as where you move it.

Article continues below

The extra few minutes spent checking the transfer rules could save you a considerable headache later.

News.title: Man charged with rape of boy, 14, in Portsmouth alleyway 'moments after they first met'
News.content:
Man charged with rape of boy, 14, in Portsmouth alleyway 'moments after they first met'

Sadiq Farhad Azad, 33, is accused of raping a 14-year-old boy and stalking a woman in her 20s in Portsmouth

View Image A boy was allegedly attacked in an alleyway off London Road in Portsmouth (file) (Image: Google Maps)

A man is alleged to have raped a 14-year-old boy in an alleyway in Portsmouth.

Sadiq Farhad Azad, 33, of no fixed address, has been charged with rape of a boy aged 13 to 15, stalking involving fear of violence or serious alarm or distress (section 4a stalking), and criminal damage to property valued at less than £5,000.

Hampshire Police received a report on August 11 that a 14-year-old boy had been raped in an alleyway off London Road in Portsmouth by a man he had spoken to on a bus but did not previously know. The incident was reported to have taken place between 7pm and 8pm on August 6.

Police received a separate report on Tuesday, September 1, that a man had been stalking a woman in her 20s for a year and had criminally damaged a family member's car.

Following enquiries into both incidents, Azad, who is an Iraqi national, was arrested and charged, the force said on Saturday afternoon.

Article continues below

He has been remanded in custody and is due to appear at Portsmouth Crown Court on Monday, September 7.

News.title: 'I thought it was a gym injury' but man's pea-sized lump was stage 3 breast cancer
News.content:
'I thought it was a gym injury' but man's pea-sized lump was stage 3 breast cancer

James Richards was 36 when he was diagnosed with breast cancer and is now welcoming Coronation Street's new storyline hoping it will highlight that it is not just a woman's disease

View 6 Images James was diagnosed with stage 3 breast cancer (Image: James Richards)

Fans of Coronation Street are set to follow Kit Green’s devastating diagnosis of stage three breast cancer. For many watching, it may be the first time they realise that men can get a disease still overwhelmingly associated with women.

‌



The Weatherfield police detective is floored to discover his health concerns result in the cancer diagnosis - something shared by more than 400 men in the UK every year. While it is rare compared with more than 55,000 women, Kit’s story reflects a very real experience faced by hundreds of men every year.

‌



James Richards knows the statistics only too well for in 2023, at the age of 36, he was diagnosed with stage three breast cancer. At the time, life was looking good - his career was going well and he had moved in with his partner, then came the shock diagnosis.

‌



View 6 Images Kit is facing a devastating diagnosis (Image: ITV)

He says: "Breast cancer was the last thing I thought would turn my life upside down. In truth, it wasn’t something I had ever seriously considered could happen to me. And it was that lack of awareness that stopped me contacting my doctor when I first found a pea-sized lump just behind my nipple.

"I put it down to 'just one of those things', or perhaps some sort of injury picked up at the gym, and carried on with my life as though nothing had happened. I did that for three months before I finally, and reluctantly, booked an appointment with my GP. Thank God I did.

‌



"A week later, I found myself in a breast clinic having a mammogram, ultrasound and biopsy. A few days after that came the diagnosis, followed by a treatment plan that would involve months of chemotherapy, surgery and radiotherapy.

"Coming to terms with cancer was one thing, but being diagnosed with what I - and much of society - still saw as essentially a 'women’s disease' brought its own feelings of embarrassment, isolation and, at times, shame.

"What I hadn’t expected was to discover just how much of the world around breast cancer still assumes the person going through it will be a woman. From information about wearing bras, to support services I couldn’t access because I was a man, I repeatedly found myself in a healthcare system that knew men could get breast cancer, but often didn’t seem designed for us."

‌



View 6 Images James was one of more than 400 men diagnosed with breast cancer in 2023 (Image: James Richards)

He says he "couldn’t see himself" in the position he found himself in - not in the literature, the support being offered or the awareness campaigns that could have flagged up the risk. As a result, during treatment, he decided to do something about it and founded moobs, the UK’s first organisation dedicated specifically to improving awareness and support for men affected by breast cancer.

"Since then, one of the things I’ve learned is that my experience is far from unique," he explains. "Again and again, I hear from men whose stories are strikingly similar to mine: they didn’t know they could get breast cancer, they delayed seeking help, and when they entered the breast cancer system, much of what surrounded them felt as though it had been designed for somebody else.

‌



"That is why Kit’s Coronation Street storyline matters. Putting a man’s breast cancer diagnosis in front of millions of viewers is an opportunity to do more than simply remind men to check themselves."

View 6 Images James Richards founded moobs

He adds: "We should also be asking whether the support waiting for them if they do receive a diagnosis is good enough." James says he believes there are five things which "we need to do better" for men affected by breast cancer.

‌



Men need to know they can get breast cancer

He says: "If there is one thing we need to do better, it is making men aware that they can get breast cancer - it’s the whole ethos behind moobs. Like all cancers, the earlier breast cancer is discovered, the better the chances of a good outcome.

"We don’t need to frighten men into thinking breast cancer is common, but they do need to know that it is possible and understand the changes they should be looking out for. Prostate Cancer UK has done an excellent job of getting men to think about their risk of prostate cancer, why should breast cancer be any different?

"This matters because research has shown a 19% higher mortality rate among men diagnosed with breast cancer than women with the disease. Awareness has to be part of that conversation, because if men don’t know breast cancer is something they can get, how can we expect them to recognise when something might be wrong?"

‌



Patient information needs to be more inclusive

James says: "Once I was diagnosed, I was bombarded with a huge amount of information about breast cancer, but nearly all of it had been written with women in mind. One of the first pieces of information I was given included advice about wearing a loose-fitting bra."

View 6 Images James said he knew he had to act after finding much of the information and support was not suitable for men (Image: James Richards)

He adds: "That might sound trivial on its own, but when you have just been told you have cancer, every reminder that the system wasn’t really expecting someone like you makes you feel a little more isolated. Throughout treatment, I received information about services, events and support that were either explicitly for women or clearly written on the assumption that the person reading it would be one.

‌



"Nobody is suggesting that information for women should disappear. Women make up the overwhelming majority of breast cancer diagnoses and their needs obviously have to remain central, but making information more inclusive of everyone who gets the disease does not take anything away from women."

Support services need to be genuinely open to men

"While I was going through treatment, one of the hardest things was the perceived lack of support available to me; but that becomes even harder when the support that does exist actively excludes you," he says. "Every time I checked in at the breast clinic, I would have to explain that I was there because I had breast cancer, with staff often assuming I had come to the wrong department.

"Having to repeatedly disclose my diagnosis in public was embarrassing enough, but one of my lowest points came when I was referred to a physiotherapy class for people with breast cancer, only to be turned away because I was a man and the class was for women only.

‌



"And this kind of experience isn’t unique to me. One man moobs has supported had told me he was refused his tamoxifen prescription because it was assumed the medication was intended for his wife and that his name had been added in error.

"These incidents might seem small individually, but they add up. You find yourself repeatedly having to explain that, yes, you really do have breast cancer and, yes, this service or medication really is for you. Men don’t need to be separated from breast cancer care, we simply need to be properly included in the treatment and support that already exists for people with the disease.

Research needs to reflect that men get breast cancer too

James says: "Although the treatment I received from my oncology team was second to none, one of the realities of being a man with breast cancer is that much of the evidence behind the treatment pathway has been built around women. This was something I came up against again and again. At one stage, I was heading towards major surgery that I later discovered would have been unnecessary, largely because the established pathway was based on 'what we do for women'.

‌



"It was only after doing my own research and independently speaking to people at the cutting edge of breast cancer in men that I was able to question that approach and ultimately avoid it. But the problem extends far beyond primary treatment and affects how I think about my future too.

"Some of the drugs I take to reduce the risk of my cancer returning have very limited evidence around their effectiveness and long-term impact in men. In many respects, it feels like I am going into parts of treatment blind.

"And because breast cancer in men is most commonly diagnosed later in life, there is also far less long-term evidence for someone diagnosed as young as I was. I don’t have generations of men diagnosed in their 30s whose experiences over the following 20, 30 or 40 years I can look to.

‌



"Of course, breast cancer in men is rare, and that makes research more difficult, but the rarity of a disease cannot become a reason not to try. If we want men to receive treatment based on evidence that reflects them too, they need to be included in the research that shapes those decisions."

The language and imagery around breast cancer needs to change

James says: "When you think of breast cancer awareness, you traditionally think of pink ribbons, bras and images of women. Although awareness campaigns have achieved enormous things, they have also created such a strong association between breast cancer and women that many men simply don’t see themselves as being at risk - and the language reinforces that.

View 6 Images James founded moobs to help others in his position (Image: James Richards)

‌



"The iconography and language around breast cancer awareness has to be more inclusive. Men need to see and hear from other men who have had the disease, so that breast cancer feels like something they are part of the conversation around too.

"And when breast cancer in men is talked about, we should be careful not to make it sound like a separate condition. It isn’t “male breast cancer”; it’s breast cancer. We don’t assign gender to other cancers, so why breast cancer? Unintentionally, that language can only widen the awareness gap further.

"Ultimately, awareness is still the most important thing. Men need to know that breast cancer is something that can happen to them, and that is why Coronation Street telling Kit’s story is such a positive and important step. Putting that message in front of millions of viewers could genuinely save lives.

Article continues below

"But awareness also has to be backed up by a breast cancer system that recognises men once they enter it. If a man receives the same diagnosis as Kit and me, the world waiting for him should feel like it was designed with him in mind too."

News.title: Hurricane Lowell live: Hawaii declares state of emergency after El Nino fuels Cat 4 storm
News.content:
Hurricane Lowell is forecast to turn northward and approach the islands of Kauaʻi and Niʻihau on Monday, the National Weather Service reported.

Hurricane Lowell is closing in on Hawaii as residents prepare for potentially dangerous conditions from the powerful Pacific storm.

Lowell remains a major hurricane, with maximum sustained winds of around 150mph, although forecasters expect it to weaken as it approaches the islands.

The latest forecast suggests the storm's centre will pass west of the main Hawaiian Islands, rather than making a direct landfall. However, the situation remains serious, particularly for Kauai County, where tropical-storm conditions, heavy rain, dangerous surf and coastal flooding are possible.

Heavy rainfall could trigger flash flooding and mudslides, while large swells are expected to produce dangerous surf and rip currents across parts of the islands.

The exact track remains uncertain, and even a relatively small change could alter the severity of conditions experienced on Kauai.

Follow our live coverage below for the latest updates

News.title: Santa María Canchesda Fair: 'Multiple people injured' after 'explosion' at festival in Mexico
News.content:
Santa María Canchesda Fair: 'Multiple people injured' after 'explosion' at festival in Mexico

Emergency teams are carrying out rescue and extraction operations for people who were left under the rubble following the explosion, according to local media.

View 2 Images

At least 20 people have reportedly been injured after a fireworks explosion during a religious festival in Mexico.

‌



The blast happened on Saturday night in the community of Santa María Canchesdá, in the municipality of Temascalcingo, Mexico.

‌



The explosion occurred during preparations for the community's patron saint festivities, according to local reports.

‌



A structure next to the church reportedly collapsed following the blast, with emergency teams sent to the scene to search for and assist people who may have been trapped beneath the rubble.

Local reports initially suggested that more than 30 people could have been injured, although there is currently no confirmed official casualty figure.

The local disaster response authorities have been mobilised, with rescue teams carrying out operations at the scene.

‌



View 2 Images An ambulance was seen arriving at the scene

Footage circulating on social media appears to show the aftermath of the explosion, with debris scattered around the area and emergency personnel responding to the incident.

Authorities have urged members of the public to stay away from the scene to allow emergency crews to reach those affected and carry out rescue operations.

Article continues below

There has been no official confirmation of any fatalities at this stage.

Santa María Canchesdá is a community in the municipality of Temascalcingo, in Mexico's State of Mexico. The community is home to the historic Santa María Canchesda church.

Further details are expected as authorities assess the full extent of the damage and confirm the number of people injured.

News.title: US strikes three Iranian oil tankers after aircraft carrier targeted with ballistic missiles
News.content:
US strikes three Iranian oil tankers after aircraft carrier targeted with ballistic missiles

The latest strikes came nearly a week after the US and Iran resumed attacks following a month of relatively calm relationships as tensions in the Middle East heat up again.

View 2 Images (Image: US Central Command (CENTCOM)/AFP via Getty Images)

US forces struck three Iranian oil tankers after Navy warships were targeted with ballistic missiles, the American military said.

‌



And officials warned that it would “if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet”.

‌



Experts called it a dangerous escalation after Iran’s previous attacks at sea targeted commercial shipping.

‌



The strikes, a day after US President Donald Trump sought to minimise the conflict as “small potatoes," keep up a new tilt back toward fighting after six months of on-again, off-again war that began with US and Israeli attacks on the country on February 28.

Both sides have sought to inflict both military and economic pain, and negotiations have collapsed.

The military’s statement said an American aircraft carrier and a destroyer evaded “multiple unprovoked Iranian attacks” while patrolling in the region and no US personnel were hurt. It was not clear when the Iranian missiles were fired.

‌



View 2 Images (Image: US Central Command (CENTCOM)/AFP via Getty Images)

The statement said that two Iranian oil carriers were “permanently disabled” and the third, unladen one, was destroyed.

The US statement called the tankers part of a shadow network helping to fund Iran’s powerful Revolutionary Guard and its armed proxies in the region.

‌



A spokesperson with Iran’s joint military command later warned that strikes against US military ships would be more severe if the US continues to interfere with Iranian shipping, the state broadcaster reported.

That Iran targeted a US aircraft carrier with a ballistic missile “indicates that Tehran is becoming increasingly willing to accept risks it previously sought to avoid, including directly threatening some of the most important US military assets in the region,” Danny Citrinowicz, an Iran expert at Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies, said on X.

Earlier, Iranian state television had said that four US missiles struck a tanker about six miles from Kharg Island, home to a terminal through which the country exports most of its oil.

‌



Kharg Island has been repeatedly targeted during the war, including in US strikes on military sites there in March.

The US said that one tanker was struck off Kharg Island and another was struck near Jask, east of the Strait of Hormuz.

The unladen tanker was hit in the Gulf of Oman, and the US said its crew had been “directed to abandon ship.” The statement shared what it called video footage of the strikes.

‌



After the US statement, Iran’s state broadcaster reported the two other tankers attacked, saying their crews had evacuated.

“We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet,” said Admiral Brad Cooper, the head of US Central Command.

Between the war and the disabling of ships during the US blockade of Iranian ports, it is not immediately clear how many Iranian oil tankers have been targeted.

‌



On May 8, the US military said it fired “precision munitions” into the smokestacks of two Iranian oil tankers, both unladen.

The latest strikes came nearly a week after the US and Iran resumed attacks following a month of relative calm, with the Strait of Hormuz and Iranian communities along it again being targeted.

At least five people were killed earlier in the week during a US bombardment of southern Iran. One strike hit a wedding.

‌



Masoumeh Zarei, 13, was wounded in the attack. She spoke to The Associated Press at a hospital while being treated for injuries to her abdomen.

She said the wedding celebration had already begun when she set out to join it. She never made it there. She was knocked unconscious when a telecommunications tower was struck. Her next memory was of waking up in a hospital.

“The party had just started, and we wanted to go there,” Ms Zarei said, her voice hoarse. “I had made my nails really pretty for the party, but everything changed.”

‌



Her friend, 14-year-old Kiana Karimi, also was wounded and in intensive care. She told the AP that she heard five explosions.

“The first three explosions at the telecommunications tower threw us to the ground,” Karimi said. “I quickly got up to pick my brothers up off the ground. Then there were two more explosions, and after that I don’t remember anything.”

The Trump administration appears to have adopted a dual-prong approach to the conflict, responding militarily to attacks on the strait while going after foreign financial institutions that handle Iran’s money.

‌



Vice president JD Vance on Thursday said there was no prospect for renewed talks as long as Iran goes after ships, while noting that major military operations ended in July.

But Tehran’s hardline new senior leaders have signalled the willingness to dig in after weathering decades of sanctions.

The elected government of Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, however, has said that it favours a negotiated end to the war.

‌



Iran has found ways over the years to circumvent sanctions — and now the US blockade — and get its oil to buyers to help ease growing economic pressures. That relies in part on a shadow fleet transporting its oil.

Meanwhile, the issue that helped lead to the war — Iran’s nuclear programme — was meant to be addressed in negotiations that fell apart soon after the US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in mid-June.

Now diplomats say the US, Britain, France and Germany seek to refer Iran to the UN Security Council for failure to comply with its nuclear nonproliferation obligations.

Article continues below

Instead, Tehran’s new leverage focuses on the strait that is crucial to global oil and natural gas shipments and was seen as an international waterway before the war began.

The US military has been helping to guide ships through the strait as Tehran asserts control and targets some vessels, but overall traffic remains low.

News.title: Barnsley fire live as emergency services rush to massive scrapyard blaze
News.content:
Several fire crews are currently on the scene following an 'incident' in Barnsley at a scrap metal and tyres site

Firefighters are currently battling a major blaze in Barnsley where locals across the region say can be seen for miles.

Ten fire engines and several specialist vehicles are attending a fire on Boulder Bridge Lane in Carlton, Barnsley. The blaze is believed to be affecting a scrap metal and tyres site.

South Yorkshire Fire and Rescue said in a statement it is working to bring the incident under control. Residents are being urged to avoid the area and keep their windows and doors closed due to a "large amount of smoke".

News.title: Putin holds three-hour Kremlin talks with Trump envoys on ending Ukraine war
News.content:
Putin holds three-hour Kremlin talks with Trump envoys on ending Ukraine war

The Kremlin later described the meeting as "highly useful", although there was no immediate announcement of agreement to end the war in Ukraine

View 3 Images (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

Vladimir Putin has held more than three hours of talks with Donald Trump's envoys as the US makes another attempt to broker an end to the war in Ukraine.

‌



US special representatives Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met the Russian president inside the Kremlin on Saturday, with newly released images showing the trio sitting together for the high-level discussions.

‌



The Kremlin later described the meeting as "highly useful", although there was no immediate announcement of a breakthrough or agreement.

‌



The talks followed Trump's announcement that Witkoff and Kushner were travelling to Moscow with a new proposal intended to bring the conflict to an end.

View 3 Images (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

At the beginning of the meeting, Putin welcomed the two Americans and said the situation was "not simple". He also asked them to convey his "best wishes" and words of gratitude to Trump.

‌



The discussions come as fighting between Russia and Ukraine continues and civilian casualties mount.

At least seven people were killed in Russian strikes on Ukraine on Saturday, according to Ukrainian officials.

Moscow and Kyiv have agreed to temporarily refrain from attacking each other's capitals while the diplomatic discussions take place.

‌



The Kremlin said Putin had ordered Russian forces not to strike Kyiv for three days beginning at midnight on Saturday.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy later said his forces would similarly refrain from attacks on Moscow from Saturday through Monday.

View 3 Images (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

‌



Witkoff and Kushner are expected to travel to Kyiv on Sunday for talks with Zelenskyy.

The visit would mark their first trip to the Ukrainian capital, although both men have previously travelled to Moscow and met Putin, most recently in January.

Despite the renewed diplomatic effort, significant differences remain between Moscow and Kyiv over the terms of any potential settlement.

Article continues below

Russia continues to demand that Ukraine surrender territory it claims and abandon its ambition to join NATO, conditions Kyiv has rejected.

News.title: Temperatures could climb to 28C in late burst of warmth
News.content:
Temperatures could touch 28C (82F) in parts of the UK on Sunday as summer-like warmth makes a brief return.

A southerly wind will draw in a shot of hot and humid air from the near continent, pushing UK temperatures above average.

The hottest locations in south-east England could reach 27 or 28C (82F), while England and Wales more widely will see temperatures in the mid-20s Celsius.

It comes as parts of central and southern Europe have been experiencing a spell of intense heat, with some locations exceeding 45C.

News.title: Aviation faces hotter, stormier skies – and passengers might have to accept more disruption
News.content:
As the country sweltered through one of the many heatwaves of a baking summer in late June, towering thunderclouds were gathering over the south of England and across much of northern Europe. It was a Saturday, and with the holiday season getting under way, thousands of passengers were heading to London's Heathrow and Gatwick airports to catch flights abroad. It was always going to be a very busy day.

What followed, however, was chaos for travellers. As air traffic controllers struggled to route aircraft around the storms, airspace became heavily congested and many planes due to fly were simply forced to wait on the ground. In the end, some 900 flights to and from both airports were delayed, some by up to 11 hours. Dozens more were cancelled. At airports across Europe, passengers expecting to fly into London also faced long waits and uncertainty.

The weather in the UK may now have cooled, and passengers may soon forget their experiences. But some within the industry believe what happened in June should be seen as a warning.

The timing in this case was clearly unlucky. But there are concerns that such incidents are only going to become more common as the effects of climate change mount up around the world and weather systems are likely to become increasingly unstable, making disruption more likely and adding to costs for airlines, airports and travellers.

Tim Atkinson, an airline risk consultant and former pilot, says the very crowded skies over the UK and northern Europe mean the region is particularly exposed.

He thinks there is a real risk, for example, that all of London's airports could be affected by storms at the same time, potentially with major consequences in the air and on the ground.

"What we're seeing now is very rapid climate change," he says.

"We're going from the kind of weather activity which takes out an airport, and which the system kind of copes withâ¦ to a situation where, with very little predictability, it would be possible to lose all of the London airports from real-time operation quite swiftly and with little notice".

Such a scenario, he thinks, would make the disruption for passengers caused by the incident in June seem relatively minor â and could even put lives at risk. But how likely is it?

News.title: Nigel Farage tells BBC he 'wasn't listening' during foreign donor talks filmed undercover
News.content:
There's no question the allegations in the Channel 4 film have been embarrassing for Reform, and disrupted what they hoped would be a conference about their plans for office if they win the next General Election.

Everywhere around the huge, draughty exhibition hall in Birmingham are giant posters and placards saying, "Reform - the first 100 days".

They wanted to herald their deal with a serious contender to be the next French President, Jordan Bardella, to deal with small boats.

They were keen to highlight the promise to cut income tax if they win the election, scheduled to be in 2029.

They wanted to talk about their proposals for education, welfare, planning, and the rest.

Party members, delighted to have a reason to get together, have taken part in those sessions, applauded and cheered in the hall; gone wild for Farage on stage.

But for the rest of the country, most of the noise from the conference will have been the huge and awkward story about the toxic mix of politics and money.

What is harder to assess is the impact this mess will have on Farage's standing with the public, after a tricky summer and a recent poll slump.

At the top of the party there is a quiet admission that what has happened here is a genuine mistake.

One senior figure told me they could brush off other claims of murky funding, confident nothing had gone wrong - but they conceded these claims do matter, and that for a certain vital percentage of voters, it would "cause them to ask questions".

No one is pretending it's just what Farage tried to joke was a "little, local difficulty".

And there is a private acknowledgement that stories like this can be off putting to voters beyond Reform's no doubt very enthusiastic base.

Another party source told me they were "totally blindsided" by the revelations; stunned "there'd just been no diligence" and in disbelief at how Jukes and Orr, who both say they'd done nothing wrong, seem to have behaved.

A different member of the party's top team said, "hopefully, it's just growing pains". In other words, Reform's developed so fast that sometimes mistakes are made. But they told me: "The party has to step up â sometimes the people that got us here, aren't the people for the next stage".

Among Farage's fans at the conference, I found different views. One member was convinced the party is treated unfairly: "It's the blob, it's all against him," she said.

But another young Reform enthusiast rejected that, telling me: "It's all documented and there on camera â Nigel has to be more careful about what party members say."

But there is a sense of "here we go again". When I asked another member what they thought of the financial scandal, a weary answer, "Which one?"

This time last year in the same conference complex, Reform felt like they were simply sweeping all before them. Twelve months on, they are having to work harder, the scrutiny is more intense, and the pressure only growing.

Farage's claim that he "wasn't listening" to the conversation was telling â to get to power without more of these kinds of serious embarrassments, he may have to pay more attention to what is going on.

News.title: Disruption at Port of Dover as masked 'stop the boats' protesters block roads
News.content:
There has been major disruption at the Port of Dover due to a large group of masked men holding a demonstration.

Hundreds of protesters, dressed in black and wearing face coverings, blocked roads and were heard chanting "stop the boats".

Traffic was stopped from going in and out of the port, with the government saying it condemned "the behaviour in Dover and the travel disruption it has caused".

Kent Police, which made no arrests, described it as a "spontaneous" protest, while Dover and Deal MP Mike Tapp said questions need to be asked around why it appeared the police "didn't know about it".

Officers moved the crowd from the port to Dover Priory railway station at about 11:30 BST and said "all involved had dispersed by 12:00".

Paul King, Reform UK councillor for Dover West, said he had been told it was a "stop the boats protest".

Kent Police has not yet commented on who was behind the demo.

Anti-hate organisation Hope Not Hate claims that the Patriot Platform network arranged the protest, saying the group began meeting in July and has brought together members of anti-migrant groups from around the country.

Demonstrators told the BBC they did not want to talk to the media, although one said "send them back" and another said "stop the boats" when approached.

Far-right activists Tommy Robinson and Danny Thomas both posted about it on X, praising those involved.

Thomas wrote: "The experience on the ground today, was the overwhelming majority of the women and local people we spoke to were thankful that people were actually doing something."

He praised protesters for showing "discipline" and said they had "stuck to the plan".

News.title: Why more women carry the 'mental load' - and how couples can share it
News.content:
"My head's always full," says mum-of-three Stacie Matthias. "I go to sleep with a mental to-do list."

She's talking about the concept of the "mental load" - the burden of planning, organising, remembering and anticipating tasks that keep a household running.

These tasks include: remembering school trips, checking for updates in parents' WhatsApp groups, noticing which parts of the house need cleaning, monitoring how much sleep children get, scheduling doctors' appointments and buying school uniforms.

According to academics, this is work that in heterosexual couples disproportionately falls to women - particularly mothers - alongside the bulk of physical household labour.

All relationships and households are different, of course, but studies suggest clear patterns.

Children in the UK have just gone back to school from the summer holidays, and Stacie, 37, from Stockport, says her mind often feels especially busy in September.

"It's that feeling of always having something to remember, organise or worry about that makes this time of year particularly full-on," she says.

For Stacie this list of responsibilities leaves her mind feeling like a washing-up bowl that's being filled up throughout the day.

"If someone's not helping you remove those pots and pans, your water's overflowing by the end of the day," she says, "and you're at tipping point."

News.title: Majority Russian-speaking city in Ukraine considers language ban in the arts
News.content:
Ukraine's third-biggest city Odesa will decide this week whether to back a controversial plan to ban the Russian language in the arts.

The proposal being considered by councillors in Odesa on the Black Sea coast aims to add to existing restrictions on Russian imposed by national legislation.

It is particularly significant because Odesa is overwhelmingly Russian-speaking, although the ban would only affect public spaces and everyday usage of Russian would remain unaffected.

For millions of Ukrainians, Russian is their first language including many of the troops defending the country in its war with Russia. But Ukrainian is the only state language and spoken by the majority, and some see Russian as a tool of Russian influence.

The proposal in Odesa, which is targeted daily by Russian drone and missile strikes, calls for a complete halt to Russian-language content in music and literature, in streets, parks, public institutions and state-run arts and entertainment venues. It would also recommend a ban in privately owned spaces.

In a city famous for Russian-language writers and musicians, it has provoked strong passions.

The ban would extend in public spaces to old Odesa songs almost universally known throughout the former Soviet Union. All Russian-language books would be removed from display in public libraries. Currently, they can be shown, but not prominently.

News.title: The next James Bond: the (00)7 questions fans want answered
News.content:
Back in May, Amazon MGM Studios who now control the Bond franchise confirmed the casting process was under way, external. But little detail beyond that was given, the statement only saying: "While we don't plan to comment on specific details during the casting process, we're excited to share more news with 007 fans as soon as the time is right."

It now seems that the right time is fast approaching. In an interview with Deadline, external Amy Pascal, one of the next film's producers, was asked whether we might have news on who would be playing Bond by the end of the year. She replied: "I would say the end of the year is a good bet."

Last month entertainment writer Daniel Richtman said, external on social media: "I hear they're in the final round of casting for James Bond and might have already found their guy."

His post on X was followed up by journalist Jeff Sneider, external who said: "Heard the same rumour. First it was down to seven, then three. Now 'they may have found their guy'. Who knows at this point? But for some reason, I don't think it's any of the so-called frontrunners, including the Aussieâ¦"

The Aussie is almost certainly a reference to Euphoria and Wuthering Heights star Jacob Elordi, who was brought up in Brisbane and Melbourne before moving to the US to pursue his acting career.

News.title: Why Munya Chawawa is 'jumping ship' from socials to Shakespeare
News.content:
Comedian, content creator and documentary maker Munya Chawawa became a star in the "golden era" of online video, but says his stage acting debut in Shakespeare is part of a move to "jump ship" from social media.

Recently, he has been immersing himself in footage of the UK's 1990s illegal rave scene.

It was a time of hedonism and freedom surrounded by political and media panic - and is the setting for a modern take on Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream, in which Chawawa will appear.

"I've obviously done a super-deep dive into rave culture and watched loads of rave footage from all these little free parties where they would find an empty field," he says.

While some footage exists of those illicit outdoor parties, they came before everyone had phones and cameras - and Chawawa, 33, feels a pang of nostalgia for that age of analogue abandon.

"I absolutely miss an era where we were dancing for ourselves and not for a digital world somewhere," he says.

News.title: Jaguar Land Rover confirms planned job cuts
News.content:
Car manufacturer Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) has confirmed it is opening a voluntary redundancy programme, a year on from a cyber attack which brought production to a halt for more than a month.

The firm said it needed to save about Â£1.7bn over the next two years as it seeks to adapt to "evolving global market conditions".

It was reported by The Times on Saturday that as many as 4,000 jobs may be lost due to the impact of tariffs and a drop in sales.

The firm told the BBC it had not confirmed the numbers. It said the decision to cut jobs was to help "simplify" the organisation as well as "improve efficiency and build greater resilience".

"Today, we informed our colleagues, and trade union partners that JLR is opening a voluntary redundancy programme offering salaried and management team members the opportunity to leave the business," a spokesperson said.

"We will share further information with our colleagues first."

Unite general secretary Sharon Graham said the union had been warning about a "perfect storm" hanging over the automotive industry for some time.

"Death by a thousand cuts has been going on under the nose of successive governments," she said.

She added there had been "intensive" discussions over the weekend about mitigating jobs losses adding that she and Business Secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, would be meeting JLR's chief executive, PB Balaji, next week.

"This is an incredibly worrying and stressful time for JLR workers," said Unite national officer, Des Quinn. "Unite is working round the clock to deliver the best possible outcome."

News.title: Heathrow Airport train services resume after trackside fire disruption
News.content:
Trains to and from Heathrow Airport were halted after a trackside grass fire caused delays and cancellations.

National Rail said there was a "major disruption" to services following the incident which began shortly after 16:00 BST.

A statement said all lines were blocked between London Paddington station and Heathrow's terminals, as well as Reading, due to "a failure of the electricity supply caused by a fire next to the track".

In an update on Sunday morning, rail operators said the fire had been extinguished and normal services had resumed.

Pictures on social media showed crowds of stranded passengers at Paddington, one of London's main rail hubs.

London Fire Brigade said six fire engines and around 40 crew members were tackling the blaze near Scrubs Lane, North Kensington.

Great Western Railway, external cancelled its services to Reading and no Elizabeth line or Heathrow Express services were running between Paddington and Heathrow on Saturday night.

The airport advised passengers to leave extra time for their journeys, adding that the Piccadilly line, which runs services to the airport, also has delays.

Network Rail Western said some services on Sunday morning could face delays and cancellations, caused by trains being displaced by the disruption.

Earlier on Saturday, Heathrow's southern runway was closed while crews tackled a grass fire on the airfield.

It caused some disruption with at least two flights diverted elsewhere. Heathrow apologised for any disruption and said the fire was extinguished quickly.

That comes weeks after another grass fire near Heathrow's southern runway which forced 18 flights to divert and destroyed a large area of grassland.

While weather has cooled across much of the UK in recent days following record-breaking heat over the summer, fire crews have still been warning of wildfire risks.

The Met Office's Fire Severity Index, external shows that if a wildfire was to occur, it would have a "high" fire severity in most of south-east England and some of the Midlands.

The fire severity is "exceptional", the highest level on the index, in some parts of London including Heathrow, as well as on the Essex and Suffolk coasts.

News.title: King and Queen join Highland games fans at Braemar Gathering
News.content:
King Charles and Queen Camilla have joined cheering crowds watching Highland games events at the annual Braemar Gathering in Royal Deeside.

The event, which draws spectators from around the world, is held on the first Saturday of September every year and coincides with the monarch's annual summer holiday at nearby Balmoral.

Among the events watched by the spectators were tug-of-war, caber tossing, hammer throwing, Highland dancing and a parade of pipe bands.

This is the fourth Games that the King has attended since his coronation.

News.title: UK support for Falkland Islands 'unwavering' after Argentina restates claims, No 10 says
News.content:
It is not yet clear how or to what extent the sanctions will be imposed or tightened. In Argentina, a current law already allows for restrictions of activities of oil companies participating in projects considered unauthorised on the islands.

Two oil companies â Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum â are due to begin extracting oil in the Sea Lion oilfield off the Falklands coast within two years, something Milei said Argentina could not allow.

A joint statement from the two firms on Friday said it had the valid licences granted by the government of the Falkland Islands, "and with the full support of the UK government."

The project is due to deliver its first oil in 2028, Rockhopper and Navitas said the partnerships' timetable would not be affected.

The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles from the islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil - described by Rockhopper as a field containing "highly marketable crude".

Milei also announced plans for a naval base in Tierra del Fuego in the south of Argentina, saying Trump and the US were "assessing their historical position in regard to the Falklands", which Argentina refers to as Las Malvinas.

"That is not empty words as they understand that Argentina is a reliable partner and a valuable ally for decades to come," he said, describing the UK as a nation "in decline".

On Thursday, President Trump hinted the US would not help the UK in any future Falklands conflict because Britain "had not been there to help me" during his war with Iran.

Trump's latest remarks on the islands come after he previously said the US position on the Falklands is one of many under review.

On Friday, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the UK would "resolutely uphold" the self-determination of the islands.

Writing on X on Friday, Miliband said the Islands would remain British as that is the "overwhelming position of the islanders."

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting also said Britain's commitment to the Falkland Islands was "absolute and unshakeable".

"Milei's statement overnight tells us more about domestic politics in Argentina than it does about the Falkland Islands," he wrote in his own post on X.

In an earlier statement, Downing Street said it was "not the first time" the Argentine government had made economic threats against the Falkland Islands.

"We are clear that the Falkland Islanders' right of self-determination extends to the right to exploit their own natural resources," it said.

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said "Britain does not surrender to bullies".

"If (Milei) wants a stronger Argentina, he should build its economy, not threaten others."

Although the US is formally neutral, Washington provided support for Britain's campaign to retake the islands after the Argentinian invasion in 1982.

Argentine forces landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim in 1982, sparking a 74-day war over the territory as a British military task force ejected them.

The conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel.

In a sign of the ongoing tensions between the two countries over the issue, Argentina players celebrated their victory over England in the World Cup by waving a banner in support of their country's territorial claim.

News.title: Police probe after child dies in woodland
News.content:
A police investigation has been launched following the unexplained death of a child in woodland.

Emergency services were called to reports of a child in cardiac arrest on land near Strawberry Lane, Cheslyn Hay, Staffordshire, at about 08:45 BST on Saturday.

An air ambulance was sent to the scene, but the child was pronounced dead by paramedics a short time later, Staffordshire Police said.

The force, which has not confirmed the age of the child or any other details, is currently treating the death as unexplained.

Roads in the area were closed throughout the day while investigations took place and officers were expected to remain at the scene throughout the evening.

News.title: Cleveland police chief proud of force but being 'let down' by funding
News.content:
A Volkswagen Passat carrying five young men drove the wrong way down the motorway near Middlesbrough in the early hours of the morning before colliding with a marked police car.

Officers had been pursuing the car for almost seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when the Passat turned on to the dual carriageway, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said.

Fuller, whose force covers an area of north-east England that includes Middlesbrough and Teesside, recalled being asleep when the duty commander rang her with the news.

"No matter how tragic and devastated you feel, we swing into action and we do what we need to do," she said.

The home secretary announced this week that Cleveland Police would be given an extra Â£2m to deal with the fallout from the crash, with 200 officers drafted in from elsewhere.

Fuller told the BBC on Friday that she was grateful for the support the force had been given, but added: "I need that all the time."

Cleveland's Labour police and crime commissioner has previously said the force needed an extra Â£20m a year to hire more officers and crack down on organised crime.

Cleveland Police is grappling with the highest recorded crime rate of anywhere in England and Wales, Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures for the year to March show.

It also ranks highest for burglary, sexual offences, violence with injury, and criminal damage and arson.

Fuller said Cleveland Police had also experienced the largest decrease in the number of officers since 2010 and was staffed as if it were a rural force.

"It absolutely needs to change," she said.

Fuller expressed hope that reform to policing across the country was on the horizon, and that Cleveland Police would become one of the "big, strategic forces that have the resource, the flex and the capability to surge when they need to surge".

She added: "In the meantime, we need additional funding... to take us to that point."

Recent inspections show Cleveland is one of the most improved forces in England and Wales, with performance levels also judged to be some of the best in the country.

The force has recently arrested 87 people for offences linked to organised crime gangs and over the past two years 16 people have been jailed for such crimes.

Fuller denied that gangs had control over parts of Middlesbrough, describing it as a "complex" area to police, with high rates of school absence, drug addiction and mental health issues.

"We're doing the very, very best with what we've got - and we absolutely do need more."

Authorities say high deprivation and unemployment in the area are fuelling organised crime.

"When young people have little aspiration or hope, who don't have confidence in the state, then unfortunately criminals exploit these people," Fuller said.

"They give confidence, and they give them hope, and they give them aspiration. And sadly what that means is young people doing things without thought of consequences."

News.title: 'I'd rather die than ring the police': Distrust and fear in Middlesbrough after A66 crash
News.content:
All but one of the residents who speak to us do so on the condition of anonymity. They are worried that showing their faces could place them or their homes at risk.

What message do the attacks send to people on this street, I ask one.

"Well, they should be scared, shouldn't they, that something's going to happen to their property if they say anything or get involved. So we don't."

Victoria, who moved here several years ago, says the escalating violence cannot be separated from the wider condition of the town.

"This is a social problem, especially in this area. Teesside has been massively neglected and ignored," she says.

The attack in Acklam is far from Middlesbrough's only recent case of a vehicle being used as a weapon. Back in May, a tractor was driven into a house on Priory Road, and since the A66 crash Cleveland Police has investigated at least two further rammings.

Detectives have also linked their wider investigation to a caravan fire on Attlee Road in Grangetown.

"It's getting worse," a nearby resident says. "They're always balaclava-ed up as well, do you know what I mean?"

He blames drugs.

"It can't be anything else. Why would you be like you are unless it was drugs?" he says.

Whether every incident is part of a single feud has not been established. But taken together, the rammings, fires and arrests have created a powerful sense that violence is being used to intimidate, punish and send messages.

What is most unsettling for these residents is the sense that nobody is fully in control.

Grangetown and South Bank are communities still living with the void left by the decline of heavy industry. Both now rank among England's most deprived neighbourhoods.

In South Bank, we see a group of teenagers tend three ponies tethered on the grass. Two perform wheelies on electric scooters while another uses a long stick to scatter rubbish.

On the adjoining estate, more than a dozen homes have boarded-up windows.

On a wall are the words "RIP 2UZZI", said locally to have been the nickname of Jakub Matusiak, who lived one street away.

One 17-year-old boy tells us he knew him. "He was my best mate," he says. "It's sad."

Elsewhere, three letters are repeated: "FTP" - an expletive directed at the police.

I ask the teenager if he would call the police if another young person approached him carrying a knife.

"No," he says. Before adding: "I've never needed the police in my life. I'd rather die than ring the police."

Again and again, the young people we speak to express a profound distrust of the police.

Cleveland's Chief Constable Victoria Fuller said what we'd heard was "horrifying".

"Yes, there are a small minority of people in the Grangetown area who blight those communities. But we will continue relentlessly to serve our communities."

The scale of the challenge facing the force and the community it serves is not new.

The area has some of the highest police-recorded crime rates in England and Wales.

Its leaders have been warning for years that its resources did not match the demands placed upon it.

But recent inspections show Cleveland is one of the most improved forces in England and Wales, with performance levels also judged to be some of the best in the country.

The force has recently arrested 87 people for offences linked to organised crime gangs and over the past two years 16 people have been jailed for such crimes.

Since the crash, more than 200 additional officers have been deployed in Middlesbrough and surrounding communities. Their immediate task is to suppress the violence and identify those directing it.

There is also the question of restoring order and rebuilding trust and confidence.

News.title: Lauryn Hill, Wyclef and Giggs among surprise guests at Jay-Z's long-awaited UK show
News.content:
Jay-Z's first headline solo show in the UK in more than a decade saw him celebrate hip-hop culture alongside a host of special guests, including Lauryn Hill, Wyclef Jean and Giggs.

The US rap superstar rolled back the years for more than two hours - playing hits like 99 Problems, Empire State of Mind and Dead Presidents - as he took to the stage at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on Friday night for the first of two shows in London this weekend.

The run is part of his Jay-Z 30 tour, which is marking the 30th anniversary of his debut album, Reasonable Doubt, and his culture-shaping career that followed.

Fans of his wife BeyoncÃ© had hoped she would join him on stage, like she did at two of his three New York shows this summer, as she was also celebrating her 45th birthday on Friday.

After days of waiting anxiously, Lu Haitao's family could finally breathe a sigh of relief when the Chinese man was rescued from a tunnel in Nepal where devastating floods killed more than 1,300 people.

Rescuers carried out Lu from a 225-meter (740-foot) hydropower tunnel and evacuated him by helicopter Saturday, 10 days after the floods. He was taken to a hospital and was in stable condition, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported.

The Aug. 26 floods were likely caused by a glacier collapse and nearly 4,900 remain missing, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency. On the Tibet side of the border, 31 people died and 531 were missing, Chinese official news agency Xinhua reported Friday.

Lu recalled climbing to the highest point inside the tunnel and thinking the whistles he heard from the rescue crews were in his imagination, according to audio shared by CCTV. He told a Chinese embassy staffer that the emergency personnel initially could not hear him when he shouted toward their lights.

“When they shone before my eyes, I couldn’t believe it,” he said. “When they shone before my eyes, I no longer shouted. I had lost hope.”

Lu Hairong, Lu’s sister in China, told state media Red Star News that she received a call about the rescue before the news emerged. But she only found it believable after seeing him in a picture in the news.

Her 49-year-old brother, who is married with a son, was previously a farmer from Henan province in central China and took additional work, mainly carpentry, during his spare time. He headed to Nepal for work with a fellow villager in February, his first time working overseas, she told Red Star News.

She told Cover News, another Chinese state media outlet, that Lu had not shared his exact working location and she could only watch the news sent by others in a mutual aid group for families of the missing, unable to eat or sleep well.

“It’s a stroke of sheer luck amid the misfortune,” she said of the rescue.

Lu’s cousin, Lu Haiqing, said her mind went blank after learning he was missing on the sixth day after the floods. She then searched for Nepal news every day and used artificial intelligence to translate Nepali to Chinese. She wept every day on her way to work, Chinese news portal Jiupai News reported.

On Saturday, Lu's cousin received a picture from his sister asking her to help confirm his identity. The man looked very similar but she needed to call another relative to help confirm, the report said.

“This day has finally come,” she was quoted as saying. “There is hope when one doesn't give up.”

The new hosts of The Grand Tour have been approved by former stars Jeremy Clarkson, Richard Hammond and James May, all of whom gave the incoming motorheads advice ahead of filming.

Replacing former presenters are social media star and train enthusiast Francis Bourgeois, as well as YouTubers Thomas Holland and James Engelsman, best known for their motoring channel Throttle House. It’s fair to say they have big shoes to fill.

“They’ve been very supportive, very warm, very open in just saying, ‘Go ahead – make it your own,’ even though we have been sensitive in honouring what the show is all about, and keeping car enthusiasm central,” Bourgeouis tells The Independent, days before the new season’s premiere on Prime Video this Friday (4 September).

open image in gallery Thomas Holland, Francis Bourgeous and James Engelsman are ushering in new era for ‘The Grand Tour’ ( Prime Video )

May had a more hands-off approach – and it was effective in its simplicity. “His sentiment was, ‘Don’t ask me – just do your thing,’” Holland explains. “It was the right thing to hear. It was like Yoda.”

Clarkson made a cameo in episode one, in which he told viewers: “I have been watching what they have been up to and I think you are going to love it.” Executive producer Andy Willman said on TellyCast that the Clarkson’s Farm star was happy to endorse the new version of the show after realising the new presenters weren’t “s***”.

Holland has admitted that “there was a lot of trepidation and fear” when he was first approached about becoming one of the new hosts, and was left wondering: “Do I do this?” But he also knew it didn’t matter what he was thinking: “Obviously I was going to do it”. He also addressed concerns any fans might have about this new era of the show, urging them to “give it a go”.

Nobody’s more surprised he’s the new host of The Grand Tour than “train guy” Bourgeois, who gained widespread popularity for his infectiously enthusiastic videos about trainspotting, which would often go viral on TikTok and Instagram. Five years ago, if you’d told him he’d be replacing Clarkson and co as host of the motoring show, he “would have considered what kind of mushrooms were on my al funghi pizza”.

His casting on the show was backed by his co-hosts thanks to his extremely niche car knowledge. “It was a huge green flag early on,” Engelsman says. “We all had the same reaction – ‘but he’s the train guy.’ But he’s also the car guy.” (Bourgeois worked for six months as a mechanical engineer at Rolls-Royce.)

open image in gallery New ‘Grand Tour’ host’ Francis Bourgeois – not just ‘the train guy’ ( Prime Video )

Holland, who is originally from Canada and studied biology, founded Throttle House in 2015 “out of boredom”. The channel initially focused on BMW builds and occasional car reviews, but began to gain momentum when Engelsman joined in 2018.

Engelsman, who is from the UK, became part of Throttle House after suggesting ideas to Holland and asking to be part of his videos. The duo had their first meeting in person at a gathering of Miata car owners.

Of the new trio, Bourgeois is arguably the most famous, having amassed millions of followers and celebrity fans for his trainspotting videos.

The 24-year-old, real name Luke Nicolson, gained widespread popularity for his infectiously enthusiastic videos about trainspotting, which would often go viral on TikTok and Instagram, and even featured cameos from singer Joe Jonas and the Prince and Princess of Wales.

open image in gallery YouTube stars Thomas Holland and James Engelsman are bringing their car camaraderie to motoring show ( Prime Video )

Beyond social media, Bourgeois has ventured into modelling, collaborating with brands including Gucci and The North Face, and has authored a book titled The Trainspotter's Notebook. He also hosted the Channel 4 digital series Trainspotting with Francis Bourgeois, which featured appearances from footballer Jesse Lingard and musicians Sam Ryder and AJ Tracey.

The Grand Tour races back to screens on Friday (4 September).

TV presenter Andi Peters has addressed Miriam Margolyes’ questioning of his race live on air while presenting This Morning.

Actor Margolyes, 85, has become increasingly known for her unpredictable chat show appearances, and her comments about Peters’ heritage on the ITV daytime series on Thursday (3 September) left show bosses so “nervous” they were edited from the episode that was added to catch-up service ITVX.

After Margolyes started impersonating co-host Christine Lampard’s Northern Irish accent, she asked Peters: “What accent would be normal for you? What are you?”

open image in gallery Andi Peters was questioned over his race by Miriam Margolyes on 'This Morning' ( YouTube )

Peters replied: “What am I? I’m me,” to which the Harry Potter actor said: “Well, you’re a mix, aren’t you? So you’ve got a Black daddy and a white mummy.”

He informed Margolyes that both of his parents are Black, following which she used an outdated phrase. When the host said that he “didn’t know there were shades”, Margolyes stated: “There are shades.”

At this point, producers expressed their concern over the conversation in Peters’ earpiece, with the host saying: “They’re getting nervous now.”

“Don’t be nervous,’ Margolyes said, adding: “We welcome everybody, and that’s what I want to write about in my book.”

open image in gallery Miriam Margolyes' comments left 'This Morning' producers 'nervous' ( YouTube )

After the episode aired and the clip went viral online, broadcaster Jeremy Vine wrote on Instagram: This is seriously nerve-wracking. No filter. Andi Peters dealt with it brilliantly, but note at the end – ‘They're getting nervous' [the producers].’

Peters wrote back: “Thanks JV. As you know we have to be ready for ANYTHING!!!”

The Independent has contacted Margolyes, Peters and ITV for comment.

In 2023, Margolyes expressed her “regret” over asking the late Friends star Matthew Perry whether “he was an alcoholic” on The Graham Norton Show.

open image in gallery Andi Peters addressed ‘This Morning racism row on Instagram ( Instagram )

The theatre and film star, whose credits include The Age of Innocence and Harry Potter and the Philospher’s Stone, appeared on Norton’s BBC chat show in 2020 alongside the actor, who died in October 2023.

Margolyes said, upon reflection, she “really wishes” she hadn’t asked him that question, adding that it “was one of the few times” she “didn’t quite ‘mesh’ with another guest” on a chat show.

She wrote in her memoir: “Matthew was expecting a bland conversation that stayed on the surface of things, but I was warming to my theme and immediately launched in, burrowing deeper.” At one stage, when she shared an X-rated anecdote, Perry comedically declared: “I honestly don’t think I’ve ever been more uncomfortable in my life.”

Dolly Parton’s sister has urged fans to show more compassion in the wake of the Queen of Country’s death.

Stella Parton, 77, shared an update on how she is coping with the grief via a Friday Instagram post writing that the family has been subjected to “incredible pressure and insensitivity from strangers.”

“There is a tremendous amount of AI and endless garbage being posted everyday and it’s been challenging to absorb and/or ignore,” she continued.

“As time passes, those who are in the business of exploiting the loss and tragedies of others on a daily basis will move on to the next stampede of endless misinformation.”

She reminded fans of the “positive influence” her sister had on others, and urged them to “show more compassion and wisdom as we move forward in life.”

open image in gallery Dolly Parton’s sister Stella has urged fans to ‘show more compassion and wisdom as we move forward in life’ ( Getty )

“Use my sister’s life as an example for tolerance and respect toward others,” Stella wrote. “It’s not about the most clever comments, fake AI garbage, or snarky tweets.”

“At the end of the day or the end of your life, how will you feel about yourself? It’s not about what other individuals you will never meet think of you.”

Parton’s niece, Lainey Parton, shared a touching tribute to her aunt August 29, confirming the Queen of Country had been laid to rest the day prior at a private family funeral at Woodlawn Memorial Park and Mausoleum in Nashville, Tennessee.

“I wanted to wait until after my granny was laid to rest yesterday before I tried to put any of this into words,” Lainey wrote of her “Aunt Granny.”

open image in gallery Parton was laid to rest last week at a private family funeral at Woodlawn Memorial Park and Mausoleum in Nashville, Tennessee. ( Getty )

“From the time I was little, my granny always had a way of making me feel like I was enough. She never made my dreams feel too big or made me feel like I couldn’t do something. She believed in me before I even knew how to believe in myself.”

Parton was buried next to Carl Dean, her husband of 60 years, who died in March 2025.

Her death had been announced by her nephew, Bryan Seaver, in an Instagram video posted August 25. The musician’s representatives later confirmed she died following a “brief battle with cancer.”

Parton’s niece Jada Star revealed that the family deliberately kept the late country star's cancer diagnosis private to avoid causing concern for her fans.

Star, who is the daughter of Parton’s younger sister Freida, paid tribute to her aunt at the Grand Ole Opry in Nashville after her death by performing “The Orchard,” which is a duet she originally recorded with the late country music legend.

After her sister’s death, Stella also disclosed that the “9 to 5” singer offered to allow her medical team to test experimental cancer drugs during her final days in the hope of helping future patients.

“She told me recently that if there was no hope for her, she would still allow her medical team to try experimental drugs in the hope of helping others in the future,” Stella wrote on Facebook.

“My sister was always thinking of others and if you want to honor her legacy, show more kindness, lift others up and give more of your time and resources as she continued to do to the very end.”

Spider-Man: Brand New Day has set yet another impressive record in the U.S. box office.

The Marvel blockbuster, which stars Tom Holland as the web-slinging superhero, is now the fastest movie to cross the $900 million threshold in domestic theaters. The sum was made in just 36 days, which beats the 50 day record set by 2015’s Star Wars: The Force Awakens.

As reported by Variety, the Marvel-Sony project is projected to make $22 million over the four-day Labor Day weekend, pushing beyond its domestic total to $922 million.

It is only a matter of time before the movie knocks The Force Awakens off the top spot to become the highest-grossing domestic release of all time. The record is currently set at $936 million.

This isn’t the first box office record that the Tom Holland flick has broken — and it won’t be the last. After just three weekends of being released, the blockbuster broke the $2 billion mark at the global box office, becoming just the eighth film to reach that milestone.

open image in gallery ‘Brand New Day’ has now surpassed $2.33 billion at the global box office, making it the third highest-grossing movie of all time ( Sony/Marvel )

The seven other films that have made over $2 billion at the box office are: 2009’s Avatar ($2.9 billion), 2019’s Avengers: Endgame ($2.7 billion), 2022’s Avatar: The Way of Water ($2.3 billion), 1997’s Titanic ($2.2 billion), 2015’s Star Wars: The Force Awakens ($2.07 billion) and 2018’s Avengers: Infinity War ($2.03 billion).

The previous installment in the Spider-Man franchise, 2021’s Spider-Man: No Way Home, narrowly missed out on the landmark by finishing with a total box office of $1.9 billion.

Brand New Day has now surpassed $2.33 billion at the global box office, making it the third highest-grossing movie of all time behind Avatar ($2.9 billion ) and Avengers: Endgame ($2.7 billion). Brand New Day overtook the 2022 film Avatar: The Way of Water, which made $2.3 billion at the global box office.

open image in gallery Tom Holland will reportedly make more than $100 million for ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ ( AFP/Getty )

The movie has been a big hit with critics. In a four-star review for The Independent, Clarisse Loughrey called the film “the best Spider-Man movie in more than 20 years.”

She added: “Brand New Day offers a maturation not only of its hero, but of the franchise’s entire vision, too.”

“While returning screenwriters Chris McKenna and Erik Sommers provide a sense of continuity in the character, its director Destin Daniel Cretton (of Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings fame) and his frequent cinematographer Brett Pawlak have simultaneously allowed the series to feel completely revitalised.”

Holland is expected to earn more than $100 million for starring in the movie, according to a new report by The Wrap.

Insiders told the outlet that the British actor, 30, was paid $20 million upfront for the blockbuster. That means he has the potential to receive another $80 million or more in backend bonuses, which are typically paid out to actors and directors once a movie covers its production and distribution costs.
