News.content:
“I don’t know if it’s streetwise but he knows how to win,” Maresca said, who is in line to hand Fernández his debut against Coventry on Saturday. “When you want to compete or win, it’s much more important to have players that already know how to do that than players who have never done it in the past.

“Enzo is not the only one. This squad has many players who know how to win titles and how to compete and this is what we are looking for.

“I know Enzo quite well and I know what he can bring to the team. He is a winner, [has] a winner’s mentality and knows how to win [after] the World Cup, Club World Cup [success].

“I just said he is a winner and when you belong to the squad and another winning player arrives, they are always happy.

“I can promise you that in the last four or five days, four or five players from the squad were asking if was coming or not because they wanted him to be with us. It’s very important that he is with us.”

Maresca said he planned to use Fernandez predominantly as a No 6 or No 8 depending on the game. “I see Enzo as a six, a little bit more deep, or [an eight] a little higher arriving in the box,” he said.

News.title: Newcastle’s limitations exposed by Bournemouth before hosts fight back for draw
News.content:
A reality check is not necessarily a bad thing. There has been a lot of hype and excitement on Tyneside and a self-congratulating tone to their own end of summer appraisals.

But this was a reminder of the team’s limitations and the fact that only three of their eight summer signings started the game, with two more coming off the bench, underlined they are a work in progress.

In truth, that is fine. It is the start of September and the Premier League campaign is only three games old. They have a new manager and a new-look team. There has been a significant amount of change in a very short period of time.

It was not the easiest summer, and despite the insistence from senior figures at the club that they had always remained calm and methodical during their summer reset, there was a whiff of crisis only a few weeks ago.

When Eddie Howe quit as manager and Bruno Guimarães, the captain, forced his move to Arsenal at the start of August, Newcastle looked in disarray. So, to have started the season unbeaten from three games against Liverpool, Tottenham Hotspur and Bournemouth is encouraging.

It is also worth highlighting just how good the visitors were. In the first half Bournemouth were superb, rushing Newcastle, forcing mistakes and pouring forward in numbers. In Alex Scott, just as he was in their victory here last season, Bournemouth had the best player on the pitch.

That opens up another conversation. Newcastle played like this a lot at home in Howe’s final season in charge, especially in the second-half of the campaign, but tended to lose not draw the game.

On this occasion, they secured a decent point with a late equaliser thanks to substitute Ramsey, who looked good when he replaced the off-colour Lewis Miley.

Bournemouth will feel they should have held on. They had taken a deserved lead through Marcus Tavernier, who took advantage of a static and ball-watching Amar Dedić to bundle home from close range.

News.title: Relentless Springboks give All Blacks 15 minutes of hell to lead series
News.content:
There will be no repeat of the All Blacks historic Test series victory in South Africa 30 years ago, after the home side ruthlessly ensured they will lead 2-1 going into the concluding weekend.

And the manner in which the Springboks blew away their fierce rivals in the last 15 minutes made Rassie Eramus’s men overwhelming favourites to finish the job in America next Saturday.

However, there were passages of this brutal battle that suggested that Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry could still produce a finale worthy of the billing if New Zealand can learn the lessons from this brutal encounter at the FNB Stadium in Johannesburg.

There was a late Kiwi try to give the scoreboard a humdinger hue but Erasmus’s side were well deserving of their second victory in as many Saturdays over their fierce rivals, and credit to the South Africa coach for outwitting counterpart Dave Rennie without needing to change his starting XV just before the kick-off, like he did seven days before.

Amazing what one can do with a simple but chilling game plan. The old scoundrel knew that if he slowed it down and let his scrum walk round the All Blacks scrum that his backs would have the precious space.

Yet, however it might feel away from Springbok turf, New Zealand will still fancy their chances of levelling it, especially after matching their opponents’ haul of four tries. Their fly-half, Ruben Love, missed five simple-enough points and until that last quarter it was an even contest. Yet, as it tends to, South Africa’s physical intensity and their almighty scrum eventually prevailed.

News.title: Gasly takes shock Italian GP pole and denies Russell
News.content:
Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of and qualifying for the Monza Grand Prix.

Before the weekend’s racing, George Russell was, at least publicly, less than bullish about his chances in Italy.

He did, though, believe he would deliver a better showing than he had in recent weeks.

“I don’t know if we can say we’re favourites this weekend, but we probably have a greater opportunity than we’ve had in the last two races where it’s been less about the power unit and more about the chassis,” he said.

“It’s so close right now, that last tenth in qualifying can be the difference of a couple of positions, which can change the podium. Right now, I don’t know who is going to be the team to beat.”

Russell was almost a minute off winner Lando Norris of McLaren in Hungary, finishing seventh in his Mercedes. Two weeks ago, in the Netherlands, he took the last spot on the podium, with Norris winning again.

However, in the second practice session on Friday and FP3 today, Russell was quickest. He led his former colleague, Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton, who was second fastest.

Red Bull’s Max Verstappen hinted at a rare good weekend as he was third fastest, about a third of a second behind Russell.

Russell, of course, needs a win soon, or he is in danger of seeing the championship run away from him entirely, as Kimi Antonelli already leads him by 59 points in the world title chase.

Perhaps psychologically just as pressing is that erstwhile teammate Hamilton is tied with Russell on 183 points, in third because he has one victory compared to Russell’s two. Slipping down the rankings could knock his confidence.

Russell has not secured pole for the last four races, so a strong showing in qualifying might be the boost he needs ahead of Sunday’s race, while Norris is looking for a pole position hat-trick.

News.title: ‘It’s just a useless gimmick’: Telegraph readers react to Dyson’s latest gadget
News.content:
Would you spend over £400 on a toothbrush? Telegraph readers aren’t convinced.

The new Dyson CameraJet has just launched, retailing for £419.99, which brushes, flosses and mouth-washes in one, with the help of a camera.

After Rebecca Astill gave her verdict on the gadget, we asked Telegraph readers for their views and whether Dyson can convince them to trade in their old faithfuls.

They share the toothbrushes they swear by, from manual to electric models, and whether they see any reason to upgrade. Here’s what they had to say.

Why readers are unconvinced

The majority of readers seem unconvinced by the CameraJet, with John arguing that a toothbrush and a smartphone “sounds like two accidents waiting to happen. Squirted in the eye with mouthwash as you drop the phone down the toilet”.

“It’s just a useless gimmick,” argues reader Donald Mckie, a retired NHS dentist. “The average patient wouldn’t have a clue what they would be looking at in their mouth on a phone screen,” he adds.

“Dyson as a brand is an aspiration for many but I don’t know how this appliance would improve anyone’s oral health.”

In his view, “the tank for the mouthwash at 12.5ml is far too small, the industry average will be somewhere near 250-300ml” to last long enough and successfully dislodge sticky plaque.

He also questions the picture quality of the camera with water spray, saliva, lips, facial hair and toothpaste in the way. “People nowadays will expect pin sharp detail, which I doubt this will deliver.”

News.title: DiCaprio’s Amazonian warrior queen
News.content:
It was while she was in hiding after recovering from the sixth attempt on her life, that the activist Juma Xipaia got a call asking if she would agree to be the subject of a documentary. The first female chief of the Middle Xingu region of the Brazilian Amazon, Xipaia was well known in Brazil for her passionate attempts to protect her indigenous community from the effects of deforestation, illegal gold-mining and – in particular – the catastrophic environmental consequences of the $11 billion Belo Monte hydroelectric dam project, a wildly ambitious and destructive endeavour that has affected livelihoods, fish stocks, ecosystems and biodiversity, with legal challenges still ongoing today.

Thirty-four-year-old Xipaia’s outspoken resistance and exposure of corruption relating to the dam’s construction led to the threats on her life. The last attempt was by poisoning, via a food delivery company, which resulted in her being on a ventilator with 70 per cent organ failure. She was on the verge of death, when, she says, she had a dream that she was given a choice – to take the easy path of dying, or the difficult path of coming back, and because she’s a fighter, that’s the one she chose. And a week later she walked out of the hospital.

Leonardo DiCaprio described the activist as one of the most incredible people he’d ever met Credit : Lalo de Almeida/Folhapress, FSP

Like many activists representing indigenous communities she walked a tightrope between protecting the interests and traditions of her people, and not being perceived as standing in the way of progress in terms of the economic development that benefits Brazil as a whole, a paradox that was defined when President Lula da Silva regained power in 2023, and brought Xipaia into government.

Richard Ladkani, a film director who has made vibrant environmental documentaries such as The Ivory Game (about poaching) and Sea of Shadows (marine activists), was the man who called her. It was 2019, when Brazil was still under the brutal rule of Jair Bolsonaro and destruction of the Amazon was at its peak – an area of rainforest the size of Belgium was burned during his presidency, and thousands of illegal goldmines flourished, contaminating the forest, polluting the river with mercury (mercury is used to bind gold) and bringing crime and disruption to previously pristine areas.

Film-maker Richard Ladkani in the Brazilian Amazon Credit : Courtesy of Malaika Pictures

“All summer long we had seen these dramatic apocalyptic images,” says Ladkani. “And I was posing for photos at the premiere of Sea of Shadows, with [executive producers] Leo DiCaprio and Jane Goodall, when Leo leaned over and whispered, ‘So Richard, what’s next?’

“And I said, 'We've got to do something about the Amazon.’”

DiCaprio came onboard as producer, and Goodall as an ambassador. Ladkani knew he had to find a powerful central figure to provide human and emotional context, someone who would be the voice of the Amazon. He drew up a list of possible candidates, until the Brazilian journalist Eliane Brum told him “do not make a decision until you have spoken to Juma Xipaia – when she speaks, the world listens. She can silence a whole room with her energy.”

‘For a long time I had been seen as a soldier, an army of one’

Right now, in a small restaurant in New York, Xipaia is not really in the mood to talk. It is February, and it’s snowing, and Ladkani, Xipaia and her husband, Hugo Loss, are here to publicise the resulting documentary, Yanuni – which took six years to make – at a screening attended by UN representatives and Brazilian diplomats. The recent news about Trump’s exploits in Venezuela has shaken them all and, more specifically, Juma has had a bad experience with American food which doesn’t really agree with her. She is a little reticent at first, but soon opens up with the help of an interpreter, and explains to me what it meant to be a cacique (chief), and how she was selected.

Indigenous leader Juma Xipaia and her husband Hugo Loss in the city of Aracaju, Brazil Credit : Lalo de Almeida/Folhapress, FSP

“I never chose to be a cacique,” she says, “but I couldn’t stay quiet in the face of exploitation of my people – there was violence, and women being harassed and raped.” She is referring to the collateral damage that importing thousands of workers to build a dam inevitably brings. “Usually the role of cacique is given to the oldest male in the community – my dad and my uncles and my brother were all caciques, but the elders knew that they could trust me never to negotiate our rights with corporations or politicians, never to compromise. For a long time I had been seen as a soldier, an army of one. I accepted the position for two years, with the goal of strengthening on our territories and bringing sovereignty to our people.”

Xipaia was born in 1991 and had an idyllic childhood, she says, growing up in Tucumã, a small indigenous community along the Iriri River, about 250 miles west of the city of Altamira. They lived in wooden houses and ate fruit and nuts from the forest and fish from the river, and in 2006 she moved to Altamira for her education. But threats were encroaching her community, with land opened up for mining and farming, and in 2011, a licence was granted to construct the Belo Monte Dam, to stop up parts of the Xingu River, one of the most species-rich areas of the Amazon.

Aged just 21, Xipaia spoke out against the dam at a public hearing, but despite lawsuits, protest from indigenous people and large sections of society, construction went ahead. Xipaia attended law school in Altamira and studied plans put forward by Norte Energia, the company that built Belo Monte, helping to expose corruption that was going on within. In 2015, at the age of 24, she became a cacique, the first female leader of her people. Other communities had been bought off by Norte Energia with gifts of stoves, fridges, TVs.

In November 2019, she led a protest of angry Brazilian landowners and farmers to disrupt the Amazon: Center of the World international conference in Altamira. But by now she had become a target, and by the time Ladkani called her she had survived six attempts on her life, including her car being rammed with children in the back, and a threat to kidnap her son. She went into hiding for a year and she didn’t want to talk to anyone.

“She thought, the only way I’m going to survive is if I stop talking, because when I talk, people want to kill me,” Ladkani says. But she was finally convinced to take a call from him, and from the first moment, he says, he knew he had found the voice for his film. “Her poetry is the thing that stands out – the way she can describe emotions and feelings and put things into context, I felt it was unique. And when she told me the story of how she almost died because of the poisoning, I was in tears.

“I told her I wanted her to be the voice in the film and also offered her the role of producer. Because I knew nothing of indigenous life and I needed her to lead the way.”

An aerial view of the Belo Monte hydroelectric dam in Altamira Credit : CARLOS FABAL

It was a struggle from the word go. Xipaia was not happy about a translator being involved because of security reasons; she couldn’t trust anyone. So Ladkani, who is Austrian, took intensive lessons in Portuguese and within six months was fluent. “It was a key thing to show that I meant business and took her concerns very seriously,” he tells me.

The security budget for the film was huge, they needed the best, most experienced people: safe houses, secure drivers. And the arrangements had to extend for a year after filming was completed – a total of seven years. “Leo was extremely important here because he raised the first third of the budget, and this encouraged other philanthropists to be part of it.”

Filming began in 2020. There was no script and Ladkani didn’t know what he was going to get from it, just that he needed to tell the story of the pillaging of the Amazon via Xipaia’s voice.

And in the end it was a wild ride: it started with Xipaia leading protests against Bolsonaro, but after Lula was elected in 2023, he established a Ministry for Indigenous Rights, of which Xipaia was made state secretary, implementing a series of bills for the protection of the forest and employing lawyers, biologists and engineers to combat the destruction of the Amazon.

Juma Xipata and Leonardo DiCaprio at the Yanuni Premiere during the 2025 Tribeca Festival in New York City. Credit : John Nacion/Getty Images for Tribeca Festival

The film documents her move from her village to set up home in Brasilia with her son; getting together with her husband Hugo Loss, head of special operations for Ibama (the Brazilian Institute of Renewable and Natural Resources), an elite outfit conducting raids on illegal mines; and the birth of their first child, who was called Yanuni.

It was a lengthy, exciting journey, an improvisation which resulted in thousands of hours of film. “I just had to go with the unpredictable. The strength of any documentary is when unforeseen things happen, because a twist in direction is the greatest thing of any film structure.

“And we had that multiple times. I had chosen a woman to be the voice of the Amazon and two years later she became the second most powerful woman in the Indigenous Ministry – I get goosebumps now at the sheer luck. That was the first twist, and then Hugo enters her life, who happens to be this charismatic soldier of an elite force who would take me to the frontline of the Amazon resistance, and then Juma becomes pregnant and gives birth to Yanuni. Holy s**t. If I had written that as a script, everyone would have thrown it out as complete fiction.”

‘I said, how dangerous is it? And he said, “Well, the risk of you dying is 50 per cent”’

Leo DiCaprio was a producer on the film (rather than his usual role of executive producer), which meant he was far more involved. “He not only provided the money, but he gave me meaningful support throughout the production,” says Ladkani. In November 2021 DiCaprio attended Cop 26 in Glasgow, where he met Xipaia for the first time. “That meeting was spectacular – Leo posted a picture of the two of them together and said that she was one of the most incredible people he’d ever met.” The resulting attention helped to protect Xipaia, because a public profile is to some extent a safeguard. “There she is next to DiCaprio, so she’s not just a voiceless indigenous person from somewhere in the Amazon.”

There were many technical challenges. Because of security, Ladkani couldn’t film in the normal way, with lighting and a crew. “I had a second cinematographer, a brilliant guy from Brazil, called Fábio Nascimento, and I took him with me when I could – but that was only 30 per cent of the time. The rest I shot alone. I downsized my gear and basically shot the film with a DSLR, like a photo camera, so I looked like a tourist. To an outsider, I was just a white gringo taking pictures.” Xipaia had a hidden microphone beneath her shirt. If Ladkani was ever confronted, he claimed to be a YouTuber.

“Security demanded that we shot the film incognito, and that became its strength, because I was embedded within the family to the extent that they stopped noticing me,” says Ladkani.

An illegal gold-mining ship destroyed by Ibama in the Brazilian Amazon – it is dangerous work, with agents risking serious injury and even their lives Credit : Courtesy of Malaika Pictures

Hugo Loss’s job involved protecting indigenous communities and flying over the forest and rivers of the Amazon routing out illegal goldmines, dredgers and excavators. His small team lands, arrests the miners and sets fire to all the expensive equipment, which is too bulky to confiscate. In the film we see massive plumes of thick black smoke rising above the forest. Penalties for environmental crime are insubstantial, but, says Loss, “It’s not for President Lula to change those things, it’s Congress, and it’s hard to change the law. But destroying the equipment is a real deterrent, because the machines are expensive, so it’s a risky investment.”

An illegal gold mine in the Brazilian Amazon Credit : Courtesy of Malaika Pictures

Loss and Xipaia met when her village was attacked in 2020 by illegal goldminers; she was in Altamira, a two-day boat ride away. She put out a cry for help on social media and Loss, who was also in Altamira, saw it and responded right away. He picked Xipaia up in a helicopter and asked her to take him to the exact location of the miners’ dredger. The attackers spotted them and ran, but Ibama were able to seize their boat and secure the area. “He saved her village and her people and her parents from an immediate attack and they fell in love and have been together ever since,” says Ladkani.

“I’m usually very shy about these things but from the first time I saw her in the helicopter I couldn’t stop thinking about her,” admits Loss. “Three months later I was doing an Ibama operation on land to remove some illegal loggers and I saw a hawk’s nest and I took a picture of it and sent it to her,” says Loss.

“It’s the bird whose feather I wear in my headdress,” interrupts Xipaia, shyly. She admits that she had first met Loss before the helicopter ride, at a meeting, but he was leaving as she arrived. “He shook my hand and I made eye contact with him and something told me – I can’t really explain what – that he was going to be my husband.”

Loss holds a Master’s degree in social anthropology from the University of Brasília and is one of Ibama’s most experienced field agents, yet he spent a good part of his career sidelined by Bolsonaro, who had no interest in protecting the environment. In February 2023, under Lula, he was appointed Ibama’s coordinator of enforcement.

Loss has taken part in hundreds of operations. His job is a dangerous one. We watch him flying helicopters over swathes of forest to spot mines, or patrolling the rivers looking for dredgers. Recently one of his team was killed in an ambush, another got burns over 60 per cent of his body.

Hugo Loss, Xipaia’s husband, on a mission to destroy illegal mining equipment for Ibama, Brazil’s government enforcement agency

Ladkani asked to accompany Loss on a raid. “Hugo told me, it's too dangerous, the risk of you dying is too high. It’s a small team, and you would be taking the place of a soldier on the helicopter so we would be down one security man, which means our job is much harder, and by the way, if we get into a gun fight, we are not your bodyguards, we are there to finish a job. You would have to save yourself.

“I said, how dangerous is it? And he said, ‘Well, the risk of you dying is 50 per cent.’ I laughed – and then I realised he wasn’t joking.

Film-maker Richard Ladkani in the Brazilian Amazon Credit : Courtesy of Malaika Pictures

“Of course I had to think about that – I have a wife and two daughters. My wife and I discussed it. She grew up in a war zone in Beirut, so she understands threats, and how you can mitigate risks as well. She is also the producer of this film. We have had a long journey together – making conflict zone films like Sea of Shadows and The Ivory Game was no joke. But this one felt like a different level because of the 50 per cent quote.” He smiles.”‘I did hostile-environment training and we augmented the security to a degree where I felt it wasn’t 50 per cent any more.”

An illegal airbase in the Brazilian Amazon being destroyed Credit : Courtesy of Malaika Pictures

So Ladkani joined the team, and the resulting episode is terrifying: they are patrolling the river when they find a huge illegal dredger, used for gold mining. They board the dredger, its crew of illegal miners are put in a small boat and dispatched, and Loss’s team set fire to it. Attempting to get away, they realise their boat is still attached to the dredger by a chain, and they have only moments before an oxygen tank below the deck of the dredger explodes. Loss has to shoot the chain, but he has to hit it while it is taut, or the bullet would glance off. “The oxygen tank is steel and if it had exploded we would have been killed by the fragments if we were within 100 metres of that boat – and we were six metres away. It was Hugo who shot the chain – it took 50 shots at least. When Juma saw that footage she broke down and sobbed,” says Ladkani.

Do you like your job? I ask Loss.

He smiles. “Yes I do.”

Back in the 1970s, when two major roads were originally carved into the Amazon rainforest, of which 60 per cent is in Brazil, it opened it up for settlers to devastating effects – the population of the Brazilian Amazon quadrupled and millions of acres of trees were cut down for timber or land clearance and farming, and the rivers became polluted. Thousands of garimpeiros (prospectors) arrived, bringing disease, destruction and violence.

Indigenous people from the Mura tribe in a deforested area inside the Amazon rainforest near Humaita, Amazonas State, Brazil Credit : Ueslei Marcelino/REUTERS

Despite the protected reserves created by Lula during his first tenure (2003 to 2011), when Bolsonaro took over, he vowed that he would not demarcate a single millimetre of Indigenous land.

There was reason to be hopeful when Lula was re-elected in 2023, especially when he created the Ministry for Indigenous People. But it was an uphill struggle, and Xipaia left the post of State Secretary after about two years, and retired to her territory, where she still is. “She realised that it would be years, if not decades, before change could happen and she felt that her power was with activism from the front lines rather than being in an office in the city,” says Ladkani. “And what really hurt was her children having to grow up in the city and not having the connection to nature that she had.”

Smoke from illegal fires lit by farmers rises in Manaquiri, Amazonas state Credit : MICHAEL DANTAS

There has been a lot of progress, Juma says, compared to the Bolsonaro years “when it was genocide”. “It is hard to quantify all the changes because even though there was a change in the administration, it is important to understand that the government structure is very colonialist, no matter who is in power, and everything takes time. I entered the ministry when it was just being born.

“It was hard working in an office every day and not spending time with my children, and my son Tuppak [eight] told me that he wanted to go back to the forest, he was having a hard time at school in the city. I did not want to rob my son of that kind of childhood – being in the territory and getting his knowledge from the forest.”

I ask Loss and Xipaia if, with the way things are now, they are more inclined to hope or despair. “Most of the time I don’t think about the future,” says Loss. “I just focus on doing my work, one operation at a time.”

A wildfire consumes land deforested by cattle farmers near Novo Progresso, Para state, Brazil Credit : MICHAEL DANTAS/AFP via Getty Images

Xipaia thinks. “It depends where I am. When I’m in the forest with my family, there is immense fulfilment which is hard to explain; it gives me the hope and energy to keep wanting to protect it, and I want the whole world to get to know it.

“When I walk through the forest and harvest food there with my family and my people, it reminds me of what my ancestors were doing. The innocence of children, the idea of clean water, food without toxins – this gives me hope.”

“I don’t feel despair,” says Ladkani. “I feel like we’re in a war. There are plenty of good people fighting back, and that gives me hope. And there are lives on the line that we need to care about, which is the indigenous people, who are the frontline of our defence. They are defending nature for us so we need to make sure that they are heard and seen and respected. And we hope that the film puts a human face to that.

“We can’t pretend that destroying the biggest ecosystem on the planet is OK. If we lose the Amazon, we all lose.”

Yanuni will be released later this year

News.title: Alexander Isak starts to justify £125m price tag with double
News.content:
Emersonn, Ipswich’s Brazilian striker, did not see the ball in the opening exchanges and, by the time he did, Liverpool had zoomed into the distance to such an extent that you felt it was going to be impossible for them to peg their visitors back.

“I hate having to talk about good performances when you do not get points,” O’Neil declared to a room full of raised eyebrows and you can only assume his message was to ensure that morale in the dressing room was not drooping.

What damage was inflicted with Liverpool’s first significant attack. Gakpo, the subject of an £80m bid from Manchester City, was never going to allow transfer speculation to disrupt his focus and he nudged a perfect little ball into Isak’s path in the sixth minute to show his wellbeing.

The next move announced the return of Isak. One touch gave him an avenue to shoot, the next was a shot with his right foot that was so hard from 16 yards, on an angle, it bent the wrists of Kjell Scherpen as it howled into the net. Critics will feel Ipswich’s keeper should have done better.

Your first thought was to think of the first goal Isak scored in English football in September 2022, a similarly venomous drive, against Liverpool at Anfield. He oozed quality that evening, his pace and skill had Jürgen Klopp’s defenders persistently fretting and this is what he was doing again.

It was no coincidence that three minutes later, he came up with another wonderful goal. This one owed much to the beautiful pass Gakpo presented to him, an inch-perfect through ball with the outside of his right foot, but Isak still showed great poise to bamboozle Scherpen.

News.title: Forced displacement in the West Bank could be ‘crime against humanity’, says UN report
News.content:
Israel’s forced displacement of more than 33,000 Palestinians in the West Bank could amount to a “crime against humanity” and involves “ethnic cleansing”, according to a report published by the UN.

A report by the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) said that Israeli actions in the area had sparked the “largest and longest displacement crisis in the West Bank since 1967” – the year in which Israel captured the territory.

The report said “large-scale, long-term and systematic displacement of over 33,000 Palestinians from refugee camps … during Israel’s Operation Iron Wall [which] raises serious concerns of the crime against humanity of forcible transfer”.

It added: “The documented use of airstrikes, armoured bulldozers and controlled detonations, to render entire camps uninhabitable, to force the displacement of their residents and to prevent their return, in the absence of imperative military necessity to justify such destruction and displacement, are not permissible under international law, appear to amount to collective punishment and raise concerns of ethnic cleansing.”

The 27-page report covers the period December 5, 2024 to January 31, 2026.

In January 2025, Israeli forces launched “Operation Iron Wall” in the northern West Bank in a bid to counter what they said were terrorist threats.

They destroyed hundreds of homes, cut off water and electricity, and barred humanitarian access to the Jenin, Nur Sham and Tulkarm refugee camps.

By October 2025, 52 per cent of structures in Jenin camp, 48 per cent in Nur Shams and 36 percent in Tulkarm had been destroyed or damaged.

The three camps are among 19 in the West Bank established to shelter Palestinians after the 1948 Nakba, and are administered by the UN Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA).

Although still referred to as refugee camps, they are in fact now densely packed towns.

Sports.title: Daryz, Gstaad and Opera Ballo feature on stellar Arc Trials Day
Sports.content:
Daryz, Gstaad, Opera Ballo and Benvenuto Cellini all line up on an outstanding Arc Trials Day from ParisLongchamp on Sunday.

4.35 ParisLongchamp - Arc hero Daryz returns en route back to Arc

Prix de l'Arc de Triomphe hero Daryz returns to ParisLongchamp en route to his defence of Europe's most prestigious race, tackling the Prix Foy.

Francis-Henri Graffard's star returns having not being seen since his third in the Prince Of Wales's Stakes - where there were excuses for the run given his misbehaviour in the stables prior to the race. That run is the only blemish to an otherwise seamless four-year-old campaign to date, which has seen him win the Prix Ganay & Prix Aga Khan IV, showing a devastating turn of foot in both.

He was beaten at this meeting last term by Japanese raider Croix Du Nord in the Prix du Prince D'orange but bounced back with that famous victory a month later, seeing off Minnie Hauk in a pulsating renewal of the Arc.

Bay City Roller is currently 14-1 for the October showpiece and is a really interesting contender in both this and the Arc, having delivered his second Group 1 success when dispatching his rivals in the Coronation Cup at Epsom in June. He flourished in soft conditions that day and easing conditions combined with a return to a favoured track could see him go close.

Both the Antoine Griezmann-owned Uthred and Quest For Magic have an enormous amount to find on ratings and should be nowhere near the front two - although the latter did defeat Prix Vermeille contender Rabbit's Foot in Listed company last time out.

3.25 ParisLongchamp - Star Gstaad reopposes Opera Ballo and Ten Bob Tony

Star three-year-old Gstaad reopposes two of his rivals from the Sussex Stakes in Sunday's feature Qatar Prix du Moulin de Longchamp for a pot just shy of £400,000 to the winner.

Aidan O'Brien has been unlucky to bump into the brilliant Bow Echo on three of his four starts this year, going down to George Boughey's phenomenon in the 2000 Guineas, St James's Palace Stakes and Sussex Stakes by a cumulative three lengths. Clearly a star in his own right, Ryan Moore's mount cruised to an emphatic triumph in the Irish 2000 Guineas earlier in the campaign and with Bow Echo now retired, is arguably best of the European milers.

Image: Gstaad

Both Opera Ballo and Ten Bob Tony had to give Gstaad 8lbs the last day but that is reduced to 6lbs and both will hope that will be enough to close the deficit of just under three lengths.

Opera Ballo is a Group 1 winner this year, taking out the Jebel Hatta at Meydan in January before subsequently topping that up with an impressive weight-carrying display in the bet365 Mile at Sandown against some top rivals. He then was defeated in the Queen Anne by Ten Bob Tony, who bought up his sole Group 1 success with a dramatic finish - defying odds of 50/1. Kieran Shoemark's mount stayed on well after a bad start in the City Of York Stakes recently and could go even closer.

Erdenali represents the lethal duo of Francis-Henri Graffard and Mickael Barzalona and cannot be discounted. This gelded son of Caravaggio should have retained his unbeaten status in Group 3 company last time but was boxed in and only managed third when sent off the odds-on favourite.

2.50 ParisLongchamp - Sparan Nua and Sunly lock horns in competitive race

Sparan Nua and Sunly lock horns in a very competitive Group 1 Qatar Prix Vermeille.

Sparan Nua looked to relish the step up to a mile and half last time out in the Yorkshire Oaks, finishing with a late run but failing to displace King George winner Kalpana.

Sunly returned this year with big expectations, taking out a Group 3 at Saint-Cloud before running Aventure very close in the Group 2 Prix Corrida. This form has been boosted given the Wertheimer mare has since won the Group 1 Prix Jean et Louis Romanet. Sunly's run in behind Calandagan in the Grand Prix de Saint-Cloud last time out was very eye-catching and she could be hard to beat here with Colin Keane booked.

Survie recently took out the Grade 1 Christophe Clement Turf Stakes at Saratoga and comes here with Ryan Moore in the saddle. George Boughey's charge - who is owned by the Coolmore powerhouse - did struggle with a previous yard around ParisLongchamp but seems to have been rejuvenated in Newmarket.

Tattycoram recently beat Tiffany at Headquarters, who has since boosted that form - winning a Group 1 in Germany.

Also at ParisLongchamp...

Arguably Europe's star two-year-old thus far in 2026, Avec Toi takes on four rivals in the Qatar Prix la Rochette at 12.58pm. Labelled a "machine" by trainer Christopher Head after a stunning success last time, all eyes will be on this daughter of No Nay Never - who takes on unbeaten contenders Vignelli and Imperial Strike.

Christopher Head could take out the first two Group contests on the card, given he saddles the promising Data in the Qatar Prix d'Aumale at 1.33pm. She was excellent in Group 3 company the last day and if she handles the step back up in trip and hike in class, she looks the one to beat. There is British representation in this race, with Ed Bethell fielding Rogue Passion.

Irish Derby winner Benvenuto Cellini is the star attraction in the 4pm Qatar Prix Niel for Aidan O'Brien. The Ballydoyle representative showed his brilliance at the Curragh following his controversial failed start in the Epsom equivalent, before running well in third in the King George. Francis-Henri Graffard fields Varandir in opposition, with Zaraki also a big contender for the Fabre team.

Elsewhere...

2.20 Fontwell - Royal Rhythm looks to defy 9lbs rise

2.55 Fontwell - Coastal Command returns for the King and Nicky Henderson

4.40 Fontwell - Jiar Madrik chases four-timer

11.00 Del Mar - five-runner Grade 1, with the winner often heading to the Breeders' Cup Juvenile

Sports.title: Gauff progresses at US Open, compatriots Fritz, Anisimova, Keys knocked out
Sports.content:
Coco Gauff ensured the watching American public had something to cheer at the US Open as she progressed to the fourth round on a day when Taylor Fritz, Amanda Anisimova and Madison Keys suffered shock defeats.

Gauff, US Open champion in 2023, was facing world No 40 Cristina Bucsa, and though far from her best, did enough to grind out a 6-3 6-4 success to progress to the last 16.

The 22-year-old will next face the winner of compatriot Iva Jovic or the Philippines's Alexandra Eala for a quarter-final spot.

"I think it was way different playing in the day than at night. Once I was down that break I just told myself I need to accelerate through my shots," Gauff said.

"She's a tricky player and sometimes she can pick it up and slow it down, so it was tough for me to get a rhythm but I'm just happy with how I fought through even when I wasn't playing my best."

Yet, the American charge faltered badly at Flushing Meadows after stunning defeats for Fritz, Keys and Anisimova.

Fritz blows two-set lead in shock defeat

Sports.title: Aberdeen and Kilmarnock end losing streaks with draw
Sports.content:
Aberdeen and 10-man Kilmarnock battled out a tetchy 0-0 Premiership draw at Pittodrie as both sides brought their losing streaks to an end.

Quality chances were at a premium with Aberdeen's Tony Yogane hitting the inside of the post in the first half but Dons goalkeeper Marius Muller was the busier goalkeeper throughout.

Aaron Tshibola saw red for the visitors for a second booking with eight minutes remaining but Aberdeen were unable to capitalise on the extra man.

In the first of a double-header between the sides, they meet again at Rugby Park in the Premier Sports Cup next weekend, both were looking to arrest poor league form.

Aberdeen had not scored in their previous three league games, having only taken points from their opening day win over Hearts at Pittodrie.

Killie had lost all four of their Premiership matches so far, and were keen to avoid becoming the first side to lose their first five of the season - the last having been current Killie boss Neil McCann's Dundee side in 2018.

Both managers made changes, with Aberdeen making four after the defeat at Celtic in midweek, and McCall swapping three after the loss to St Mirren.

The home side showed some smart early initiative as Stuart Armstrong and Kevin Nisbet combined to create an opening after just two minutes, but Armstrong opted for an extra pass and the chance was gone.

Killie captain Greg Kiltie flashed wide of the left-hand upright from 20 yards, before, midway through the first half, Aberdeen's Nesta Guinness-Walker threw himself in front of a Jamie Brandon effort after Mitchy Ntelo gave away possession cheaply in midfield.

Aberdeen moved Lewis Smith infield and he flashed an effort over the bar, before Yogane curled an effort off the inside of the far post after cutting inside from a Smith pass.

Muller pushed another Kiltie effort past the far post and Aberdeen's Dan Happe saw a header held by Max Stryjek as the first half drew to a close.

The home side made a triple change at the interval, switching to a 3-4-1-2 formation, and soon after sub Toyosi Olusanya just failed to connect with a ball across goal which was put wide by Smith at the back post.

That sparked a period of pressure that saw an Ayoub Mouloua header held by Stryjek, after McCann had been booked following a VAR review of a potential handball in the Killie box.

Armstrong saw an effort from distance held, before Muller pushed a Cathal McCarthy header over and then impressively denied Kiltie from point-blank range.

Image: Referee John Beaton shows Kilmarnock's Aaron Tshibola a red card

Tshibola was denied by the masked Muller, the goalkeeper diving high to his left to push a 25-yard free-kick over.

Ten minutes from time, good hold-up play from Mouloua created an opening for Chris Cadden, his effort blocked by a sliding challenge from George Stanger.

Killie were reduced to 10 men when Tshibola was dismissed for a challenge on Mats Knoester, having been booked for a first-half foul on Smith.

What the managers said...

Aberdeen boss Stephen Robinson

"It was a tired performance. We looked jaded after the two games through the week - that was always the fear. We tried to freshen things up, but it was a performance that lacked energy.

"We got a reaction at half-time with the changes, but we lacked the finishing touch and the quality needed. We got what we deserved.

"I didn't think we were going to get any more energy out of the team if we didn't make changes. We got more energy, but whether we got more quality is questionable.

"I don't think we deserved it today. A draw was probably a fair result, but at home we have to expect better."

Kilmarnock boss Neil McCann

"We should have won. We were definitely the best team today. We leave with a point and we're proud of that point, but we probably deserved three.

"Coming away to a team like Aberdeen on our travels, we can't be disgruntled with a point. The most pleasing thing is that when big questions are asked of you, you can answer them back positively.

"Today we showed that we're brave. We gave a glimpse of a wee bit of what we're capable of. It's going to take more time. There's new players coming in who have to understand what we demand.

"We've had a great week this week, and I think there's a wee bit of determination that they want to start showing that they're better than what they've served up in terms of points."

Sports.title: Villa take first point but rue missed chances in Hull stalemate
Sports.content:
Aston Villa picked up their first Premier League point of the season, but were left to rue missed chances in their 0-0 draw against Hull City.

After an improved performance against Arsenal, Unai Emery was hoping for better fortunes in what was his 200th game in charge of the Villans.

A positive start saw Nicolas Jackson head wide in the opening couple of minutes, before youngster George Hemmings managed the club's first shot on target of the season in the first quarter of an hour.

However, the reigning Europa League champions often lacked the imagination to concern the newly promoted Tigers, who looked the most threatening during the first 45 with their collection of long-range efforts.

That was until the start of the second half, which saw Villa spurn two glorious opportunities.

First, some neat interplay between Emi Buendia and Jackson left John McGinn one-on-one with Konstantinos Tzolakis, only for the Scot to blaze his shot too high. Three minutes later, an even better chance fell for Buendia, who couldn't keep his effort down after being left unmarked inside the penalty area.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Emiliano Buendia has a chance to put Villa ahead but sends the ball over the bar

From that point on, it was the hosts looked most likely and who should've stolen the points.

Mohamed Belloumi saw a stunning curling effort crash off the crossbar just after the hour mark. Then at the death, Ryan Giles picked out Oli McBurnie inside the penalty area, but the hero from the Championship fluffed his lines when a first Premier League goal for the Tigers looked inevitable.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mohamed Belloumi hits the bar

While not three wins from three, the stalemate does mean that Hull remain unbeaten, something unfathomable at the start of the campaign. Meanwhile, Villa's first point is enough for them to climb out of the bottom three.

Emery taking positives from another goalless outing

Despite failing to score for the third successive match, Unai Emery was pleased with what he saw from his Aston Villa side as they continue to regroup after losing several key players.

"I'm positive. The result is not enough but how we planned and how we played and how we created some chances to score, I think we deserved more," Emery told Sky Sports.

"We avoided mistakes we made before. We avoided transitions. Through our positioning and keeping possession we tried to dominate and then in the end we had the chances to win.

"Of course they are very excited in front of their home supporters. They had some chances, but overall in 90 minutes, I can feel comfortable with how we are progressing."

Despite the positivity, the Spaniard admitted there was no avoiding that his side needed to be more clinical in the final third moving forward.

"We weren't clinical. We had four very good chances to score and of course if we do the match can change. When you don't you have to be careful defensively of the transition."

Hull's incredible start continues to blow Jakirovic away

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Curtis Davies and Ashley Young assess Hull City's flying start to the Premier League season after seven points from their opening three games, comparing it with previous promoted sides and examining how those teams went on to fare

While many tipped them to be the favourites for relegation, Hull's incredible start to the season continued to be the story of the third weekend of the new Premier League campaign. Even boss Sergej Jakirovic couldn't hide the fact that he would've jumped at the chance to take seven points away from his first nine.

"Amazing. If somebody offered this to me at the start of the season I would sign it immediately," Jakirovic said post-match.

"Especially with who we were against. This is a great example for us that we have to continue like this as it shows us that we can compete at this level."

He also has high hopes for his Deadline Day arrivals, who feature in different capacities at the MKM Stadium.

Sorba Thomas and Brooke Norton-Cuffy made their debuts off the bench following their deadline day arrivals, while Robinio Vaz and Christos Mouzakitis remained on the bench. Tim Iroegbunam and Ilyas Ansah were not part of the squad, but were also signed on the final day of the window.

"They are very high potential players," Jakirovic added.

"They need time. Okay, Sorba came from Stoke with pre-season, but some players they didn't have a pre-season. This is right now a problem."

200 up for Emery, but a brand new challenge dawns - or is it?

Image: Unai Emery reached 200 games in charge of Aston Villa

Analysis from Sky Sports' Callum Bishop:

"One point from three games. Zero goals and just one shot on target. Key names like Morgan Rogers, Youri Tielemans and Ollie Watkins gone. Some might say this is a new mountain for Unai Emery to climb as Aston Villa boss. And what a mountain.

"Let's not forget last season though. It took Villa five games to get off the mark in terms of goals in the league. They didn't win a game until the end of September. By Christmas, there were suggestions they were even in a title fight.

"That's how quickly fortunes and perceptions can change in the Premier League, and Emery has shown he knows just how to overcome this very obstacle. If he couldn't he wouldn't have been celebrating his 200th game in charge of Aston Villa tonight.

"Is that to say that a similar turnaround is coming. No. He did still have Premier League proven talent to help him turn things around in attack. The signing of Ibrahim Mbaye is exciting. George Hemmings has potential. Nicolas Jackson brings energy. But you'd probably back none of them to be more clinical than Watkins inside the 18-yard-box.

"But Emery has time and again found a way. He even said post-match that this is the position he found himself in last season. He's reminded his players of that. So, while the table looks bleak and the lack of goals is a talking point, refrain from jumping to conclusions. Villa's boss is playing the cards he's been dealt and as Jamie Carragher and Thierry Henry have already argued, there's few better at doing so."

Sports.title: Swansea miss chance to go three points clear with Wrexham draw
Sports.content:
Championship leaders Swansea and visitors Wrexham fought out a 0-0 draw in a passionate all-Welsh affair.

Chances were hard to come by on a night when the sold out signs went up at the Swansea.com Stadium and there was more graft than craft on show.

Neither goalkeeper was tested until Zan Vipotnik slid Moussa Yeo’s cross into the arms of Anthony Patterson nine minutes from time, while Kieffer Moore tested Swansea’s Lawrence Vigouroux in stoppage time.

Red Dragons boss Phil Parkinson might have felt Swansea should have been reduced to 10 by then following Ben Cabango’s lunge on Callum O’Hare.

Celebrity investors had stayed away with no sign of Swansea pair Snoop Dogg and Luka Modric or Wrexham co-owners Rob Mac and Ryan Reynolds.

The Pontarddulais Male Voice Choir were present, though, and a rousing pre-match rendition of Max Boyce's 'Hymns and Arias' lifted the crowd.

Swansea sat top of the table at kick-off with 10 points from four games and head coach Vitor Matos suggesting in his programme notes that they were building something special.

Wrexham had experienced a trickier start, but travelled in good spirits after recording a first win of the season at Millwall on Wednesday.

Both camps ignored the old adage of never changing winning teams - Swansea making three and Wrexham five - with the visitors handing a debut to O'Hare, a £6.5million deadline day signing from Sheffield United.

There was a lively start befitting of a derby with Ryan Longman leaving a calling card on Josh Key, much to the displeasure of Swansea supporters.

Swansea started the better and there were loud shouts for a penalty, at least from the home crowd, after 18 minutes.

Melker Widell played the ball into a central area and it struck the hand of Longman, but referee Elliot Bell was not interested.

Wrexham slowly settled, enjoyed greater possession and found space with raking diagonal balls.

One such pass from Callum Doyle released Danny Imray down the right and the wing-back got past Josh Tymon.

Imray's cross found O'Hare in the box but he was quickly surrounded by Swansea defenders and the opportunity was lost.

The first genuine chance came five minutes after the restart when Sam Smith nodded Ben Whiteman's pass into the path of O'Hare.

He took a good touch to create shooting space but his effort went across the face of goal.

Wrexham went close again when Josh Windass, one of four substitutes introduced after 62 minutes by Parkinson, drove into a congested penalty area and struck Max Cleworth before drifting wide.

Referee Bell was surrounded by angry Wrexham players after Cabango took out O'Hare on the touchline. But the verdict was a yellow card, not red, as Swansea took a one-point lead at the top.

What the managers said

Swansea's Vitor Matos speaking with Sky Sports:

“Happy with the clean sheet. Keeping clean sheets is quite important for building momentum. At the other end, of course I’m not happy because we could’ve won the game. We had the chances to do that. We knew it would be a quite physical one and our pitch didn’t help us as well. It was quite heavy so it was hard to keep the quality and speed we wanted.

On being a point clear at the top of the Championship: “It doesn’t mean a lot. There’s still a long way to go. It’s more important to keep the desire to fight for every game.

“We have a really tough trip to Southampton. If we keep that the desire then we have a good chance to compete.”

Wrexham's Phil Parkinson speaking with Sky Sports:

"We'll take the point. It was always going to be a tough game. I thought the lads stuck to the task at hand and grew in confidence, belief and quality as the game went on. In the end we probably had the best changes to win the game."

On Ben Cabango not being sent off: "A couple of things. Firstly Cabango grabs Kieffer [Moore] around the neck on the halfway line. That's a definite bookable offence that wasn't given. Then he has the challenge which is a straight red. It's a dangerous, out of control challenge. One which can really injure a player and the same referee sent off Callum Doyle against Oxford last year for a challenge that was nowhere near that level.

"I'll be interested when he reviews that challenge and see how he sees them in the cold light of day. Those challenges that are out of control and can injure players are the ones that, in my book, they're the ones that are reds."

Sports.title: Allen fight ends in bizarre fashion as Carty falls through ropes in round one
Sports.content:
Dave Allen's heavyweight clash with Thomas Carty at Croke Park ended in a bizarre no contest after the Irish favourite fell out of the ring during the first round.

The chief support for Katie Taylor's final fight before retirement was over after just 82 seconds with Carty - seeking the biggest win of his 12-bout career - unable to continue.

Allen caught Carty on the back of the head with a clubbing right hand and the Dublin southpaw tumbled through the ropes as much through momentum as the shot itself and onto the floor, where he was laid on his back.

After receiving medical attention - including oxygen for several minutes - Carty then walked back to the changing room and the fight was abandoned.

Allen, a 34-year-old journeyman from Doncaster, looked as bemused as the 80,000 crowd at the way the fight had ended.

The Irish fans booed as replays were shown on the giant screens and Allen was filmed saying: "That's one of the most bizarre things I've ever seen in my life."

Neither fighter spoke to the media immediately after the strange conclusion.

Sports.title: Arteta v Alonso, part one: a desire for control and the theory behind the chaos | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
Control v chaos. On the one hand, the forces of order, regimented, playing in precise patterns and, on the other, something darker, more visceral, a method that acknowledges the imperfection of the human soul, the unknowability of football in all its randomness; better, that second way says, to attempt to ride the fury than to believe it might be harnessed.

When it began, a decade ago, that’s how the Pep Guardiola v Jürgen Klopp rivalry appeared. Apollo v Dionysius. Two fundamentally opposed ways of seeing the world. But in time, the two crept towards each other. Klopp moved away from the heavy metal of his Borussia Dortmund years to something more conservative. Guardiola experimented in multiple directions, slowly abandoning the possession-oriented idealism of his past to something less radical but also less predictable.

The temptation, after the first two weeks of the season, is to cast Mikel Arteta and Xabi Alonso in a similar light. Arsenal are yet to concede a goal. They dominated the Community Shield from the first minute, beat a shambolic Manchester City 3-0 and gave the sense that they could easily have won more comprehensively had they been minded to do so. They were no more troubled in beating Coventry by the same scoreline in their opening league game and, while they were rather less dominant, they were still extremely comfortable against Aston Villa on Monday and had been slowly increasing the pressure when Bukayo Saka gave them the lead just before the hour.

Arteta has become more controlling over his seven years at Arsenal, not just in his micromanagement but in his demands from his team. Tactical plans are sophisticated and negotiable only in the final details. In their third successive season of finishing second he spoke repeatedly of the need to reduce, to zero if possible, the xG of the opposition. If they have no chances, they cannot score, and if they do not score, they cannot win.

Last season it was a refrain heard less often; Arsenal did reduce their opponents’ opportunities, conceding seven goals fewer than they had the previous season. There were those who criticised them on aesthetic grounds, bemoaning their reliance on set plays and occasional bouts of excessive pragmatism, but it worked. They were the best team and they won the league, in the end, fairly comfortably. All else is taste, subjective.

Might, it will be asked, there be a more expansive approach this season? Might, with the burdens of yearning and doubt lifted, the insistence on control lessen? Might this be a breezier, a freer and easier, Arsenal? Might that even make them more effective in Europe, more capable of beating Paris Saint-Germain?

View image in fullscreen Bukayo Saka scores Arsenal’s winner at Aston Villa on Monday. Photograph: David Klein/Reuters

Probably not. Arsenal played as they did in the Champions League final out of necessity, not choice. They were exhausted. Only three PSG players had played more than 2,000 minutes in the league last season; nine Arsenal players had – and given the relative strengths of the Premier League and Ligue 1, theirs were harder minutes. In such circumstances an open game is impossible.

Accepting the role played by fatigue, in fact, has been one of Arsenal’s great strengths; last summer’s business was characterised by the accumulation of squad depth over acquisition of the very highest quality. This summer has been about upgrading where possible. They’ve seemingly done that well in midfield and at the back, although losing three players who can operate from the left wing while signing only Christos Tzolis seems a risk, even with Max Dowman likely to be more involved. It’s possible, likely even, that a more relaxed outlook will allow Arsenal to play with a greater freedom but it would be a surprise if the tactical emphasis were not still on control.

Chelsea’s case is more complex; the sense of chaos of Alonso’s opening two games has surely not been deliberate. He is no Kloppite; his heritage is of John Toshack and Rafa Benítez, Vicente Del Bosque and Guardiola. Like Arteta, four months his junior, he came through the youth ranks at Antiguoko in San Sebastián; they are not so different in their formation. When Alonso won the league at Bayer Leverkusen, they had 62% possession. Although they pressed hard, they were not part of the high-tempo, high-turnover Bundesliga trend. Yet in beating Fulham 3-2, Chelsea had 38% possession, and in beating Brighton 4-3 they had only 26%.

Game state is partly responsible. In both games, Chelsea had the lead early and could afford to allow their opponents the ball. The front three of João Pedro, Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers have excelled playing on the break. There have been glimmers of the sort of interactions Leverkusen produced, the modifications that prevent Alonso’s 3-4-2-1 from experiencing the blockishness that means the formation is more often a tool for counterattacking sides, most notably when Maxence Lacroix advanced from central defence to set up Rogers’ goal against Fulham. But they take time to develop; perhaps the idea for now, as patterns are assimilated, is to lean into the basic simplicity of shape, the security the two screening midfielders in front of the back three should offer.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Chelsea have won their opening two Premier League games this season. Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Nigel French/Apl/Sportsphoto

The problem is, it hasn’t yet worked – although that may in part be down to personnel. Having sold Enzo Fernández without signing another central midfielder, though, Chelsea look short in midfield (in as much their bloated squad can look short of anything). If Roméo Lavia can remain fit, and if Reece James’s minutes can continue to be rationed, the issue should not be insoluble, but Moisés Caicedo’s knee problem complicates things, especially with Alonso seemingly unwilling yet to trust the 22-year-old Argentinian Valentín Barco from the start. Without Caicedo, that is not a midfield that is going to create much, and may struggle even with ball retention.

It’s possible that on Sunday, in a game Chelsea are not expected to win, it is easier to maintain shape and discipline, that a destructive pairing works more naturally. Only by making the game a midfield slog to be decided by which team’s forward line can best exploit breakdowns can Chelsea feel they have an edge. That may end up looking like control against chaos, like possession against turnovers. It may even be so. But for Alonso that is a matter less of ideology than of expediency.

Sports.title: Glasner claims VAR was ‘guessing’ after Forest are denied winner against Spurs
Sports.content:
Oliver Glasner argued there was insufficient evidence to disallow Neco Williams’s goal against Tottenham, accusing the video assistant referee Peter Bankes of guessing that the Nottingham Forest defender handled and said ruling it out weakens the officials’ authority. Midway through the second half, Williams stooped to head in on the goalline as Sandro Tonali attempted to hook the ball clear after Morgan Gibbs-White’s deflected effort bobbled towards the net.

Glasner conceded at least one angle showed Williams appeared to handle the ball, seemingly to protect himself as Tonali went to clear the ball with his left boot, but said the footage was too unclear to disallow the goal. “I don’t think VAR can intervene when he’s guessing,” said Forest’s head coach. “It was not clear and obvious. We had a briefing before the season that the threshold for VAR intervention should be very high and this is why it was a wrong intervention for me.

“I’ve watched five or six different angles and to be fair, from one angle you can guess that the ball touched the arm because the shirt [of Williams] moves a little bit, but it’s not clear whether it’s [because of] the ball or Tonali on the goalline. I know refereeing a Premier League game is really difficult – refereeing a training session is sometimes really difficult – but we are told to support the referee, to keep the threshold for VAR intervention very high, to strengthen the referee’s decision and they didn’t do that today. With these kinds of situations, you weaken the referees.”

Bankes checked the goal and then the referee, Craig Pawson, took to the mic before awarding a Spurs free-kick amid a chorus of boos from the home support: “After review, the ball touches the hand of Nottingham Forest’s No 3 before the goal is scored.” Williams was adamant he did not handle the ball. “I headed it in between my arms,” said the Wales defender, who this week signed a new four-year contract. “If you’re going to pause it, it’s going to look like it hit my arm but it didn’t. I have seen all the images and at not one moment can you tell that has clearly hit my arms because it never. I knew straight away I’d headed it down in between my arms.”

The disallowed goal was undeniably the moment of an underwhelming contest. For the third successive league match, Tottenham failed to score and this time they did not even muster a shot on target. Dominic Solanke heading on to the roof of the Forest goal, 88 minutes on the clock, was as threatening as they got. Omar Marmoush wellied a shot wide after Spurs countered at speed. Mykhailo Mudryk was brought off the bench for his first competitive minutes for 645 days after a doping suspension but Spurs were blunt. Aside from a 5-1 win against a Charlton B team in the Carabao Cup, their season so far reads: five goals against and none scored.

View image in fullscreen Spurs’ Mykhailo Mudryk came on as a late substitute for his first competitive appearance for 645 days. Photograph: Andrew Boyers/Action Images/Reuters

Apart from Gibbs-White’s effort in the buildup to the disallowed goal, Forest’s only other shot on goal was a daisy-cutter from James McAtee. The Spurs league debutant Sávio, a £75m arrival from Manchester City, showed a few neat touches but he and Destiny Udogie were withdrawn after an hour on the advice of Tottenham’s medical department. “I’m not happy when we have the plan but it is for my advantage, my business, the management of the players after their injuries,” said De Zerbi, who accepted his team lacked quality in the final third. “We have to make better decisions, to keep more calm when we are very close to do something important.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

No wonder both teams remain winless. Spurs’s date at home to Everton next weekend has taken on another layer of significance and the same applies to Forest’s trip to Aston Villa. Vinai Venkatesham, the Tottenham chief executive in attendance, could be forgiven for wondering when Spurs will see the fruits of their £300m-plus spend, much of the focus on sharpening their attack. They turned to Mudryk, who thrived under De Zerbi at Shakhtar Donetsk, after the failure to sell Richarlison halted moves for preferred targets Cody Gakpo and Iliman Ndiaye. This was not the desired result. “We bought very, very good players but you can’t just build the team with the names like in Football Manager,” De Zerbi said.

Sports.title: High-flying Hull stay unbeaten by holding off Aston Villa in stalemate
Sports.content:
It’s never dull in Hull, as the saying goes in these parts, and after just three games the Premier League is proving to be quite some ride for Hull City supporters.

Having embarrassed Manchester United here on the opening day and won at Coventry last weekend, this deserved point and third successive clean sheet merely reinforced Sergej Jakirovic’s belief that his men can beat the drop.

You have to go back to Bolton’s excellent start in 2001-02 to find a promoted side who began the season with three straight victories. The Tigers failed to emulate Sam Allardyce’s team, but they came closest to a winner as the Algeria winger Mohamed Belloumi hit the crossbar with a stunning second-half shot before the substitute Mohamed-Ali Cho and Oli McBurnie threatened late on.

“We could have won, but they also had a few chances in the second half,” said Jakirovic, who signed a two-year contract extension on Friday. “We won’t be ungrateful for seven points after three games and another clean sheet. It’s a great result for us and we showed we can compete at this level.”

For Aston Villa, it was another largely impotent display which saw them fail to score for the third match running as the captain, John McGinn, and Emiliano Buendía spurned decent second-half opportunities.

Villa failed to manage a shot on target when being hammered 4-0 at Brighton and losing 1-0 at home to Arsenal; here they managed just one, a tame shot by George Hemmings early on.

Unai Emery chose to take the positives from Villa’s display as he patiently rebuilds the club after a summer of major upheaval which saw a number of key players leave and 10 new faces arrive.

View image in fullscreen George Hemmings had Aston Villa’s first shot on target of the Premier League season, 13 minutes into their third game. Photograph: Craig Brough/Action Images/Reuters

“The result is not enough, but I think we deserved more,” he said. “We weren’t clinical but of course to win matches, you need goals. We created chances today to score and we must improve but we are rebuilding.”

Ambition pulsed loudly at a sold-out MKM Stadium before kick-off as a huge amber banner inscribed with the words “One family, one dream” was paraded on the pitch. It said much for the togetherness that Jakirovic has fashioned within his squad and the connection with the club’s supporters during a remarkable few months in the Tigers’ history.

Desire was visible and audible in the stands and on the pitch, but Villa almost led inside the second minute when Nicolas Jackson headed Ian Maatsen’s teasing left-wing cross wastefully wide.

Hull were unfazed and Belloumi beat Ross Barkley twice, including with a delightful nutmeg, before breaking clear down the right flank. His low cross was cleared, but it hinted at the possibilities on offer for the hosts.

In the 13th minute, Villa finally fashioned their only effort on target this season as Hemmings’s low shot was comfortably saved by Konstantinos Tzolakis.

If Villa could not see off a promoted side widely tipped for an immediate relegation this season, could they really consider themselves ready to start climbing the table? A neat passing sequence should have brought a Villa goal in the 50th minute but McGinn could only lift the ball harmlessly over Tzolakis’s crossbar from less than 12 yards out.

Three minutes later, Villa went even closer as Hemmings outstripped the Hull captain, Lewie Coyle, down the left flank and showed intelligence to pick out Buendía with a neat cut-back. Buendía should have buried the chance but he blazed wildly over, much to his disgust.

In the 65th minute, Hull went agonisingly close to scoring when Belloumi collected possession from a short corner and curled a stunning left-foot shot against the bar. There was a resilience to the hosts, and the collective desire that carried them to promotion last season will be needed over the next 35 games if they are to defy the odds and beat the drop.

It was evident again late on when the Hull substitute Lucas Herrington – on his 19th birthday – produced a vital block to repel Tyrone Mings’s shot. Cho’s close-range effort was then repelled by Zion Suzuki before McBurnie failed to properly connect with Giles’s cross as Hull looked likeliest to nick a late winner.

Sports.title: Haaland edges Manchester City past Coventry as Fernández sparkles on debut
Sports.content:
Enzo Fernández started for Manchester City after Nico O’Reilly’s back injury during the warm-up and sparkled, showing why the club paid a British-record-equalling £125m for the midfielder. The winner came courtesy of Erling Haaland’s 300th goal in club football and Fernández had a key part, feeding Antoine Semenyo, whose cross from the right was crashed home.

In the second half Coventry hammered away, but their wait for a first top-flight goal since Mustapha Hadji’s second in a 3-2 defeat at Aston Villa on 5 May 2001 goes on. The visitors did not like losing, but were heartened by holding the star-studded hosts to a slender win, though the bottom line is all three of their Premier League outings on their return have been defeats.

Frank Lampard said: “I don’t think we deserved to lose. I’m disappointed we didn’t get what we deserved – which was a point. We can walk out of here with our heads held extremely high.”

Enzo Maresca’s men have a maximum nine points so can be supremely satisfied. “Today was not a nice win, a bit ugly,” he said. “In the first half we deserved more goals – we scored one but could have scored one or two more.”

The manager said of Fernández: “The reason Enzo was on the bench [initially] was because he arrived only a few days ago. I know how frustrating it was for him in the last weeks but in the end he played some minutes and was quite good. Nico felt something in his back – not serious.”

Ayyoub Bouaddi, bought for £85m, was on the bench for the hosts, as Fernández lined up alongside Rayan Cherki in a 4-1-2–2-1 that had Semenyo and Iliman Ndiaye, another new home signing, stationed behind Haaland.

View image in fullscreen Enzo Fernández shoots on his Manchester City debut. Photograph: Phil Noble/Reuters

Coventry, with Ethan Pinnock and Frank Onyeka replacing Caleb Yirenkyi and Loum Tchaouna from the XI that lost at home to Hull, could have taken the lead when Abdukodir Khusanov played the ball back to Gianluigi Donnarumma and it slipped under the goalkeeper’s boot, but the Italian scrambled it clear. The visitors should then have bridged the 25 years to Hadji when a Semenyo pass meant for Rúben Dias was intercepted by Taiwo Awoniyi. But when the striker ran in his radar failed, and the shot was pulled wide.

The longer Coventry stayed level the better their prospects. Cherki fed a galloping Haaland and he twisted and let fly, but Carl Rushworth’s save was equal to the shot. Then, dazzling Cherki footwork – after a pass from Fernández – was followed by an effort that struck a post.

The frame of the goal and Rushworth could do nothing to stop Haaland’s opener. This time Fernández curved a pass in behind for Semenyo, the right-winger spun the ball over, and Haaland did the rest.

This was 26 minutes in and Coventry were under siege. Fernández collected the ball along the right, looked up and aimed a cross for Haaland but it failed to beat the first man. Then Cherki, again in Fred Astaire mode, made space and saw an effort blocked.

Maresca wants his wingers to be more direct – utilising the pace of Ndiaye and Semenyo – and the tactic spun Coventry. So, too, did an impish Cherki flick which put Haaland in again: he rode a challenge when going down might have brought a penalty, before shooting. Rushworth once more thwarted the Norwegian.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Frank Lampard and the Coventry players applaud their fans but their wait for a Premier League goal goes on. Photograph: Phil Noble/Reuters

For Coventry, Jack Rudoni did better than Awoniyi with a header at close range, but Donnarumma flew to his left to prevent an equaliser. This showed the hope Lampard’s men carried but they had to finish any chance as these were scarce.

Ndiaye was fairly quiet on debut and when Cherki’s work took the ball to him in the area he should have pulled the trigger but refused.

Maresca said of the Senegalese: “Ili just had two sessions with us – most of the time he was moving in the wrong way, he needs to learn. When Marc Guéhi has the ball [at centre-back] he was dropping a lot – we didn’t need that, we needed him in the final third, that space was for Josko [Gvardiol, the left-back].”

The manager was more enthused about Elliot Anderson. “Really impressed not just today, he was very good against Palace, and against Bournemouth,” said Maresca. “The best thing with Elliot is day by day he wants to be better.”

Bouaddi’s home debut came on 75 minutes for Fernández and the 18-year-old showed composure during Coventry’s late-game bombardment, which included Ellis Sims forcing a point-blank save from Donnarumma.

Sports.title: Scottish Premiership: Celtic’s Yang completes fightback to see off St Mirren
Sports.content:
Yang Hyun-jun scored the winner as Celtic came from behind to beat an impressive St Mirren side 2-1. St Mirren were heading for the top of the Premiership when Nikolas Agrafiotis netted from the spot midway through the first half.

Liam Scales conceded the penalty with a handball but made amends when he headed home six minutes after the break. And Yang finished off a counterattack midway through the second half after good pressing from Camilo Durán.

The victory in Paisley made it five wins from five league games for the champions and inflicted St Mirren’s first Premiership defeat. Martin O’Neill’s side were made to work all the way by a Saints side who played with tempo, invention and managed 19 shots at goal.

O’Neill later lamented the unavailability of Yang for some crucial games – the 24-year-old will now fly to Japan for the Asian Games and miss the midweek trip to St Johnstone and two games against Rangers, plus the Europa League opener against Ferencvaros.

“We are going to miss him. He’s in really fine form at the moment,” the manager said. “But he’s signed off with a brilliant goal. He’s in great form and he’ll work for you going backwards. He doesn’t mind doing the hard graft.”

Rangers striker Ryan Naderi accepted a gift to score the only goal against Motherwell at Ibrox, but they fear their captain Lawrence Shankland faces a lengthy spell on the sidelines after a hamstring injury suffered early on in the game.

Naderi, who came on for Shankland in the eighth minute, dispossessed Alex Paulsen as the Motherwell goalkeeper attempted to dribble the ball past him outside his box and the German had the simple task of rolling the ball into the net to score what proved to be a 12th-minute winner.

Motherwell dominated possession and created several chances but Rangers were more effective in the final third and should have added to their lead. Kim Min-su missed a first-half penalty and the debutant striker Kevin Kelsy was among those to pass up good opportunities after he came off the bench.

View image in fullscreen Lawrence Shankland leaves the pitch unaided but his manager later revealed the club fear his hamstring injury is significant. Photograph: Steve Welsh/PA

Rangers ultimately saw out the game without any late scares as they recorded a third consecutive Premiership victory.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Of Shankland, the Rangers manager, Derek McInnes, said he fears the injury is similarly significant to the one that kept him out for two months early in 2026. McInnes said: “He has a similar feeling to the hamstring injury he had at Hearts last January. We don’t want to speculate too much but he says it feels similar, in the same area, so we’ll get him scanned on Monday.
