Sports.title: Briatore questions Monaco GP appeal integrity in explosive Italian GP press conference
Sports.content:
Alpine Formula 1 boss Flavio Briatore has questioned the fairness of the appeal procedure against the Monaco Grand Prix results, claiming one judge has a close relationship with McLaren.

Pierre Gasly was one of several drivers penalised in Monaco for exceeding the pitlane speed limit, which was later found to be the result of an incorrect measurement by FOM. Gasly lost his third place, but Alpine launched a right of review against the penalties, with the FIA race stewards agreeing to rescind the Frenchman's penalty.

McLaren and Red Bull appealed against that decision, as the other drivers involved had already served their penalties and didn't have the opportunity to get those rescinded.

Following a lengthy procedure, the FIA's International Court of Appeal ruled in favour of the appellants and reinstated Gasly's two five-second penalties, dropping him to seventh as Red Bull's Isack Hadjar reclaimed a podium spot.

Read Also: Formula 1 Gasly loses Monaco GP podium as penalties reinstated following McLaren and Red Bull appeal

In a statement the Alpine expressed "its disappointment and frustration" with the ruling. But in the FIA's Italian Grand Prix press conference on Friday, executive advisor Flavio Briatore went much further, suggesting the hearing had been unfair as he claimed one of the four judges, Italian-American Filippo Marchino, had links to McLaren.

"I think it's very unfair. We accept the decision, but what is very strange was there were four judges on the panel and one of the judges acted like a prosecutor," Briatore said. "It was four judges, and this one was really a prosecutor against the FIA, against us, against FOM.

"Afterwards we found out what is the reason why this guy was so nasty. It's very linked with McLaren. We have a nice picture of this guy [giving a] speech for McLaren in 2018 at MSO Beverly Hills. He has a foundation, it's called One Drop Foundation and McLaren gave two or three McLaren cars, and this was quite unfair.

Flavio Briatore, Executive Advisor of Alpine F1 Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

"We accept the decision, we accept everything, but it's quite strange to have one guy in the panel linked to the team. This is unfair. The judge normally needs to be independent completely."

Sitting alongside Briatore, McLaren team principal Andrea Stella was visibly taken aback by those accusations.

"I find that this conference is going in a direction that is quite insulting for McLaren, for the reputation of a team that deserves a lot of respect," Stella shot back. "And if anybody makes these kinds of allegations, which seem quite serious, they are going to have to take the responsibility for what they are saying in a public forum.

"The hearing, the whole International Court of Appeal was conducted to the highest standards, and we should not question this case like it's been done."

Commenting on the Monaco appeal outcome, which also moved up McLaren driver Oscar Piastri up from fifth to fourth and earned the two additional championship points, Stella said: "It's a decision that definitely we welcome. It's very important, because it adds clarity in relation to the application of Article 1.1.1 of the International Sporting Code of the FIA, which is foundational for anything that derives from there.

"We appealed because we wanted to make sure that this clarity was sought. We had concerns which were beyond the fact that we might have lost two championship points. Probably these two championship points are not going to make any difference. We were concerned about the application of sporting equality and fairness. This is important and this is not only important for McLaren.

Andrea Stella, McLaren Photo by: Eric Le Galliot

"In fact, not only Red Bull applied, but all teams were present in the hearing because this was a very important moment in terms of clarification as to how we apply the rules, as to how we apply consistency, and also in the specific case, consistency is related to the methodologies that are valid through our race weekend."

Briatore returned to F1 in June 2024 as an executive advisor to then-Alpine CEO Luca de Meo. Earlier in his career, the Italian helped steer the Benetton and Renault teams to consecutive world championships, with Michael Schumacher and Fernando Alonso respectively.

But he was subsequently handed a lifetime paddock ban for his instrumental role in the 2008 Singapore 'Crashgate' scandal. Briatore had been implicated in a plot that involved his driver Nelson Piquet Jr crashing deliberately to cause a safety car intervention that helped his team-mate Alonso win. That lifetime ban by the FIA was overturned in 2010, with the Italian a regular paddock presence as a dealmaker until his official return with Alpine.

Sports.title: Piastri handed three-place grid drop for impeding Lawson | Formula 1
Sports.content:
The stewards have issued Oscar Piastri a three-place grid drop for impeding Liam Lawson during qualifying for the Italian Grand Prix.

Piastri originally qualified third on the grid but will now start from sixth place. Charles Leclerc will take third place on the grid, followed by Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen.

The stewards ruled Piastri did not intend to delay Lawson but did impeded him at the Rettifilo chicane. The incident occured after Piastri left the pits as the two Red Bull cars overtook him. Max Verstappen narrowly made it past without being held up but Piastri was unable to avoid getting in Lawson’s way.

“On leaving the pits, the driver of car 81 [Piastri] was advised [by his race engineer] ‘Verstappen, Lawson and Sainz just crossing, Sainz has pitted, just Verstappen and Lawson, watch out for them as you join’. The driver of car 81 stated that he was not alerted to the fact that [Verstappen] and [Lawson] were on push laps but realised as he was almost at turn one that Verstappen was on a push lap. He slowed significantly and kept to the right to allow Verstappen to pass but was unable to do anything to avoid impeding Lawson who was close behind.

“The stewards accept that with the information he had, and the situation he was placed in, the driver of car 81 had, at this stage, no other options available and hence, inadvertently, and also unnecessarily, impeded car 30 [Lawson].”

Piastri previously received a penalty for impeding Nico Hulkenberg during final practice at the Japanese Grand Prix earlier this year.

Sports.title: How “clever” Verstappen spoiled Russell’s bid for pole in qualifying at Monza | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff punched the team’s monitor in fury after George Russell lost pole position for the Italian Grand Prix.

Russell was held pole position after the drivers’ first runs in Q3 but fell to second on the grid behind Pierre Gasly when the drivers completed their final runs.

After the session Wolff said “we got done over by Max in the final run when preparing.”

As Russell’s team mate Andrea Kimi Antonelli will serve a grid penalty for a power unit change this weekend, Mercedes arranged for Antonelli to run a short distance ahead of his team mate to give him a ‘tow’. However Verstappen disrupted this on their final runs.

The McLaren drivers led the field out of the pits at the end of Q3. Verstappen followed them both out with the two Mercedes behind him.

However immediately after leaving the pits Verstappen went across the run-off at turn one. “Tyres are extremely cold somehow,” he told his race engineer Gianpiero Lambiase.

As the gap between Verstappen and the McLarens grew, Verstappen told Lambiase: “I’m not going to catch up to them.”

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

On the straight approaching the final corner, Parabolica, Verstappen slowed down significantly and pulled to the inside of the track. As Antonelli drew up alongside on the left of the Red Bull, Verstappen moved back onto the racing line.

This forced Antonelli to slow down and brought Russell onto his tail. Russell’s run through the first sector was compromised and his time through there was slower than his previous effort.

“It didn’t go to plan,” said Wolff afterwards. “I think Max was very clever there.

“He just slowed it down, made Kimi and George bunch up. So throughout the lap, George was much too close to Max to do a proper lap and that cost us both.”

Wolff suggested the team should have chosen “another guy to follow than Max.”

Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies apologised to Verstappen at the end of the session after he qualified sixth. “It’s frustrating but much improved compared to yesterday.”

Verstappen, who complained about his car performance degrading during the session, said: “It’s bad, this car is made out of paper, it just loses two tenths already just in ride.” He likened his car to a Fiat Punto during practice.

Sports.title: Gasly takes surprise Monza pole ahead of Russell, Piastri and the Ferraris | 2026 Italian Grand Prix qualifying report
Sports.content:
Pierre Gasly will start the Italian Grand Prix from pole position after beating George Russell by six hundredths of a second in qualifying.

The Alpine driver was in contention for the quickest time throughout qualifying. Just over 24 hours since he learned he had lost his podium finish in the Monaco Grand Prix, and at the same track where he scored his only Formula 1 victory six years ago, Gasly claimed his first pole position and the first for his team in their current guide.

The first runs in Q3 left four different cars separated by less than a tenth of a second: Russell, who gained a tow from team mate Andrea Kimi Antonelli approaching turn one, Oscar Piastri, Gasly and Charles Leclerc. Hamilton in the other Ferrari found himself without a tow and was seven-tenths of a second slower than his team mate.

McLaren’s hopes of strengthening their position on their final runs faded when Piastri went off at the first corner. He secured third on the grid but his team mate Lando Norris running behind him was unable to improve and wound up a lowly ninth.

Russell appeared to have secured pole until Gasly nabbed it off him. He had also set the quickest time earlier in the session in Q1, though team mate Franco Colapinto had to settle for eighth place.

Hamilton improved to claim fifth ahead of a frustrated Max Verstappen. The Red Bull driver said his car degraded throughout the session.

The pace of the Alpines created a headache for several teams, notably Ferrari, who were fortunate to get both their cars through into Q3. Gabriel Bortoleto came within a thousandth of a second of beating Hamilton into the top 10 shoot-out and Charles Leclerc was only seven-thousandths faster than his team mate.

A frustrated Liam Lawson missed Q3 after being held up by Piastri at the Rettifilo chicane on his final lap. But Lawson didn’t just direct his frustration at the McLaren driver: he also described his team’s tactics as “appalling”, saying they “left me out to dry”. The stewards will investigate the Piastri incident after qualifying.

Oliver Bearman split the Audis in his upgraded Haas. Lawson came next, followed by Carlos Sainz Jnr and the other Haas of Esteban Ocon.

Yuki Tsunoda failed to make the cut for Q2 in his second appearance for Racing Bulls this year. Alexander Albon, who will take a power unit change penalty, also dropped out in the first round after giving his team mate a tow. The Aston Martins were slowest of all behind the Cadillacs.

Sports.title: Verstappen told Red Bull his car has “less power than a Fiat Punto” in practice | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen made his dissatisfaction with his car clear in final practice for the Italian Grand Prix.

“Mate I have less power than the Fiat Punto,” he told race engineer Gianpiero Lambiase as he prepared for his final run. “I can’t do anything, I can’t even race with them.”

Verstappen made his comment shortly before his run-in with Lewis Hamilton at the Rettifilo chicane late in the session.

Verstappen told his team several times during the session he needs to use the slipstream of another car to have a competitive straight-line speed at the track.

“It’s just slow driving by yourself,” he said early in the session. Following another run he told Lambiase: “I need the tow. You can see the difference again, this is slow.”

“I have no power in the laps,” he added on another run. “I can’t even stay close.”

Verstappen hit a top speed of 331kph on his fastest run as he passed the pits. As is typical with the current cars, his speed tailed off long before he reached the braking zone for the first corner.

The Red Bull driver ended the session third-fastest behind George Russell’s Mercedes and Lewis Hamilton’s Ferrari. His team mate Liam Lawson was 12th fastest, six-tenths of a second off Verstappen.

Sports.title: Russell fastest ahead of scrapping Hamilton and Verstappen in final practice | Formula 1
Sports.content:
George Russell was quickest again in the final practice session ahead of qualifying for the Italian Grand Prix.

He led Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen, who almost collided at the Rettifilo chicane in the final minutes of the session.

The incident began after Verstappen’s race engineer Gianpiero Lambiase told him he could pass Hamilton as both drivers prepared to start their final laps. Verstappen passed Hamilton heading into Ascari, but the Ferrari driver re-passed him approaching the next corner.

Verstappen immediately tried to re-pass Hamilton on the straight but fell back behind the Ferrari, either out of choice or because his car ran low on energy before his rivals. When they reached the chicane, Verstappen dived down the inside while Hamilton swerved onto the run-off area to avoid contact.

“He caused that,” claimed Verstappen. “I got blocked by Max,” said Hamilton.

The pair were separated by a tenth of a second at the end of the session. Andrea Kimi Antonelli, who will start the race from the back of the grid due to a power unit change penalty, was fourth-fastest.

Russell was fortunate to emerge from the session without incurring the wrath of the stewards. He clearly held Oscar Piastri up in Lesmo One yet they opted not to investigate. He also had to slam on his brake to avoid crossing the pit exit line when the light turned red at the end of the session.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Piastri went quickest of all through the first sector but ended up only eighth. His team mate Lando Norris was a tenth of a second quicker and the pair were separated by Charles Leclerc’s Ferrari and Arvid Lindblad’s rapid Racing Bulls. His usual team mate Liam Lawson was only 12th in his Red Bull.

The two Alpine drivers completed the top 10. The Williams drivers were much lower down and both are under investigation for potential yellow flag infringements.

As the cars’ lack of energy means they are losing significant amounts of speed on the straight, drivers used practice to work out how to best improve their lap times by getting a tow from another driver. Lambiase advised Verstappen “I would not recommend starting the lap closer than five seconds to Stroll” as the Red Bull was gaining around three seconds per lap on the Aston Martin.

Temperatures remained high at the Monza circuit, with the track surface hitting 53C during the session.

Prior to the session Cadillac were fined €30,000, all but €5,000 of which was suspended, but Colton Herta’s Clutch Deactivation System did not operate when his car stopped in first practice.

Sports.title: Court of Appeal issues defence to Briatore’s allegations of bias over Gasly decision | Formula 1
Sports.content:
The International Court of Appeal has issued a statement in reaction to the allegations of bias made by Alpine executive director Flavio Briatore yesterday.

The ICA, which is independent of the FIA, ruled against Alpine and the governing body in a case brought by Red Bull and McLaren over a decision made in the Monaco Grand Prix three months ago. The court reinstated two penalties issued to Alpine driver Pierre Gasly which the Monaco stewards previously struck out. Gasly fell from third place to seventh in the classification as a result.

Briatore suggested one of the four ICA judges involved in the decision, Filippo Marchino, favoured McLaren. In response the ICA defended the integrity of its selection process.

“The FIA Courts are aware of public comments questioning the independence and impartiality of the judges of the panel that decided Case ICA-2026-06-07-08-0,” it said in a statement issued by ICA president Laurent Anselmi, ICA vice-president Waltraud Wunsch, International Tribunal president Rui Botica Santos and vice-president Gerard Martin.

“The FIA Courts wish to make clear that the appointment and participation of the judges in that case, like for any other case, were conducted in accordance with the applicable FIA judicial procedures and usual practice, which are inspired by the highest standards like the IBA Guidelines on Conflicts of Interest in International Arbitration.

“All judges are elected by the FIA General Assemblies, some of them upon proposition of a group of at least five F1 teams in accordance with the FIA Statutes. They are all subject to the independence and confidentiality requirements contained in the FIA Judicial and Disciplinary Rules, make annual disclosures of interests to the FIA Compliance Officer, and sign a specific declaration of independence for each particular case in consideration of the issue at stake and the parties involved, which is served to the parties.”

The ICA pointed out all parties involved in the case, including Alpine, had the opportunity to raise any concerns they had over the selection of judges.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“At both the beginning and conclusion of the hearing, the parties were invited to raise any issue concerning the proceedings or the composition of the Court,” they said. “None did so.

“No objection was raised during the hearing concerning the manner in which the Court questioned the witness or conducted the proceedings.”

Marchino, a US-based lawyer, was one of four judges involved in the decision. Michael Grech presided over the hearing and Tomas Borec and Luigi Fumagalli were also appointed.

“The ICA emphasises the importance of constituting panels with judges from different cultural and geographical backgrounds,” the statement continued, “This helps ensure that the deliberations and discussions reflect a diversity of legal traditions, perspectives and approaches, further strengthening the fairness, independence, credibility of the process and access to a fair trial.

“A Court’s decision can leave room for various interpretations and comments as for its legal merits; that is fair and accepted by all the judges. The Court is confident in the soundness of the proceedings and the integrity of the judges. The FIA Courts remain committed to the independence and impartiality of their judges and to the integrity of the judicial process.”

Sports.title: Muhammad Ali, Richard Dunn, And The AccuPunch
Sports.content:
Both stood 6’3″, but nearly everything else separated them. Ali traveled with an international promotional circus and commanded million-dollar purses. Dunn was a former paratrooper and working scaffolder who balanced his trade with professional boxing. Their meeting was not part of the original plan.

German promoters anticipated that Bernd August would win the vacant European championship and provide Ali with a German challenger. Dunn ruined the arrangement by stopping August in the third round at London’s Royal Albert Hall seven weeks before the Munich date.

That victory sent Bradford’s working-class champion into a fight with the most famous athlete in the world.

Dunn was Ali’s third championship opponent in barely three months. Ali stopped Jean Pierre Coopman in February, struggled through 15 rounds with Jimmy Young in April, and returned against Dunn only 24 days later.

The champion traveled between Puerto Rico, Maryland, and West Germany while completing three training camps and fulfilling three promotional commitments. Money helped drive the pace. His large entourage, expensive lifestyle, and business obligations required a steady supply of purses.

Ali’s performance against Young showed what the schedule was costing him. He looked slow, poorly conditioned, and frustrated as Young made him miss before leaning through the ropes to escape exchanges.

The judges awarded Ali a unanimous decision, but the scores did not erase the criticism. Young had exposed how much of the champion’s timing and movement had disappeared since his physical peak.

Munich gave Ali an opportunity to look dominant again. Dunn held three respected championships, but his direct, aggressive style offered fewer complications than Young’s movement and defensive tricks.

The promotion struggled before either boxer reached the ring. A dispute involving $225,000 from Ali’s purse and German taxes placed the event in danger only days before the fight.

A late compromise kept the card alive. Ali’s purse was reported at approximately $1.6 million after adjustments, while Dunn received about $100,000, easily the largest payday of his career. Ali also helped cover a shortage in the challenger’s money.

The champion spent another $100,000 purchasing 2,000 tickets for American servicemen stationed near Munich. Even that gesture did not rescue the live gate.

The main event began around 3 a.m. local time to place it on NBC during American primetime. That decision served the television audience but punished German ticket buyers. High prices and the brutal starting hour helped leave thousands of seats unsold.

Roughly 11,000 people were inside the 12,700-seat Olympiahalle, but about 4,000 reportedly attended with complimentary tickets. Estimates placed the promoters’ losses between $300,000 and $500,000. Ali and Dunn received their money. The local backers were left with the bill.

Ali frequently described southpaws as awkward opponents. Karl Mildenberger had given him uncomfortable moments from the left-handed stance during their 1966 championship fight, creating the belief that the alignment itself caused Ali trouble. Dunn demonstrated the limits of that theory. A southpaw stance changes punching angles, but it does not automatically provide timing or defense. Dunn approached Ali upright, followed him instead of cutting off the ring, and often began his attacks with looping punches.

Those wide shots gave Ali time to recognize what was coming. Dunn also advanced without consistent head movement, leaving a direct lane for the champion’s right hand.

A quicker and more deceptive southpaw might have punished Ali’s low left hand and tendency to pull away from punches. Dunn lacked the speed and disguise required to take advantage. His stance altered the angles, but his technical flaws gave Ali the solution.

Ali waited for Dunn to square himself and drove short rights through the opening. The fight showed that his difficulties were not caused by southpaws alone. They came against opponents who knew how to use the stance.

Dunn pressed forward from the opening bell and tried to force a physical contest. His activity kept Ali from treating the bout as an exhibition, but much of his work struck gloves, arms, or empty space.

The challenger’s bravery soon worked against him. He continued marching forward after Ali established his advantages in speed, timing, and power. Instead of changing his approach, Dunn kept presenting the same openings.

Ali was more than 10 pounds lighter than he had been against Young. He remained heavier and less mobile than the dazzling fighter of the 1960s, but the lower weight helped him look sharper.

The champion stayed patient during the early rounds, studied Dunn’s attacks, and gradually began sitting down on his punches. Once he committed to the right hand, Dunn lacked the defensive reactions to protect himself.

Ali dropped him three times in the fourth round. Each knockdown exposed the difference between determination and defensive ability at championship level.

Dunn rose from another knockdown in the fifth, but a short right sent him to the canvas again. Referee Herbert Tomser stopped the fight at 2:05 as Ali theatrically wound up his right arm from a neutral corner.

Ali later credited taekwondo instructor Jhoon Rhee for teaching him the short right used in the finish. Rhee called it the “AccuPunch” and said its quick delivery was based on a technique Bruce Lee had shown him.

The punch was designed to remove the physical warnings that normally precede a power shot. Instead of drawing back the hand or first rotating the shoulder, the boxer sent the fist directly toward the target and brought the rest of the body behind it.

That approach suited the opening against Dunn. The challenger was advancing with his head high and his guard separated. Ali released the right from close range before Dunn recognized the attack.

The exaggerated arm motion came afterward, when Ali knew the contest was finished and began performing for the crowd.

It gave him the 37th knockout of his professional career. Ali never stopped or officially knocked down another opponent.

The Dunn victory was the last time Ali increased the pressure, repeatedly floored an opponent, and ended a fight before the final bell.

His later victories depended more heavily on endurance, clinching, defense, and carefully rationed attacks. Ken Norton forced him through another punishing 15 rounds. Earnie Shavers hurt him badly before Ali rallied in the final round. Leon Spinks outworked him in their first fight and pushed him through 15 more rounds in the rematch.

Ali retained the ability to produce combinations and fight through exhaustion, but he was no longer an offensive finisher. His legs moved less, his punches carried less force, and too many rounds were spent on the ropes while opponents worked.

Dunn became the final opponent Ali was able to erase once he decided to attack.

Ali had little time to recover. Just 33 days after beating Dunn, he faced Japanese professional wrestler Antonio Inoki in a mixed rules exhibition at Tokyo’s Nippon Budokan.

Inoki spent much of the 15-round contest on the canvas, repeatedly kicking Ali’s legs while remaining outside punching range. Ali absorbed more than 100 kicks and left with severe swelling, bleeding, an infection, and two blood clots.

Three months later, he defended his championship against Norton at Yankee Stadium and escaped with a disputed decision after another exhausting 15 rounds.

The sequence captured the reckless pace of Ali’s career. He fought Young in April, Dunn in May, Inoki in June, and Norton in September. His body received little opportunity to recover between major events.

Thousands of people lined the streets of Bradford to welcome Dunn home. They honored a working scaffolder who had risen to challenge the most famous boxer in the world.

His championship run ended five months later when Joe Bugner stopped him in the first round. Dunn retired after a 1977 knockout loss to Kallie Knoetze.

The Munich promotion lost money, but the fight gained historical importance. Dunn became the final opponent Ali stopped, permanently linking the Bradford heavyweight to The Greatest.

Sports.title: Dave Allen’s 40 Fight Plan Gets Bizarre Twist
Sports.content:
Officials had several possible outcomes to consider after watching the replay. Allen could not receive a stoppage victory because the punch was ruled an accidental foul rather than a legal blow. A disqualification would have required the referee to treat the foul as intentional.

Trainer Jamie Moore accepted the no contest despite Allen’s visible unhappiness inside the ring. “He’s gone to hit him in the side of the head. He’s turned his head, he’s hit him in the back of the head, and he’s fallen out of the ring,” Moore told IFL TV. “Dave can’t win on an unintentional foul, but he can’t lose either. So it’s got to be a no contest. By the rules, they’ve done the right thing.”

Under the unified rules commonly used in professional boxing, a fighter knocked out of the ring receives 20 seconds to return without assistance. An injury caused by an accidental foul before four completed rounds generally produces a no contest or technical draw, depending on the governing commission. There were no completed rounds available for a technical decision.

Consequently, neither boxer could be awarded a win from such an unusual sequence. The brief fight was erased competitively, leaving both men without a satisfactory result after completing full training camps.

Falling outside the ring also carried more danger than an ordinary knockdown. Carty dropped from the elevated platform into an area containing chairs and other ringside equipment. Medical personnel therefore had to consider the impact outside the ropes rather than judging his condition solely by the punch.

Before the ending, Carty had used his southpaw jab and attempted to press Allen. Moore was encouraged by how quickly his fighter closed the distance. Allen reached Carty at close range earlier than anticipated and forced the type of physical exchanges that suited him.

“I thought he hurt him a couple of times,” Moore said. “I was over the moon with the way it was going up until that point. It was just over way too quickly to tell anything.” Allen now has one appearance remaining under his 40-fight limit. The Carty contest counts as his 39th professional bout even though it ended without a winner.

A rematch would settle the unfinished business, but it would also require Allen to use his intended last appearance on another meeting with a tricky southpaw. He could instead pursue a larger domestic payday and leave Carty as one of the strangest opponents listed on his record.

Sports.title: Katie Taylor Defeats Flora Pili!
Sports.content:
The two-time undisputed champion controlled the opening rounds with her jab, speed, and movement. Pili made the third round competitive, but Taylor continued landing the cleaner punches as the fight progressed.

The action increased during the seventh, with Taylor getting the better of the exchanges. Pili switched to southpaw in the ninth and remained in that stance during the final round, but Taylor adjusted and finished strongly.

The judges scored the fight 100-90, 100-90, and 98-91. David Irving was the referee.

Paddy “The Real Deal” Donovan (16-2, 12 KOs) stopped Tyrone “The Mighty Celt” McKenna (25-7-1, 8 KOs) at 2:33 of the fourth round in their welterweight contest.

A body shot from Donovan dropped McKenna in the second round, with referee Paul McCullagh administering an eight-count. McKenna suffered a cut over his right eyebrow during the final minute of the fourth, and the ringside physician stopped the fight.

Taylor Bevan (10-0, 9 KOs) stopped Emmet Brennan (6-1, 1 KO) just 36 seconds into the sixth round of their super middleweight bout.

Bevan dropped Brennan near the end of the third round and put him down again with a left to the body at the bell in the fifth. Two more knockdowns followed early in the sixth before referee Padraig O’Reachtagain stopped the contest.

Joe McGrail (14-0, 7 KOs) stopped Matthew “Bam Bam” Boreland (7-1, 2 KOs) at 3:03 of the fifth round in their super bantamweight fight.

McGrail dropped Boreland with a combination in the closing seconds of the round. Boreland failed to beat referee Padraig O’Reachtagain’s count.

The heavyweight fight between Dave “White Rhino” Allen (27-9-2, 20 KOs) and Thomas “No Carty No Party” Carty (11-1, 9 KOs) ended in a first-round no contest.

Allen landed a right hand to the back of Carty’s head, sending him through the ropes and out of the ring. Carty was unable to continue, and the contest was ruled a no contest at 1:22. Emile Tiedt was the referee.

Molly “Meatball” McCann (5-0, 1 KO) defeated Sylwia Doligala by unanimous decision after eight two-minute rounds in their bantamweight bout.

McCann controlled the fight with her pressure and work rate. The judges scored it 80-72, 80-73, and 79-73. Paul McCullagh was the referee.

Paul “Ravishing” Ryan (12-2, 4 KOs) defeated Paddy “Pat-Man” Gallagher (17-7-1, 10 KOs) over six rounds in their middleweight contest.

Gallagher hurt Ryan badly in the fifth and had him leaning halfway through the ropes. Gallagher suffered a cut over his right eyebrow during an action-packed final round, but Ryan had done enough to receive the decision. Referee Paul McCoy scored the fight 58-55.

Heavyweight Adam Olaniyan (4-0, 4 KOs) stopped Matej Hudak (6-3, 6 KOs) at 2:59 of the first round.

Olaniyan landed a right hand to the chin in the closing seconds of the round. Hudak took the count on one knee before referee Emile Tiedt waved off the fight.

Bobby Flood (4-0, 2 KOs) defeated Jack “Mad Dog” Swallow (4-14-1, 1 KO) by decision in their four-round super welterweight bout.

Flood controlled the contest from start to finish. Referee David Irving scored it 40-36.

Mikey Sheehan and David Diamante served as the ring announcers.

Sports.title: Damian Knyba Is Anthony Joshua’s Perfect Fury Test
Sports.content:
He lacks Wladimir’s speed, timing, defense, and destructive power, but the basic construction is similar. That familiarity should benefit Joshua, who spent years studying Wladimir, training alongside him, and eventually fighting him at Wembley in 2017.

Facing Knyba would not reproduce Fury’s movement, feints, stance changes, or ability to invent his way through a difficult fight. It would give Joshua experience against another towering heavyweight who knows how to keep the action at long range and smother opponents once they get inside.

The matchup becomes more appealing because Knyba is not harmless. His power is respectable enough to test the weakness that now defines Joshua’s career.

Joshua’s punch resistance and recovery can no longer be trusted after his fights against Daniel Dubois and Kristian Prenga.

The younger AJ survived a crushing right hand from Wladimir, regained control, and stopped him in the eleventh round. He had the physical resilience and confidence to fight his way through a crisis. That version of Joshua is gone.

Against Dubois, the consequences of catching AJ cleanly and denying him time to recover were obvious. Once hurt, Joshua became rigid, lost track of incoming shots, and struggled to restore order.

His fight with Prenga provided more evidence that Joshua no longer processes hard punches as well as he once did.

Although Knyba does not punch like Dubois, he hits hard enough to stop Joshua. His height allows him to generate leverage on the straight right, particularly when an opponent remains directly in front of him or pulls back without changing angles.

AJ would have to close the distance behind his jab, keep his head moving, and remain defensively responsible after throwing. One lazy exit or mistimed entry might give Knyba the opening needed to wreck the Fury fight.

That danger is precisely what makes Knyba a worthwhile warm up. A harmless opponent would tell Eddie Hearn nothing about Joshua’s readiness.

The blueprint for beating Knyba was supplied by Agit Kabayel, who stopped him inside three rounds in January. Kabayel refused to conduct the fight from the outside, where Knyba’s 86 inch reach gave him the advantage. He applied pressure, shortened the distance, and forced the taller man to work at an uncomfortable pace.

There is little doubt that Joshua possesses the strength and power to follow that approach, but his recent habits create doubts.

Under Ben Davison, AJ has often settled into cautious outside boxing built around the jab and isolated right hands. That approach may suit him against shorter opponents who must cross open space to reach him. It makes less sense against Knyba, who owns the longer reach and wants a slow fight at the end of his jab.

AJ cannot afford to admire Knyba’s size from the outside. He would need to attack the body, force him backward, and make him reset his feet. Knyba becomes much less effective when denied the time and space required to extend his punches.

That would test Joshua’s willingness to take calculated chances. Moving into mid range places him closer to Knyba’s right hand, but remaining outside allows the Polish heavyweight to dictate the pace. Finding the balance between aggression and recklessness has repeatedly escaped AJ.

Reaching Knyba would solve only the first part of the problem. Against Andy Ruiz Jr., he regularly wrapped up and smothered the shorter fighter whenever Ruiz crossed the distance.

Fury uses that tactic even more effectively. He leans his weight across an opponent’s shoulders, forces him to carry the load, and drains his legs during long clinches. It is not glamorous, but it has become a vital part of his heavyweight style.

While Knyba cannot match Fury’s inside craft, he can give Joshua a physical rehearsal for those wrestling exchanges. AJ would have to keep his arms free, create enough room to punch, and avoid wasting energy trying to overpower a taller man in static clinches.

Too much muscular weight has caused Joshua to burn energy unnecessarily in previous fights. Continually wrestling with a heavyweight of Knyba’s size would test both his conditioning and his patience.

Frustration with the holding may tempt Joshua into lunging from too far away. That is where the straight right becomes dangerous.

Knyba’s victory over Andy Ruiz Jr. supplies more than a recognizable name for the promotion. It connects him directly to the most damaging defeat of Joshua’s career.

The loss to Ruiz destroyed Joshua’s aura at Madison Square Garden in 2019. Although AJ comfortably won the rematch, questions about his confidence and punch resistance followed him from that night onward.

By beating Ruiz, dropping him in the seventh round, and controlling much of the fight with his jab and reach, Knyba added a former unified champion to his record. The official scores were 117-110 and 114-113 twice, although the two narrow cards understated his control.

That creates an easy promotional story. Joshua would be fighting the man who just dominated his old conqueror while testing himself against the physical dimensions he will encounter against Fury.

The psychological angle should not be exaggerated. Beating Knyba would not erase what happened against Ruiz. It would still allow Joshua to show that he can dominate the fighter who just reduced Ruiz to a fading former champion.

Hearn cannot treat Knyba as an opponent controlled entirely by Matchroom. The Polish heavyweight signed a multiyear promotional agreement with Bob Arum’s Top Rank in 2023 and remains listed on the company’s roster. That introduces promotional politics.

From Top Rank’s perspective, the money and exposure attached to a Joshua fight may be tempting, especially after Knyba rebuilt himself by beating Ruiz. The company would also know that his size and right hand give him a genuine chance to spoil the larger plan.

Calling Knyba a warm up sacrifice would undersell his value. He has already fought Kabayel for an interim heavyweight title and now owns a win over Ruiz. Top Rank would likely want proper compensation and a favorable arrangement before placing him across the ring from one of Matchroom’s most valuable fighters.

Warren’s connection to Fury adds another consideration, although he does not control Knyba’s contract. Anyone invested in Fury versus Joshua must decide if the preparation value justifies placing AJ in another dangerous fight first. The financial calculation may ultimately kill the idea.

Heavy investment from Turki Alalshikh in both Joshua and Fury has helped keep their fight alive as one of the largest events available in British boxing. Sending Joshua against a towering heavyweight with a hard right hand creates a direct threat to that investment.

If Knyba knocks out AJ, the Fury fight loses much of its commercial power. It may still happen because of the names involved, but it would no longer carry the same sporting value or sense of occasion.

That gives the match its central contradiction. Knyba is the ideal warm up for Fury because he reproduces several of the physical problems Joshua must solve. He is also the wrong warm up from a business perspective because he carries enough power to destroy the entire plan.

On experience and technical development, Joshua should be able to pressure Knyba, attack his body, and exploit the weaknesses Kabayel exposed. But “should” offers little comfort with Joshua now.

Winning would not require Knyba to outbox him for 12 rounds. He would only need to survive long enough to land one clean right hand on a fighter whose recovery has badly deteriorated.

That is why the fight works. Knyba can prepare Joshua for Fury’s dimensions, force him to solve the clinching problem, and test the punch resistance Fury would attack. If AJ cannot safely handle that assignment, he has no business moving directly into the Fury fight.

Sports.title: Taylor Retires Undisputed After Dominating Flora Pili
Sports.content:
Before retiring in front of more than 80,000 fans, Taylor (26-1, 6 KOs) added the vacant WBC title to her WBA, IBF, WBO, and Ring championships. Pili (12-1, 2 KOs) suffered her first professional defeat after struggling to match Taylor’s speed, timing, and work rate.

There were no knockdowns, and Taylor was rarely in serious danger. It was a controlled farewell rather than another punishing war, with the 40-year-old boxing intelligently and refusing to give Pili the exchanges she needed.

From the opening bell, Taylor took the center of the ring and began setting the distance with her jab. She pressed behind the lead hand, landed the right hook, and put together quick combinations before Pili could answer.

During the opening two rounds, Pili looked tentative. She waited too long for Taylor to finish punching and then found the target had already disappeared. Taylor moved her head, changed position, and made the French challenger reset before beginning another attack.

Four-punch combinations allowed Taylor to score without remaining in front of Pili. Whenever the challenger attempted to close the distance, Taylor either countered her coming forward or tied her up before she could build any offense.

The difference in hand speed was clear. Pili had difficulty timing Taylor’s entries, while Taylor repeatedly beat her to the punch and moved away before the return fire arrived.

That pattern continued through the third round. Taylor stabbed with the jab, stepped into range with combinations, and smothered Pili’s attempts to respond. She did not need to take unnecessary chances because Pili was giving away rounds with her low output.

More urgency came from Pili in the fourth as she tried to push Taylor backward. Her pressure briefly made the fight more physical, but she still struggled to land cleanly. Taylor met her with counters and refused to remain trapped along the ropes.

The challenger continued advancing in the fifth, only to run into Taylor’s sharper punches. A clean left hook from Taylor closed the round and reinforced her control of the fight.

One of Pili’s better jabs snapped Taylor’s head back early in the sixth. Taylor responded quickly with punches through the middle and a counter right hand, preventing Pili from building on the moment.

The Frenchwoman’s punches looked slower, and her attacks usually came one shot at a time. That made it easier for Taylor to read what was coming and answer with combinations. Pili remained durable and willing, but she could not produce enough offense to change the direction of the contest.

Her best work came in the seventh and eighth rounds. Pili connected during a flurry in the seventh after Taylor had attacked the body, while the referee warned Taylor for using her head.

In the eighth, Pili crowded Taylor more effectively and landed a short right hand inside. The closer distance made the action rougher and took away some of Taylor’s room to operate. Those were the only rounds that offered Pili a reasonable argument on the scorecards.

Even during that stretch, Taylor continued finding openings with the jab and combinations. When Pili forced her toward a corner, Taylor punched her way out or held before the challenger could extend the exchange.

A more disciplined approach returned from Taylor in the ninth. She stayed near the edge of Pili’s range, slipped in a right hand, and changed levels with attacks to the body and head.

Despite continuing to come forward, Pili was following rather than cutting off the ring. Taylor controlled where the exchanges took place and rarely allowed her challenger to plant her feet long enough to throw sustained combinations.

The crowd rose as Taylor opened up in the 10th. She increased her output, fired fast combinations, and exchanged with Pili through the closing seconds. Taylor finished as the stronger and busier fighter before receiving a standing ovation at the final bell.

The wide scores accurately reflected the action. Pili had brief moments when her pressure made Taylor uncomfortable, but she never consistently solved the champion’s jab or timing.

It was a smart way for Katie to end a career filled with demanding fights. She did not chase a dramatic knockout or allow the emotion of the night to pull her into a reckless exchange. Instead, she relied on the speed, movement, combination punching, and experience that carried her to championships in two divisions.

The victory gave Taylor every major title at 140 pounds and a third reign as an undisputed champion. More importantly, it allowed her to leave boxing with her belts, her record intact apart from one defeat, and the final image of a packed Croke Park standing in appreciation.

Sports.title: Katie Taylor vs Flora Pili Live Results and Fight Updates
Sports.content:
Undercard action

Paddy Donovan stopped Tyrone McKenna in the fourth round after a cut forced the doctor to end their welterweight contest at Croke Park. Donovan dropped McKenna with a body shot in the second and continued targeting him with sharp, accurate punches. A damaging blow also opened a severe cut over McKenna’s right eye. Blood poured from the wound in the fourth, leaving the ringside doctor with little choice but to wave it off. The Limerick southpaw was patient behind his lead right hand, body attack, and head movement while McKenna struggled to catch him cleanly. .

Dave Allen’s heavyweight fight against Thomas Carty was ruled a no contest following a frightening incident in the opening round. Allen landed a short punch during a clinch near the ropes approximately 1:22 into the contest. Replays showed the shot catching Carty around the back of the head as the Irish heavyweight lost his balance. Carty tumbled through the ropes, landed awkwardly at ringside, and caught his foot in a chair. Medical personnel administered oxygen before determining that he could not continue, and officials treated the incident as an accidental foul. The crowd booed the ruling.

Taylor Bevan stopped Emmet Brennan 36 seconds into the sixth round after scoring five knockdowns in their super middleweight contest. Brennan had some early success, but Bevan’s sharper combinations and heavier punches soon took control. The Welsh prospect dropped Brennan twice during a punishing third round. A left hook to the body sent the Dublin fighter down again in the fifth. Bevan registered two more knockdowns at the beginning of the sixth before Brennan’s corner threw in the towel.

Molly McCann (5-0) defeated Sylwia Doligala (8-3-2) by unanimous decision after eight rounds in their super bantamweight bout. The judges scored the fight 80-72, 80-73, and 79-73. McCann controlled the action from the opening bell with steady pressure, a high work rate, and combinations to the head and body. Doligala remained durable but spent much of the contest moving backward and struggling to establish her offense. The accumulated punches left Doligala with swelling beneath one eye and blood on her vest by the later rounds. McCann completed the eight-round distance comfortably and earned her fifth win since leaving mixed martial arts for professional boxing.

Super bantamweight Joe McGrail (14-0, 7 KOs) stopped Matthew Boreland (7-1) with a left hook to the body in the fifth round of a 10-round scheduled bout. The win earned McGrail the vacant WBA Continental Gold title. Boreland fought competitively from the opening bell and began building momentum as the rounds progressed. McGrail remained composed, worked to the body, and found the decisive opening late in the fifth. His sharp left hook dropped Boreland, who remained down for the referee’s full count. The stoppage gave the 23-year-old Liverpool southpaw his seventh knockout and handed Boreland his first professional defeat.

Paddy Gallagher (17-6-1 entering) was initially announced as the majority decision winner over Paul Ryan (11-2 entering) after six competitive middleweight rounds. The score was given as 58-55 for Gallagher, but later reports stated that the referee’s card had been read incorrectly. The actual score was reported as 58-56 for Ryan, leaving the announced result subject to an official correction. Gallagher applied steady pressure and used his experience to force exchanges throughout the fight. The taller Ryan worked from his southpaw stance, boxing at range and looking to counter the advancing Belfast veteran. There were no knockdowns, and the result remained in question while the fighters’ official records were being updated.

Bobbi Flood (4-0, 2 KOs) defeated Jack Swallow (4-14-1) by unanimous decision over four rounds in a junior middleweight fight. The referee scored the contest 40-36, giving Flood every round. The 21-year-old Dublin native controlled the action from the opening bell with his cleaner and more consistent punching. Flood used his amateur experience to outbox Swallow, who remained durable but offered little effective offense. No knockdowns occurred as Flood continued piling up points without placing himself in unnecessary exchanges. The Croke Park crowd supported the local prospect throughout his comfortable points win.

Heavyweight prospect Adam Olaniyan (4-0, 4 KOs) overwhelmed Matej Hudak (6-3, 6 KOs) for a first-round stoppage on the preliminary card. The aggressive 20-year-old immediately closed the distance, established his jab, and hurt the much heavier Hudak with combinations upstairs.

A sustained flurry sent Hudak to a knee as blood flowed from his nose and face. Referee Emile Tiedt stopped the fight after Hudak covered up without returning fire. Eddie Hearn is extremely high on Olaniyan, who has the raw talent and marketability to become Matchroom’s flagship heavyweight after Anthony Joshua retires.

Sports.title: WBO Orders Denzel Bentley–Yoenli Hernandez, Blocking McKenna Unification
Sports.content:
“OFFICIAL 🚨 WBO orders negotiations for Denzel Bentley vs. Yoenli Hernandez in the middleweight division. Both teams have 20 days to reach an agreement,” the WBO announced.

Bentley and McKenna had agreed to an IBF and WBO unification targeted for late 2026, but the fight still needed approval from both organizations. The WBO’s decision to enforce Hernandez’s mandatory removes the most important piece of that plan.

McKenna captured the vacant IBF title by defeating Etinosa Oliha in Dublin last month. Bentley became the full WBO champion in July after Janibek Alimkhanuly relinquished the belt before going up to super middleweight.

That created an opportunity to bring two titles together, and the Bentley–McKenna matchup made sense for both champions. Neither man is tied to one of the division’s established stars, while a unification would have given the winner a stronger negotiating position against WBC champion Carlos Adames or WBA champion Erislandy Lara.

Hernandez was never likely to step aside quietly. The Cuban contender earned his position and had already petitioned the WBO to enforce his title opportunity. Once the organization recognized him as Bentley’s mandatory, approving McKenna as a voluntary opponent became much harder to justify.

The WBO order does not permanently kill Bentley–McKenna. Bentley can face Hernandez first and return to the unification if he keeps his title. Hernandez would inherit that opportunity if he wins.

Bentley’s team can also request an exception allowing him to fight McKenna first, but the organization’s decision to order negotiations suggests it wants the mandatory completed without another delay. A unification agreement between the champions does not automatically override Hernandez’s rights.

The worst outcome for Bentley would be surrendering the WBO belt to preserve the McKenna fight. That would turn a two belt unification into a defense of McKenna’s IBF title and remove much of the contest’s value.

Postponement is more likely. Bentley can deal with Hernandez and revisit McKenna afterward, provided both champions still have their belts and their promoters remain interested.

For McKenna, the order forces him to find another opponent or remain inactive while Bentley fulfills his obligation. His own IBF mandatory situation may create another obstacle if the delay lasts too long.

The Bentley–McKenna agreement arrived before either organization had sanctioned the fight. The WBO has now made its position clear: Hernandez has the first claim on Bentley, and the unification must wait unless an exception is granted.

Sports.title: Jaron Ennis Threatened Crawford’s Mount Rushmore Campaign
Sports.content:
The comparison with Norris’s 1991 victory over Leonard was not flattering to Crawford. Leonard entered that fight trusting the timing, intelligence, and psychological control that had allowed him to solve younger and physically stronger opponents. Norris denied him the time required to think. His hand speed, combinations, and youthful reactions kept Leonard behind throughout the fight.

Norris dropped Leonard twice and won a lopsided unanimous decision. The younger man did not need a greater historical reputation or a deeper collection of accomplishments. He only needed to be faster on that night. That was the danger Ennis represented.

Few fighters solve problems inside the ring as well as Crawford. He often uses the opening rounds to study an opponent’s rhythm, distance, reactions, and preferred attacks. Once he recognizes the patterns, he begins switching positions, taking away weapons, and landing increasingly damaging counters.

That process worked brilliantly against Errol Spence Jr. Crawford read Spence’s jab, punished his predictable entries, and transformed a major welterweight fight into a one-sided beating.

Boots presented a different type of puzzle. He could attack with fast combinations from both positions, change the angle of his punches, and continue punching after the first countering opportunity had passed. His natural size also meant Crawford would not automatically control the exchanges through strength.

Giving away early rounds while collecting information becomes far more dangerous against a younger opponent who can bank them behind speed and activity. Crawford would need to identify Boots’ patterns without allowing the fight to escape him or suffering damage during that process.

The Norris comparison fits here. Leonard still knew more about boxing than Norris, but his knowledge could not slow the younger fighter’s hands or restore the reactions he once possessed. Ring intelligence only takes over after a fighter creates enough time and space to use it.

Those openings might have been available against Boots. The younger man also might have closed them too quickly for Crawford to capitalize.

The business calculation made the decision easier. By the time Crawford defeated Spence in July 2023, he had already taken everything he needed from the welterweight division. He had become undisputed, beaten the other leading fighter of his era, and delivered the signature performance of his career.

The athletic danger Ennis presented was not matched by a comparable payday. He did not possess Spence’s commercial following, Saul “Canelo” Alvarez’s drawing power, or the historical value attached to winning championships in higher divisions.

Beating Boots would have strengthened Crawford’s record. Losing to him might have changed how the public viewed his entire welterweight reign.

That was a poor exchange for a fighter already in his late thirties. Modern stars expect enormous compensation for accepting enormous danger. Remaining at 147 to face the youngest, largest, and most explosive opponent available for less money violated every sensible rule of career management.

Leaving the division allowed the Spence destruction to serve as Crawford’s final welterweight image. He advanced toward larger purses and championships elsewhere while Ennis inherited the welterweight class without receiving the fight that would have connected one generation to the next. That was smart business. It also protected Crawford’s historical argument.

A place among boxing’s greatest fighters has become part of Crawford’s public case. Once a fighter begins making a Mount Rushmore argument, controlling the final stage of his career becomes essential.

A decisive loss to Boots would have supplied Crawford’s critics with an image they would never stop using: an older great being outsped, outworked, and overpowered by his successor. Most fans would not carefully account for Crawford beginning his championship career at lightweight or Ennis being a natural welterweight. They would remember who controlled the fight.

There was less for Crawford to gain because Boots belonged to the next generation. Clearing out your own era establishes dominance. Remaining long enough to be tested by the leader of the following era invites a very different ending.

Floyd Mayweather Jr. understood that distinction. He faced Canelo while the younger fighter was still developing, then retired before age and declining reactions left him vulnerable to the next wave. Crawford followed the same basic principle: leave the division while the signature victory remains vivid and pursue only the opportunities that pay enough or add enough historical value.

None of this proves Crawford feared Ennis. Fear is unnecessary when basic arithmetic produces the same decision. Boots brought greater youth, natural size, explosive combinations, and minimal commercial compensation compared with the danger involved.

By reading the business correctly, Crawford protected his legacy. Davis merely explained the physical truth behind that choice.

This was not simply another challenger. Ennis was the one welterweight capable of damaging Crawford’s Mount Rushmore campaign while paying him less for the privilege. Leaving 147 allowed Crawford to avoid discovering if his timing and intelligence could overcome the same youthful speed that made Leonard look old against Norris.

Ghana News.title: Road inspections not to witch-hunt contractors – Kwame Agbodza
Ghana News.content:
The nationwide inspection of road projects is not intended to witch-hunt contractors, Roads and Highways Minister Governs Kwame Agbodza has said, insisting that the exercise is aimed at ensuring projects stay on course and are completed within agreed timelines.

Mr Agbodza said regular visits to construction sites were necessary to give the government a clear picture of progress, identify obstacles affecting projects and determine where contractors needed support to improve delivery.

He said the exercise had already encouraged several contractors to increase the pace of construction.

“We don’t go around just trying to look for trouble for contractors, but indeed, many of the Big Push contractors and other contractors are doing very well,” he said.

Speaking during his working visit to the Northern Region on Saturday, September 5, as part of the nationwide inspection tour, Mr Agbodza assured contractors facing challenges that the government remained ready to support them to meet their obligations.

“Don’t worry, with our support, you can also complete your work on schedule,” he said.

Ghana News.title: Inter Milan mount stunning comeback to beat Napoli
Ghana News.content:
Reigning Serie A champions Inter Milan came from 2-0 down to earn a superb win against last year's runners-up Napoli.

Lautaro Martinez scored twice for the hosts - including a 90th-minute winner - either side of a Marcus Thuram header.

Inter were two behind when Napoli scored twice in three minutes at the start of the second half.

Napoli's second came in strange circumstances when the Inter defence switched off, assuming a loose ball was going out of play.

It was kept in and played to Rasmus Hojlund, who swept a shot into the far corner.

But Inter - who have won their opening three league matches of the season - recovered and are still unbeaten at home in Serie A since November 2025.

Napoli, who finished last season 11 points behind Inter, have lost back-to-back Serie A games following a home loss to Como last weekend.

After a goalless first half, Napoli caught Inter cold with a one-two punch.

On 50 minutes, Max Allegri's team took the lead when Matteo Politano scored into the bottom corner on his second attempt after his first effort was blocked.

Then three minutes later, no Inter players were paying attention when the ball appeared to be heading for a throw-in.

But it stopped short of the sideline and was picked up by Giovanni Di Lorenzo, who pulled it back to Hojlund on the edge of the area.

Hojlund made a yard of space away from Inter midfielder Curtis Jones, and curled into the far corner for his second goal in as many league matches.

England international Jones came on at half-time for his second appearance since joining from Liverpool in the summer - and was instrumental in driving Inter to come back and win.

Inter got one back just three minutes later, when Federico Dimarco brilliantly kept in an overhit cross. His first-time pull-back was turned home by Martinez from close range.

Thuram came close to an equaliser when he struck the post, but with eight minutes to play, the Frenchman did get his goal with a header planted into the right-hand corner.

And the victory was earned in remarkable circumstances as Martinez bundled in from close range before celebrating wildly with home fans at San Siro.

While Jones was brought on, fellow England player John Stones was an unused sub.

Another English summer signing, Djed Spence, was not in the squad for the third successive Serie A match as he recovers from a fitness issue.

Ghana News.title: Modric plans to play for Croatia past 41st birthday
Ghana News.content:
Luka Modric turns 41 on Wednesday but is not ready to retire from international football just yet.

The Croatia FA has announced that their captain intends to continue playing for the national team in upcoming Nations League games, including against England.

His decision coincides with the return of Slaven Bilic as manager, with the former West Ham boss helping to guide Modric's fledgling international career in his first stint in charge of the Croatia side, between 2006 and 2012.

Modric earned his first senior cap in March 2006, just before Bilic was named Croatia manager for the first time, and has since gone on to make 202 appearances for his country.

He was expected to call it a day after this summer's World Cup, when Zlatko Dalic's side were knocked out in the last 32 by Portugal.

"Of course, Luka's decision makes me extremely happy," said Bilic, who was manager of Croatia when they denied Steve McLaren's England side qualification for the 2008 Euros.

"We are all aware what he brings to Croatia, both on and off the pitch.

"I'm looking forward to working with him again, after 14 years, and we both share a strong ambition to keep Croatia a top, successful team, shoulder to shoulder with the best teams in the world."

Modric, who currently plays for AC Milan, won the Golden Ball at the 2018 World Cup in Russia, when he helped Croatia reach the final, where they lost to France.

He was also part of the side that finished third in Qatar, four years later.

After playing his part in McLaren's "wally with the brolly" moment at Wembley in the 2008 Euro qualifiers, Modric helped Croatia reach the quarter-finals in Austria and Switzerland.

Croatia's next internationals are in the Nations League - away to the Czech Republic on 26 September and Spain on 29 September.

They then host England in the competition on 3 October, with the return fixture at Wembley on 12 November.

Ghana News.title: Bayern fail to score for first time in 59 games
Ghana News.content:
Bundesliga champions Bayern Munich failed to score for the first time in 59 competitive matches as newly promoted Schalke held them to a goalless draw in Gelsenkirchen.

Luis Diaz came closest to putting Bayern in front when he spurned one-on-one chances either side of half-time.

First, he shanked a shot wide with only Loris Karius to beat, before he saw a tame chip over the goalkeeper, which was cleared well before it reached the goal line.

After opening the season with a thumping 5-1 win against VfB Stuttgart and a 4-1 victory over second-tier side Osnabruck in the DFB Pokal, Bayern manager Vincent Kompany opted to rotate his side.

Harry Kane and Michael Olise watched from the bench as Bayern dominated possession, but did little with it in a disjointed first-half performance.

England captain Kane came on at the break, but it was not until the introduction of Olise and Jamal Musiala with 35 minutes remaining that Bayern began to ramp up the pressure.

Musiala was included in the squad for the first time this season after suffering seizures during two pre-season matches.

Bayern's Konrad Laimer sliced into the side netting from close range, before Kane forced Karius into a stunning fingertip save with a late drive destined for the top corner.

Bayern could not penetrate a compact and disciplined defence as Schalke held on to collect their first point of the season.

This was Kane's 96th Bundesliga appearance, and he needs two more goals to reach 100 in the competition. The record for the fewest matches to reach a century is 129.

Kane began the day having scored against all 20 teams he had faced in the Bundesliga, and has now netted against 20 out of 21.

It is the first time in 67 Bundesliga matchdays - almost two years - that Bayern will not finish on top of the table.

Bayern host Bodo/Glimt in their opening Champions League game on Thursday before travelling to Bundesliga newcomers Elversberg on 13 September.

Ghana News.title: Bawumia preparing new cocoa policy package for farmers – Annoh-Dompreh
Ghana News.content:
The New Patriotic Party's 2028 flagbearer, Dr Mahamudu Bawumia, is preparing to unveil a new policy package for Ghana’s cocoa sector, with a focus on addressing concerns raised by farmers and making cocoa production more sustainable, Minority Chief Whip Frank Annoh-Dompreh has disclosed.

According to the Nsawam-Adoagyiri MP, the proposed measures are expected to offer a fresh approach to some of the longstanding challenges confronting cocoa farmers, including producer prices, rising input costs, disease, ageing farms and declining yields.

He said the initiative followed extensive consultations between a Minority parliamentary team and cocoa farmers across the country.

Speaking at Duayaw Nkwanta in the Ahafo Region on Friday, September 4, 2026, Mr Annoh-Dompreh said the team’s findings were presented to Dr Bawumia in June.

The former Vice President subsequently referred the report to the NPP’s Policy Committee on Agriculture, Food Security and Agribusiness for further technical assessment, expert consultations and the development of costed policy options, with an assurance that “the cocoa farmer will not be abandoned.”

Mr Annoh-Dompreh was speaking after joining Tano North MP Dr Gideon Boako to present 84 motorised spraying machines to cocoa farmer groups to support disease control and improve productivity.

His comments come amid concerns over the current producer price of GH¢2,587 per 64-kilogramme bag for the 2026 light crop season, equivalent to GH¢41,392 per tonne, with the anticipated Bawumia proposal being positioned as a potential alternative to address farmers’ concerns and strengthen the sector.

Ghana News.title: Wa-Tumu-Bolga road upgrade will unlock agriculture, trade – Agbodza
Ghana News.content:
The ongoing upgrade of the Wa-Tumu-Bolgatanga road corridor is expected to open up new economic opportunities for communities across the Upper West Region by improving the movement of farm produce, goods and people, Roads and Highways Minister Governs Kwame Agbodza has said.

Mr Agbodza said the government was determined to complete the various road projects along the corridor within its four-year mandate, despite the significant financial obligations inherited from previous administrations.

He said the government would continue to prioritise projects considered essential to national development while working within available resources.

He explained that completing the Tumu Road and other projects towards the border would constitute one of the government's biggest direct investments in the area during its first term.

According to him, improved connectivity would strengthen agriculture, facilitate trade and create opportunities for residents, particularly young people and farmers who depend on reliable roads to transport their produce to markets.

The Minister expressed optimism that motorists would soon be able to travel safely and smoothly from Wa through Tumu to Bolgatanga as work progresses on the different sections.

Regional Highways Engineer Livistone Damali said construction was ongoing on almost all sections, while Sissala East MP Mohammed Issah Bataglia and Tumu Landlord Baba Tommy Kantong welcomed the projects and expressed hope that they would provide a lasting solution to the area's longstanding road challenges.

Ghana News.title: Ghana Maritime Authority readies oil-spill response vessel for deployment
Ghana News.content:
The Ghana Maritime Authority’s (GMA) multi-purpose oil-spill response vessel christened “MV Esther Ocloo” has undergone a ten-day work-up programme to make the ship operationally ready for deployment.

The ten-day work-up training, organised by the Ghana Navy in collaboration with the GMA, was to determine the operational readiness of the vessel and prepare it for deployment since its acquisition in 2023.

Dr Ali Kamal-Deen, the Director-General of the GMA, speaking during a closing ceremony of the work-up training, at the Sekondi Naval Base said part of the programme was to ensure the MV Esther Ocloo was crewed with Ghana Navy personnel and some officers of the GMA for operational efficiency.

He said: “Having acquired the vessel in 2023, there hasn’t been any attempt to crew the vessel but upon assuming office, management led by myself has been working with the Ghana Navy to crew the vessel so that it can be effectively deployed.”

He stated that the ten-day work-up training, therefore, signalled that the ship was ready to be deployed to protect Ghana’s maritime environment and its offshore oil and gas installations.

“It is no longer going to be a vessel that is going to sit at the harbour but now going to be available for deployment to protect Ghana’s maritime environment and perform roles that will assist in the protection of our offshore oil and gas industry to ultimately meet the regulatory mandates and responsibility of the GMA,” Dr Kamal-Deen added.

He expressed appreciation to the leadership of the Ghana Navy for supporting the GMA to effectively deliver on their mandates.

He also assured the crew on board the MV Esther Ocloo of their welfare to ensure they properly took care of the vessel for its continuous and effective deployment.

Commodore Stephen Billins Nyam, the Flag Officer Commanding (FOC) the Western Naval Command, said the ten-day work-up was significant as it provided a structured basis for determining the vessel ‘s readiness and ensuring that the personnel entrusted with its operation were adequately prepared for the responsibilities ahead.

He said: “The comprehensive nature of this training has revealed valuable insight into the capabilities of the vessel and the level of preparedness of the personnel operating her.

“From the perspective of the Command, the completion of this work-up provides an important basis towards the effective employment of the MV Esther Ocloo.”

Commodore Nyam acknowledged the collaboration between the Ghana Navy and the Ghana Maritime Authority towards enhancing Ghana’s maritime security, noting that Such engagements promoted a better appreciation of respective roles and provided a foundation for more effective coordination at sea.

The MV Esther Ocloo was named after Ghanaian entrepreneur Esther Afua Ocloo.

The 40-metre-long vessel serves as a strategic asset for oil-spill detection, recovery, surveillance and environmental protection, while supporting Ghana’s efforts to develop a safer, cleaner, and more sustainable maritime sector.

Ghana News.title: Ayariga turns to drones, AI to tackle Agbogbloshie waste mountain
Ghana News.content:
The government is deploying drones and artificial intelligence to determine the volume of waste accumulated at Agbogbloshie as it prepares for a major operation to clear the decades-old heap from the heart of Accra.

The exercise is expected to involve hundreds of trucks, heavy-duty equipment and personnel drawn from several institutions.

Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs Minister Mahama Ayariga said the waste mountain had reached such an alarming scale that its removal had become a national priority.

He disclosed that he had visited the site three times within his first week in office and, during his latest visit, climbed to the top of the heap, which he estimated to be about the height of a 10-storey building.

According to Mr Ayariga, President John Dramani Mahama has directed the Ministries of Local Government, Finance, Roads and Highways, and Defence to jointly develop a comprehensive plan for the evacuation.

The government is mobilising the Ghana Armed Forces, Jospong Group, private contractors and dump trucks from Metropolitan, Municipal and District Assemblies, while technical teams use drones and AI to map the site and determine the logistical requirements.

The Minister said the waste would be transported to an engineered landfill site off the Nsawam Road, with authorities considering a 24-hour operation subject to final arrangements and presidential approval.

He acknowledged that the movement of large numbers of trucks could temporarily disrupt traffic, but urged Ghanaians to accept the inconvenience, stressing: “Let all of us be inconvenienced by the problem, and if we are all sufficiently inconvenienced by the problem, the danger of reverting to the problem will be minimised.”

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.
