World.title: Bystanders rescue SUV occupants who crashed into Rideau River in Ottawa
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Two people whose SUV crashed into the Rideau River on Friday morning are safe after several others who were in the area rushed into action to rescue them.

Emergency services responded to the single-vehicle collision around 5:50 a.m. at the corner of Riverside Drive and Walkley Road near Mooney's Bay, according to Ottawa paramedics.

They said an SUV went into the water and that two people inside had made it back to shore. They were assessed by paramedics and released at the scene.

CBC News saw a long silver pole on the road and boats labeled "Ottawa Fire" on the water around 6 a.m. on Friday.

Lesley Tomlinson had been out for a run that morning and was near the intersection when she heard the sound of a car braking and skidding.

She told CBC the SUV had skidded through the intersection, hit the light pole, went over the embankment and crashed into the water.

"I was dumbfounded," she said.

The intersection of Riverside Drive and Walkley Road is seen at around 6 a.m. on Friday after the crash. (Gabrielle Huston/CBC)

'He can't swim!'

"There was definitely a moment of panic as to, how do I help these people?" Tomlinson said.

Two other people emerged on the scene to help, she said. One woman came out of a house nearby and called 911, while another woman who'd been in a car behind the SUV pulled over and jumped into the water.

Tomlinson said she watched her help the driver out of the car and then go around to the passenger's side, yelling: "He can't swim!"

A former lifeguard, Tomlinson dove into the water. When she reached the car, it was mostly submerged and the passenger was holding onto it.

"I was very assertive and I told him that he was not to touch me, he was not to put his arms around me, that that would mean we would both drown," Tomlinson recalled.

"I told him that he is going to lie on his back and I am going to hold his head and I'm going to bring him in. ... We got him into that position just as the car completely submerged."

First responders are seen at the scene of the crash Friday. Speaking about the help she provided, Tomlinson said that 'if you're not aware of lifeguard procedures, you really can't help someone who can't swim.' (Gabrielle Huston/CBC)

'You really need basic swimming skills'

Tomlinson said she swam with him to shore while supporting his head.

Speaking to CBC News afterwards, she said it didn't hit her how extraordinary the situation was in the moment.

Tomlinson emphasized that it was a group effort to help, saying the woman who had pulled over and jumped in first was "the real superstar."

Later that day, Tomlinson went to work as a teacher and told her students about what happened.

"I felt it was so important to impress upon them the ability to swim. The driver was not a strong swimmer but he could keep his head up ... the other person couldn't swim and didn't know what to do," she said.

"I really think the takeaway from this whole thing is that you really need basic swimming skills because you never know what situation you're going to be in."

Police told CBC on Saturday that the SUV had been recovered from the Rideau River.

World.title: Rescuers in Nepal pull 2 people alive from the debris 10 days after devastating floods
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Two more people have been rescued alive in Nepal 10 days after devastating floods hit the country, including a worker trapped in a hydropower tunnel and a woman found inside a damaged home. More than 5,000 people remain missing.

Rescuers in Nepal pulled out a Chinese man and a woman in separate operations on Saturday, 10 days after devastating floods hit the country, as teams continued searching for thousands of missing people.

The man was rescued from a hydropower tunnel, according to a social media post by the country's prime minister's office, bringing the total to three workers pulled alive from the Trishuli hydropower project. Two Nepalese workers were rescued on Friday.

Nepal's army said a joint rescue team of Nepalese military personnel and South Korean disaster experts rescued the man from a 225-metre tunnel and that he was undergoing a health assessment. Images showed him being evacuated by helicopter, with an army medic checking on him during the flight.

A photo released by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV showed two rescuers carrying the man out of the tunnel.

CCTV shared audio of the man talking to an officer, saying how he repeatedly shouted whenever he saw the rescue crews' lights, but they could not hear him.

"When they rescued me today, when they shone [the light] before my eyes, I couldn't believe it," he said.

The man was taken to hospital and was in stable condition, according to CCTV.

Rescue efforts have increasingly focused on 12 hydropower projects across Nepal, where about 900 workers are missing and roughly 500 are believed to be trapped in various tunnels, authorities said. Specialized rescue teams from India, China, South Korea and the United States have been searching through debris, damaged structures and tunnels at the projects, hoping to find survivors.

WATCH | 2 Nepalese workers rescued on Friday: 2 workers rescued from buried Nepal tunnel | Duration 1:54 Two workers were rescued from a hydroelectric tunnel nine days after devastating flash floods in Nepal. Nearly 5,000 are still missing, including 29 Canadians.

In flood-hit Nuwakot town, a woman was rescued alive from a house, Nepal's army spokesperson said Saturday. Officials said she was airlifted to Kathmandu for treatment.

Images released by Nepal's army showed rescuers finding the woman covered in mud inside the damaged house. They gave her bottled water before pulling her to safety, wrapped in a grey blanket.

At least 1,300 people were killed in the Aug. 26 floods, which were likely caused by a glacier collapse, and more than 5,000 remain missing, according to Nepal's disaster management agency.

World.title: Snowbirds take their final flight over Toronto until the 2030s at this weekend’s air show
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The 77th Canadian International Air Show at this year's CNE marks the final Toronto appearance of the iconic Snowbirds. The nine-jet aerobatics team is set to be replaced in the 2030s at the earliest, after far exceeding their intended lifespan. CBC's Tyler Cheese was at the airshow and spoke to attendees about what this last flight means to them.

Snowbirds take their final flight over Toronto until the 2030s at annual air show

The 77th Canadian International Air Show is roaring back into the city this Labour Day weekend, with high-flying demonstrations at Toronto's lakeshore.

This year's air show marks the final Toronto appearance of the Snowbirds, a nine-jet aerobatics team, until their fleet is replaced in the 2030s at the earliest.

The significance of this weekend's performances isn't lost on Maj. Maciej Hatta, the pilot tasked with leading the Snowbirds as they fly in tight formations around the city.

"It's on our minds," he told CBC Radio's Metro Morning.

"[But] obviously I can't be thinking about that the whole time, because we've got a nine-plane formation to worry about leading around the city safely."

WATCH | A former Snowbirds commanding officer on grounding the squadron: CBC News Network's David Common speaks to Retired LCol Dan Dempsey about the Snowbirds | Duration 6:58 Get the latest on CBCNews.ca, the CBC News App, and CBC News Network for breaking news and analysis.

The team's signature CT-114 Tutor jets were ordered by the military as training aircraft in 1961 and have been used for performances for more than five decades.

Hatta, who grew up outside Toronto, says seeing the Snowbirds fly as a child is part of what inspired him to become a pilot in the first place.

"It is touching to hear that everybody's got a slightly different Snowbird story, whether it was watching from a condo in downtown Toronto, or… somebody's dad or or mom working on the team as a technician or pilot,” he said.

Replacements coming ‘as quickly’ as possible: Ottawa

Military officials have been warning for decades that the Tutors have gone far past their intended lifespan and needed to be replaced.

In May, Defence Minister David McGuinty announced that the planes would be grounded after a busy summer performance schedule, ending with a final appearance at the Grey Cup in Calgary.

The Swiss-made, turbo-prop CT-157 Siskin II has been chosen to replace the Snowbird squadron.

"Negotiations are underway with the manufacturer and we intend to procure those aircraft as quickly as we possibly can," McGuinty said at the time.

On Friday, Canadian veterans gathered to watch the Snowbirds during their final rehearsal before the air show.

"This is a wonderful day," said retired air force pilot Mort Lightstone as aircraft zoomed overhead, "These aircrew men and women are a national treasure."

A 77-year Labour Day weekend tradition

This year's air show will also have demonstrations by a Royal Canadian Air Force CF-18 and an RCMP Black Hawk helicopter — though a last-minute schedule change saw the United States' F-16 demonstration team drop out.

The daily performances run from noon to 3:40 p.m. every day from Saturday through to Monday.

The Canadian International Air Show, now in its 77th year, is an end-of-summer fixture — though not one everyone enjoys equally.

PHOTOS | Canadian Snowbirds, RCMP Black Hawk Helicopter, Pink Jet part of this year's lineup:

The noise associated with the event is routinely criticized for being disruptive for people and pets alike, and for upsetting Torontonians who are struggling with PTSD or memories of war.

Hatta says he understands those concerns, but encourages Torontonians to think of the show as a way to inspire future pilots and technicians who may one day help save lives, for example as a part of a search-and-rescue mission.

"There's a little more to it than meets the eye," he said.

On its website FAQ, the air show writes that the show complies with "all regulations, including those published by Transport Canada relating to noise."

World.title: Woman injured in bear attack in Whistler backcountry
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A woman was taken to hospital on Friday after a bear attack in the backcountry near Whistler.

The B.C. Conservation Officer Service (BCCOS) said a group of three hikers ran into two bears near Conflict Lake in the Callaghan Conservancy around 5 p.m. PT on Friday.

The service said one of the bears attacked a woman before disengaging.

Whistler Search and Rescue president Brad Sills said it helped transport conservation officers to the scene, and to evacuate the woman by helicopter.

He said the woman had a severely lacerated leg. B.C. Emergency Health Services said the victim was transported to hospital in stable condition.

BCCOS swept the area and killed an adult male black bear at the attack site due to safety concerns, it added.

However, the service said it has not been able to confirm if a black bear or grizzly bear was responsible for the attack.

Sills said the area is known grizzly habitat, and hikers in the area need to take precautions including making plenty of noise.

“It’s not enough to call out intermittently when you’re hiking, when you’re in known grizzly bear terrain, you need to be calling out all the time,” he said.

The BCCOS said officers were returning to the site on Saturday.

B.C. Parks has closed trail access in the area and is urging people to stay away.

World.title: Billy Ray Cyrus reacts to Miley changing her stage name
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When pop singer Miley dropped the Cyrus from her name on her social media accounts earlier this week, tongues started wagging.

Was this the act of a distraught singer, mourning the loss of her honorary godmother, Dolly Parton?

Had she fallen out with her famous father, country singer Billy Ray Cyrus?

Or did it have something to do with the release of her upcoming album?

Billy Ray Cyrus is clearing up the confusion today with a post on social media.

" I always called my little girl Miley. Just … Miley," he wrote on Instagram, alongside a picture of him with his children when they were young.

Miley was named Destiny Hope Cyrus at birth, but as a baby she smiled so much, her father told Ellen DeGeneres, he started calling her Smiley — then Miley, and the name stuck.



Around this time, Billy Ray Cyrus also introduced his young daughter to country music icon Dolly Parton, whom he befriended while performing as her opening act on tour. He asked Parton to play the role of godmother to Miley.

Both Cyruses have publicly expressed how keenly they are feeling the loss of Parton, who died last week.

Billy Ray Cyrus, who turned 65 on the day of Parton's death, says family is more important to him right now than ever before, and he doesn't begrudge his daughter performing under a single name.

"I told @miley yesterday I felt good about her going with her first name. I mentioned Dolly and Cher. Thinkin' about it more and more … Elvis ... Prince … and so on. It’s a natural progression for an iconic superstar legend. "

This does not appear to be an official name change for Miley, merely a rebrand.

Her tenth studio album, Bass Persuades, is due to be released on Sept. 18, and she has also announced two concerts at the Hollywood Bowl in Los Angeles in October.

" I’ve sat in those seats many times, but I’ve never taken the stage. L.A. is my heart and I’m bringing it home," she wrote this week on Instagram.
