World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Sheinbaum delivers her second-year report as trade tensions simmer
World.content:
Listen to this article

The week of Aug. 31, President Claudia Sheinbaum delivered her second annual government report, reflecting on the state of the nation as her second year in office draws to a close. She touted falling homicides and a stable economy, only to face a pointed rebuttal from opposition leaders who accused her administration of manipulating crime statistics and shielding officials tied to drug trafficking.

Mexico continues to grapple with security challenges on a variety of fronts, a fact underscored by a car bomb in Zacatecas Sunday night — the state’s third such attack in four days. But Mexico’s security forces remain active and on Monday claimed a high-profile target: Soldiers and marines killed Luis Enrique Barragán, alias “R5,” the accused leader of extortion against Michoacán’s avocado growers, in a shootout in Tocumbo.

Trade friction with Washington ran through much of the week. A dispute over cheese naming rights is complicating already-strained talks over the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA). Mexico continues to push back against the threat of U.S. tariffs, and Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard met U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on the sidelines of a G20 gathering Wednesday to press Mexico’s case against tariffs on steel, aluminum and cars.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Sheinbaum’s second-year report meets a sharp opposition response

President Sheinbaum delivered her second annual government report Tuesday, a 67-minute address touting a 51% reduction in homicides since taking office, record foreign direct investment and a stable economy. She said her administration’s relationship with Washington “has had its challenges” but reiterated that “sovereignty isn’t negotiated, handed over or shared.”

Opposition senators offered a starkly different account. PAN’s Ricardo Anaya disputed the government’s homicide figures, arguing that reclassified deaths obscure a rising toll, while PRI’s Alejandro Moreno accused the administration of an unspoken “pact” with organized crime, pointing to the unresolved U.S. extradition request for Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya. Sheinbaum has said her administration won’t shield anyone who has committed a crime.

The president also used Wednesday’s press conference to accuse the Trump administration of trying to “create divisions” within her cabinet ahead of November’s U.S. midterms, calling it part of a long-standing U.S. pattern of pressuring “independent governments.” Her approval rating stood at 68% heading into the report, among the highest of any Mexican president at this point in a term, according to polling firm El Financiero. Along with the high approval rating, the newest results of the MND Sheinbaum Index™ found an almost 10-point increase in the president’s performance.

Security: Zacatecas car bomb and a cartel leader’s death

Eleven people, including a policewoman, were injured Sunday night when a car bomb exploded outside a municipal police station in Ojocaliente — the third explosives attack in Zacatecas in four days. Authorities are investigating whether the blast was retaliation for the Saturday capture of an alleged Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) sicario. The explosion damaged 30 properties and 13 vehicles; classes were suspended and army troops deployed to the municipality.

The next day, Mexican Army and Navy forces killed Luis Enrique Barragán Chávez, known as “El Güicho” or “R5,” in a shootout in Tocumbo, Michoacán. Federal Security Minister Omar García Harfuch identified Barragán as the leader of the Cártel de Los Reyes and the main coordinator of extortion against avocado producers in the state; the U.S. had offered a $3 million reward for his arrest on drug and firearms charges.

At her Friday mañanera in Zacatecas, Sheinbaum’s Security Cabinet reported the state’s daily homicide rate fell 85% in August compared to September 2024, and that more than 3,800 people have been arrested there since she took office. Defense Minister Ricardo Trevilla Trejo, responding to a Fox News report on U.S. anti-drone operations at the border, said the drones are mainly used by migrant smugglers and declined to confirm Mexican military involvement in the U.S. takedowns.

Mexico-U.S. trade relations: Tariffs, cheese and an uncertain USMCA

Mexico-U.S. trade talks hit a snag over cheese this week, with U.S. officials pressuring Mexico to amend a May agreement with the European Union that grants regional-name protections to products like Parmigiano Reggiano and manchego. The U.S. government’s position is that these names are generic; the European Commission says the deal isn’t open to amendment, leaving Mexico caught between two trading partners.

Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard met U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on the sidelines of a G20 Innovation Ministerial in North Carolina on Wednesday, pressing the U.S. to lift tariffs on Mexican cars, steel and aluminum, which Mexico calls unjustified. Sheinbaum said Thursday her government is working to secure a better tariff agreement, noting that most Mexican exports still enter the U.S. duty-free under the USMCA.

The tariff dispute traces back to Washington’s decision not to renew USMCA in its current form for a further 16 years, leaving the pact’s future — and Mexico’s manufacturing-heavy states — in limbo pending ongoing bilateral talks.

Economy: The peso strengthens as growth forecasts improve

The peso hit a 28-month high against the dollar on Friday, trading at 16.863, reviving talk of a “super peso.” Analysts attribute the gains partly to peso strength and partly to the dollar’s weakness. A stronger peso cuts import costs and inflation but squeezes exporters’ margins and remittance values, with agricultural states like Michoacán most exposed.

Earlier in the week, Banxico raised its 2026 GDP growth forecast to 1.5%, up from 1.1%, citing stronger-than-expected second-quarter growth, while flagging USMCA uncertainty and geopolitical tensions as downside risks.

Mexico’s tourism sector added a bright note: The World Travel & Tourism Council ranked Mexico fourth globally in tourism-generated GDP, behind only the U.S., China and Germany, with Quintana Roo cited as the main driver.

Looking ahead

Trade talks with Washington remain unresolved on both cheese labeling and industrial tariffs, with no clear timeline for a new USMCA agreement as bilateral dialogue continues. Meanwhile, Hurricane Marie, a Category 2 storm off Baja California Sur, is expected to weaken to a Category 1 by Saturday as it moves out to sea, though Conagua warned that atmospheric instability could keep bringing rain to the country’s interior into next week. Zacatecas remains under heightened security following last week’s car bomb attack, with federal, state and municipal forces reinforcing operations in Ojocaliente.

Some good news to end the week

Mexico News Daily

World.title: The singing frog that came to symbolize midcentury Mexico
World.content:
While it may be a fine place to avoid New Orleans’ sweltering heat, Tulane University’s Doris Z. Stone Latin American Library serves a much larger purpose as a repository of Mexico travel and tourism ephemera, including magazines, hotel brochures and highway maps.

Together, the collection offers a unique look at how the United States’ southern neighbors were constructed as attractive vacation destinations throughout the midcentury.

Mexico especially loomed large in the imagination of U.S. tourists. It was a period when, as historian Mauricio Tenorio notes, Mexico was understood as a “Brown Atlantis” — where revolutionary thought fermented, and the Pan-American Highway promised access to exotic adventures. Everyone wanted to meet Frida Kahlo and visit Teotihuacán, all while dreaming up global politics anew.

Two brochures found in the Mexican ephemera collection tell how Mexico feted itself for an international community, including the crooning amphibian that would become the country’s unofficial mascot during the time.

The singing frogs of Taxco

First is a trifold brochure from arguably Mexico’s most famous nightclub during the second half of the 20th century — Cantarranas. However, the site didn’t always host the international glitterati.

Located in the silver-mining town of Taxco, roughly 2.5 hours outside of Mexico City, the estate was initially conceived in 1538 by Hernán Cortés, who ordered its construction so that he could extract the region’s precious materials.

Dubbed Hacienda Cantarranas, – literally “singing frogs” due to the loud chorus of frogs living in the nearby area – Cortés’ son Martín de Cortés oversaw its construction, which featured large stones along a hillside. Over the years, the infrastructure took its toll on the unstable land it was built on and was ultimately abandoned in favor of a new locale.

For the next four centuries, the site was nothing more than a derelict ghost of Mexico’s colonial past. That is, until one entrepreneur saw an opportunity.

Antonio “Tony” Reyes Ramírez, who would later become Taxco’s minister of tourism, officially opened Cantarranas in 1957. Eager to capitalize on its history, Reyes Ramírez kept the name and leaned on its playful imagery in his marketing materials.

Cantarranas quickly developed a global reputation as a lively hangout throughout the 1960s and 70s, and even featured prominently in a popular television show of the time.

The brochure for Catarranas promises tourists a night of “flamenco dancing by Estela Calderón,” “Carl Brice directly from Nassau, Bahamas,” “Primitive African Drums by the owner and Manager of Cantarranas Tony Reyes,” and “The Latin American Rhythms of the great pianist Juan García Esquivel.”

The nightclub also housed several distinct spaces, including the “Twilight Room,” the “Patio,” the “Flamenco Room” and the “Mulata Room.” Newspapers of the time reported that, inside Cantarranas, “the audience moves en masse from room to room as each show finishes.”

During that same decade, the brochure from Tulane notes that Cantarranas was chosen as the backdrop for an episode of the NBC series, “I Spy,” entitled “Return to Glory,” which aired Feb. 23, 1966.

In it, Alexander Scott – played by Bill Cosby – is tipped off by U.S. intelligence to visit Cantarranas, where he rendezvouses with the wife of a deposed president of an unnamed Latin American country. Famed Mexican actress Dolores del Río plays the part of the wife, as Cosby and costar Robert Culp try to negotiate the democratic leader’s return to his home nation.

Cantarranas’ popularity continued to grow throughout the early- to mid-1970s.

A newspaper article from 1974 lists several of the club’s attractions, including “Flying Indian Men,” a discotheque called “The Psychedelic Cave,” bullfighting lessons, a piñata party, and calypso songs by Carl Brice.

However, as a new decade dawned, Cantarranas was beginning to lose its luster.

An article from 1978 reported that “Cantarranas is a little rough around the edges.” Two years later, the club was described as “the kind of place that you wouldn’t miss if you missed it. But worth it if you’re utterly bored.”

Unable to sustain itself any longer, in 1983, the Mexican state of Guerrero acquired the property and converted it into a culinary school and arts center. In 1992, it changed hands once again, this time to the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México as a school for foreign nationals.

Despite its short life, Cantarranas heralded Mexico’s midcentury miracle as its nascent legacy was beginning to be forged.

The birth of Señor Frogs

Twelve years after Cantarranas opened, another Mexican restaurateur, Carlos Anderson, was cooking up a similar concept that would come to define the Mexican resort experience well into the 21st century – Señor Frog’s.

First opened in Mazatlan in 1969, Señor Frog’s capitalized on that same midcentury swagger, with waiters slinging tequila shots and cajoling spontaneous conga lines in a neon cave. It’s unclear why Señor Frog’s succeeded where Cantarranas ultimately failed, but it did.

It wasn’t just the nightclub scene, either. The Tulane collection includes another brochure with a singing frog on it — this one from Pemex or Petróleos Mexicanos, the company formed in 1938 by the Mexican government to sell the nation’s significant oil supply.

The brochure includes maps of Mexican highways and invites travelers to explore the best routes. There is no mention of Cantarranas, or Taxco, or even nightclubs. However, at this point the singing frog had become emblematic of Mexico’s exotic sights, electric nights and cultural spectacle.

From Hacienda Cantarranas to Tony Reyes’ “Singing Frogs” bar, through a national oil company and today’s Señor Frog’s franchises, the brochure in Tulane University’s Doris Z. Stone Latin American Library chronicles the birth of a national symbol, while documenting how tourists were meant to imagine the delights of midcentury Mexico – strange, inviting and culturally savvy, not unlike a crooning amphibian.

Kevin M. Anzzolin earned a PhD in Romance Languages and Literatures from the University of Chicago. He is the author of “Guardians of Discourse: Literature and Journalism in Porfirian Mexico,” published by the University of Nebraska Press (2024), which received an Honorable Mention from LASA-Mexico for Best Book in the Humanities in 2025. He currently teaches language and literature courses at Christopher Newport University (Virginia, USA). He also publishes in more public fora.

World.title: Is Mexican-made kombucha underrated?
World.content:
There are few drinks in history with an eccentrically bubbly origin story like kombucha.

The fermented probiotic can be traced back to China around 221 B.C. during the Qin Dynasty, when it was consumed as a “remedy for immortality” by those who considered the yeasty, naturally carbonated black tea a source of long-lasting health and vitality.

The long history of kombucha

In 414 B.C., the Smithsonian reports, the cloudy beverage was imported to Japan by a Korean doctor named Kombu, in order to treat Emperor Inkyo. To further complicate its history, Japan already had its own form of kombucha, made from kombu (brown seaweed) and cha (tea).

According to Forbes, kombucha began to spread during the global trade expansion of the 20th century, when the fermented Chinese tea variety migrated into Europe, with Russia and Germany having adopted it as “kambucha” and “kombuchaschwamm,” respectively.

In 1955, Italian piano prodigy Renato Carosone delivered a hit single, “Stu Fungo Cinese!” (translated as “The Chinese Fungus!”), which was rooted in a Chinese mushroom infusion similar to kombucha.

The drink gained mainstream popularity in China during the 1960s, ’70s and ’80s, with homebrews known as “Stomach Treasure” touted as digestive tonics.

Finally, in the 1990s, kombucha entered the North American market, largely thanks to major U.S. brands like GT’s Kombucha.

In the past decade, kombucha’s ubiquity — and value — has skyrocketed as one of the fastest-growing beverage markets on the continent. Now a mainstream supermarket item, North American kombucha sales generated revenue of US $2.1 billion in 2025, with revenues expected to top US $4 billion by 2033.

Of course, the United States accounts for much of the lion’s share. But a market study revealed that Mexico is predicted to have the continent’s largest compound annual growth rate for kombucha in the coming years.

So what has taken kombucha so long to work its magic in Mexico?

Mexico as a country of many beverages — except kombucha, until recently

In my personal recollection, the Eurasian style of kombucha was never plentiful in Mexico. As a child, I could get all sorts of aguas frescas, carbonated sodas and any flavored drinks imaginable. As I grew older, that evolved into other forms of consumption (micheladas, carajillos, etc.). But I have no memory of ever seeing kombucha on a restaurant menu, at a cafe or in mercados.

Here’s my theory: With all of the other beverages that are made in, and often native to, Mexico — including tepache, a naturally fermented pineapple drink — the craft of Asian and Western kombuchas couldn’t get a foothold. In a country where you can easily get tequila, mezcal, pulque, sugar cane aguardiente, rum, atole, arroz con leche and so much more on practically every corner in any pueblo (often made by someone in the neighborhood with generations of family knowledge, ancestral practices and native ingredients at their disposal), kombucha didn’t necessarily have much demand. I’ve watched señoras prepare natural tea remedies from flowers they’ve handpicked from their gardens. But getting offered kombucha inside someone’s home? Never.

It wasn’t until the mid-to-late 2010s that I started to notice kombucha — commercially and independently bottled — as a relatively more common option around Mexico.

Kombucha in Veracruz and other states in Mexico

Near my home in downtown Xalapa (a region known for its rich and deeply rooted coffee history), all of the new-school cafes now offer kombucha, with a noticeable amount of homebrewed and locally made brands available. While recently enjoying my neighborhood on foot, I popped into a few nearby cafes — touted for their espressos, flat whites and other caffeinated brews — and was excited to see artisanal kombucha on nearly every menu. I asked the owner of Marcelo whether she has noticed a rise in kombucha’s popularity and consumption; she confirmed that within the past five years (by her estimation) kombucha has exploded with trendiness across Mexico. She even started to experiment with brewing her own batches, but after failed attempts, opted to get her supply from LindaSol Fermentería, a micro-kombuchería located a few miles from her cafe in Xalapa.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by the pickle (@thepickleofbrighton)

My personal go-to is Agua Brava, made by the chef at Bravo Pizza, a small pizzeria that opened in Xalapa two years ago. Their kombucha flavors rotate weekly and are made in-house and bottled on-site. Among other favorites that I’ve found in Veracruz are Komboocha Puerto (from the port city of Veracruz), Dominga Kombucha (from Cholula, Puebla) and Naran Fermentos (from Xalapa). Mexico City, Guadalajara, San José del Cabo and other cities are no different, offering their own unique brands like Cali Kombucha in Baja California Sur. Data and testimonials suggest that kombucha first infiltrated Mexico’s market roughly a decade ago, when Mexican-owned brands like the aforementioned Cali Kombucha and Brew Lab from Oaxaca launched their brands around 2015 and 2016, respectively.

To highlight the Mexicanization of kombucha since then, “kombucherías” are now a thing in Mexico — as evidenced in the social media reel above, made by a British tourist tasting Oaxacan kombucha in Mazunte. Spoiler: It’s “banging.”

Kombucha a la mexicana: Basil jamaica, pineapple coconut, and more

Though you won’t casually walk past a kombuchería on every corner, you’re likely to encounter a local kombucha brewer in your neighborhood, who might directly sell unmarked jugs or labeled microbatches of their SCOBY-made (Symbiotic Culture Of Bacteria and Yeast) concoctions. You’ll also find it in most grocery markets with a cosmopolitan clientele, or in small businesses that are dedicated to holistic living and organic products.

Often, the flavors have a tropical Mexican vibe: maracuyá, tamarindo, coconut, mango. Some brands add additional ingredients like ancho chile peppers, jalapeño, honey or kiwi for an extra kick of spice, sweetness or tang. Puebla’s Domingo Kombucha has a killer guayaba option — subtly effervescent, fruity and mellow. Mexico City’s Umani offers canned options including orange turmeric, Mexican pepperleaf and fig. Bruja Sana from Yucatán emphasizes herbally minty options with green, earthy additions like romero and hierba buena.

Many of Mexico’s leading kombucha brands are independent, and offer or encourage other lifestyle supplements like yoga and Pilates classes, SCOBY workshops and more. It’s far from commercial profit and mass-made consumer-targeted sales; instead, kombucha offers a doorway into a wider range of health-centered practices and mindful consumption with regional flavor.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: New episode: ‘Confidently Wrong’ podcast tackles expat money habits and mistakes
World.content:
Money affects everyone living in or traveling to Mexico. It is with that in mind that Mexico News Daily has launched a new weekly series called “Mexico and My Money.” You can read about the thinking behind the series here: Mexico and My Money: A new series MND on personal finance.

Our team recently conducted a survey of over 700 expats living in 25 states throughout Mexico about how they handle money while living in the country. The results were striking: Despite wariness of Mexican banks, 71% of respondents own a home in Mexico and nearly eight in 10 have made some kind of investment here — in real estate, a business, stocks or bonds. Nearly one in five respondents said they’d been victimized by a financial crime, with stories ranging from a landlord who kept a deposit “without cause” to a household employee who stole from a family over eight years. You can see the full results here: Mexico and My Money: What you told us about your personal finance habits and hang-ups.

In this week’s episode of “Confidently Wrong,” George and I dig into those results. We talk about banking in Mexico, cash and credit cards, the money mistakes expats wish they’d avoided. You will learn what are others doing differently and about best practices for money in Mexico. Check it out!

Confidently wrong about Mexico and my money: Episode 7 - Season 3

Watch this video on YouTube

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: Why isn’t the peso at 37 to the US dollar? A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
Here is a mindblowing number to think about: If the peso had performed similarly from 2020 to the present as it did in the previous 25 years (from 1995 to 2020), the current exchange rate would be near 37 pesos to the US dollar!

That statistic puts into perspective how incredible the current exchange rate of 16.86 (as of Friday) really is. With the peso back near record highs in what seems like an unbreakable trend, I thought it would be a good time to do a refresher on the topic of the MXN:USD exchange rate.

For decades, the peso reliably lost about 10% of its value against the dollar every year. Although that devaluation was bad for some and good for others, its consistency and predictability allowed businesses, governments and families to plan around it. The fact that the past five-plus years have been so dramatically different — so unpredictable — has had some real impacts on Mexico.

With that in mind, I thought I would share some of the top columns I have written about the peso over these past several years to help us understand why its its happening, if it might continue, and what we can do about it. Each one tackles a different angle of the story. Please enjoy.

When will the Mexican peso begin to behave rationally again? — Why the peso stopped following its old, predictable rules — and what “rational” behavior would even look like now.

Is the peso punching above its weight? The results of our latest MND Peso Index™ — Our MND Peso Index™ compares real prices in Mexico and the U.S. to understand the real value of the peso.

Mexico in Numbers: The peso’s wildest swings since 2000 — A numbers-driven look back at 25 years of exchange rate history.

What’s next for the peso? — A forward-looking read on where the exchange rate could realistically head next.

Is the peso about to peak? — The signs that suggest the peso’s historic run might be nearing its limit.

How to stop a speeding super peso — What tools the government and Banco de México actually have to slow the peso down, and whether they’re likely to use them.

How can we predict what will happen next with the Mexican peso? — A practical framework for reading the signals, so you’re not just guessing.

Pros and cons of the superpeso — Who wins and who loses when the peso gets this strong, and why it’s not all good news.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

Brazil votes on Sunday, October 4, 2026, in the first round of a presidential election that polls show heading for a runoff between President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro. This page becomes our live results blog the moment polls close: vote counts, turnout, state-by-state maps, market reaction and what the numbers mean for the October 25 runoff.

Until then, it carries the state of the race, the mechanics of the count, and what to watch on election night. For weekly polling numbers, see our Brazil Election Poll Tracker; for the full landscape, the Brazil Elections 2026 Complete Guide.

Live Results — October 4, 2026

Live desk opens at 17:00 BRT (20:00 UTC) on Sunday, October 4. Brazil’s fully electronic voting system typically delivers a reliable national picture within two to three hours of polls closing. We will publish the TSE’s official count as it lands, with analysis of what each update means for a potential runoff. Bookmark this page — the newest entries will appear at the top.

Latest pre-election update — September 5, 2026: Four late-August pollsters agree on the shape of the race. Lula leads the first round with 37–41% against Flávio Bolsonaro’s 30–37%, while Augusto Cury holds third with up to 11%. All runoff simulations sit inside the margin of error: Real Time Big Data shows a 44–44 deadlock, and Vox Brasil puts Flávio fractionally ahead, 45.1% to 44.5%. Free TV advertising began on August 28; both front-runners skipped the first debate on August 23.

When Will We Know the Result?

Brazil uses a fully electronic voting system run by the Superior Electoral Court (TSE). Polls close at 17:00 BRT, and because votes are counted digitally at each polling station and transmitted centrally, the TSE typically publishes a solid national picture within two to three hours. In recent elections the outcome of the first round was clear the same evening.

Official results flow through the TSE’s results portal; we relay them here with context as they arrive. A candidate wins outright on October 4 only with more than 50% of valid votes — blank and null ballots do not count toward that threshold. Prediction markets currently give a first-round victory only about a 12% probability.

What to Watch on Election Night

The 50% question. Lula’s only path to avoiding a runoff is clearing half of valid votes — no late-August poll puts him close, but undecided voters and Cury’s soft support are the swing factors.

Cury’s real vote. Augusto Cury’s poll surge to 7.8–11% is the campaign’s wild card. Whether those voters show up — or drift back to the front-runners under Brazil’s “useful vote” logic — decides how big the runoff gap looks on Sunday night.

State races. Governor contests in São Paulo, Minas Gerais and Bahia run in parallel and shape the second-round map; Senate races, including Michelle Bolsonaro’s bid in Brasília, are decided in one round.

Markets. The real and the Ibovespa have moved on every major poll release. A clear Lula first-round win and a tight-but-runoff outcome price very differently — watch the Sunday-night and Monday-morning reaction in our markets coverage.

The State of the Race — September 2026

The final stretch begins with Lula in front but unable to close out the election in one round, Flávio Bolsonaro competitive in every runoff simulation, and Cury reshaping the arithmetic from third place. Both front-runners carry rejection rates near 50%, the highest in the field, leaving very few persuadable voters for the runoff.

Government approval stands at 45% against 51% disapproval (Real Time Big Data, Aug 27–31). For the full survey-by-survey record, use the poll tracker; for candidate profiles and the electoral calendar, the complete guide.

Frequently Asked Questions

When will Brazil’s 2026 election results be announced?

The TSE begins publishing the official count shortly after polls close at 17:00 BRT (20:00 UTC) on October 4. Thanks to fully electronic voting, a reliable national picture typically emerges within two to three hours.

Will there be a runoff?

Very likely. A candidate needs more than 50% of valid votes to win on October 4, and no late-August poll puts Lula near that threshold. The runoff would be held on October 25. Every Brazilian presidential election since 2002 has gone to a second round.

Who is leading the 2026 Brazil election?

Lula leads every late-August first-round poll, by margins of two to eight points over Flávio Bolsonaro, with Augusto Cury third at up to 11%. Runoff simulations between Lula and Flávio are all tied within the margin of error.

Where can I follow official results?

On the TSE’s official results portal and here — this page runs as a live blog from 17:00 BRT on election day with the count, turnout and analysis.

World.title: Bolivia Inflation Slows as Boliviano Loses Value
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

BOLIVIA · ECONOMY

Key Facts —What happened: Bolivia’s year-to-date inflation through August 2026 is 3.01%, down from 18.09% a year earlier. —How big it is: August’s monthly rate was 1.10%. —What it means: Prices are rising much more slowly than in 2025, easing pressure on households and businesses. —The catch: The low number hides fuel shortages and a currency devaluation that could push prices up again. —Who it hits: Anyone earning or saving in bolivianos, plus foreigners with local currency or fixed incomes. —What comes next: Watch for fuel supply and exchange rate moves, which could reverse the disinflation trend.

Bolivia’s inflation has slowed sharply in 2026. But fuel queues and a devalued currency complicate the picture.

The numbers behind the headline

Bolivia’s national statistics institute, known as INE, released the latest consumer price data on September 3. The monthly inflation rate for August 2026 was 1.10%.

That pushed the year-to-date figure to 3.01% for the first eight months of 2026. The twelve-month rate, which compares August 2026 with August 2025, stands at 5.02%.

Through July the year-to-date figure had been just 1.89%. August alone added more than a percentage point.

In the same period last year, year-to-date inflation was 18.09%. That means prices rose six times faster over the first eight months of 2025 than over the same months of 2026.

What drove prices up in August

The main culprit behind August’s monthly rise was chicken. INE says chicken meat had the largest single impact on the index.

INE blamed the chicken price rise on delayed restocking at poultry farms after 53 days of blockades. It says prices began falling again in the second week of August as supply normalised.

July had seen a rare monthly decline of 2.79%, which helped keep the year-to-date figure low. That drop was driven by price decreases across several product categories.

So the August increase is a reminder that prices can still jump, even in a year of low overall inflation.

Why the big fall from 2025 to 2026

INE’s releases explain which products moved rather than why the overall rate fell. Much of the fall is arithmetic.

Prices rose so fast in 2025 that the same months of 2026 look calm by comparison. That year closed with annual inflation of about 20%, the highest in nearly four decades.

The June currency float is the other factor to watch. The government ended the fixed exchange rate on 29 June 2026, saying it wanted to restore economic stability.

Without named economists or officials giving specific reasons, the full explanation remains open. But the base effect alone explains much of the drop.

Fuel shortages and the currency shift

The low inflation number does not mean Bolivia’s economy is trouble-free. Bolivia has faced repeated fuel shortages through 2026, with long queues for diesel and petrol.

Diesel and gasoline have been hard to find at times, which affects transport and food production. These shortages could push prices up again.

Bolivia scrapped its fixed exchange rate on 29 June 2026, ending about fifteen years of a fixed dollar. The rate jumped from 6.96 to 9.73 bolivianos to the dollar overnight and has gone on sliding.

At 12.58 bolivianos to the dollar today, the boliviano has lost about 45% of its dollar value since the float. The central bank now publishes a single rate.

Valid for 5 to 7 September, in place of the old fixed pair of 6.96 to sell and 6.86 to buy.

What this means for your wallet

If you live in Bolivia and earn bolivianos, slower inflation is good news. Your salary goes further than it did a year ago.

But the currency devaluation means imported goods are more expensive. If you buy electronics, medicine, or anything from abroad, you will feel the pinch.

For foreigners holding bolivianos, the currency’s drop in value is a concern. Even with lower inflation, your money buys fewer dollars than before.

If you are on a fixed income in bolivianos, the lower inflation rate helps. But watch out for fuel-related price spikes.

How the exchange rate affects inflation

Bolivia’s currency, the boliviano, has historically been pegged to the dollar. That peg kept inflation low for years.

But the peg came under strain as dollar reserves fell. The central bank spent reserves to defend it, and a parallel market rate emerged.

The float in June was a major shift. The official and parallel rates have converged.

The parallel rate now trades close to, and sometimes just below, the official one. So far, the effect on inflation has been limited.

But if the currency keeps sliding, inflation could pick up.

What the inflation data does not tell you

The consumer price index measures a basket of goods and services. It does not capture everything.

The index records the official fuel price, not the hours people spend queuing for it. Shortages affect production and transport costs, which eventually hit prices.

So the low inflation number may understate the real cost pressures facing Bolivians. The index also lags behind sudden price shifts.

For a full picture, you need to watch both the index and the queues at petrol stations.

What to watch next

The next INE report will show September’s inflation. If fuel shortages persist, monthly figures could rise.

Watch the exchange rate. If the boliviano weakens further, imported inflation will follow.

Also watch government policy. Any changes to fuel subsidies or price controls could have a big impact.

For now the direction is good. But in Bolivia, inflation can turn quickly.

The bottom line for foreigners

Bolivia inflation is much lower in 2026, which is a relief after 2025’s spike. But the economy is still fragile.

Fuel shortages and a weaker currency are real risks. If you hold bolivianos, consider the exchange rate risk.

If you are planning to move to Bolivia or invest, the lower inflation is a positive sign. But do not ignore the underlying problems.

Keep an eye on monthly data and the exchange rate. They will tell you more than the year-to-date number.

Understanding Bolivia’s inflation history

Bolivia has seen extreme inflation before. In the 1980s, hyperinflation wiped out savings and forced radical reforms.

The country later adopted a currency peg to the dollar. That brought stability and low inflation for decades.

But the peg created vulnerabilities. When dollar reserves fell, the pressure on the boliviano grew.

The 2025 spike was a reminder of those risks. The 2026 slowdown shows how quickly conditions can change.

How INE measures inflation

INE, the national statistics institute, tracks prices in cities across Bolivia. It surveys a range of products each month.

The basket includes food, housing, transport, and other goods. Each item gets a weight based on what households spend.

The monthly inflation rate compares prices from one month to the next. The year-to-date rate compares prices from January to the current month.

The twelve-month rate compares prices with the same month last year. Each measure tells a different story.

Who feels the change most

Low-income households feel inflation most. They spend a larger share of income on food and fuel.

When chicken prices jump 25%, as they did in August, it hurts families that rely on it for protein.

Pensioners and workers on fixed incomes also suffer. Their earnings do not adjust quickly to price changes.

Businesses face uncertainty too. They must decide whether to pass higher costs to customers or absorb them.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Bolivia’s current inflation rate? Bolivia’s year-to-date inflation through August 2026 is 3.01%. The twelve-month rate is 5.02%. How does this compare to 2025? In the same period of 2025, year-to-date inflation was 18.09%. The drop is dramatic. Why did inflation fall so much? Mostly base effects — 2025’s prices rose so fast that 2026 looks calm against them. The June currency float and the easing of last year’s supply disruptions are the other factors. Is the low inflation good news for foreigners? It is mixed. Lower inflation helps, but the boliviano has devalued, which hurts those holding local currency. What could make inflation rise again? Fuel shortages and further currency devaluation are the main risks. Watch monthly data.

World.title: Brazil’s C6 Bank Agrees to Buy Alymente in Benefits Push
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

BRAZIL · BANKING

Key Facts —What happened: the lender agreed to buy Alymente, a Brazilian corporate benefits startup, to enter the benefits market. —How big it is: Alymente serves over 100,000 workers and about 1,200 companies, according to figures the companies released. —What it means: the lender gains a ready platform and team in a market worth over R$150 billion a year (about US$29.3 billion). —The catch: The deal price is undisclosed, and the purchase still needs Central Bank approval. —Who it hits: Rivals like Flash, Caju, Swile, and traditional issuers Ticket, Alelo, and Pluxee face a new heavyweight. —What comes next: After approval, Alymente will be rebranded as C6 Benefícios, and its team of about 40 will join the lender.

C6 Bank is buying Alymente, which manages meal and transport benefits for Brazilian workers. The market is worth over R$150 billion a year, about US$29.3 billion.

What Alymente does

Alymente is a Brazilian fintech founded in 2017. It offers a multi-benefits card issued by Mastercard that covers food, transport, and well-being.

The card also includes services like telemedicine, psychological support, and gym access. Companies give these cards to employees as part of their compensation package.

How meal and food cards work for workers

In Brazil, many companies provide meal and food allowances through prepaid cards or vouchers. Most meal and food benefits are set by collective bargaining agreements.

Companies that offer them through the federal PAT scheme get a tax break. Workers use these cards at supermarkets, restaurants, and other approved merchants.

The market’s size and appeal

The Brazilian corporate benefits market moves more than R$150 billion per year. That is about US$29.3 billion at R$5.11 to the dollar, the Central Bank’s PTAX rate of Friday 4 September 2026.

That figure covers meal, food, transport, and other employee benefits. Banks want a slice of this flow because it generates fees and deposits.

It also deepens relationships with corporate clients. They may use other banking services.

C6 Bank’s strategy

C6 Bank is a digital bank that has been expanding its services for businesses. Buying Alymente gives it an instant presence in the benefits market.

It brings an existing client base and technology. The bank plans to rebrand Alymente as C6 Benefícios and integrate its team of about 40 professionals.

This move is part of C6’s broader push into corporate banking. It follows a trend of banks buying fintechs to gain new capabilities.

Competition in the benefits sector

The market is crowded with both traditional players and newer fintechs. Traditional issuers include Ticket, Alelo, and Pluxee, which was spun out of the French group Sodexo.

Newer flexible benefits startups include Flash, Caju, Swile, and Raiô. These companies offer single cards that cover multiple categories, aiming to replace older voucher models.

What the acquisition means for the market

C6 Bank’s entry comes as four operators already hold roughly 80% of the segment. That concentration shapes what C6 can achieve with Alymente.

The deal puts a bank inside a market that fintechs opened. Whether other banks follow is not yet clear.

Regulatory approval and next steps

The deal still depends on approval from Brazil’s Central Bank. Until then, the transaction is not complete, and no closing date has been set.

Reports in the Brazilian press say approval could take two to three months. Once approved, Alymente’s brand will be retired, and the operation will operate as C6 Benefícios.

The price, and when it closes

The price the lender is paying for Alymente has not been disclosed. Neither company has published a price, and both have kept the financial terms confidential.

The exact closing date is also uncertain, as it depends on regulatory approval. No firm date has been set.

Alymente’s growth and client base

Alymente has grown to serve over 100,000 workers and about 1,200 client companies. The figures come from the two companies, released with the deal.

Its clients include well-known names like Heineken, Nissan, BIC, and Pernod Ricard. The startup operates nationally across Brazil, offering a flexible benefits platform.

This scale made it an attractive target for the lender’s expansion plans.

The role of Mastercard in the deal

Alymente’s card is issued by Mastercard, a global payment network. This partnership will continue under the new C6 Benefícios brand.

Mastercard’s involvement adds credibility and reach to the benefits card. It also allows C6 to use an established payment infrastructure.

Potential impact on workers and companies

For workers, the change may bring more integrated financial services. They could see their benefits card linked to other C6 banking products.

For companies, the acquisition could mean more streamlined benefits management. C6 may bundle benefits with corporate banking services, offering convenience and cost savings.

The broader context of bank-fintech deals

This deal is part of a wider trend of banks buying fintechs to gain new capabilities. In Brazil, digital banks like C6 are expanding beyond traditional banking.

They are moving into areas like payroll loans, insurance, and now employee benefits. These moves aim to capture more of a customer’s financial life.

Buying a fintech is often faster than building a service from scratch. It brings an existing client base, technology, and a team that knows the market.

What the numbers do and do not prove

The R$150 billion (about US$29.3 billion) market figure shows the size of the opportunity. But it does not mean C6 will capture a large share quickly.

Alymente’s 100,000 beneficiaries are a small fraction of the market. The real test will be whether C6 can grow this base using its banking relationships.

Neither company disclosed a price, so the deal’s valuation cannot be assessed. Without a price, analysts cannot calculate the potential return.

The lack of a closing date adds uncertainty. Regulatory approval could take longer than expected, delaying any benefits for C6.

How this affects everyday workers

Workers who use Alymente cards may not notice an immediate change. The card will keep working as before, even during the transition.

In the long run, they might see new features or integrations with C6’s banking app. This could make managing benefits and money easier.

C6 has said it plans to add payroll and salary consolidation to the platform. For now, cards keep working while the deal waits for approval.

What to watch for next

The first milestone is approval from Brazil’s Central Bank. Once that happens, C6 can start integrating Alymente into its operations.

Watch for announcements about the new C6 Benefícios brand and its product lineup. C6 may yet disclose the price.

Competitors will likely respond to C6’s entry. They might cut prices, add features, or seek their own acquisitions.

The benefits market is evolving quickly, and this deal could accelerate that change. More consolidation is possible as banks and fintechs compete.

How Brazilian benefit cards work in practice

An employee receives a card loaded with a monthly amount for meals or food. The employer sets the value, often through union agreements.

The card works like a debit card at approved merchants. Single-purpose cards cannot be used for cash withdrawals or outside their category.

Flexible cards, like Alymente’s, let workers use one card for several needs. The system aims to ensure money is spent on its intended purpose.

The regulatory change that opened the market

Brazil’s PAT program, created in the 1970s, gave tax breaks for companies offering meal benefits. For decades, only a few accredited companies could issue these vouchers.

Changes in 2021-22 allowed fintechs to enter the market. This opened the door for new players like Alymente and its rivals.

Rules in force since last year cap merchant fees at 3.6% and require interoperability between issuers. These rules reshape the economics of the market C6 is entering.

the lender’s entry is a direct result of this regulatory shift. It allows a bank to compete in a space once closed to it.

What the lender is and who owns it

the lender is a Brazilian digital bank that started operations in 2019. It offers checking accounts, credit cards, and loans through an app.

JPMorgan Chase holds 46% of the lender, having raised its stake from the 40% it bought in 2021. The bank was founded by a group of former BTG Pactual executives.

C6 has been expanding its corporate services to compete with larger banks. Buying Alymente fits that strategy by adding employee benefits.

The acquisition gives C6 a new product line without building from scratch. It also brings a team that already knows the benefits business.

What the deal does not tell us

Neither company has disclosed a price. The financial terms of the agreement remain confidential.

The companies did not disclose the structure of the consideration. There is no word on earn-outs, stock, or cash breakdowns.

The closing date is uncertain, pending Central Bank approval. Reports suggest two to three months, but that is not a guarantee.

Without a price, it is impossible to judge if C6 overpaid or got a bargain. The real value will show only in future results.

World.title: Argentina Trade Deficit With Brazil Widens on Month in August
World.content:

ARGENTINA · TRADE

Key Facts —What happened: Argentina trade deficit with Brazil widened to US$380 million in August 2026. —How big it is: The deficit is up from US$40 million in June, but down from US$613 million a year earlier. —What it means: The monthly gap has grown since midyear, driven by a rebound in car imports. —The catch: The year-on-year narrowing hides a monthly widening, so the trend is not improving. —Who it hits: Brazilian carmakers gain sales, but Argentine consumers face costly imports. —What comes next: Watch September data to see if the monthly widening continues or reverses.

The August deficit is a sharp widening on the month, even though it is far below last year. Car imports are rebounding from a weak June.

A wider deficit on the month, narrower on the year

Argentina trade deficit with Brazil widened to US$380 million in August. That is up sharply from June, when the gap was just US$40 million.

Compared with a year earlier, the deficit is much smaller. In August 2025 it stood at US$613 million.

The monthly path since June shows the shortfall growing. Abeceb put the first-half deficit at US$993 million, against US$2,947 million a year earlier.

Cars drive the trade between the two neighbors

Cars and auto parts are the biggest item in Argentina’s imports from Brazil. Abeceb counts automotive purchases at US$554 million in August, down from US$730 million a year earlier.

Passenger car imports fell 25.6% to US$267.4 million. Imports of road passenger transport vehicles dropped 41.2%, and parts and accessories fell 25.5%.

Why car imports are rebounding from June

The June deficit was unusually low because car imports collapsed. That month, the automotive complex likely saw a sharp drop in purchases.

August imports of cars and parts rose from that low base. That is why the monthly deficit widened, even though it remains below last year’s level.

Exports rose, but not enough to offset imports

Argentina’s exports to Brazil grew 6.7% in August to US$1.099 billion. A key driver was goods-transport vehicles, mainly mid-size pickups, up 44.3% to US$313.5 million.

But that increase was smaller than the rise in imports. The deficit widened because Argentina bought more from Brazil, not because exports fell.

What the numbers mean for the wider trade picture

A deficit that widens because imports recover is not necessarily bad. It can signal stronger domestic demand, which is healthy for the economy.

But the August figure is still far below the record deficit of 2025. That year, the bilateral gap exceeded US$5 billion, an eight-year high.

The role of government policy

Argentina has been opening up to imports, not closing down. More than 90% of imported new cars pay no tariff in 2026, according to industry sources.

Currency controls still apply to companies, though most were lifted for individuals in 2025. They are no longer the main brake on car imports.

The real driver now is domestic demand. When the economy slows, car imports fall; when it recovers, they rise.

How the bilateral trade relationship works

Brazil is Argentina’s biggest trading partner. Argentina is Brazil’s biggest partner inside South America.

They share a long border and a history of economic integration through Mercosur, the Southern Common Market. Its full members are Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay and Bolivia, which joined in 2024.

Venezuela is suspended. Mercosur removes tariffs on most goods traded between members, so cars and auto parts flow easily across the border.

Brazil is usually the stronger exporter in this pair. Its larger industrial base produces more vehicles than Argentina can absorb.

Who is affected by the swings in car trade

Brazilian carmakers feel the swings first. They gain sales when Argentina buys more vehicles, and lose when it buys fewer.

Argentine consumers face higher prices when imports are restricted. Dealerships may offer less variety when imports shrink.

Workers in both countries are indirectly affected. Auto plants and parts suppliers employ thousands of people across the region.

Brazil exports more vehicles to Argentina than it imports from it. That makes Brazil’s auto sector more sensitive to Argentine demand.

What the numbers do and do not prove

The August figures show a rebound in car imports from a weak June. They do not prove that Argentina’s trade position is deteriorating in a lasting way.

One month of data is not a trend. The deficit could narrow again if demand slows or if export growth accelerates.

The numbers also do not capture the full picture of competitiveness. A wider deficit driven by stronger imports can be a sign of economic recovery.

Economists would need several months of data to see a real shift. For now, the August result is a snapshot, not a turning point.

What to watch next

Watch Brazil’s official trade data for September. It should clarify whether the monthly widening continues or reverses.

Also watch Argentine car sales figures. If they keep rising, imports from Brazil will likely stay high, and the deficit may widen further.

A healthier path would be for Argentine exports to grow faster. That would require better competitiveness and more investment, which take time.

Why the automotive sector matters so much

The automotive industry is a pillar of both economies. It employs hundreds of thousands of workers directly and indirectly, according to industry groups.

Cars are also a major source of export revenue for Brazil. Argentina is a leading buyer of its vehicles.

Brazilian car factories feel Argentine downturns quickly. That is why analysts watch this trade flow closely.

The sector is also politically sensitive. Governments on both sides protect local production with tariffs and quotas.

How Mercosur shapes the trade

Mercosur was created in 1991 to boost regional trade. The bloc removes tariffs on most goods traded between members.

That makes cars cheaper to import from Brazil than from elsewhere. But Mercosur has limits, and non-tariff barriers still exist.

The automotive trade is managed by special agreements within the bloc. These set rules on how many cars can cross the border.

The human side of the trade swings

Behind the numbers are real jobs and families. In Brazil, auto plants in cities like São Paulo depend on exports.

In Argentina, dealerships and repair shops feel the impact of changing car flows. They sell more vehicles and parts when imports rise.

Small businesses that supply parts to the auto industry are also affected. They gain orders when production picks up.

The full social cost is hard to measure. But it goes beyond the factory floor to the wider community.

How Argentina’s economy affects the trade

Argentina has struggled with high inflation for years. That erodes purchasing power and makes big purchases like cars less affordable.

The government has tried to control inflation with high interest rates. That makes car loans expensive, so fewer people buy.

These factors combine to reduce car sales and imports. The trade deficit with Brazil is one symptom of a deeper economic problem.

What could change the trend

A recovery in Argentine consumer confidence could boost car demand. That would likely increase imports from Brazil again.

Alternatively, Argentina could boost its own auto production. That would reduce the need for imports.

New trade deals or investment could also shift the balance. But those take years to materialize.

Expect the deficit to keep moving with Argentine demand. The most likely scenario is continued volatility.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Argentina’s trade deficit with Brazil widen in August? The deficit widened because Argentina imported more cars and auto parts from Brazil than in June. Imports rose from a low base, while exports grew only modestly. Is a wider trade deficit always bad for Argentina? No. A deficit that widens because imports recover can signal stronger domestic demand. It is a problem only if it reflects a loss of competitiveness. How important are cars in Argentina-Brazil trade? Cars and auto parts are the largest category in Argentina’s imports from Brazil. In August, they accounted for US$554 million of the US$1.479 billion in total imports. What does this mean for Brazilian carmakers? Brazilian carmakers gain sales when Argentina buys more vehicles. Argentina is a key export market for Brazil’s auto industry, so stronger demand there helps Brazilian factories. Are the August figures official? The US$380 million figure comes from Argentine media and the consultancy Abeceb. Brazil’s trade ministry has not yet published a country-specific breakdown for August, but it typically does so in the following weeks.

World.content:

BRAZIL · BUSINESS

Key Facts —What happened: CSN named Fabio Schvartsman as its new CEO on September 3, 2026. —How big it is: CSN is one of Brazil’s largest steelmakers, with mining and cement operations. —What it means: Benjamin Steinbruch steps back after 24 years as CEO, returning to board chair. —The catch: Police allege officials may have interfered in procedures involving CSN. —Who it hits: Investors and partners in CSN, plus Rio state environmental agencies. —What comes next: Schvartsman takes over with the company named in a police file in which it is not accused of wrongdoing.

The Steinbruch family hands day-to-day control to an outsider. A separate police inquiry alleges officials may have interfered in procedures involving the company; CSN declined to comment and those named deny wrongdoing.

A new leader at CSN

Brazilian steelmaker CSN has a new chief executive. Fabio Schvartsman took over the role on Thursday, September 3, 2026.

He replaces Benjamin Steinbruch, who led the company for 24 years. Steinbruch goes back to chairing the board, a post he held from 1995 to 2023.

Who is Fabio Schvartsman?

Schvartsman is a seasoned executive. He ran Vale from 2017 to 2019, stepping aside weeks after the Brumadinho dam collapse of January 2019.

The company is controlled by the Steinbruch family. Schvartsman is the first chief executive from outside it in decades.

The police investigation

Separately, Brazil’s Federal Police are investigating alleged irregularities in Rio de Janeiro’s environmental licensing. The probe is called Operação Sem Refino.

Part of the case file was released by Supreme Court justice Alexandre de Moraes. G1 reported on September 4 on the police findings.

The police found cument says investigators found messages indicating that state officials may have interfered in procedures involving CSN’s interests.

These are allegations, not proven facts.

What the police say about CSN

The police report says investigators found messages between then state environment secretary Bernardo Rossi and then Inea president Renato Bussière. Inea is the state environmental institute.

According to police, the two allegedly acted on issues related to CSN’s environmental liabilities. They also monitored administrative procedures involving CSN at Inea.

Both deny wrongdoing. Bussière says Inea never issued an operating licence to CSN.

Neither man has been charged in this strand.

CSN declines to comment

CSN declined to comment on the investigation’s conclusions. The company was approached but did not respond to the specific police findings.

No prosecutor has charged CSN, and no court has ruled against it. The police report describes suspected favorable treatment by state officials, not wrongdoing by CSN itself.

The broader investigation

Operação Sem Refino focuses on suspected fraud in environmental licenses for the Refit refinery in Rio. The refinery was formerly known as Refinaria de Manguinhos.

Police also allege money laundering and tax evasion linked to Refit and the fuel sector. The investigation has at least two phases, with the second launched on August 14, 2026.

Allegations against state officials

Police say the evidence points to what they call a criminal organization inside Rio’s environmental agencies. They allege it worked against technical advice to serve private interests.

None of this has been tested in court. Police quote a message they attribute to Rossi, telling Bussière to ‘atropela o Ibama’, or override Ibama.

Rossi denies pressuring Inea and says his conduct was administrative. Bussière denies any irregularity and says Inea never issued an operating licence to CSN.

What this means for CSN

The leadership change comes at a turbulent time for CSN. The police document names the company among those whose administrative procedures allegedly drew political interference.

Police have not named CSN as a target of the investigation. Investors will watch how Schvartsman handles the situation.

Asked about Brumadinho, Steinbruch told NeoFeed that Schvartsman ‘will now show that this was not his doing’. He said the market’s view of him is very good.

The road ahead

Schvartsman takes over while the company is named in a police file in which it is not itself accused of wrongdoing. The allegations are serious but unproven.

CSN’s board, now led by Steinbruch, will support the new CEO. The family remains in control, but the day-to-day leadership has changed.

Background on CSN

CSN, or Companhia Siderúrgica Nacional, is a major Brazilian steelmaker. It also operates in mining, cement, and logistics.

The company was founded in 1941 and is based in São Paulo. It has been controlled by the Steinbruch family for decades.

How the environmental licensing works

In Brazil, environmental licensing is shared between federal and state agencies. Ibama handles federal licenses, while state institutes like Inea manage state ones.

Companies need licenses to operate and expand. These licenses require technical studies and public consultation.

Who is affected by the allegations

The allegations could affect CSN’s reputation and stock price. Investors may worry about legal risks.

They also affect public trust in Rio’s environmental agencies. The police probe suggests possible corruption in the state’s oversight.

What the numbers do and do not prove

The police report includes messages and other evidence. But it does not prove that CSN acted illegally.

It only suggests that state officials may have favored the company. CSN has not been charged with any crime.

What happens next

The investigation will continue, and more phases may follow. CSN might issue a statement in the coming days.

Schvartsman will need to address the allegations with investors. His leadership will be tested early.

Understanding the Refit refinery case

The Refit refinery is central to the police investigation. It was formerly known as Refinaria de Manguinhos.

Police suspect fraud in how its environmental licenses were granted. They also allege tax evasion linked to the fuel sector.

The role of Rio’s state government

Police say former governor Cláudio Castro helped create a favorable environment for Refit. Castro’s defence says the contacts were purely institutional and brought no improper benefit.

He has not been charged. The investigation involves several state agencies, including the finance and environment secretariats, plus Inea.

What investors should watch

Investors will track any official statements from CSN. They will also watch for new phases of the police operation.

The company’s stock price may react to news. Legal risks could affect its valuation.

The challenge for Schvartsman

Schvartsman must balance daily operations with the ongoing probe. He has experience leading a major mining company.

His track record at Vale may reassure investors. But the allegations could still create uncertainty.

What is confirmed and what is not

Schvartsman became chief executive on 3 September 2026. Steinbruch moved to the board chair.

CSN declined to comment on the investigation’s conclusions. No prosecutor has charged CSN and no court has ruled against it.

The significance of the Steinbruch era

Benjamin Steinbruch led CSN for 24 years. During that time, the company grew into a diversified industrial group.

His departure from the CEO role marks the end of an era. The family still holds control through the board.

How CSN’s leadership change affects its operations

A new CEO can bring fresh strategy and management style. Schvartsman’s experience at Vale may influence CSN’s direction.

The company’s day-to-day operations are unlikely to change overnight. But investors will watch for any shifts in priorities.

The role of Inea in Rio’s environmental oversight

Inea is the state environmental institute responsible for licensing and enforcement. It operates under the state environment secretariat.

The police probe suggests that some Inea officials may have acted improperly. This raises questions about the agency’s independence.

What the police probe means for Rio’s business climate

The investigation could affect how companies view Rio’s regulatory environment. Investors may demand more transparency in licensing.

State officials face scrutiny over their decisions. This could lead to reforms in environmental oversight.

World.title: Panama Now Hosts 192 Multinational Headquarters
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

PANAMA · BUSINESS

Key Facts —What happened: Panama’s commerce ministry says 192 multinationals now hold SEM regional headquarters status. —How big it is: The list, updated to May 2026, was announced on September 2, 2026. —What it means: SEM offers tax breaks and immigration perks to attract corporate regional hubs. —The catch: The ministry did not confirm how many jobs or how much investment these firms bring. —Who it hits: Foreign executives and their families can get residency through the program. —What comes next: A newer EMMA regime extends similar benefits to manufacturing services.

Panama’s SEM scheme now counts 192 multinational headquarters. The ministry says they have created about 10,000 jobs, roughly half filled by Panamanians.

What is the SEM regime?

SEM stands for Sedes de Empresas Multinacionales, which means Multinational Company Headquarters in Spanish. It is a special status that Panama gives to foreign companies that set up a regional office in the country.

The goal is to make Panama the home base for a company’s Latin American operations. In return, the company gets tax breaks and easier immigration rules for its staff.

The program is run by a special unit inside the Ministry of Commerce and Industries, known as MICI. That unit tracks every company that holds the status.

Panama created this regime to attract high-value corporate jobs. It wants to be the place where global firms manage their regional business.

The new numbers

On September 2, 2026, the Ministry of Commerce and Industries (MICI) announced that 192 companies now hold SEM status. The list was updated to May 2026.

Panama closed 2025 with 188 SEM companies, so four have joined since. The ministry did not name them.

The ministry published the news on its own website. A Panama newspaper repeated the same figure the next day.

MICI publishes SEM and EMMA companies on the same list, which runs from 2007 to May 2026.

What SEM offers

Panama created SEM under Law 41 of 2007 and reformed it under Law 57 of 2018. Headquarters pay 5% income tax on what they earn serving group companies abroad.

The regime also brings immigration perks. Executives and their families get faster visas and residency.

These perks make Panama more attractive than other Latin American hubs. Executives can move with less paperwork and keep more of their income.

The benefits are not automatic. Companies must apply and meet specific requirements set by the ministry.

How EMMA fits in

EMMA is a newer regime, created by Law 159 of August 31, 2020. It is aimed at multinationals that provide manufacturing-related services, not just headquarters.

EMMA offers similar terms, including a 5% income tax rate and relief from Panama’s sales tax, the ITBMS, on certain services. It also provides immigration perks like permanent residency.

Tax advisers describe EMMA as a version of SEM built for manufacturing services. It lets companies do more than manage regional offices.

The two programs are tracked together on the ministry’s public list. That list covers both SEM and EMMA firms from 2007 to May 2026.

Jobs and investment

The ministry says these companies provided 8,359 direct jobs in 2024. It puts the running total at about 10,000 jobs by early 2026, roughly half held by Panamanians.

Investment totals are still not published. Jobs are, and about half of them go to Panamanians.

Earlier reports from March 2026 mentioned 13 new licenses in 2025. They projected US$37.3 million in investment.

Infobae reported in January that multinationals were weighing new investments in Panama. That suggests the pipeline of new companies is still active.

Who benefits

The main beneficiaries are foreign executives who get to live and work in Panama with their families. The regime makes it easier to obtain visas and residency.

Panama also benefits from the jobs and spending these companies bring. Local professionals get opportunities to work for global firms without leaving home.

Local service providers also gain. Lawyers, accountants, and real estate agents serve the needs of these multinational teams.

The program aims to create a multiplier effect. Each headquarters can support many local jobs beyond its own staff.

The bigger picture

Panama has long positioned itself as the logistics and business hub of Latin America. The SEM regime is a key part of that strategy.

The country’s dollar-based economy and strategic location help. But the tax and immigration incentives are what seal the deal for many multinationals.

Panama is not the only country courting regional headquarters. But it has the longest-running scheme in Central America.

The SEM regime is one tool in a broader plan. Panama wants to diversify beyond the canal and become a knowledge economy.

What the ministry has not said

The ministry did not confirm which companies were the latest to join the SEM regime. It also did not provide a breakdown by sector.

The MICI portal keeps a public database of SEM and EMMA companies from 2007 to May 2026. That is the best place to check the full list.

The tax terms sit in the law rather than in the announcement. Law 57 of 2018 sets the 5% rate.

Investment totals are still not published. That makes the programme’s full return hard to judge.

What comes next

Panama is likely to keep promoting both SEM and EMMA to attract more multinationals. The government sees these regimes as a way to create professional jobs and diversify the economy.

For foreign companies, the message is clear: Panama wants to be your regional home. The SEM regime is the door, and EMMA widens it.

The ministry may release more details in future announcements. Investors should watch for updates on new licenses and policy changes.

The government has signaled it wants to keep both programs active. That suggests stability for companies already in the system.

Why Panama targets multinationals

Panama’s economy depends heavily on services like banking, logistics, and trade. Multinational headquarters bring high-value jobs that support those sectors.

These companies also create demand for local lawyers, accountants, and other professionals. That helps Panama move beyond its historic reliance on the Panama Canal.

The canal alone cannot sustain the country’s growth. Panama needs new engines of economic activity.

Multinational hubs also bring global connections. They link Panama to corporate networks across the region.

How the SEM regime works in practice

A company applies to MICI for SEM status. Once approved, it can set up a regional office that manages operations across Latin America.

Companies must meet minimum staffing and spending commitments. Those details are not public in the latest announcement.

The application process involves several government agencies. It can take months to complete.

Once approved, the company must renew its status periodically. That keeps the regime accountable.

What the numbers do and do not prove

The jump from 188 to 192 companies shows steady, if slow, growth. But it does not prove that Panama is winning a race against rivals like Costa Rica or Colombia.

The company count on its own says little. The jobs figure is the more useful number, and it points to about 10,000 posts since the scheme began.

The four new companies could be small or large. The count does not reveal their economic weight.

Jobs are the better measure, and the ministry now publishes them. Export and investment totals are still missing.

What foreign investors should watch

Investors should watch for updates from MICI on new SEM and EMMA licenses. They should also look for changes in tax law that affect these regimes.

The government has signaled it wants to keep both programs active. That suggests stability for companies already in the system.

Investors should also monitor the political climate. Changes in government could alter the incentives.

Finally, watch how Panama’s neighbors respond. If they sweeten their own deals, Panama may need to adjust.

How Panama compares with neighbors

Costa Rica and Colombia also offer incentives for regional headquarters. Panama’s edge is its location and dollar-based economy.

But those countries have lower labor costs in some sectors. Panama must compete on more than just tax breaks.

Panama’s canal and banking sector give it unique advantages. No other country in the region has both.

The SEM regime is just one factor in a company’s decision. Infrastructure, security, and quality of life also matter.

The role of the Ministry of Commerce

The Ministry of Commerce and Industries, known as MICI, runs the SEM program. It processes applications and keeps the official list.

MICI also promotes the regime abroad. It works with investment agencies to attract new companies.

The ministry’s announcement on September 2 led on jobs rather than on the company count. It said about half of the posts go to Panamanians.

For more information, companies can contact MICI directly. The ministry’s website has contact details and the public list.

Historical growth of the regime

The SEM regime started in 2007. Since then, it has grown steadily to 192 companies.

The public list covers the full history from 2007 to May 2026. That shows how the program has evolved.

Early years saw slower growth. Recent years have added a few companies each year.

The growth is not explosive, but it is consistent. That consistency may appeal to investors.

Potential risks and limitations

The SEM regime depends on government policy. A change in leadership could alter the benefits.

Global economic downturns could also slow new investments. Multinationals may delay expansion plans.

Panama faces competition from other hubs. If rivals offer better deals, companies may go elsewhere.

Investment totals are still not published. That makes the programme’s full return hard to judge.

It is a special status Panama grants to foreign firms that set up regional offices. How many companies are in the SEM regime? As of May 2026, 192 companies hold SEM status. The Ministry of Commerce and Industries announced this on September 2, 2026. What benefits does SEM offer? SEM offers a 5% income tax rate on qualifying income, plus easier visas and residency for executives. The exact details are set in the law. What is the EMMA regime? EMMA is a newer regime for multinationals providing manufacturing-related services. Created by Law 159 in 2020, it offers similar benefits to SEM, including a 5% income tax rate and residency options. Where can I find the list of SEM companies? The Ministry of Commerce and Industries (MICI) publishes a public list on its website. It covers SEM and EMMA companies from 2007 to May 2026.
