World.title: The lonely crusader against Gianni Infantino
World.content:
That being said, it’s impossible now to bring back the Russian teams. Because of the way they are used, the national teams, it’s so hard to separate from the propaganda. But that is a failure, I’m not happy to say that it’s impossible; it’s sadly so, even though we are in 100 percent solidarity with Ukraine. It’s never good to make kids never play with each other. That is the aim, that they could play with each other and not be affected by the war. But that’s not possible now, football would stop and Ukraine would not play. So then we are there, and that’s a sad situation, but happening because of war.

When it comes to the Israel situation, we have always said, and we will always say, when you have a breach of FIFA statutes, it needs to be treated. It was delayed, delayed, delayed for many years, that they play with teams from [settlements in] Palestinian territories, which is not allowed by FIFA statutes. And then it’s politically very difficult, but legally not so difficult. So then you need sanctions, and then what the sanctions should be. You’ve got to look at precedents. Do you have any similar cases where you play in other people’s territories? What about Crimea? What about former Yugoslavia? Maybe you have some precedent. What’s the sanction? If it’s not changed, you increase the sanctions, because you need a rules-based system. And you need territory lines.

Klaveness at a press conference in Oslo on August 7, 2026. | Terje Bendiksby/NTB via Getty Images

When we played Israel, we gave the money to the victims of Gaza, not because we did not want to give to the victims of October 7th, but because there were ongoing attacks on the kids in Gaza, and they were poor, they needed the money.

In the end, it’s all about having bridges that are actually working when this is over, when people come to terms, you need to be effective bridges that speak to both sides. For us, we have had projects in Palestine for very many years, decades, educating girls and women there to be coaches; also in Jordan, in this area. So it’s an area [where] we know how difficult it is, how many good people live there on both sides. You know, in Israel, Jordan, everywhere. So we feel very connected to the region because of these projects.

Daria Zakharova contributed to this report.

World.title: Why Macron’s space summit risks blowing up on the launchpad
World.content:
Six participants with first-hand knowledge of the summit's organization described it to POLITICO as a poorly coordinated event with an unclear outcome. They were granted anonymity to discuss sensitive matters.

“It’s falling behind schedule, it hasn’t really been coordinated with the major players in the European space sector, and it’s not entirely clear what its purpose is,” said a senior space expert involved in the summit’s preparation.

“And now that the White House has effectively decided to use it against Emmanuel Macron, it’s becoming even more awkward — it shows that, from a diplomatic standpoint, they didn’t do what they should have done,” they added.

Next week’s event aims to gather the international community — including leaders, large corporations, startups and researchers — to discuss issues including the regulation of space activities, competitiveness, security and defense, and space exploration.

Macron is keen to ensure that France and Europe remain credible space powers, with an independent launch capability and their own global satellite communications system, in an effort to reduce dependence on U.S. technology.

The French president's office insisted Friday that the absence of SpaceX and Blue Origin — two of the world's leading space companies — will have little impact on the summit.

World.title: Witkoff and Kushner set to visit Moscow then Kyiv on Sunday
World.content:
Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff listen as Vice President JD Vance speaks during a news conference. | Pool photo by Jacquelyn Martin/Getty Images

The men have been key U.S. mediators in the stalled Ukraine peace talks.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s special envoys Steven Witkoff and Jared Kushner will visit Moscow and Kyiv in the coming days in an apparent attempt to restart stalled negotiations to end the Ukraine war, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Telegram.

“We discussed today that Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will visit Moscow and then Kyiv on Sunday,” the Ukrainian president wrote.

No details about the substance of the meetings have been released, but a U.S. official told CNN Friday that Witkoff and Kushner intend to press for a diplomatic solution to end the conflict.

World.title: US peace envoys set for Kyiv visit after talks with Putin
World.content:
US peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are due to meet with Ukrainian officials in Kyiv on Sunday following talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

 

The pair met the Russian leader in Moscow on Saturday as they discussed a plan to end the war in Ukraine, which began in February 2022 following Russia's full-scale invasion of the country.

A White House official told the AFP news agency that the duo had met with Putin to "advance President Trump's agenda of peace in the Russia-Ukraine War."

"The two sides discussed substantive plans for next steps, which will be announced in the coming weeks, and look forward to equally productive meetings tomorrow in Ukraine," they said.

Yuri Ushakov, a Kremlin aide, called the talks "extremely frank" and said that the US side had "put forward a number of ideas on possible routes to a settlement."

He added that the Russians had told the Americans that Moscow was "confident" it could seize the rest of eastern Ukraine.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he had also spoken with Witkoff and Kushner on Saturday and reaffirmed Kyiv's commitment to pausing strikes during their visit.

"From the moment of this conversation, we are ready to observe a ceasefire in airstrikes against the cities involved in the negotiation process," he wrote in a post on social media. "From now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow, and we expect the Russians to do the same regarding Kyiv".

Putin has ordered his forces to halt strikes on Kyiv for three days while the envoys make their trip, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told the Russian news agency Interfax. The pause was in place from midnight Saturday, he said.

US President Donald Trump told reporters on Friday that Witkoff and Kushner would be bringing a "proposal to end the war" to Kyiv and Moscow.

"I sent Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, two great negotiators. They've done a great job, and we sent them over to see whether or not we can get something done," he said. "And there may be a good chance that we'll do it".

Zelenskyy said on Saturday that the Ukrainian plan for discussions with the envoys had been approved and that Kyiv was ready for a "substantive conversation."

World.title: Exhibition celebrates legacy of 80-year-old Hungarian painter Sándor Pinczehelyi in Pécs
World.content:
A retrospective exhibition of the oeuvre of 80-year-old Sándor Pinczehelyi has opened at the M21 Gallery in the Zsolnay Cultural Quarter in Pécs. Long before the Iron Curtain came down, the artist was already combining Soviet totalitarian insignia with the symbols of Western affluence.

 

The exhibition features 150 works by the Munkácsy Prize-winning artist, who has been named Artist of Merit and Artist of Excellence, offering a comprehensive selection spanning six decades of his career.

"In European art circles I am known as someone who, in the earlier socialist period, worked with symbols such as the hammer and sickle, the paving stone and the star. One such piece is my iconic work with the hammer and sickle you can see here. There is virtually no art book dealing with that period in which this work is not reproduced."

Divided into nine thematic sections, the genre-spanning exhibition guides visitors from his earliest works to the present day through photographs, paintings, spatial sculptures, prints and enamel pieces. Alongside well-known works, visitors can also see pieces that have never been published before. The exhibition also presents works that were shown at the exhibitions in Turin and Berlin.

World.title: Shein’s stock market debut was a major flop. Does it signal the death of ultra-fast fashion?
World.content:
Shein’s ultra-fast fashion empire has taken a dramatic fall following its post-IPO valuation collapse.

 

The e-commerce platform, which is headquartered in Singapore but outsources much of its manufacturing to China, failed to go public in London and New York following concerns around its supply chain and heavy criticism of its environmental impact.

Shein therefore pivoted to the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, where it was valued at around $27 billion (approximately €23.24 billion) on 1 September. It may seem like a huge financial win, but it’s 70 per cent lower than its private market peak of almost $100 billion (€86 billion) back in 2022.

Why was Shein’s IPO such a flop?

“Capital markets aren’t acting out of pure altruism: they’re reacting to material financial risk,” sustainability expert and founder of tech company E&S Solutions Ildiko Almasi Simsic tells Euronews Earth.

“Shein’s delayed public listings and severely discounted valuation prove that investors now recognise ESG issues as direct threats to terminal value.”

Simsic argues that a business model that has been exposed to multiple controversies, such as forced labour and hazardous chemicals in clothing, carries an “enormous risk profile”.

She says environmental and human rights issues have now crossed over from “ethics to equity”, signalling a watershed moment for the fast-fashion industry.

But what makes Shein so controversial in the first place, and can its super cheap garments and on-trend styles ever become sustainable?

Shein’s controversial supply chains

“For years, ultra-fast fashion grew by leveraging hyper-fragmented, outsourced supply chains that kept prices absurdly low while keeping liabilities at arm’s length,” Simsic tells Euronews Earth.

“But that model created a massive structural vulnerability. When your business relies on thousands of sub-contractors operating in grey regulatory zones, supply chain oversight isn’t just an operational headache – it becomes a central business risk.”

Shein’s supply chain has been shrouded in controversy since its conception. In 2022, an investigation by environmental NGO Greenpeace Germany found hazardous chemicals above the EU regulatory limits in seven of 47 Shein products tested.

At the time, Shein acknowledged the chemical contamination and pledged “substantial improvements” to its chemical management.

However, a 2025 investigation found that little had changed. Greenpeace purchased 56 garments from Shein across eight countries and analysed them for hazardous chemicals. They found that 18 of 56 (32 per cent) of the garments exceeded the EU limits, including children’s clothing.

Among other chemicals, the plasticizers phthalates and water- and dirt-repellent “forever chemicals” (PFAS) were detected. These are hazardous chemicals that have been linked to various health concerns, including cancer, reproductive disorders, growth disorders in children, and immunodeficiency disorders.

Workers in producing countries are often exposed without protection, while chemicals are discharged untreated into waterways and soils, Greenpeace Global campaigning network

“Consumers are also at risk as they can be exposed to these chemicals through several ways – directly through the skin, by inhaling textile fibres in the air and, in the case of small children, through mouthing contaminated clothes.”

In 2023, Shein admitted to finding two cases of child labour in its supply chain during the first nine months of the year.

The firm introduced new rules so that any child labour or forced labour violations have become grounds for immediate termination of contracts.

“Both cases were resolved swiftly, with remediation steps including terminating contracts with underage employees, ensuring the payment of any outstanding wages, arranging medical checkups and facilitating repatriation to parents/ legal guardians as needed,” Shein said at the time.

“Following appropriate remediation, the contract manufacturers were permitted to resume business.”

Despite Shein’s clampdown on labour violations, concerns of poor working conditions remain rife. A 2025 investigation by the BBC found that workers were sitting behind sewing machines for around 75 hours a week in contravention of Chinese labour laws.

Many employers told the publication that they only have one day off each month and have to endure 12-hour shifts, which didn’t include breaks for lunch and dinner, often working until past 10pm.

A 2024 report by Swiss advocacy group Public Eye also found that excessive overtime was still common for many workers – despite Shein promising to improve conditions following previous probes.

Can Shein ever be sustainable?

As Shein geared up for going public, scrutiny on its fast-fashion model grew stronger.

The company’s draft prospectus included the slogan “We believe in doing well by doing good”. However, according to Public Eye, this was removed from the final document.

Shein insists that “commitment to sustainable and responsible growth is woven into the fabric” of its business model. However, the expected IPO proceeds allocate just 10 per cent to sustainability and corporate responsibility.

An investigation by global nonprofit Rest of World found that between July and December of 2021, Shein added anywhere between 2,000 and 10,000 SKUs (stock keeping units, or individual styles) to its app each day.

This is because Shein orders small batches of each garment, sometimes as low as a few dozen pieces, then waits to see how consumers respond. If a particular item seems to be selling well, Shein orders more.

“A model that floods the market with thousands of new daily styles at single-digit price points can only exist by passing its true costs onto labour and the environment,” Simsic says.

“Cheap prices are an illusion created by systemic outsourcing. When garments are produced at a fraction of a cent per stitch, it almost guarantees non-compliance with fair wages, excessive overtime, and cheap, fossil-fuel-derived synthetic fabrics.”

The expert acknowledges that while efficiency and tech-driven demand forecasting can reduce excess inventory, it cannot bypass the “physical limits of planetary resources or basic human rights”.

“Ultra-low cost and sustainability are fundamentally incompatible concepts,” she adds. “One inherently undermines the other.”

Can fast fashion survive the scrutiny?

Shein’s scrutiny has gone far beyond complaints from environmentalists and individuals. Earlier this week, France passed a law targeting companies known for selling large volumes of low-quality clothing at rock-bottom prices.

“The harmful effects of ultra-fast fashion on our environment and our economy are well known and documented,” says Mathieu Lefevre, the minister for ecological transition.

Under the bill, firms like Shein are assessed under two criteria: the volume of clothing placed on the market and the cost of repairing garments relative to their purchase price.

The per-item fee will vary on a set scale according to how each product scores on both of these standards.This year, companies will pay fines such as a 50-cent levy on underwear falling into the ultra-fast fashion category, rising to €2 for T-shirts, €9 for jeans and €12 for a jacket.

The levy could reach up to €19.50 per item by 2030, though the cap remains at 50 per cent of the product’s pre-tax price.

Beijing has bitten back, urging France to abandon the law and describing it as “clearly discriminatory” due to Shein – and sites like Temu – being located in Asia.

“Should France persist in this course of action, China will take necessary measures to safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises,” says commerce ministry spokeswoman Huang Ling. “France will bear full responsibility for all consequences arising from this.”

Simsic argues that while fast-fashion giants will still be able to survive new laws like this, it’s likely they won’t reach their historical growth model.

We’re witnessing a decisive shift from voluntary corporate sustainability to hard, enforceable law. Ildiko Almasi Simsic Sustainability expert

“Historically, labour issues or toxic chemical findings were managed by public relations or board-level sustainability committees. Today, with legislation like the EU’s Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive and Extended Producer Responsibility, these are strict legal compliance matters carrying fines of up to five per cent of global turnover.”

Simsic adds that if non-compliance directly threatens a company’s bottom line through hefty regulatory penalties and import bans, growth will inevitably slow. It means sites like Shein will have no choice but to internalise these costs, by investing heavily in supply chain traceability and safer materials.

Euronews Earth has contacted Shein for comment.

World.title: The Euronews Travel autumn bucket list: Our top picks for holidays in Europe
World.content:
Forget mourning the end of summer. Autumn might just be one of the best times of year to travel in Europe – bringing fewer crowds, lower prices and destinations at their most atmospheric.

 

From crisp countryside walks and fiery autumn colours to cosy cafés and seasonal celebrations, these are the trips on the Euronews Travel team’s bucket list for the “-ber” months.

Saskia O’Donoghue: Why I choose Bavaria (and Malta)

If I’m honest, autumn is my absolute least favourite time of the year, with trees slowly dying and the nights drawing in. I think my hatred of the season is down to how miserable it is in England, where I call home. More recently, I’ve been trying to embrace autumn in other places which do it properly.

Last year, I visited Czechia and Nova Scotia in Canada, both of which manage to make the fall very enjoyable. This year, I’m planning to head to Bavaria when the summer crowds have thinned, and the landscape turns shades of gold, orange and deep red.

Despite my reservations about autumn, I’d happily spend my days wandering around Munich, hopping between cosy beer halls and markets, before heading south towards the mountains and, of course, the castles.

Neuschwanstein might be a little obvious as a must-see, but I’m not sure I’d ever get bored of seeing something that looks quite so spectacular surrounded by autumn colours.

Long walks followed by hearty Bavarian food, a local beverage and somewhere suitably cosy to warm up by an open fire? That sounds pretty close to the ideal autumn holiday – and it might just convert me into an autumn lover.

If I still despise it, I’ll head back to Malta, where I have happy memories of sunbathing in November and the sun setting at a non-depressing hour!

Sigulda is known as Latvia's autumn capital Artis Butkevics/Unsplash

Dianne Apen-Sadler: Why I choose Latvia

As a travel journalist, I’m constantly being asked to share recommendations for my top spots in Europe, and nine times out of 10, I’m going to talk about either somewhere in the Balkans (think more Belgrade and Skopje than Budva and Split), or the Baltics.

With its picturesque – and UNESCO-listed – city centre, brilliant museums, and superb craft breweries, Latvia’s capital Riga has all the hallmarks of a great weekend break, and one that can be enjoyed equally in the peaks of summer or the depths of winter (or, for the purposes of this article, in autumn).

But the place I’m most excited about visiting during leaf-peeping season is Sigulda, Latvia’s "autumn capital", which lies around 45 minutes outside of Riga by train.

Come October, the banks of the Gauja River are transformed into shades of orange – which also just happens to be my favourite colour! – and the Sigulda Cable Car and Turaida Castle offer the best vantage points.

Who needs New England when we have spots like this right here in Europe?

Scotland is famous for its beauty in autumn – and for good reason B K/Unsplash

Mike Starling: Why I choose Scotland

I don’t want to come across like I’m a stay-at-home Brit, but as someone who’s been based outside of the UK for many a year now, it’s always nice to go back to the motherland. However, even though I am English, I would say forget London, the Cotswolds and the Lake District and head “north of the border”.

Scotland is lovely at any time of the year, but in autumn it’s perfect – especially if you’re heading outdoors. Of course there may be the odd rain shower (or five), but the autumnal colours of the trees, glens and lochs make any hike, walk or outdoor adventure truly worth it. Then there’s the golf… truly spectacular.

Also, once you’ve finished 18 holes or “bagged a Munro” – reaching the summit of a Scottish mountain that is at least 3,000 feet (914.4 metres) high – you can then enjoy the country’s warm hospitality. Literally. Think log-burning fires in pubs, hearty food and a dram of whisky. What’s not to like?

Monte Carlo, Monaco Lazar Gugleta/Unsplash

Fakhriya M. Suleiman: Why I choose Monaco

Monaco’s luxury appeal has always been attractive to me. But as a principality on the French Riviera that only spans two square kilometres, the summer crowds? Less so. However, shoulder season travel to an autumnal Monaco? Now, that I wouldn’t turn down.

I’ve heard so much about exploring the city-state leisurely on foot. I picture myself taking in the futuristic architecture of Mareterra or the vibrant colours in Fontvieille's Princess Grace Rose Garden.

While I’m always game for new experiences (such as visiting Monaco for the first time…) admittedly, and paradoxically, I’m also a creature of comfort. I know I’d feel right at home travelling from Doha’s shopping paradise to Monte Carlo’s. My walking adventure will continue to the shopping promenade, where I’d work up an appetite before sampling Monte Carlo’s gastronomy scene.

The two-Michelin-starred Blue Bay by Chef Marcel Ravin offers guests an experience between Caribbean and Mediterranean cuisine, alongside a sea view. All that’s missing is a plane ticket.

Rome in autumn Nicolò Salinetti/Unsplash

Maya Abu Hajleh: Why I choose Italy

Italy is somewhere I’ve wanted to visit. I love the idea of walking around the streets, trying different food, sitting in little cafés and not really having to rush anywhere.

I’ve always liked the thought of living somewhere small and cosy, where you know the people around you and everything feels a bit slower. Maybe I’d find it boring after a while, but I actually want to experience it myself before deciding that.

As someone who’s lived most of their life in the Gulf, I’m used to hot weather and seeing a lot of desert and dry surroundings. That’s why I’d love to experience something completely different, like Italy in the autumn, with all the trees changing colour, the mountains, the lakes, and little towns.

I think one of my favourite things would honestly be walking through Italy’s beautiful streets and stepping on all those dry, coloured leaves after they’ve fallen. I think I’d really enjoy that slower kind of life, even if it’s just for a little while.

The New Forest in the south of England, known for its wild ponies, is particularly beautiful in the autumn Richard Loader/Unsplash

Rebecca Ann Hughes: Why I choose England

It’s been an intense summer in northern Italy, where I live. We’ve been more in heatwaves than out of them; long stretches of +35C degrees and 95% humidity. So I’ve found myself unexpectedly longing for what I’d normally consider a very mundane holiday idea – walking in the British countryside.

Europe has no shortage of spectacular hikes and natural parks, but I want that unmistakable environment of Britain’s forests: mizzling rain, the peaty, damp smell of fallen leaves underfoot, glimpses of scrabbling squirrels, and the warm country pub.

I’m lucky to have family living in two great spots of the English countryside (given I’m from Scotland, I’m heading in the opposite direction to editor Mike for a change of scenery!). My aunt lives in the Lake District, the ideal terrain for lung-busting hikes up mountain peaks or meanders around lakeside paths.

My uncle lives down south in the New Forest, where I’m envisaging delving into dark woods or striding across open heathlands – and making friends with the wild ponies that roam freely.

World.title: Two pilots killed in Phantom  F-4 jet crash during Greek air force annual show
World.content:
A twin seat Phantom F-4 jet crashed at Tanagra air base during an air show held as part of Athens Flying Week 2026, killing the two pilots, according to officials.

 

The crash occurred during a display, in front of thousands of people, the circumstances of the crash remain unclear.

According to information from ERT, the aircraft suddenly began to lose altitude and plunged to the ground. An explosion followed immediately after the impact.

Athens Flying Week, taking place this year on 5 and 6 September, is one of the largest air shows in south-eastern Europe.

The programme features formation flying, high-difficulty manoeuvres and parachute jumps.

In the wake of the crash, Defence Minister N. Dendias is cutting short his schedule at the Thessaloniki International Fair and is returning to Athens. Organisers have also cancelled remaining events planed over the week end.

Wildfire in forested area

The crash of the fighter jet sparked a fire at Tanagra, which spread to the surrounding forested area.

Some 115 firefighters and 36 vehicles are operating at the scene with three ground teams. Meanwhile, nine aircraft and four helicopters are being deployed periodically, one of them coordinating the operation.

Firefighting aircraft and vehicle operate at the crash site of the Hellenic Air Force F-4 Phantom fighter jet ΑΠΕ ΜΠΕ

During Saturday afternoon, an alert was sent via the 112 emergency number to inform people in the wider area of the fire.

Later on Saturday afternoon, the situation of the fire had improved.

At the same time, because of the fire, police closed the service road of the Athens–Lamia national motorway and the Oinoi provincial road at Oinoi.

World.title: Paris drops Mercator projection: France now looks smaller on world maps
World.content:
A shrunken Africa, a Greenland and a northern Russia that seem to stretch into infinity: that is about to disappear from the maps used by French diplomacy.

 

Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot announced on Friday that his department is abandoning the so-called Mercator projection, which artificially enlarges polar regions and visually downplays the size of equatorial areas. France will now use instead the Eckert IV projection, which reflects the true proportions of the continents more accurately.

As a result, France will appear smaller on the map compared with countries close to the equator, just like the United States or Russia.

'A map is never entirely neutral'

In a speech at the Sorbonne university during the public event "La Fabrique de la diplomatie" or "The making of diplomacy", the French minister said that "the time has come" to "correct" how the world is perceived through maps inherited from 16th-century Western navigators.

In a speech delivered at the Sorbonne for the public event "La Fabrique de la diplomatie", the French minister said that "the time has come" to "correct" how the world is perceived through maps inherited from 16th-century Western navigators.

"A map is never entirely neutral. Take the Mercator projection, the one every one of us has known since childhood. The areas we see on it do not correspond to actual areas: (...) The United States, Russia, China take on a disproportionate visual importance compared with Africa, Latin America or South-East Asia," the French foreign minister said.

Jean-Noël Barrot also cited the example of Greenland, which is roughly the same size as the Democratic Republic of Congo or Algeria, even though it "seems almost as vast" as the entire African continent.

"Changing the map obviously does not change the world. But correcting a representation that distorts it is already an act of truth," he stressed.

The ministry began reducing its use of the Mercator projection in 2021

Meanwhile, French diplomatic maps will not change overnight but the process is already underway, Euronews has learned from a diplomatic source. The ministry began reducing its use of the Mercator projection in 2021, "with the aim of providing a more accurate geographical representation of the world."

The projection has been "gradually phased out" across all public diplomacy websites, the source said.

"The advantages and biases associated with each type of representation are presented at various events attended by the ministry's cartographers," the Quai d'Orsay added, citing the European Heritage Days and the International Geography Festival in Saint-Dié-des-Vosges.

"France will continue this work, prioritising map projections suited to different purposes and providing a more accurate reflection of geographical realities in its diplomatic communications."

French diplomats nevertheless acknowledge that the Mercator projection remains relevant "in a limited number of cases", including regional or local uses around the equatorial zone, as well as for navigation charts.

At the UN, a cartographic victory for Africa

The announcement in Paris comes as, in New York, the world map is also being redrawn. A few hours later, the United Nations General Assembly officially abandoned the Mercator projection in favour of a projection based on the Equal Earth model, created in 2018 and closer to the real proportions of the continents.

The non-binding resolution, entitled "Correcting the map"and sponsored by Togo, was backed by 164 member states. The African Union had already adopted Equal Earth in March, and the text now encourages countries to do the same.

Only the United States voted against, denouncing what it called a "radical ideological project", notably because of a passage in the resolution stating that "correcting cartographic distortions relating to the size of continents constitutes an act of cognitive justice and memorial reparation".

Six countries – Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova, Serbia and Ukraine – abstained.

The United Nations General Assembly adopts an African proposal for a new world map In favor: 164 Against: 1 Abstentions: 6

The UN stresses that the resolution does not ban the Mercator projection, "nor does it impose a single map". The resolution "encourages governments, educational institutions, international organisations and technology companies to make use of the Equal Earth projection, or of other so-called 'equal-area' maps that preserve the true proportions of surface areas.

France has therefore joined this movement, but has opted to adopt the Eckert IV projection, created in 1906. It is similar to the Equal Earth projection recommended by the UN, though not identical. Both represent the size of the continents much more faithfully than the Mercator projection, but they differ slightly in the shapes they give to the landmasses.

As the UN points out, Mercator mapping will not disappear altogether. Digital platforms such as Google Maps also currently use a version of this projection.

In French schools, most world maps are still in Mercator. "You can find Eckert or Peters* in some textbooks, but that is very rare," says Grégory, a senior history and geography teacher in Rennes, speaking to Euronews.

It remains to be seen whether the maps used in schools will also follow the shift launched by the foreign ministry.

*another equal-area projection, which provides a better representation of the continents' true surface area – Euronews.

World.title: US drafting post-war plan for the Middle East, report says
World.content:
The Trump administration has begun working on a post-war strategy for the Middle East, aimed and reshaping the balance of power in the region by tightening pressure on Tehran and expanding normalisation between Israel and neighbouring countries, Axios reported, citing two US officials and two other sources familiar with the matter.

 

The US outlet said that the plan remains in its early stages but that it could set out US policy towards the Middle East for the remainder of US President Donald Trump's time in the White House.

The unnamed sources told Axios that three key pillars had been discussed as part of the plan - building "regional alignment" among US allies to deter and constrain Iran, working to wind down the regional consequences of the 7 October 2023 attacks on Israel, and broadening the Abraham Accords while pursuing normalisation of relations between Israel and Saudi Arabia.

Discussions over the plan, which are likely to be impacted by the US' upcoming midterm elections as well as Israel's October legislative elections, have also looked at the possibility of the US acting as a guarantor for the so-called regional alignment, working towards a security agreement between Israel and Syria, and implementing the next part of Trump's Gaza plan.

President Donald Trump disembarks Air Force One at Morristown Airport, Friday, Sept. 4, 2026, in Morristown, N.J. Julia Demaree Nikhinson/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved.

The regional alignment strategy would not represent a major shift in US policy, as successive administrations since the 1979 Iranian Revolution have sought to curb Tehran's regional influence by strengthening relations and alliances with Gulf states.

But Washington may seek to turn these efforts into a more structured framework that includes closer defence and security coordination among allies, against the backdrop of what the US sees as a shift in the regional balance of power amid the Iran war.

A push for a normalisation agreement between Saudi Arabia and Israel is a goal Washington has been pursuing for years but which has stalled as Riyadh has tied any move in such a direction to tangible progress towards resolving the situation in Gaza and the creation of a Palestinian state.

These efforts build on the "Abraham Accords" agreed to in 2020 under Trump's first administration, which normalised relations between Israel on the one hand and the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Morocco and Sudan on the other.

Since then, Washington has worked to widen the circle of countries joining these accords, seeing them as one of the tools for reshaping relations and alliances in the Middle East and reducing the influence of Iran and its allies in the region.

The other pillar, which focuses on addressing the regional repercussions of the Hamas militant group's 7 October attack and the ensuing war in the Gaza Strip, could see the issue tackled in three main ways.

Firstly, moving to the next phase of Trump's plan for Gaza, which, according to previous reports, includes arrangements for the reconstruction of the Strip, the disarmament of Hamas and the establishment of a transitional administration.

The second could be an effort to reach a security agreement between Israel and Syria, which would come amid sweeping political changes in Syria since the fall of Bashar al-Assad's regime at the end of 2024 - as well as new authorities' attempts to recast the country's regional and international relations.

And thirdly, implementing an agreement between Israel and Lebanon that would limit Hezbollah's military capabilities. This comes as part of efforts linked to the ceasefire deal reached by Israel and the group in 2024, which provided for the withdrawal of Hezbollah fighters to north of the Litani River and the deployment of the Lebanese army in the south of the country.

Israel has since accused Hezbollah of trying to rebuild its military capabilities, however, while Lebanon has continued to report Israeli air strikes on its territory.

A final plan has yet to take shape

While the planning continues, one of the sources told Axios that it had not yet fully come together.

"They are cooking it, but it is not yet cooked," they said, adding: "The idea is to tie a whole lot of things in the region together — how you create a regional alignment after the war. It is still unclearif all U.S. allies in the region will be on board."

World.title: Ebola: Why children are last to be treated in medical crises
World.content:
In the latest Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, children are more likely to die than adults. But it's not always due to the disease. Specific medicines for younger people are often harder to come by.

The current Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has been devastating. Since the outbreak began in mid-May, more than 3,000 people have died.

Almost half of people infected with Ebola are expected to die, and the mortality rate is particularly high for young children. According to a commentary by Doctors Without Borders recently published in medical journal The Lancet , the mortality rate for children under the age of 5 is over 60%.

But often, it's because of a lack of medication and information on how to use it with young patients, rather than then disease itself.

"Children must be centered in Ebola treatment and prevention research," the aid organization wrote in early September .

At the heart of the debate is the EBO-PEP study, which began mid-July. The study looks at an experimental antiviral drug called obeldesivir, which is being studied for its ability to protect people exposed to the Bundibugyo Ebola virus, the strain responsible for the current deadly outbreak.

But children weighing less than 30 kilograms (about 66 pounds) and around 12 years old or younger, were not included in the original study. But that could change soon with protocols to include children weighing over 20 kilograms.

Children under the age of 5 are significantly more likely to die from Ebola fever than adults Image: Benediction Murhabazi/AFP

Children weighing less than 20 kilograms — that is, roughly 6 years old or younger — won't be included in the treatment. There is an alternative treatment for them: Another antiviral drug, remdesivir, given intravenously. But as Doctors Without Borders argued, a 10-day course of infusions is difficult to administer during an outbreak, especially for young children.

According to Neal Russell, a pediatric doctor based in London who consults for Doctors Without Borders and who was also the lead author of the Lancet commentary, young children are at particularly high risk from Ebola. This could be due to their weakened immune systems, underlying health conditions, or the fact that treating them for Ebola is especially challenging in an outbreak.

For example, children are often harder to diagnose than adults because early symptoms resemble other illnesses, and young children often find it difficult to describe their symptoms accurately. Other issues include the fact that children cannot always be accompanied into an Ebola treatment center by their parents or caregivers, something that is especially important in their recovery. Younger Ebola patients also require closer monitoring and specially trained staff.

Ebola outbreak in DR Congo outpaces efforts to contain it To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ebola in Berlin

In May, an American doctor was treated at Berlin's Charite hospital after contracting the Bundibugyo Ebola virus while caring for patients. His wife and their four children were also considered at high risk. The medical team in Germany decided to treat the family prophylactically with an experimental antibody drug called MBP134.

"Of course, a careful risk benefit assessment had to be carried out," said Han Ngoc Le, a doctor at the hospital who was involved in the treatments.

The available data about the drug's impact on children was very limited. But at the same time, the children were at high risk of catching Ebola after close contact with their sick father.

In the end, all the family remained healthy and no apparent side effects were seen. It's unclear whether the experimental treatment prevented infection in the children. Such a small sample can't be mapped onto the larger population either.

But the test was valuable nonetheless. "The mere fact that the antibody was so well tolerated even in 1-year-olds and children under 12 is a valuable finding upon which future studies can build," Le said.

Why do such gaps in knowledge exist?

Le explained that, from a medical perspective, children cannot simply be thought of as "small adults."

Their metabolisms function differently, they react differently to medications, their pharmacokinetics — what a body does with a drug — are simply different. The same sort of cautions also apply to pregnant women.

That's why dosages of medication can't simply be transferred from adults to children. It's also why any new medications require separate studies so that specific dosages can be determined and potentially special formulations can be developed. Children might require kid-friendly syrups instead of adult-size tablets, for example.

DR Congo launches Ebola trial for high-risk contacts To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"All of this creates extra costs," said Marc Biot, access coordinator for Europe at Doctors Without Borders, who works to ensure people in need can get affordable, good-quality medical products. He said research institutions and pharmaceutical companies often see investing extra in pediatric studies as a lower priority.

"It is faster and it can be cheaper if you only focus on adults," said Biot — which is why treating children and pregnant women usually only becomes part of the research at a later stage of drug development. "That is our plea — a plea not only to the scientists, to the pharmaceutical companies, but also to those who fund and allow trials to happen — to allow that to happen on the same speed for adults as for children and pregnant women."

Biot said it's sad to see that pressure is needed to make it happen. "Whenever you start a clinical trial, you also should include pregnant woman or children," he argued.

A difficult balance

None of this is new. In 2020, the Global Accelerator for Pediatric Formulations network was founded — supported by the World Health Organization(WHO) — to accelerate the development and availability of child-friendly medicine worldwide.

This isn't an issue limited to Ebola. Russell pointed to the 2024 mpox epidemic in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where children made up a large proportion of those infected or killed.

Although a vaccine existed for mpox, it wasn't made for children. The WHO advised it be used "off label" for minors, but they tended to get it a lot later than adults anyway. Experts say they've observed similar patterns with other diseases including HIV, tuberculosis, and during the COVID-19 pandemic.

When it comes to the development of medicines and vaccines, the first samples are often made for adult patients Image: Thomas Lohnes/AFP/Getty Images

"When you're doing a research study, which is not in an emergency, [it makes sense] to protect children and pregnant women from any potential harm of an investigational product," said Russell. "But when you're in an emergency, the balance between protecting those people from any potential harm from research, and protecting them from the very fatal disease, changes."

Berlin-based doctor Le believes children and pregnant women should be considered right from the beginning of any new clinical trials. "They shouldn't be excluded from participation just like that," she said. "Instead, sub-studies or parallel studies should be set up from the outset."

Russell calls for a similar approach. He wants to see all people benefit equally from scientific progress during a health crisis — especially in a health emergency, when the most vulnerable should not be the last to benefit from that progress.

"No matter who you are, you should have the same opportunity to have access to these medical products," he said.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Hungary begins hunt for corrupt regime's billions
World.content:
Hungary's new prime minister promised he would recover billions stolen or diverted by the previous administration. A new "super authority" is about to begin that work. Its success or failure will have a big impact.

Asset recovery — it sounds bureaucratic but behind this phrase is one of the most important campaign promises made by Hungary's new government.

Hungary's new prime minister, Peter Magyar, and his Tisza party want to retrieve funds and assets that went — in some dubious ways — to the family of ousted Hungarian leader Viktor Orban or his allies, various oligarchs, or frontmen. The new government wants those funds back for state use, and it also plans to hold the beneficiaries accountable under law.

Billions of euros were stolen or diverted and, if social media is to be believed, many Hungarians want to see the individuals responsible behind bars. Magyar has talked of a sum of around €60 billion ($70 billion), though other estimates suggest the real amount could be three times that much.

Orban, allies lived lives of luxury

Observers say the success or failure of the asset recovery will almost certainly influence the future of Magyar and the Tisza party.

The huge sums of money are linked to images of decadent luxury under Orban. The former Hungarian prime minister's family, party members, and friendly oligarchs lived on luxury estates, flew in luxury jets, vacationed on luxury yachts, and repeatedly won billions worth of public contracts.

Orban-affiliated entrepreneurs, artists, academics, and journalists were also generously supported with public funds for years. Often their main qualification was loyalty to the former prime minister.

Former Prime Minister Viktor Orban has alleged that his successor has 'dismantled the rule of law' since coming to power Image: Balint Szentgallay/NurPhoto/picture alliance

Those lifestyles contrasted with the lives led by Hungarians in poverty, the image of neglected public infrastructure, poor conditions in schools and hospitals, and the exodus of many young Hungarians from the country, as well as a huge deficit in the state budget, some 7.5% of Hungary's national income. These contrasts explain why there is such a popular desire for justice.

It's been almost four months since the new Magyar government took office and anti-corruption actions have officially started.

At the end of July, the new government established the National Asset Recovery Authority, or NVVH — a sort of "super institution" with very broad powers and independence.

Hungary hasn't had an authority like this in its modern history. The way state assets were privatized in the 1990s after communist rule was problematic, as it often was elsewhere in the former Soviet bloc. When Orban first came to power in 2010, there was a half-hearted attempt to address the corruption of the previous government under Ferenc Gyurcsany, but it came to nothing.

Hungary new PM lifts lid on Orban-era government luxury To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

This time, things are meant to be different.

The NVVH will investigate where public funds flowed and how assets like real estate were used. Although no specific date has been set, the investigations will primarily focus on the Orban government's time in power, so dating back to 2010. The authority is also meant to make sure this cannot happen again, and will look into how public funds and assets are to be used in future.

The NVVH has both policing and prosecutorial powers, so it can investigate cases and bring charges. The authority is accountable to Hungary's parliament.

Controversy around new anti-corruption body

But the creation of the NVVH has not been without controversy.

Late last week, parliament appointed Anna Unger, 46, a political scientist at Eotvos Lorand University in Budapest, to head the new anti-corruption and asset recovery body. Unger is an expert on political systems, democratic institutions, and party financing and was chosen out of almost 100 other applicants in a process with several stages.

Some were surprised at Unger's appointment, as she wasn't really a public figure. Her research has included political corruption but she's not a recognized expert on the topic, nor is she a lawyer. Observers had expected a lawyer or an anti-corruption expert to get the job, somebody like Miklos Ligeti, head of legal affairs at Transparency International Hungary since 2012.

Anna Unger was named head of the new accountability organization in late August Image: Attila Kisbenedek/AFP

Ligeti also applied for the job but is reportedly being considered for a position as a deputy director. Unger will have four deputies with different duties and responsibilities. Katalin Tasnady, a well-known prosecutor with around two decades of criminal law experience, was made the NVVH's deputy chief of investigations.

Government representatives said Unger had presented a comprehensive political vision for the agency's work. During her parliamentary hearing, she said that under Orban, Hungary saw more than just what one might call classic corruption. An almost feudal system had prevailed, she argued. That was why in addition to restitution and asset recovery, the system had to be thoroughly investigated and exposed so that it would never happen again, Unger said.

No justice in next 6 years?

Unger caused the biggest upset when she said it would be folly to expect legally binding verdicts in any major corruption cases during the NVVH's first six-year term.

Robert Puzser, a popular commentator and personality on social media, called Unger's statement "devastating." Voters had given Magyar "unprecedented power to hold the country's plunderers to account," he said on Facebook, and if Hungarians had to wait more than six years, it could cause the collapse of this new government.

The new prime minister himself reacted angrily to critics who said the NVVH should have had a lawyer at its head.

"Nobody promised people they could vote for the leader of the NVVH as if it was a [reality TV] casting show," he wrote on Facebook. Plenty of experts thought Unger was absolutely suitable for the job.

In a podcast on the 24.hu media outlet, political science Gabor Torok surmised that the way that the NVVH had been established indicated that it would be a "strong political institution" that aimed to come to terms with the recent past.

Torok said the public expects the Tisza party to thoroughly reckon with the old system, and the new government will only be able to maintain the public's trust if it doesn't look like the "culprits of the previous order" are getting away with their past crimes, he said.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Saxony-Anhalt: Far-right AfD eyes power in German state vote
World.content:
09/06/2026 September 6, 2026 Polls open in Saxony-Anhalt state election

Polling stations have opened in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt, where voters are choosing a new state parliament.

Around 1.7 million people aged 18 and over are eligible to vote. Polling stations opened at 8 a.m. local time (0600 GMT/UTC) and will close at 6 p.m., when counting begins.

Voters are electing the members of the new state parliament in Magdeburg.

They can cast two votes: one for a direct constituency candidate and one for a political party.

The new parliament will subsequently elect the state premier.

The state returning officer expects a preliminary final result in the early hours of Monday morning.

World.title: Indonesia: Flights canceled as Anak Krakatau volcano erupts
World.content:
The spread of ash after the volcanic eruption of Anak Krakatau has impacted thousands of passengers, as flights were canceled at Jakarta's international airport.

Hundreds of flights were canceled at Jakarta's international airport after Indonesia's Anak Krakatau volcano erupted early Sunday morning, more than 150 kilometers (93 miles) away.

The volcano produced a fountain of lava and loud sounds heard up to 700 kilometres (435 miles) away, Indonesia's geological agency said in a statement.

The cloud of ash was detected up to a height of 6,000 meters (20,000 feet) on the Java side of the volcano and a plume of up to 15,000 meters (50,000 feet) on the ‌Sumatra side and some parts of Banten province in Java, the ‌meteorological ​agency BMKG posted on its website.

No incidents of casualties were reported, and no evacuation orders were issued.

Danger remains in Indonesia in the wake of volcano eruptions To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The closest township is more than 16 kilometers (10 miles) away, but the authorities warned residents and visitors to stay at least 3 kilometers (1.9 miles) from the volcano's active crater.

Two new eruptions were recorded on Sunday, the volcanology agency warned.

Indonesia cancels flights

The ash spread across parts of the capital Jakarta and Lampung province on the southern tip of Sumatra island, Indonesia's Center for Volcanology and Geological Hazard Mitigation said.

The spread of ash after the volcanic eruption of Mount Anak Krakatau disrupted operations at Jakarta's international airport.

Soekarno-Hatta International Airport posted on ‌Instagram that it had ⁠suspended ⁠flight operations until 9:30 a.m. (0230 GMT) due to volcanic ash.

New volcano eruptions hit Indonesia To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Due to increased activity from the Mount Anak Krakatau eruption, Soekarno-Hatta International Airport has temporarily suspended flight operations from 5:30 a.m. to 9.30 a.m.," the airport said.

The disruption of flight operations has impacted more than 22,000 passengers, the transport ministry said in a statement, adding that 209 flights were affected, particularly to and from Singapore.

Anak Krakatau lies in the middle between Java and Sumatra in Indonesia's vast island chain, which sits on the Pacific "Ring of Fire," where earthquakes and volcanic eruptions are frequent.

Anak Krakatau means "Child of Krakatau." The volcano is the offspring of the famous Krakatau, whose monumental eruption in 1883 triggered a period of global cooling.

World.title: Saxony-Anhalt's state election will have a nationwide impact
World.content:
The parliamentary election in the small eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt could have dramatic consequences for Germany's federal government, further raising dissatisfaction with Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

Only 1.6 million eligible voters are called to choose a new state parliament in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday. The region between the Elbe River and Harz Mountains in eastern Germany is outnumbered in population by 10 of Germany's total 16 federal states.

Nonetheless, the vote has become a major challenge for the federal government coalition of the conservative Union — of the Christian Democrats and their Bavarian sister party the Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) — and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD). In the last few months, there were even rumors in Berlin that German Chancellor Friedrich Merz of the CDU could step down following this vote — or that he would be forced to by his own party.

This is because the in-part right-wing extremist Alternative for Germany (AfD) party leads the polls in Saxony-Anhalt, far ahead of the centrist parties governing at the federal level, the CDU and SPD. Even an absolute majority for the right-wing populists cannot be ruled out. If that came to pass, the election would have serious consequences for the federal government in Berlin.

A threat to Chancellor Friedrich Merz?

Political scientist Carsten Koschmieder from the Free University in Berlin does not believe Merz will give up.

"I do not have the impression that he is a person who would resign," Koschmieder told DW. "Rather, he is very glad to be chancellor and has long worked toward that." In addition, there is currently no ready successor to Merz in the CDU and CSU, he added.

An absolute majority for the AfD could, however, plunge the governing coalition in Berlin into crisis, Koschmieder said. It would also intensify pressure regarding the correct way to deal with the AfD, which is in parts right-wing extremist.

Before he was elected chancellor in May 2025, Merz set the goal of halving support for the AfD, in part by adopting a tough migration policy. The fact that this has not succeeded, and instead the CDU has lost support, has yielded him much criticism within his party. His Union of the CDU and CSU has categorically ruled out working with the AfD, as have all other established German political parties.

Could a CDU government get support from the Left Party?

It's also possible that the CDU in Saxony-Anhalt ends up forming a minority government with the SPD and the environmentalist Greens. But even such a three-way coalition is unlikely to have a majority in parliament.

This would mean it has to be tolerated, ironically, by the socialist Left Party. Ironic, because the CDU also wants to avoid any cooperation with the Left, as the chancellor reiterated in an interview with regional newspaper the Mitteldeutsche Zeitung: "Both the AfD and Left Party have such fundamental differences with the Union that cooperation is out of the question," Merz said on Tuesday.

Saxony-Anhalt election: Can the CDU stop the AfD? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Here, Koschmieder said, a double problem arises for Merz: Many local-level CDU politicians, especially in eastern Germany, consider cooperation with the AfD quite possible, and have categorically rejected working with the Left Party.

But many other conservative politicians fear the opposite: that engaging with the right-wing populists would massively damage the CDU/CSU. "There are many conservative democrats in the CDU who say: We have nothing to do with the AfD. They want to abolish our democracy; they support Russia's President Putin and oppose Western integration and European unity," Koschmieder explained.

Merz: Government stability not at risk

In other words: It is mainly for the chancellor's party that the election result in Saxony-Anhalt could become a crucial test. Merz has already identified this issue, and has made recent calls for calm.

"Outsiders are trying to drive a wedge into the Union. The result of a state parliament election does not endanger the stability of the federal government," he told the Mitteldeutsche Zeitung.

Amid far right's rise, is Germany at a breaking point? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video





The chancellor seems resolved to carry on with his government, even amid growing dissatisfaction and rising pressure. This year, he still plans to bring his controversial reforms of the old age pension system through parliament, which have been heavily criticized by members of his own party on the campaign trail in Saxony-Anhalt.

But that hasn't discouraged Merz. "The pension system is no longer sustainable because of demographics, and we have known this for years," he said.

AfD state government feared to be a security risk

Political scientist Koschmieder also thinks many CDU politicians at the state level will continue their criticism of the pension reform plans, but he added: "I do not think they will completely fail, but there will be amendments in some places."

Pressure from his own party, problems with upcoming reforms — all of this could be in store for the chancellor. And that's not all: Interior policy and security experts at the federal and state levels have warned of high risks if a possible AfD government in Saxony-Anhalt has access to sensitive data — when it comes to counterintelligence, for example.

Georg Maier, the SPD interior minister in the eastern state of Thuringia, told German media outlet RND: "If an AfD politician becomes the interior minister of Saxony-Anhalt, that would be in my view a glaring security risk for Germany."

What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

SPD hopes for success in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania

What about the Social Democrats? A possible result of 8% or 9% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt, as recently calculated by pollsters, sounds terribly low, but it would be a great improvement on what was being predicted six months ago.

In addition, the Social Democrat premier of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Manuela Schwesig, has good odds of a renewed mandate in state parliament elections there on September 20. The SPD has made a strong comeback in the polls in the coastal state since last year; with around 30% of the vote, they could form a government with the Left Party, the CDU or potentially both.

But also here, in northeastern Germany, the AfD is the strongest polling party, at around 35%.

Why voters are so unhappy with leadership in democracies To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: US envoys meet with Putin, leave Russia for Kyiv
World.content:
Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow to try to revive talks to end the war in Ukraine. The US envoys are also scheduled to visit Kyiv on Sunday.

US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Saturday evening.

"The situation is of course not simple," Putin told the US officials in footage aired on Russian state media.

Putin and US envoys held "useful" talks on a range of ideas to end the war in Ukraine, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters.

According to Russian media outlets, US envoys left Moscow after the meeting.

Earlier, US President Donald Trump said Kushner and Witkoff were traveling to Russia with a new proposal, but he did not provide any details on the potential peace plan, including whether it involved Ukraine giving territory to Russia as he has previously suggested. Instead, he said, "We have an idea for peace."

In the meeting with Putin, Kushner and Witkoff discussed "substantive plans" for the next steps toward ending the Ukraine war, the White House said, adding that more details would be announced next week.

The envoys "look forward to equally productive meetings tomorrow in Ukraine," a White House official said in a statement.

Russia, Ukraine pause strikes for three days

The Kremlin said Russian forces would pause strikes against Kyiv for three days in conjunction with the peace negotiations.

Putin "ordered that no strikes be carried out against Kyiv for three days, starting at midnight today," Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told state media.

The order came after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had already committed to pausing airstrikes for the talks.

"As with previous diplomatic visits by the American side, we will ensure the normal functioning of Russian airspace so that the negotiators can arrive safely. We are concerned about their safety, not about Russia," Zelenskyy said.

US envoys to make first visit to Kyiv

Zelenskyy announced on Friday that Kushner and Witkoff would visit Ukraine on Sunday following talks in Moscow.

Recent media reports have questioned whether the pair would indeed travel to Ukraine. Despite trips to Moscow to meet with Russian officials, the US envoys have not visited Kyiv since Trump's reelection last year.

On Saturday, Zelenskyy said he had been in contact with Kushner and Witkoff.

"I ⁠have ​just spoken ​with the US president’s ​envoys," Zelenskyy said ‌on Telegram.

"From the moment of this conversation, ​we ⁠are ready to observe a ⁠ceasefire ​in airstrikes against the cities involved in the negotiation process."

Trump had promised to end the war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year, on his first day back in office, but has more recently said that the feat was more complicated than expected. In the past, he has blamed Ukraine for the Russian invasion and a "personality problem" between the countries' leaders for the continued fighting.

World.title: German company successfully launches rocket to space
World.content:
Bavaria-based Isar Aerospace managed to launch its Spectrum rocket into orbit, 18 months after its first attempt. This is the first such launch from European soil.

A Spectrum space rocket built by German company Isar Aerospace was launched into space from the Norwegian spaceport at Andoya.

"We're in orbit! And just made European history: This is the first time a privately developed rocket reached orbit from continental Europe," the company wrote on X.

"Germany has spaceflight capabilities," said the country's Ministry for Research, Technology and Space on X, praising a "milestone that impressively demonstrates our country's innovative strength and technical expertise".

This was the German company's second attempt to launch the Spectrum rocket into space. The first attempt, which took place 18 months ago, was unsuccessful.

What is Spectrum rocket?

The Spectrum rocket is designed for small and medium-sized payloads. It carried five smal satellites and an in-flight technological experiment, the company said.

According to Isar Aerospace, the launch was for "both the vehicle's qualification mission and its first flight carrying payload."

The move is believed to bring Europe closer to being able to offer satellite flights from its own territory. Several countries voiced interest in the growing market of commercial space missions, including Britain and Sweden.

The launch of Spectrum follows months of delays Image: Isar Aerospace/dpa/picture alliance

In March, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited the launch site of Isar, a Bavaria-based company, showing support for its efforts and for European autonomy at a time when the world order is changing under US President Donald Trump.

Isar is also working on the development of a second launch site, located in Canada.

The company said that while the US launched 198 rockets last year, Europe's tally was just eight. Isar's goal is to produce some 40 rockets a year.

Competition includes SpaceX

Although the rocket is not yet ready for mass production, Isar has already received orders through 2028.

The Spectrum rocket is intended to send both civilian and military satellites into low Earth orbit, meaning a few hundred kilometers above the Earth's surface.

The industry includes Elon Musk's SpaceX and ArianeGroup, a French joint venture between Airbus and Safran that operates a spaceport in French Guiana, located in South America.

For the sake of developing new rockets and extend its testing and launch infrastructure, Isar said last week it received €200 million ($232 million) from the European Space Agency (ESA).
