World.title: Langdon Appears in Prague! Netflix Presents New Series Based on Dan Brown
World.content:
Netflix has begun filming its new series based on Dan Brown’s The Secret of Secrets, bringing Harvard symbologist Robert Langdon back to Prague.

The production officially started in the Czech capital this week, with Netflix releasing a first look at Morgan Spector as Langdon and Rebecca Hall as scientist Katherine Solomon. The series is currently untitled and does not yet have a release date.



Netflix has now added five more actors to the production. Mamoudou Athie will appear as Michael Harris, Ben Levi Ross as Alex Conan, Anamaria Marinca as Dr. Gessner, Richard Sammel as Karl Muller and Elena Saurel as Susan Housemore.

The series is being developed by Carlton Cuse, who co-created Lost and later worked on Jack Ryan, Locke & Key, Bates Motel and Five Days at Memorial. Cuse serves as co-creator, showrunner, writer and executive producer. Emma Forman is also an executive producer for Genre Arts, alongside Cuse and Brown.

Brown is involved in the project as a co-writer and executive producer.

The novel takes Langdon through several recognizable parts of Prague, including Charles Bridge and the Klementinum, as he searches for answers following Solomon’s disappearance. Netflix says the television adaptation will combine scientific ideas, historical mysteries and mystical elements.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Dan Brown (@authordanbrown)

The Secret of Secrets was published in September 2025 and became the latest installment in Brown’s Robert Langdon series. The book was released simultaneously in multiple countries, including the Czech Republic, and Prague is closely tied to its plot.

The Czech Republic is expected to play a significant role in the new television production. Prague has previously served as a filming location for a wide range of international productions, making the city a familiar setting for foreign film and television crews.

The arrival of the Netflix series could also have an impact beyond the production industry. Czech travel companies and Argo, the publisher of Brown’s books in Czech, have previously pointed to the potential for two waves of tourism connected with the project: first from readers discovering the novel and later from viewers of the television adaptation.

World.title: Prague Planetarium to Become a Concert Venue Under the Stars
World.content:
The Prague Planetarium in Stromovka will host a new series of chamber concerts combining live music with projections of the universe from September 2026.

Called Niche Nites, the series will feature 10 concerts between September 2026 and June 2027. Each performance will be accompanied by visuals projected across the planetarium’s 22-metre-wide dome, with the imagery responding to the music in real time.



The programme will take place on the final weekend of each month. Rather than staging repeated performances, each musician or group will appear at the planetarium only once, giving every concert its own programme and visual design.

The series will open on September 25 with cellist Terezie Kovalová, whose work combines classical music with pop, alternative and electronic influences.

Other performers confirmed for the programme include guitarist and composer Michal Pavlíček, who will appear with singer Bára Basiková, pianist and composer Beata Hlavenková, and singer-songwriter Lenka Dusilová. Further names will be announced by the organisers in the coming months.

Producer and dramaturg Michala Komrsková said the project is intended to present established Czech musicians in a more intimate setting than the large concert halls where they usually perform.

The planetarium’s technology will play a central role. Its dome is fitted with an LED system containing millions of diodes, allowing large-scale visual sequences to accompany the performances. The imagery will be prepared specifically for each concert rather than using a single projection throughout the series.

More recently, the planetarium was used during this year’s Spectaculare festival, which combined music by composer Rafael Anton Irisarri with visual work by Czech artists Dalibor Cée and Alex J. Jindrák.

World.title: Gipsy Kings by André Reyes to Perform in Prague This November
World.content:
The legendary Gipsy Kings by André Reyes will perform in Prague this November, bringing their distinctive mix of flamenco guitar, rumba and Latin rhythms to Lucerna Great Hall on November 29, 2026.

Led by founding member André Reyes, the group will perform some of the songs that made the Gipsy Kings famous around the world, including “Bamboleo,” “Djobi Djoba” and “Volare,” alongside newer material.



The concert is being presented by Gotobeat and will begin at 7 p.m. Tickets are online here.

From southern France to the world

The Gipsy Kings’ story began with the Reyes family and their musical roots in the south of France. André Reyes was one of the founding members of the group, which went on to combine traditional flamenco with rumba, Latin rhythms and pop influences.

Their energetic guitar playing and Spanish-language songs helped turn rumba flamenca into an international sound. Tracks such as “Bamboleo” and “Djobi Djoba” became global hits, while their version of “Volare” introduced the group to an even wider audience.

Music associated with the Gipsy Kings has sold more than 60 million records worldwide, making the group one of the most successful international acts to emerge from the flamenco-rumba tradition.

Their music has also appeared in popular culture, including their version of “Hotel California,” which featured in The Big Lebowski.

A new generation of the Reyes family

André Reyes continues the tradition today with Gipsy Kings by André Reyes, performing alongside younger members of the Reyes family.

The current show combines the group’s best-known classics with newer music, including material connected to Nací Gitano, the band’s latest project. The group is also touring internationally in 2026 as part of its Viva el Arte Tour.

For audiences, the concert offers a mix of familiar songs and new material, with the performance centred on the fast-paced guitar playing, percussion and vocals that have defined the Gipsy Kings sound for decades.

Date: Sunday, November 29, 2026

Time: 7 p.m.

Venue: Lucerna Great Hall, Štěpánská 61, Prague 1

Promoter: Gotobeat

World.title: No Tickets Needed: Six Free Events in Prague This September
World.content:
Prague is offering a packed lineup of free events this September, from an air show and science festivals to a rare public viewing of the Czech Crown Jewels and a celebration marking a local brewery’s 15th anniversary.

Here are some of the best events taking place across the Czech capital this month.



Free Sightseeing at Historic Sites

The National Heritage Institute will open selected state-owned castles, chateaux, monasteries and other historic sites to visitors for free on Sunday, September 27.

Most of the properties managed by the institute will take part, although the tours and routes available will vary by location. Free admission will cover standard tours and selected additional routes. Capacity is limited, so visitors must book a free ticket online in advance for a specific time.

The Prague 10 Science Festival returns to Gutovka on Saturday, September 12.

From 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., 25 stations will offer visitors the chance to take part in chemistry experiments, explore LEGO robotics, play math games and learn more about nature, technology and the human body.

The program will also include workshops, a competition, a toy and plant swap, and a science show by Michael Londesborough. DJ SÂN will perform from 6 p.m., with the festival continuing until 8 p.m.

Dokola Festival

The Dokola Festival will take place on September 10 and 11, focusing on creative ways to reuse items rather than throw them away.

Visitors can repair broken electronics, make furniture from leftover wood, upcycle old clothes or try making kimchi. The program will also feature talks, a clothes swap, an upcycled fashion show and stand-up comedy. Most of the program is free, although some workshops charge a nominal fee.

Břevnov Brewery Celebrates 15 Years

Břevnov Brewery will mark its 15th anniversary on Saturday, September 12, with a day of beer, live music and family activities.

From 11 a.m. to 9 p.m., the meadow beside Břevnov Monastery will feature beer from the local brewery, along with special brews from other monastic breweries from across the Czech Republic.

Live performances by HUGO, Funk Corporation and JAKSI TAKSI will accompany guided brewery tours, barrel-throwing and timed barrel-rolling competitions, as well as activities for children.

There will also be a workshop for visitors interested in learning how to brew beer at home.

Czech Crown Jewels on Display

One of Prague’s most prestigious treasures will go on public display this month, when the Czech Crown Jewels are exhibited in Vladislav Hall at Prague Castle from September 19 to 28. Admission is free.

The exhibition marks 500 years since Ferdinand I of Habsburg became King of Bohemia. Alongside the famous St. Wenceslas Crown, the display will feature the royal sceptre and orb, a coronation robe dating from 1653 and historic keys once used by guardians of the Crown Archive.

Visitors will enter through the South Gardens and Bull Staircase from Hradčanské Square. Everyone must pass through a security check, and organizers advise against bringing prams.

Letňany Airport Day

After a two-year break, Letňany Airport will once again open its doors to the public on Saturday, September 5.

This year’s event will focus on legendary training aircraft and pilot training during World War II and the postwar years.

The program will feature historic aircraft from the Czech Republic and abroad, demonstrations by the Czech Army and police, model aircraft and a chance to see the airport’s current operations.

Events will take place in half-hour blocks between 9 a.m. and 6 p.m.

World.title: Fire During C-Section at Bulovka Hospital Leaves Woman Seriously Burned
World.content:
A woman suffered serious burns during an emergency cesarean section at Prague’s Bulovka Hospital on Aug. 25, hospital spokeswoman Eva Stolejda Libigerová said.

The cesarean was performed because of an acute obstetric complication. The woman’s condition is now stable and she does not require intensive care, the hospital said. She is recovering in a standard ward with her newborn.



The hospital is investigating the incident as part of its internal procedures for reviewing patient safety and the quality of medical care. It said it would take appropriate measures once the investigation is complete.

Fire broke out during surgery

According to information obtained about the incident, medical staff were attempting to control bleeding toward the end of the operation when a fire broke out involving a surgical device.

The device was reportedly being used shortly after the patient’s skin had been treated with a disinfectant.

The woman suffered second- and third-degree burns to her inner thighs, sides, lower abdomen and genital area, according to the available information.

Two days after the operation, she was transferred to the Burns Medicine Clinic at University Hospital Královské Vinohrady for treatment. She was later returned to Bulovka Hospital’s postpartum ward.

The circumstances surrounding the fire, including how it started and whether established safety procedures were followed, are being examined by the hospital.

Previous incident at Bulovka maternity clinic

The hospital’s gynecology and obstetrics clinic was also the site of a serious medical error in March 2024.

In that case, staff mistakenly identified two patients of Asian origin. A pregnant woman who had arrived for a routine examination was incorrectly subjected to a curettage procedure, resulting in the loss of her pregnancy.

An internal investigation concluded that two employees had violated established procedures and internal rules. The hospital subsequently ended its cooperation with one of them.

Police also investigated the case on suspicion of negligent bodily harm but ultimately brought no charges.

The woman later reached a settlement with the hospital worth 2.3 million Czech crowns. One of the employees involved lost her job.

World.title: Ambiente to Open Its 35th Prague Establishment This September
World.content:
Restaurant group Ambiente is preparing to open its 35th establishment, with a second location of its Pult beer concept set to launch in Prague’s Holešovice district in mid-September.

The new venue will be located on Tusarova Street and will follow the concept of Pult in Prague 1, which opened in the Celnice building in 2021.



While both locations will focus on Czech lager, the new Holešovice branch will introduce a different food concept and its own selection of beers.

The original venue serves beers from six breweries, with an emphasis on precise storage, serving and temperature control.

A different approach to food

Food will be one of the main differences between the two Pult locations.

The original Pult in Celnice focuses largely on smaller dishes and snacks. The Holešovice restaurant will instead offer a more substantial menu designed specifically to accompany beer.

The menu is expected to focus heavily on Czech beef, including several versions of steak tartare and steaks. Unlike many restaurants where the kitchen closes earlier than the bar, the new Pult plans to serve food until closing at 1 a.m.

The restaurant will have space for around 130 guests.

Another new destination for Holešovice

The opening comes as Holešovice continues to attract new restaurants, cafés and cultural venues. The area has become home to places including Vnitroblock, Mexická, Slice Slice Baby, Eatery, Ema, Typika, Osada and Polepšovna.

Ambiente itself has expanded its presence in Holešovice this year. At the Holešovice Market, the group has opened a second location of its Myšák confectionery and Naše maso butcher shop, as well as Skô, a Slovak-focused restaurant concept.

World.title: 7 Autumn Bike Trips to Take Around Czechia
World.content:
With cooler temperatures and autumn colours arriving, September and October are among the best months for cycling in Czechia.

The country’s extensive network of marked trails makes it easy to plan anything from a relaxed day trip to a multi-day adventure.

Here are seven routes worth considering this autumn.



1. Prague–Mělník–Litoměřice

One of the easiest options for Prague residents is to head north along the Elbe. The route passes through Mělník, known for its vineyards and historic centre, before continuing towards Litoměřice.

Along the way, cyclists can see Roudnice Chateau, Mount Říp and the historic fortress town of Terezín. Mělník is particularly appealing in September, when its wine season is in full swing.

2. Znojmo Wine Route

For a combination of cycling and wine, South Moravia is hard to beat in autumn. The 63-kilometre Znojmo Wine Route connects vineyards and villages around Znojmo and is suitable for cyclists of different abilities.

September and October are also the region’s main wine-harvest season, with numerous wine and burčák events taking place.

3. Mikulov and Pálava

The Mikulov Wine Trail offers another relaxed way to explore South Moravia. The route takes cyclists through vineyards and the countryside around Mikulov, with the Pálava hills providing one of the region’s most distinctive landscapes.

It is particularly attractive in September, when the annual Pálava Wine Festival takes place.

4. Singltrek pod Smrkem

If road cycling isn’t your thing, head towards Liberec. Singltrek pod Smrkem has more than 60 kilometres of purpose-built mountain-bike trails, ranging from easier sections for beginners to more challenging routes.

The surrounding Jizera Mountains also make it a good destination for a weekend trip.

5. Bečva Cycling Trail

The almost 160-kilometre Bečva Cycling Trail follows the Bečva River across Moravia. The route can be completed over several days and is largely downhill when ridden from the river’s source towards its confluence with the Morava.

Highlights along the way include Helfštýn Castle, the Zbrašovské Aragonite Caves and the open-air museum in Rožnov pod Radhoštěm.

6. Ploučnice Cycle Path

The nearly 100-kilometre Ploučnice Cycle Path runs from the river’s source near Ještěd to Děčín. It passes through Česká Lípa, the Ralsko area and the Kokořínsko-Máchův kraj landscape before reaching the Elbe.

7. Prague–Vienna Greenway

For a more ambitious trip, the Prague–Vienna Greenway stretches 368 kilometres between the two capitals. The route passes through historic towns, castles and monasteries, including Tábor, Znojmo and Mikulov.

It takes roughly a week to complete with stops, making it better suited to a longer autumn holiday than a weekend ride.

World.title: How to Buy TikTok Followers Without Risking Your Account
World.content:
Building a TikTok audience from zero can be frustrating. Even well-produced videos may struggle to attract attention when an account has only a handful of followers.

This slow beginning encourages some creators and businesses to purchase followers in the hope of making their profiles appear more established. Follower count can influence first impressions. When visitors discover a profile with an existing audience, they may be more willing to watch its videos, explore older content, or follow the account themselves. However, purchased followers cannot replace engaging videos or genuine interaction. Low-quality services may also deliver inactive accounts that disappear quickly or create an unnatural gap between follower numbers and actual engagement. Anyone considering this approach should understand how follower services operate, what they can realistically provide, and which warning signs suggest that a seller should be avoided.

Why Creators Purchase TikTok Followers

New accounts frequently face a credibility problem. Viewers have little information to judge whether the creator is worth following, so the visible follower count becomes one of several signals they use to make that decision. A larger audience can make a profile appear more established. This is particularly relevant for businesses, influencers, musicians, and other new TikTok creators trying to build authority in a competitive category. Some creators also purchase TikTok followers to reach eligibility thresholds for particular TikTok features. TikTok commonly applies age, location, and follower requirements to features such as LIVE, although the exact conditions may differ between markets and can change over time. The important distinction is that purchased followers mainly affect appearance. They may strengthen the profile’s initial social proof, but they do not guarantee greater reach, more sales, or stronger engagement.

What Purchased Followers Can and Cannot Do

Follower count is visible to anyone who visits a TikTok profile, which means it can shape the visitor’s first impression. A profile with several thousand followers may look more credible than an otherwise similar account with fewer than 100. TikTok’s recommendation system, however, evaluates much more than audience size. Signals such as watch time, completion rate, rewatches, shares, comments, saves, and viewer satisfaction are generally more important when determining whether a video should reach a wider audience. This creates a potential problem. If an account displays 30,000 followers but its videos consistently receive only a few dozen views, the imbalance may look unnatural to both TikTok and real visitors. Brands evaluating the creator for a partnership may notice the same discrepancy. Purchased followers should therefore be understood as a limited form of social proof. They cannot:

Make weak videos more entertaining

Guarantee placement on the For You feed

Produce meaningful comments or conversations

Create loyal customers

Replace a consistent publishing strategy

Automatically generate revenue

The greatest risk comes from purchasing followers that are obviously automated, inactive, or created only to inflate account statistics. These profiles add little value and may be removed during platform cleanups.

How to Evaluate a TikTok Follower Provider

The market contains everything from established social media marketing platforms to temporary websites selling automated accounts. A professional design alone does not prove that a service is dependable, so each provider should be evaluated carefully. Platforms such as SocialWick offer clearly defined TikTok packages and a conventional ordering process. Regardless of which company is being considered, several basic checks should be completed before placing an order.

Check the Website’s Security

A provider should use HTTPS encryption to protect information submitted through its website. This can usually be confirmed by checking for the padlock symbol beside the address in the browser. Secure payment methods are equally important. Credit cards and reputable payment processors normally offer better consumer protection than cryptocurrency transfers, gift cards, or other payment methods that are difficult to reverse.

Never Provide a TikTok Password

A follower delivery service generally needs only the public username or a link to the TikTok profile. It should not require the account password, email login, recovery code, or two-factor authentication details. Requests for private credentials are a serious warning sign. Sharing this information could allow an unknown company to access the account, change its settings, publish content, or lock out the owner.

Review the Delivery Time

Instant delivery may sound convenient, but an enormous follower increase within minutes can look unnatural. A newer account is unlikely to gain tens of thousands of followers suddenly without a viral video or another clear reason. More credible providers commonly offer gradual delivery. This spreads the order across several hours or days and makes it easier to monitor the quality of the accounts being added.

Understand the Package Quality

Follower packages are often divided into labels such as standard, high quality, active, real, or premium. These terms are not standardized, so they can mean different things on different websites. A higher-priced package may include accounts with profile photos, usernames, existing posts, or more complete activity histories. Cheaper options frequently consist of empty or inactive profiles. Before paying extra for a so-called premium tier, buyers should read the description carefully and determine what the seller is actually promising. Independent comparisons of TikTok follower providers and package quality may provide additional context, but customer reviews and seller claims should still be treated cautiously.

Look for Accessible Customer Support

A legitimate business should provide a clear way to request assistance. Live chat, email support, or a functioning contact form gives customers somewhere to report missing followers, delayed orders, or payment problems. Support availability does not automatically prove that a provider is trustworthy. However, a website with no contact information, unanswered messages, and no stated resolution process presents a much greater risk.

Warning Signs That Should Not Be Ignored

Very low pricing is one of the most common signs of poor-quality delivery. Maintaining accounts that look authentic requires more resources than operating a large collection of disposable bots. Consequently, offers promising thousands of “real and active” followers for a few cents are unlikely to match their description. Other warning signs include:

Requests for passwords or security codes

Guaranteed viral results

Promises of automatic monetization

No terms of service or privacy policy

Prices far below comparable providers

Only irreversible payment methods

Broken pages or copied website content

No delivery estimate

No refund or replacement policy

Large numbers of identical customer reviews

Claims of guaranteed engagement also deserve scrutiny. No external provider can honestly promise that purchased followers will watch every video or become paying customers.

Why a Refill Policy Matters

Follower losses can occur after an order is completed. TikTok may remove suspicious accounts, users may deactivate their profiles, or low-quality followers may simply disappear. A refill policy allows customers to request replacements when the follower count drops within a specified period. Depending on the provider, this protection may last for several days or a month. The conditions should be reviewed before checkout. Some companies refill only when the loss exceeds a minimum amount, while others exclude certain packages. Buyers should also check whether the replacement is automatic or must be requested manually. A refill guarantee cannot eliminate every risk, but it shows that the provider has at least acknowledged the possibility of follower loss and established a process for addressing it.

Avoid Unnatural Growth Patterns

Sudden, unexplained growth can draw unwanted attention. An account that gains 10,000 followers overnight without publishing anything new may appear suspicious, particularly if its views and interactions remain unchanged. Gradual delivery is generally less disruptive than receiving an entire order immediately. However, spreading out a purchase should not be treated as a method for bypassing TikTok’s enforcement systems. Buying followers may still conflict with platform rules, and no delivery method can guarantee that an account will avoid restrictions or removals.

Creators who choose to purchase followers should keep the order proportionate to the profile’s existing size. Adding a modest number to an active account is less conspicuous than transforming a nearly empty profile into a large one overnight. Content should also continue to be published consistently. A larger number beneath the profile image will have little effect if visitors arrive and find outdated, irrelevant, or poorly produced videos.

Keep Engagement and Follower Numbers Balanced

Follower count is only one part of a TikTok profile. Views, likes, comments, shares, and posting frequency provide a broader picture of its actual performance. If follower growth significantly outpaces every other metric, the account may lose credibility. A profile with 20,000 followers and almost no interaction may look less trustworthy than one with 2,000 followers and an active community. Maintaining a reasonable balance requires genuine content work. Creators should continue to:

Publish videos on a consistent schedule

Capture attention within the opening seconds

Respond to real comments

Participate in relevant trends

Use searchable captions and keywords

Test different formats and video lengths

Review analytics to identify strong topics

Collaborate with creators in the same niche

These activities provide TikTok with behavioral signals that purchased followers cannot produce.

Turning Social Proof Into Organic Growth

The most practical reason to purchase followers is to improve the profile’s initial presentation. If that stronger appearance encourages more people to explore the content, it may indirectly support organic growth. This effect depends entirely on what visitors find after opening the profile. A clear bio, recognizable niche, strong video covers, and a useful collection of content can convert curiosity into a genuine follow. An inflated number without quality content is unlikely to accomplish the same result. Creators should prepare their profiles before purchasing anything. A complete profile should include:

A memorable username

A clear profile image

A concise description of the account

Several high-quality published videos

Pinned content that represents the creator’s best work

A consistent subject or visual identity

An appropriate call to action

Purchased followers may bring the profile closer to the starting line, but the content determines whether real viewers remain interested.

Final Considerations Before Buying TikTok Followers

Buying TikTok followers can improve the visible size of an account, but it should never be confused with building a real community. The number may influence first impressions, yet it cannot reproduce the value of genuine viewers who regularly interact with the content. Anyone considering a purchase should choose a provider carefully, avoid sharing login information, use protected payment methods, read the refill conditions, and remain skeptical of unrealistic guarantees. It is also important to recognize that follower purchases may violate TikTok’s rules and could lead to removals or other account consequences. The strongest TikTok profiles combine credibility with content that earns attention. Purchased followers may change how a profile looks, but sustainable growth still depends on originality, consistency, audience understanding, and videos that people genuinely want to watch.

World.title: Hungary’s housing market faces a major shift as government backs social housing
World.content:
Hungary’s housing market may be approaching one of its most important policy shifts in years. A newly published government resolution orders the preparation of the Wekerle Housing Construction Programme, promising more affordable homes, rental housing and student accommodation, with brownfield redevelopment at the centre of the strategy. Yet the plan also raises a fundamental question: can Hungary build its way out of the housing crisis through huge new urban districts, or could the infrastructure bill swallow much of the money before the first flats are completed?

The distinction is important. The government has not yet approved a detailed construction programme with a final list of projects, prices and eligibility rules. Government Resolution 1275/2026, published in the Hungarian Gazette on 31 August, instructs the minister for transport and investment, together with the finance minister, to prepare the Wekerle programme by 30 September.

Nevertheless, the political direction is already clear: after years in which Hungarian housing policy was dominated by measures encouraging home ownership, the state is preparing to give a much larger role to rental housing, institutional investors and publicly supported construction.

Why the Hungary’s housing market has become a political problem

The starting point is deteriorating affordability.

According to figures presented by Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy, an average Hungarian home was equivalent to around 5.9 years of average net earnings in 2015. By 2025, the figure had risen to 7.1 years.

Over roughly the same period, Vitézy said inflation-adjusted house prices increased by around 120%, while real wages rose by about 60%. Real rents, meanwhile, climbed by around 30%.

The situation is particularly difficult for people who cannot or do not want to buy.

Research cited by Economx estimates that Hungary faces a shortage of roughly 100,000 homes in areas where affordable housing and labour mobility are increasingly important. In Budapest, researchers found a substantial gap between rents that many households regard as affordable and actual market prices. ()

Students face another version of the same problem. According to the figures presented by the minister, approximately 320,000 university students compete for just 49,000 dormitory places nationwide. Those who cannot secure accommodation are pushed towards the private rental sector, adding demand particularly in university cities.

Construction has also been weak.

According to the Hungarian Central Statistical Office (KSH), only 12,062 new dwellings were completed in 2025, 9.3% fewer than the previous year. That compares with around 28,000 new homes at the recent peak in 2020.

There is, however, an important sign of improvement: 6,278 new homes were completed in the first half of 2026, 22% more than during the same period of 2025, KSH said. The number of homes covered by new permits and simplified notifications also rose by 29%, to 16,588. The Hungarian housing market is therefore recovering from a very low base, rather than continuing to contract uninterruptedly.

If you missed it – Looking beyond price per square metre: how Budapest, Warsaw and Bucharest’s new-build home markets differ

What the Wekerle programme would change

The government resolution makes brownfield redevelopment one of the programme’s priorities.

It also calls for increasing the proportion of affordable housing, developing institutional rental housing and student accommodation, simplifying planning and approval procedures, improving transport connections, encouraging energy-efficient construction and attracting long-term institutional investors.

The resolution goes further than construction alone. Ministers must examine tax measures that could expand housing and dormitory supply, while a new system of financial and regulatory incentives for affordable rental housing is due by the end of 2026.

Perhaps most significantly, the government has also ordered the preparation of a regulatory concept for a state housing agency, with a deadline of 31 December.

Separate government announcements have provided an indication of the potential financial scale.

The government says EUR 550 million could be drawn from EU Recovery and Resilience Facility resources. With bank and private-sector co-financing, the investment volume could exceed EUR 2 billion, while potential European Investment Bank participation could eventually push the total towards EUR 3 billion.

Large underused or former industrial areas are expected to play a major role. Vitézy has mentioned sites such as Rákosrendező and the planned Diákváros, or Student City, in Budapest as examples of the type of development being considered.

The stated ambition is to make quality rental housing available to young people for around HUF 130,000–180,000 (approximately EUR 352–487) per month, Portfolio.hu said.

That would be highly competitive by current Budapest standards.

However, neither these rental prices nor specific sites such as Rákosrendező are written into the 31 August government resolution. They should therefore be understood as policy ambitions under discussion rather than guaranteed features of the final programme.

Brownfield development could transform Budapest – but at what price?

On paper, the logic of brownfield construction is compelling.

Instead of expanding cities further into green areas, governments can turn abandoned railway yards, factories and industrial zones into new neighbourhoods. Large contiguous plots can also make it easier to construct thousands of homes together with schools, parks, shops and public transport.

There is another advantage: a successful brownfield project can repair parts of the urban fabric that have been neglected for decades.

But this is also where the greatest financial risk emerges.

Former industrial and railway land can require extensive soil remediation. Heavy metals, oil pollution and other contamination may have to be removed before residential construction begins. Roads, sewage systems, water and electricity networks, schools, health services and public transport may all need to be built almost from scratch.

Urban development consultant János Dienes, a former chief architect of Budapest’s Zugló district, has warned that the infrastructure bill for a hypothetical new district containing around 10,000 homes could reach HUF 700 billion (approximately EUR 1.90 billion).

According to his estimate, constructing the homes themselves could cost another HUF 760 billion (around EUR 2.06 billion).

Those figures are estimates, not an official budget, and the cost of individual brownfield sites could vary dramatically.

Yet they illustrate the problem facing policymakers. In this scenario, land preparation and infrastructure alone would cost more than three times the EUR 550 million of EU funding currently identified for the Wekerle programme.

A project can therefore create thousands of nominally affordable homes while still becoming extremely expensive for the state if taxpayers effectively finance the land, remediation, transport infrastructure and the difference between construction costs and subsidised rents.

If you missed it: How much does a flat in Budapest cost in 2026? Every district ranked, and what €200,000 actually buys

Would filling gaps in existing neighbourhoods be cheaper?

Critics of the mega-project approach argue that Budapest already contains numerous vacant or underused plots in established neighbourhoods.

Developing these so-called infill sites would offer a different model.

Many are already surrounded by roads, public transport, electricity, water, schools, shops and healthcare. Instead of creating an entirely new urban district, housing could be inserted gradually into the existing city.

This has a social argument as well as a financial one.

If thousands of subsidised rental properties are concentrated in one isolated location, policymakers must prevent the new development from becoming a segregated rental-housing estate. Distributing affordable homes across existing neighbourhoods could produce a more mixed urban environment.

But infill development also has limitations.

Plots are smaller and ownership is fragmented. Land in established neighbourhoods can be expensive, while local opposition to new construction can slow development. It is much harder to deliver 10,000 homes through dozens or hundreds of small projects than on one large site under coordinated ownership.

The real choice, therefore, may not be brownfield or infill construction.

A successful programme could require both: large strategic urban regeneration projects where the economics make sense, alongside smaller developments that exploit existing infrastructure.

Building new homes is not the only option

Supply is only one part of the housing equation.

Budapest has already experimented with restrictions on short-term accommodation. From 1 January 2025 until 31 December 2026, no new private or other short-term accommodation units can be registered in the capital. Existing properly registered operators are generally exempt from the moratorium.

District VI, Terézváros, has gone considerably further by effectively reducing the permitted number of days for private short-term accommodation to zero from 2026.

Further restrictions on Airbnb-type accommodation could theoretically return some properties to the long-term rental market, although the size of that effect is uncertain and stronger regulation would also have consequences for tourism and property owners.

Don’t miss it: Another Budapest district could tighten Airbnb rules as short-term rentals face growing restrictions

Another frequently discussed tool is taxation of persistently vacant investment properties. The theory is straightforward: instead of waiting years for new construction, governments can try to bring existing but unused housing stock back into circulation.

However, such measures raise their own questions, including how a genuinely vacant property should be defined, how exemptions should work and how the rules could be enforced.

The Wekerle resolution itself leaves the door open to tax-policy measures, but it does not yet specify what those measures will be.

Why it matters for foreigners in Hungary

The debate over the Hungarian housing market is not only a domestic social-policy issue.

For foreigners living, studying, working or investing in Hungary, the Wekerle programme could eventually change several parts of the Budapest property market.

International students could feel the effects first. If Hungary creates substantially more dormitory places, thousands of students who currently rent privately may leave the open market. That could reduce competition for smaller Budapest flats, particularly during the traditional late-summer university rental rush.

Foreign students should not, however, assume that the planned subsidised rental properties will automatically be available to them. Eligibility rules have not yet been published.

Foreign professionals and expatriates renting in Budapest could also benefit indirectly. Even if publicly supported apartments are reserved primarily for Hungarian residents or younger households, additional supply at the lower and middle end of the market could reduce pressure elsewhere in the rental chain.

Property investors face a more complex picture. A stronger institutional rental sector would create a new competitor to Hungary’s overwhelmingly private rental market. At the same time, the government’s explicit intention to attract long-term institutional capital could create investment opportunities in professionally managed residential developments.

Short-term rental investors must also consider the separate regulatory trend towards tighter Airbnb rules in Budapest.

Finally, large brownfield projects could change the geography of the capital itself. Rákosrendező and similar areas are not simply housing sites. If developed successfully, they could become entirely new urban neighbourhoods with transport links, retail, services and public spaces, affecting property values far beyond the boundaries of the projects.

The Hungarian housing market now faces a question of execution

The direction of policy has clearly changed. Hungary’s government is acknowledging that increasing purchasing power through subsidised mortgages alone cannot solve a housing shortage if the physical supply of homes remains constrained.

The Wekerle programme therefore represents something potentially more significant: a move towards construction, rental housing, dormitories, institutional investment and a more active state role in the housing market.

But the hardest decisions have not yet been made.

The programme must still determine who receives subsidised housing, how low rents will be financed over the long term, how much public money will be spent per completed home, who will own and maintain the properties, and how risks will be divided between taxpayers, banks, developers and institutional investors.

Above all, the government will have to demonstrate that its preferred brownfield projects offer value for money.

The first important deadline is 30 September 2026, when the Wekerle Housing Construction Programme is due to be prepared. A review of major housing investments follows in October, while proposals for affordable rental financing and the state housing agency are due by the end of December.

Until those details are available, the Wekerle programme should be viewed neither as a guaranteed rescue of the Hungarian housing market nor as an inevitable financial failure.

Its ambitions address real weaknesses: too few homes, expensive rents, inadequate student accommodation and a rental sector with little institutional depth. The decisive question is whether Hungary can translate those ambitions into homes at a cost that makes them genuinely affordable – not only for their tenants, but for the public finances as well.

World.title: Fungal infection in Hungary: drug-resistant ringworm strain raises concern
World.content:
An emerging fungal infection in Hungary has drawn attention after a new international study found that Trichophyton indotineae, a fungus capable of causing severe and sometimes drug-resistant skin infections, is being detected increasingly often around the world. The pathogen has already been identified in Hungary, although current evidence does not suggest a widespread Hungarian outbreak.

According to HVG, the fungus is behind a form of ringworm, or tinea, that has become a growing concern because infections can be more extensive and harder to treat than ordinary cases.

Despite its English name, ringworm has nothing to do with worms. It is a fungal skin infection caused by dermatophytes and typically produces an itchy, red or scaly rash, often with a circular or ring-like appearance. The infection can spread through direct skin contact or via contaminated objects and surfaces, including shared towels and shower areas.

Symptoms to watch for Common signs include an itchy, red or scaly rash, often with a ring-shaped border. T. indotineae infections can sometimes be more extensive than ordinary ringworm and may affect large areas of skin. When to see a doctor: seek medical advice if the rash is severe, spreading, does not improve with treatment, or appears after recent travel or contact with someone with a persistent fungal infection. Avoid using steroid creams on a suspected fungal rash unless advised by a doctor, as they can make the infection harder to recognise and treat.

Fungal infection in Hungary already confirmed

Hungary recorded its first scientifically described case of T. indotineae in 2025. Researchers at the University of Debrecen reported the infection in a man in his twenties who had travelled to a region where the pathogen was already endemic. Laboratory testing, including whole-genome sequencing, confirmed the diagnosis.

There is, however, an important distinction between that case and the broader concern surrounding the fungus.

The Hungarian isolate was susceptible to the antifungal drugs tested, including terbinafine, and the patient responded well to topical treatment. T. indotineae as a species is nevertheless frequently associated with resistance to terbinafine, one of the drugs commonly used against fungal skin infections.

This means the presence of the fungus in Hungary should not be interpreted as evidence that an untreatable infection is now spreading widely across the country.

If you missed it – How to see a doctor without insurance in Budapest: a tourist’s guide

Global detections are rising sharply

The latest research, published in the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s Emerging Infectious Diseases journal, examined laboratory identification data collected between 2022 and 2025.

Researchers analysed more than 1.6 million fungal spectra submitted by laboratories in 54 countries. T. indotineae was identified in data submitted from 29 countries, with the overwhelming majority of detections coming from Europe – although the authors stressed that this was partly because European laboratories were heavily represented in the surveillance network.

The proportion of T. indotineae detections within the closely related T. mentagrophytes complex nearly tripled during the study period, rising from 4.6% in 2022 to 13.1% in 2025. The number of participating centres detecting the fungus also increased substantially.

The researchers cautioned that their data do not show how many individual people have been infected. The figures are based on laboratory spectra rather than confirmed patient numbers, meaning they should primarily be viewed as evidence that the pathogen is being detected across an expanding geographical area.

Why doctors are concerned

T. indotineae first attracted significant attention in South Asia, particularly India, where dermatologists began reporting large numbers of extensive and difficult-to-treat fungal infections. It has since been reported across Europe, North America, South America and other regions.

The concern is resistance. Some strains carry mutations that make terbinafine less effective, potentially requiring different drugs or longer courses of treatment. The US CDC describes T. indotineae as an emerging public-health concern because infections can cover large areas of the body and may be difficult to treat.

International travel is one route through which infections can reach new countries, but researchers have also documented cases without recent travel history in parts of Europe, suggesting that local transmission can become established. The new study cites Germany as one country where infections among patients without recent travel have increasingly been recorded.

What people in Hungary should know

For most people, the discovery does not mean there is reason for alarm. Ordinary ringworm remains a common and generally treatable fungal infection.

However, the CDC advises seeking medical attention when a suspected ringworm infection is unusually severe or widespread, fails to improve with treatment, or follows contact with someone known to have a serious infection. People should also tell their doctor about recent travel. Steroid creams should not be used on suspected ringworm without medical advice, as they can worsen fungal infections and make diagnosis more difficult.

For Hungary, the main significance of the latest findings is therefore surveillance rather than evidence of an epidemic. The fungus has crossed the country’s borders before, and the international data suggest that European healthcare systems may encounter it increasingly often.

As T. indotineae continues to spread internationally, accurate diagnosis and monitoring will be crucial – especially because the infection can look similar to more ordinary forms of ringworm while potentially responding very differently to treatment.

World.title: Hungary Weekly Briefing is out: Migration clash, Ukraine veto and a widening budget gap
World.content:
Hungary’s political landscape remained highly active this week, with migration once again moving to the centre of the domestic and European debate, while the government continued to define its position on Ukraine, EU relations and the first major tests of the post-election political order.

In politics, the key questions centred on Hungary’s continued migration emergency, the government’s attempt to resolve the EUR 1 million-a-day EU fine, and Budapest’s decision to keep blocking parts of Ukraine’s accession process over minority-rights concerns. At home, the first signs of pressure on the new administration appeared alongside fresh polling, while Fidesz and Mi Hazánk are beginning to confront the strategic realities of opposition.

The economy and business picture was dominated by a widening budget gap, continued cost-of-living pressure and a growing list of domestic policy changes, from pensions and social spending to Airbnb regulation and the bottle-return system. Meanwhile, in diplomacy, Hungary took a firmer line on alleged Russian hybrid activity, Péter Magyar moved closer to the European People’s Party, and Budapest hosted a busy round of European and bilateral diplomatic engagements.

World.title: K-pop in Hungary is no longer just a teenage trend: it is becoming a cultural movement – interview
World.content:
K-pop in Hungary has moved far beyond fan playlists and dance covers. What began as a niche passion among teenagers has grown into a vibrant community that leads young Hungarians towards Korean language, food, fashion, travel and even performance. In an interview with Daily News Hungary, Yu Hye Ryong, Director of the Korean Cultural Center in Hungary, explains why Hungarian fans stand out in Europe, how Budapest is becoming a stage for local K-pop talent, and why parents might want to look beyond the glitter, choreography and screaming crowds. Exclusive interview:

K-pop in Hungary: development és character

Daily News Hungary (DNH): How has the popularity of K-pop changed in Hungary in recent years?

Yu Hye Ryong, Director of the Korean Cultural Center in Hungary

Yu Hye Ryong: In the late 2010s, when K-pop was still relatively new in Hungary, the scene was largely driven by teenagers and young adults, particularly fans of groups such as BTS and BLACKPINK. At the time, K-pop was consumed primarily through fan communities, with a strong focus on music and choreography.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, live performances were understandably affected, but online consumption of K-pop actually grew. The spread of short-form video content through platforms such as TikTok and YouTube Shorts made K-pop much more accessible and significantly lowered the barrier to discovering it.

Over the past few years, K-pop has developed into a much more mainstream cultural phenomenon in Hungary, with the audience growing to a point where large-scale offline events are now possible. For example, at MOKKOJI KOREA at Budapest Park in 2024, SUNMI, AB6IX and Dreamcatcher performed in Hungary for the first time. The event was free of charge, yet demand was so high that advance registration was required.

What is particularly interesting is that people are no longer consuming K-pop simply as a form of music or as individual concerts. Their interest often expands in a chain: K-pop → K-dance → K-beauty → Korean language → K-food → travel to Korea.

DNH: Why is K-pop particularly appealing to young people in Hungary? Who are the most active fans today, and is the fan base continuing to grow?

Yu Hye Ryong: One of the great strengths of K-pop is that it is not a form of content that is complete with music alone. Music, choreography, fashion, visual content, performance, the artists’ stories and fan communities all come together to create a much broader experience.

K-pop is also a culture that is easy to participate in. People do not simply listen to the music. They learn the choreography, learn the Korean lyrics and sing along, create cover videos, or form teams with friends and perform together.

From the participants we meet through our cultural centre’s programmes, teenagers and young adults are still the most active fan group. At the same time, however, the range of people interested in Korean culture is gradually expanding.

We often see people who first discovered Korea through K-pop several years ago now learning Korean, travelling to Korea, or becoming interested in Korean films, food and other aspects of Korean culture.

Ultimately, K-pop fans do not remain simply consumers of content. I think one of the most important strengths of K-pop is that it encourages people to learn about the culture they love, express themselves through it, and experience it together with others.

If you missed it: Nearly 17,000 visitors attended Korea Days – 7th KoreaON Festival on Margaret Island in Budapest – photos

DNH: Does the K-pop community in Hungary have any characteristics that distinguish it from those in other European countries?

Yu Hye Ryong: What I find particularly impressive in Hungary is the high level of participation and the strong sense of community among fans.

Hungary is not a particularly large country in terms of population, but people who are passionate about K-pop are extremely active. They form their own dance teams, practice and perform together, participate in competitions and cultural events, and regularly take part in programmes organised by our cultural centre.

We often see people who meet through one programme coming back to participate in another, forming new teams together or supporting each other’s activities.

So it goes beyond simply sharing a love of the same music. A genuine community naturally develops around that shared interest.

We consider this kind of participation very important. We believe that meaningful cultural exchange happens at a much deeper level when people do not simply watch or consume another culture, but actually learn it, practice it and create something together.

Soruce: Korean Cultural Center in Hungary

K-pop: the gateway to discovering Korea

DNH: Does interest in K-pop also lead to interest in other aspects of Korean culture, such as fashion, the Korean language, food, film, tourism and traditional culture?

Yu Hye Ryong: Yes. This is something we see very frequently through our work at the cultural centre.

For many people, K-pop serves as a kind of gateway through which they first discover Korea. They may become interested in Korean because they want to understand the lyrics of their favorite songs. Then they start watching Korean films or dramas, trying Korean food, or planning a trip to Korea. Their interests naturally expand from one area to another.

Fashion and beauty are another example. People may become interested in the fashion or makeup styles of K-pop artists and then think, “I would like to try that myself.”

The Korean language is a particularly good example. The natural desire to sing along to a favorite song can lead to an interest in Hangul and Korean pronunciation, and eventually become the motivation to actually study Korean.

In other words, the boundaries between the K-pop fandom and the broader Korean Wave fandom are relatively fluid. People who initially come to K-pop do not necessarily remain interested in K-pop alone. They often develop an interest in Korean dramas, food, language, travel, products and Korean culture more broadly.

What is particularly interesting is that this interest does not necessarily stop with contemporary culture. We have visitors who first come to the cultural centre because of K-pop and later participate in Korean language classes, Korean food programmes, film screenings, traditional music or traditional dance programmes.

That is why we do not see K-pop and traditional culture as separate worlds. K-pop can be the first door through which people discover Korea, but it does not have to be the last.

Soruce: Korean Cultural Center in Hungary

DNH: What role does K-pop play in the activities of the Korean Cultural Center in Hungary?

Yu Hye Ryong: K-pop is one of the important areas of our cultural centre’s activities. However, our goal is not simply to introduce popular K-pop content or bring performances to audiences. What matters to us is using K-pop as a way to encourage people to experience Korean culture directly and become active participants in it.

Through our K-POP Academy, we regularly offer K-pop dance classes. We also invite choreographers and other professionals working in Korea to conduct special workshops, giving Hungarian participants the opportunity to learn directly from and interact with professionals working in the K-pop industry.

Last October, we also hosted the Hungarian preliminary round of the Changwon K-POP World Festival with MondoCON. Through this programme, local participants have the opportunity to showcase their skills and challenge themselves on an international K-pop stage.

More recently, we have taken this one step further by focusing on the creation of original content planned by the cultural centre and made together with local participants.

Two examples are KCC IDOL and K-POP SINGERS. KCC IDOL is designed to allow participants to experience the entire process together — from practicing and building teamwork to preparing for and performing on stage. K-POP SINGERS expands the focus beyond dance to singing, allowing participants to learn and practice Korean songs and experience the process of recording and performing.

If I had to describe our approach in one sentence, it would be: “From audience to participant, and from participant to performer and creator.”

This year, we are taking this approach even further with a project called K-POP in Budapest. Local K-pop singers and dancers will practice together and perform in Budapest, while the entire journey — from preparation to the final performance — will be captured on film and produced as a music film centered around busking.

Rather than simply producing a promotional video introducing K-pop, we wanted to create something in which the people who actually love and practice K-pop in Hungary become the protagonists, and Budapest itself becomes the stage.

We believe that when people in Hungary take K-pop created in Korea and reinterpret it through their own city and their own experiences, creating new stories in the process, that itself can be a meaningful form of cultural exchange.

Soruce: Korean Cultural Center in Hungary

Read also: 6th DAESANG Eat and Travel Film Festival happened in Budapest as its First Edition in Europe

K-pop events in Hungary

DNH: Which K-pop programmes and events are currently the most popular in Hungary? Are there any special events people can look forward to this year?

Yu Hye Ryong: Interest in K-pop dance remains extremely high. There is a steady demand for dance classes, cover dance activities and workshops with professional choreographers, and our K-POP Academy continues to offer regular programmes.

At the same time, the ways in which people enjoy K-pop are not limited to dance. Many people also want to sing Korean songs themselves, so we are expanding opportunities for participation in the vocal field through programmes such as K-POP SINGERS.

In particular, we want to create programmes in which participants do more than simply attend an event for a day. We want them to experience a process together over a period of time: learning a song or choreography, practising together, recording and filming, and ultimately performing in front of an audience.

Through this process, participants are no longer simply spectators. They become the protagonists of the programme.

Our K-POP in Budapest project this year is a good example of this approach. Local participants will prepare their own K-pop performances, take part in busking performances and filming in Budapest, and have the entire process and final performance captured as a music film.

Going forward, we want to continue expanding opportunities for people not simply to watch K-pop, but to learn it, create together and express themselves on stage.

Detailed information about our programmes and events is available through the Korean Cultural Center in Hungary’s official website and social media channels.

Soruce: Korean Cultural Center in Hungary

DNH: What are some common misconceptions among people who are unfamiliar with K-pop? What would you say to Hungarian parents who see K-pop simply as a teenage trend?

Yu Hye Ryong: For people who are not familiar with K-pop, the first things they may notice are the spectacular performances and the enthusiastic young fans. So it is understandable that they might see it simply as a form of popular culture that happens to be fashionable among teenagers.

Of course, K-pop is popular culture, and trends inevitably change. But when we meet young participants directly, what interests us is not only what they are listening to, but what they are doing because they love it.

They learn a new language because they want to understand the lyrics of their favorite songs. They practice for hours and sometimes for months to perfect a piece of choreography or a song. They learn how to work with teammates, overcome the nervousness of performing on stage, make new friends and gain confidence.

For some, K-pop becomes the starting point for studying Korean or developing an interest in Korean food, films, history and society — and eventually even visiting Korea themselves.

So if their children are interested in K-pop, I would encourage parents to look not only at what their children are watching and listening to, but also at what they are learning and creating through that interest.

Interests naturally change as young people grow older. But the confidence they gain on stage, the discipline they develop through repeated practice, the ability to cooperate with others, and their curiosity about a new language and culture can stay with them for much longer.

K-pop can be the first door through which someone encounters Korea. I believe the role of a cultural centre is to help people who enter through that first door discover all the many other doors that lie beyond it.

Read our exclusive interview – South Korean Ambassador: Hungary is no longer just an investment destination; it’s a strategic innovation partner

Daily News Hungary is the official media partner of the Korean Cultural Centre in Hungary.

World.title: Hungary fuel prices face first major test as oil climbs and government rules out costly cap
World.content:
Hungary fuel prices are heading towards their first serious test since the government scrapped the protected-price system earlier this summer. With global oil prices climbing again, Prime Minister Péter Magyar says his government is preparing targeted help for motorists – but this time, it wants a solution that does not create shortages or cost taxpayers tens of billions of forints every month.

Global oil markets have turned sharply higher again amid renewed tensions between the United States and Iran and fears over supplies from the Middle East. Brent crude climbed above USD 96 a barrel on Saturday, putting renewed pressure on fuel prices across Europe.

That creates an uncomfortable economic and political test for the Hungarian government: what happens when fuel becomes substantially more expensive, but simply fixing the retail price is no longer considered a sustainable answer?

Hungary fuel prices back in focus

In a Saturday Facebook post, Prime Minister Péter Magyar said he had discussed the challenges facing Hungary’s economy and energy sector with Economy and Energy Minister István Kapitány.

The government, Magyar wrote, was working to provide motorists with “effective and targeted” assistance as soon as possible amid what he described as an increasingly difficult global market environment.

Crucially, however, he also appeared to draw a line under the previous model of intervention.

Magyar said Hungary needed a solution which, unlike the protected fuel price, would not lead to shortages and would not cost the state budget – and therefore taxpayers – tens of billions of forints every month, equivalent to tens of millions of euros.

The statement marks a notable change in tone after months in which government intervention in fuel prices became increasingly familiar to Hungarian motorists.

From Orbán’s protected price to a market-based system

The protected fuel price was introduced by Viktor Orbán’s government on 9 March 2026 following a surge in international oil prices. Petrol was capped at HUF 595 per litre, around EUR 1.64, while diesel was limited to HUF 615, approximately EUR 1.69 at current exchange rates.

After winning the election, Magyar initially announced that the incoming government would maintain the scheme. In April, he said an agreement had been reached with Hungarian oil and gas company MOL to preserve the protected prices without imposing additional costs on the budget.

By June, however, market conditions had changed. With filling-station prices falling below the official ceiling, the new government moved to abolish the system. Legislation nevertheless retained the possibility of introducing regulated prices again if market conditions changed disproportionately and government intervention was deemed necessary to protect consumers.

Now the international environment is deteriorating once again – and this time the government appears reluctant to reach immediately for the same tool.

If you missed it: Cost of living in Hungary: Inflation has fallen – so why do people still feel poorer?

The first real test for the new approach

The challenge is not merely the price displayed at petrol stations.

Artificially suppressing fuel prices can offer motorists immediate relief, but the previous Hungarian system also demonstrated the potential costs of broad price intervention. Magyar’s latest comments explicitly acknowledge two of those problems: supply shortages and a significant burden on public finances.

That makes the coming weeks an important test of economic policy.

For years, Hungarian consumers have repeatedly seen the state intervene when politically sensitive prices rise sharply. The risk is that such intervention gradually creates an expectation that the government should prevent market prices from increasing even when the underlying cause comes from abroad.

Magyar’s government now appears to be looking for a narrower alternative: helping those most exposed to rising fuel costs without once again fixing the price for the entire market.

The prime minister said he and Kapitány had also reviewed the direction of Hungary’s new domestic and foreign economic policy, as well as measures needed to establish a stable energy sector.

With global oil prices moving higher, those discussions may quickly become more than long-term economic planning. Hungary fuel prices could soon show whether the government is genuinely ready to move away from broad price controls when doing so becomes politically difficult.

Fidesz reacts

The Fidesz party, which suffered a defeat in April, is now launching a fierce attack on the Tisza government’s economic policy, in the hope of winning back voters.

At the same time, we must not forget that, on the one hand, this state intervention runs counter to the development of a healthy economy, and, on the other, Viktor Orbán has close ties with none other than Trump, who was in fact responsible for the rise in oil prices through the attack on Iran.

And if the war in Iran is not set to end any time soon – for which there is no indication – then further price rises are to be expected, for example in flights: Ryanair and Wizz Air sound the alarm – what could happen to air fares?

World.title: Hungary weather: Cold front this weekend, then heat, heavy rain and sharp cooling next week
World.content:
Hungary’s weather is about to change several times within just over a week. A cold front crossing the country on Saturday will bring a temporary drop in temperatures for Sunday, before summer heat quickly returns. From the middle of next week, however, a much more significant change could arrive, bringing substantial rainfall and eventually genuinely autumnal temperatures.

A cold front is moving across Hungary from the north and north-west on Saturday, 5 September. Despite increasing cloud cover, significant widespread rainfall is not expected, although scattered showers and thunderstorms may develop.

HungaroMet has warned of possible thunderstorms in several counties, particularly in the north-east and south, with storms also possible in the south-west later in the day. Wind gusts of 60–70 km/h, locally exceeding 70 km/h, may accompany stronger storms, and isolated hail cannot be ruled out. Temperatures will nevertheless remain summery, with afternoon highs between 25 and 34°C.

Sunday: Cooler, sunny and mostly dry

The cold front will be more noticeable on Sunday, 6 September, when temperatures fall by several degrees.

Mostly clear or lightly cloudy weather is expected across Hungary, with no significant precipitation. More cumulus clouds may develop in the north-east, while north-westerly and northerly winds could occasionally strengthen.

Morning temperatures will generally range between 10 and 18°C, although sheltered areas could fall slightly below 10°C. Afternoon highs are forecast between 24 and 29°C.

The cooler weather will not last long, however. Temperatures will begin rising again almost immediately as Hungary heads into another short spell of late-summer heat.

Hungary weather next week: Day-by-day forecast

Monday, 7 September: Summer returns

Temperatures will begin climbing again on Monday, with mostly dry and warm conditions expected. Forecasts currently indicate afternoon highs of roughly 27–32°C, meaning the weekend’s brief cooling will already be fading.

Tuesday, 8 September: Temperatures above 30°C again

Tuesday could be one of the warmest days of the week. Maximum temperatures are expected to reach around 28–33°C, bringing summer-like heat back to much of Hungary.

For anyone hoping that Saturday’s cold front marked the beginning of autumn, the answer will therefore be a clear no – at least temporarily.

If you missed it: another popular Hungarian lake dries out, Bölömbika lookout shows critical conditions

Wednesday, 9 September: A major change begins

The first wave of a more substantial weather change is currently forecast to arrive from Wednesday, when another cold front reaches Hungary.

One of its most striking effects could be a large temperature difference between different parts of the country. Western Hungary may already experience much cooler conditions while the east remains hot, potentially creating a 10–15°C difference between the two sides of the country.

Unlike Saturday’s front, this system is also expected to bring more significant rainfall.

Thursday, 10 September: Cold front spreads across Hungary

The effects of the front are expected to become much more widespread by Thursday.

Temperatures should fall across larger parts of the country, while rain could affect numerous regions. Current forecasts suggest this will be the point when the first major cooling phase becomes established.

The exact location and amount of precipitation remain uncertain several days in advance, so the forecast may still change considerably.

Friday, 11 September: Sharp cooling possible in western Hungary

By Friday, some western parts of Hungary could experience a dramatic change compared with the heat seen earlier in the week.

Current projections suggest temperatures in some western areas may reach only around 15°C – potentially almost 20 degrees below Tuesday’s highest values.

Eastern parts of the country may remain somewhat warmer, but the overall trend will be firmly towards cooler weather.

Catch up on the week’s biggest stories from Hungary — politics, economy, business and diplomacy, all in one place. Subscribe here: Substack

Saturday, 12 September: Autumn weather and heavier rain

A second phase of the weather change could begin around Saturday.

Forecasts currently indicate that a Mediterranean cyclone may start influencing Hungary, bringing widespread and potentially substantial rainfall. From this point, autumnal temperatures are expected across the country rather than only in western regions.

Sunday, 13 September: Widespread rain could continue

Sunday could remain cool and wet as the Mediterranean system affects Hungary.

Between 12 and 15 September, current projections suggest that repeated rainfall could bring approximately 30–70 millimetres of precipitation across the country, with larger amounts possible in western Hungary.

Such rainfall would be particularly notable after the prolonged dry conditions of recent months.

Summer first, then a real taste of autumn

The coming days could therefore bring an unusually sharp weather contrast to Hungary: temperatures above 30°C on Tuesday, the arrival of a cold front from Wednesday, highs potentially around 15°C in parts of the west by Friday, followed by widespread autumnal weather and significant rainfall over the weekend.

Meteorologists stress that forecasts for the second half of next week still carry considerable uncertainty, particularly regarding the timing and strength of the expected Mediterranean cyclone and the amount of rainfall it may bring. Nevertheless, current models increasingly point towards a much more substantial change than the brief cold front crossing Hungary this Saturday.
