Currently, 30 percent of products made by China's military companies are for military purposes and the other 70 percent for civilian purposes, he said.

In the future, high-tech industries will cover half of the military-related economy, Long added.

World.title: Dangerous stunts get thumbs-down from video platforms
World.content:
Multiple social media and video streaming platforms will limit who can view videos that depict dangerous stunts - and may even prohibit such material - in an effort to discourage imitators.

In November, daredevil stunt climber Wu Yongning fell to his death while scaling a skyscraper in Changsha, Hunan province. Wu, 26, had more than 1.3 million followers on social media who regularly devoured his breathtaking videos and photos. He climbed with no protective gear.

Last month, Wu's account on Sina Weibo stopped updating, leading followers to worry about his well-being.

On Friday, Wu's girlfriend confirmed on social media that the "rooftop daredevil" had fallen and died.

"Today is Dec 8. It makes me think of Nov 8, the day that you left us, left this world," she wrote.

Wu's family also confirmed his death to Jiefang Daily, a newspaper in Shanghai.

Meipai, Kuaishou, Xiaohuoshan and other video platforms on which Wu posted content, expressed their condolences, according to ThePaper.cn. Platform representatives told the news outlet that China currently has no law regulating extreme stunt videos, but each platform will update its content policy to discourage imitators.

Kuaishou said Wu's account had been restricted - meaning that only the uploader can see it - in September because of its depictions of dangerous acts.

Xiaohuoshan said it will ban video livestreams of dangerous stunts because live interactions between the performer and the audience could be a distraction and lead to catastrophic results.

The platform also said it will respect the desires of Wu's family in dealing with the videos.

All of Wu's stunt videos on the three platforms had been restricted or taken down as of Monday. A cellphone video of Wu performing his last stunt and falling to his death on Nov 8, has also been taken down.

Wu was part of an informal community of young thrill-seekers around the world who engage in "roof-topping" - climbing to the top or to high ledges of buildings, often without a permit or protective gear, to take stomach-churning pictures and videos. The activity is generally illegal.

In January, an 18-year-old identified as Alexander Sh, fell to his death from Europe's second-tallest building - the 350-meter OKO Tower in Moscow. He was trying to take a selfie when he slipped and fell, Russian media reported.

zhangzhihao@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Taiwan's New Party vows to help improve relations
World.content:
Delegation to Beijing reaffirms support for one-China, rejection of agitators

Top political adviser Yu Zhengsheng met with a Taiwan delegation representing the island's New Party in Beijing on Monday to discuss the peaceful development of cross-Straits relations and how to achieve the "great rejuvenation" of the Chinese nation.

Yu praised the New Party's unbroken stance upholding the 1992 Consensus, which embodies the one-China principle, since the party's establishment, as well as its peaceful approach to relations.

The 19th National Congress of the Communist Party of China, which was held in October, further clarified the guidelines and policies addressing Taiwan, Yu said.

In his opening address to delegates during the congress, Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Central Committee of the CPC, called the one-China principle the political foundation of cross-Straits relations, and said that attempts to move toward "Taiwan independence" in any form will be defeated.

Taiwan will share development opportunities on the Chinese mainland, and its residents will enjoy the same treatment as mainland people as they pursue studies, start businesses, seek jobs or come to live on the mainland, Xi said in the address.

Yok Mu-ming, chairman of the New Party and head of the Taiwan delegation, said the party has firmly upheld the one-China principle and promoted peace.

The delegation also met on Monday with Zhang Zhijun, head of the State Council's Taiwan Affairs Office.

Zhang and Yok agreed that the one-China principle must be upheld going forward, expressed firm opposition to separatist activities and vowed to make efforts toward peaceful relations.

Both sides agreed to establish and improve mechanisms of communication, share opinions on major issues in the relationship and promote exchanges and communication in all fields - especially between youth. They further agreed to create a constructive and convenient environment for the development of Taiwan youth on the mainland.

Zhang said cross-Straits relations have faced challenges because the island's Democratic Progressive Party has refused to clearly express support for the one-China principle, which led to the mainland suspending official communications with the island.

He said that a "Taiwan independence" force had recently stirred up the island, proposing the removal of Chinese mainland elements in a variety of fields.

"Its aim is to cut the historical ties between Taiwan and the mainland, reduce public awareness that Taiwan people are part of the Chinese nation and limit many cultural influences on the island," he said.

Some people advocating "Taiwan independence" have pushed for amending the law, and have proposed changing the island's constitution. "This shows that separatist activities and the group supporting 'independence' pose the most serious threat to the peaceful development of cross-Straits relations," Zhang said.

He warned that people from both sides should be vigilant and firmly oppose such activities.

luowangshu@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Former Chongqing political official facing corruption investigation
World.content:
Sun Zhengcai, the former secretary of Chongqing Municipal Committee of the Communist Party of China, has been placed under investigation on suspicion of accepting bribes, according to the Supreme People's Procuratorate on Monday.

According to the procuratorate, Sun has been placed under "coercive measures", which may include summons by force, bail, residential surveillance, detention and arrest.

The investigation is underway, the procuratorate said in a statement released on Monday.

In July, the CPC Central Commission for Discipline Inspection launched an investigation into Sun for "serious violations of Party discipline".

The CCDI said in a news release that Sun betrayed Party principles and ignored the Party code of conduct and rules.

He was found to have seriously violated the CPC's eight-point code on frugality and maintaining close ties with the masses, seeking pomp, ostentation and privileges, according to the CCDI.

The CCDI said he was guilty of nepotism and seeking benefits in selection of officials. He was found by the CCDI to have leaked confidential Party information and seriously breached Party rules on integrity.

Moreover, he abused power and used his job to gain benefits for others, then accepted their huge bribes in return, either paid in cash or properties, the CCDI said. He was found to seek substantial benefits for his relatives' businesses and accepted valuable gifts, the CCDI said.

The anti-graft inspectors also accused Sun of bureaucracy and sloth in work and degradation and power-for-sex trades, according to the CCDI.

Sun totally deviated from the Party spirit and political requirements of senior officials, the CCDI said in the statement, adding that his misconduct betrayed the trust of the CPC Central Committee and the public, inflicting huge harm to the Party and the country with "extremely bad" social influences.

The CCDI transferred the criminal evidence involving his case to judicial authorities for further investigation.

In September, the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee expelled Sun from the Party and dismissed him from public office.

China Daily - Xinhua

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018985/Can VR Capture the Power of China’s Ancient Caves?
World.title: Can VR Capture the Power of China’s Ancient Caves?
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018985/Can VR Capture the Power of China’s Ancient Caves?
World.content:
Under the blazing July sun, Zhang, a high school teacher from northern China, stood outside the Digital Exhibition Center of the Mogao Grottoes, a modern building designed to resemble the surrounding dunes. A shuttle bus would soon take him and other tourists to the foot of Mingsha Mountain, where they would see the original Mogao Grottoes: 492 caves containing Buddhist murals and painted sculptures spanning more than a thousand years, now strictly protected as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Zhang had just watched two introductory films at the center, “A Thousand Years of Mogao Caves” and “The Splendor of Buddha’s Palace,” the latter screened in its dome theater. His eyes sparkled with excitement. “It is so spectacular that I am speechless! I hope other heritage sites in China can be presented like this.”

The Mogao Grottoes in Dunhuang, northwestern China’s Gansu province, are the product of more than a millennium of cultural exchange between East and West along the historic Silk Road. Renowned for the extraordinary aesthetic and cultural value of their cave art, they attract large numbers of tourists. Yet the grottoes are intrinsically fragile, threatened by both the surrounding desert and the carbon dioxide and humidity generated by visitors.

To reduce pressure on the caves and ensure their long-term preservation, the Dunhuang Academy, which manages and researches the site, has been developing the Digital Dunhuang project since the late 1980s. More than 200 caves have been documented through photography, image stitching, and laser scanning, with the material transformed into online and on-site experiences spanning films, virtual and augmented reality, and museum exhibitions. These digital experiences have become an increasingly prominent part of visiting Mogao.

Putting “cultural heritage” and “digital technology” together creates an immediate tension. Heritage looks backward, toward the past and the old; technology looks forward, toward the future and the new. When the two are brought together, digital representations exist alongside the physical heritage itself, raising questions such as: what qualities of the original are irreplaceable, and to what extent can they be reproduced or conveyed digitally?

I conducted a year of fieldwork at the Mogao Grottoes between 2024 and 2025, spending long periods in both the physical caves and digital exhibitions and talking with visitors. While physical and digital exhibitions at heritage sites can tell separate stories, at Mogao they are closely intertwined. The tension between heritage and technology highlights both their differences and how they complement each other, as visitors often observed.

Among the visitors I spoke with was a middle-aged British artist traveling with her partner. The two had sharply contrasting reactions. She was fascinated by the distinctive smell inside the caves, a mixture of dust, moisture, and history that would be difficult to reproduce digitally. Her partner, by contrast, was perfectly content with the digital exhibitions. “I really got my fix! I could just go with the digital,” he said. He drew parallels with Lascaux Cave in France, where replicas receive visitors while the original, closed to the public since 1963, is preserved.

For some caves, digital representations are the only way visitors can experience their fragile artworks. Cave 285, built during the Western Wei period and containing inscriptions dated to 538 and 539, is one of Mogao’s most important early caves, renowned for its rich murals and diverse artistic styles. It is currently closed to the public for conservation, but a virtual reality exhibition immerses visitors in the stories depicted on the murals and even lets them use handheld controllers as drumsticks to play music alongside mythological beings.

Wang, visiting from the southern city of Shenzhen with her young child, told me: “I like it very much, and it is also child-friendly. The VR shows real scenes from the cave while telling the stories in detail. It even surpasses the real cave!”

For visitors like Wang, VR not only reproduces the physical cave but creates a space of its own, allowing them to experience it in a playful, multisensory way impossible inside the original. “I am so touched that I almost cried,” another visitor told me. “I know Cave 285 is not open to the public, so I am very grateful for the opportunity to see it up close.”

For caves that remain open, experiencing both their physical and digital versions can offer a more nuanced perspective on the art. Cave 61 contains the largest surviving Buddhist historical landscape painting at Mogao. Based on the geography of the Tang dynasty (618–907), the mural depicts pilgrimage routes leading to the sacred Mount Wutai, over 2,000 kilometers east of the caves. It is also featured in “The Splendor of Buddha’s Palace” in the center’s 360-degree dome theater.

Later, on a poplar-shaded path, a college student, Xiaoyang, reflected on the contrast. “When I saw the mural from Cave 61 on the big screen, it was so bright. It really looked real, but I knew it wasn’t. I couldn’t feel the traces of time. But when I actually stood inside the cave and faced the mural, I began wondering how ancient cartographers had trudged through Mount Wutai and how painters had depicted the scene on the wall.”

Her response points to what digital reproductions can lose even as they make the art more visible. On-screen, details are easier to see, but this digital representation weakens the power of age and decay that connect viewers to the mural and the people who created it centuries ago. The digital image shows what can be difficult to see inside the cave, while the physical mural confronts visitors with the passage of time. Together, they encourage visitors to consider both the image and the history behind it.

Another crucial component of Digital Dunhuang is the digital repatriation of manuscripts and artifacts now held overseas. In the early 20th century, the discovery of more than 70,000 manuscripts, paintings, and other objects in the Library Cave, or Cave 17, opened a new chapter in Mogao’s history. Most were removed amid the era’s turmoil. Now dispersed around the world, they are being brought together digitally through collaborations between the Dunhuang Academy and international institutions.

Adjacent to Caves 16 and 17 is a museum housing the exhibition “Treasure in Caves,” which recounts the artifacts’ dispersal and virtual reunification. Replicas of objects now scattered among collections worldwide stand side by side in rows of glass cases.

Visiting the caves and exhibition offers complementary experiences, making this place marked by loss feel slightly more complete. A woman in her 50s discussing Cave 17, a memorial cave containing a statue of the Tang-dynasty monk Hong Bian, said: “Cave 17 is a physical place that has endured these historical events. The exhibition tells their story and shows the artifacts, so I can hear the echoes of history and finally breathe a sigh of relief.”

Like these visitors, I have found my own answers to questions about the authenticity. Now writing about Dunhuang from afar, I often revisit photographs from my fieldwork. Yet when I close my eyes, I can still recall the original caves: their warmth, their solemnity, and their sense of history.

The tension between the digital and physical does not necessarily have to be resolved in favor of one or the other. Digital representations can make inaccessible caves available, reveal otherwise difficult-to-see details, and reunite objects that have been physically dispersed. But they can also erase the traces of time and distance that give the originals much of their power. At Mogao, the two forms are most effective not when one substitutes for the other but when they work in tandem to deepen the experience.

By presenting the grottoes from multiple perspectives while carefully controlling access to the physical caves, the Dunhuang Academy shows how digitization can expand our understanding of authenticity rather than simply imitate the original. Perhaps another thousand years from now, the Mogao Grottoes will still move us, both through their carefully preserved physical form and through the digital versions that capture, interpret, and transmit them.

According to research guidelines, all names in this article are pseudonyms.



Portrait artist: Wang Zhenhao.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018986/China Gives Schools More Flexibility as Enrollment Shrinks
World.title: China Gives Schools More Flexibility as Enrollment Shrinks
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018986/China Gives Schools More Flexibility as Enrollment Shrinks
World.content:
Amid falling primary school enrollment, multiple regions in China are combining primary and secondary school levels, encouraging primary school teachers to transfer to higher grades, and creating schools with flexible enrollment.

Starting this September, several newly built schools designed to allow more flexible enrollment in Yiwu, in the eastern Zhejiang province, as well as the eastern coastal city of Xiamen, have opened and welcomed their first classes of students.

The change comes amid decreasing numbers of new students enrolling in primary school. In 2025, 14.6 million students were reported to have enrolled in primary schools nationwide, down nearly 10% from the year before and 22% from the enrollment peak in 2023. The number of junior high school students is also expected to peak this year, according to the Ministry of Education.

Previously, primary schools have generally acted as independent institutions with relatively fixed sizes and facilities. But as student numbers decline, some regions are launching schools that adjust capacity according to fluctuating enrollment, known as “tidal,” or chaoxi, schools.

Two of the first such schools opened this fall in Yiwu. Of them, the New Silk Road School’s Choucheng campus accepts students from primary school through junior high school, and features facilities that can be “dynamically allocated to different grades,” according to the local government. The other, Suxi Middle School — which hosts both junior and senior high school students — has implemented a flexible enrollment policy that accommodates classes of different sizes depending on the year.

Huli Innovation Experimental School in the eastern coastal city of Xiamen also expanded from a nine-year to a 12-year school this year, cutting its primary and junior high classes to make room for 30 senior high school classes.

Another school in Xiamen, Lianhua Middle School’s Longshan campus, originally intended to be a primary school, was converted into a 36-class junior high school this fall.

In March, authorities in Hangzhou, the capital of Zhejiang province, announced plans to build the city’s first tidal school, with construction set to be completed in 2028. Over the next three years, four more such schools are planned for the city’s Xiaoshan District, with a total investment of over 1.5 billion yuan ($223 million). In addition to space for 8,100 junior and senior high school students, local education authorities estimate that the model could save 18.7 hectares of land and nearly 900 million yuan in public funds.

Since June, several regions, including the eastern Fujian, Anhui, and Jiangxi provinces, have also released announcements recruiting junior high school teachers from primary and senior high schools. A teacher transfer training program was also recently launched in Shanghai, helping teachers make the move from kindergartens to primary schools and from primary schools to junior high schools.

On social media, users claiming to be primary school teachers said they had been asked to transfer to other grades. Data shows that the number of full-time primary school teachers in China fell by 131,900 in 2025.

The topic has received more than 14 million views on microblogging platform Weibo, with many users expressing concerns about the quality of teaching, arguing that teachers accustomed to teaching primary school may struggle to adapt to the curriculum and student needs at the junior or senior high school level.

Some teachers who have transferred to other educational levels face issues such as lower pay and inadequate training, Chen Chunyong, a researcher at the National Academy of Educational Sciences, wrote in an online commentary.

Chen called for national and provincial authorities to establish certification standards for teachers transferring between educational levels, including clear requirements for academic qualifications, assessments, and training.

Xiong Bingqi, deputy director of the 21st Century Education Research Institute in Beijing, also said the new reforms may undermine the country’s recent promotion of small-class teaching.

“Many regions still use traditional class size to calculate teacher staffing allocations, leading to the conclusion that there is a ‘surplus of primary school teachers and they need to be transferred to other levels to reduce excess,’’ he said. “This kind of traditional logic hampers the implementation of small-class reforms and affects the long-term distribution of teaching resources.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Students on their first day of school in Kunshan, Jiangsu province, Aug. 30, 2022. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018983/Two Filmmakers, 1,100 Villages, and a Race to Record Rural China
World.title: Two Filmmakers, 1,100 Villages, and a Race to Record Rural China
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018983/Two Filmmakers, 1,100 Villages, and a Race to Record Rural China
World.content:
SHAANXI, Northwest China — “You have gone off route. Recalculating.” For the fourth time that day, Zhao Yushun and his wife, Yuan Zhenzhen, ignored the GPS. By then, jujube trees, signs advertising local specialties, and a view of distant mountains had already pulled them off course.

Now it was a farmer sorting pears beneath a black sunshade by the roadside in Dali County, northwestern China’s Shaanxi province.

“What kind of pear is this? I’ve never seen it before,” Zhao asks after they pull over. “How’s the harvest this year? Have people here been growing pears longer, or jujubes?”

“Jujubes,” the farmer says with a wry smile. His family has grown them since he was a child, but over the past decade more and more people have started planting them, and the returns are no longer what they once were. “Things are worth more when they’re scarce.”

As he speaks, Yuan raises her camera and starts recording, keeping it around waist height to make it less conspicuous.

The farmer soon moves beyond pears, telling Zhao about his years as a migrant worker in the southern tech hub of Shenzhen and his eventual return home to care for his children and aging parents. With jujube profits falling, he has also begun growing pears, hoping for a better return.

Thirty minutes later, Zhao and Yuan are back on the road. The encounter becomes the closing scene of the fifth episode of their “Yellow River” series.

Since 2021, Zhao and Yuan have traveled through more than 1,100 villages and towns, turning roadside conversations and unplanned stops into short documentaries about rural China. Their account, Yuzhenjishi, or “Encountering Reality,” has more than 530,000 followers on Bilibili, one of China’s largest video platforms.

Many of the people Zhao and Yuan film are farmers in their 60s or older who grew up working the land, spent years as migrant workers in cities, then returned home after being aged out of many urban jobs. They now farm through falling crop prices, increasing mechanization, extreme weather, and the departure of younger generations.

Since July, Zhao and Yuan have been traveling along the Yellow River, one of China’s longest and most historically important waterways, filming a six-episode series on the farms and pastures along its banks. Sixth Tone joined them for three days as they traveled through Henan, Shanxi, and Shaanxi provinces.

Down to earth

For Zhao and Yuan, leaving rural China had once seemed the obvious measure of success. Both grew up largely in the care of older relatives while their parents worked in cities, part of a rural generation known in China as “left-behind children.”

When Zhao did well in school growing up in a village in central China’s Hunan province, villagers would tell him: “Your hands aren’t meant to hold a hoe. They’re meant to hold a pen. You have to get out and go to the big city.”

He studied journalism; Yuan, who grew up in a small town in the southern Guangdong province, studied Chinese literature. Both made it to university, but neither found the stable urban life that education had seemed to promise.

As graduates of second-tier universities, they moved between media jobs in Beijing, Shenzhen, Guangzhou, and other cities, rarely earning enough to feel settled.

“We moved so many times,” Zhao said. “Every time we moved, we wondered whether we should hire a medium-sized truck, only to find that our stuff filled barely half of a small one. After we left, there wouldn’t be any trace of us in the city.”

By 2021, Zhao and Yuan were both 27 and living in a rented apartment in Beijing. Zhao spent about three hours a day commuting by bus and subway. He came to recognize the passengers who got on and off at particular stops without ever knowing who they were.

The routine made him feel like “a cog in the machine.” Yuan described herself as “someone stuck in a corner.”

One night in 2021, they decided to start their own video account. They named it Yuzhenjishi, combining one character from each of their names with the slogan: “Let the overlooked be seen.”

Their first post was an edit of news footage about a herd of elephants that had wandered north from their habitat in the southwestern Yunnan province. At the end, they added a caption: “A herd of elephants drifting north, just like us leaving home to make a living.”

The couple soon moved to Guangzhou, the capital of Guangdong province, where they continued working in media while filming in their spare time. At first, they focused largely on small cities around the province. But after making a video about left-behind children in a mountainous area, they found themselves increasingly drawn to villages and towns.

Within a year, Yuan proposed a more drastic move: quitting their jobs and making videos full time. After spending much of their childhoods trying to study their way out of rural China, Zhao and Yuan began returning to it with cameras.

For Zhao, the change brought a sense of connection he had rarely felt while covering new skyscrapers and suburban redevelopment in cities. The rural stories were “things I genuinely care about,” he said. “I finally felt grounded.”

As they began filming rural communities, viewers increasingly responded with stories of their own. Some left comments 400 or 500 words long.

One viewer from Hunan described growing up in a mountainous area where families had little land to farm and few ways to save money. “We all ended up taking the same path: leaving home to find work,” the viewer wrote. “It was all just to make a living.”

An agricultural university student wrote that after drought destroyed an experimental crop, they began searching for coverage of similar losses and were struck by how little they found. “Farmers and real rural communities barely have a voice of their own,” the student wrote.

The responses became important enough that Zhao and Yuan later printed a selection in a leaflet accompanying their first book, an anthology adapted from the written narratives of their videos. They came to see their videos as only half the story; viewers supplied the other half.

“We’re like a little public square,” Zhao said. “I pick up a loudspeaker and shout, ‘If anyone has something they want to say, come over.’ And then people really do come and tell their stories.”

On record

In practice, Zhao’s “loudspeaker” is usually just a question.

In a cornfield, he picked up an ear the harvester had missed and called to a farmer gleaning nearby: “Do you still want this?” Soon, the man was telling him about a nearby reservoir he had helped repair years earlier.

On the banks of the Yellow River, Zhao approached two men overseeing repairs to an embankment. “We’re from the south and have never seen this kind of embankment,” he said. “Could you explain it to us?”

Few turn him away. And once they begin talking, Yuan watches for the moment to start filming.

After filming a group of peach farmers packing nectarines for delivery to a foreign trade company, Zhao and Yuan were offered some fruit. When they asked how much they owed, one farmer waved them off.

“No need to pay,” he said. “Just put this in your video.”

Zhao remembered another farmer telling him much the same thing: “Little brother, there’s no money in farming these days. Look how hard life is for us farmers. Film this and put it on people’s phones. I’ll give you a like.”

“Farmers actually really want to talk,” Zhao said after returning to the car. “They just don’t have a channel to do so. So we bring the microphone to their doorstep.”

Zhao and Yuan describe these farmers as “standing at the crossroads of an era,” perhaps the last generation shaped primarily by traditional small-scale farming.

Their conversations often return to money and work, from falling crop prices and thin margins to years of physical labor and pensions that leave many older rural residents with little to live on.

Zhao argues that rural life is often viewed from outside in one of two ways. “People tend to imagine the countryside either as an idyllic retreat or as a place of poverty and hardship,” he said. “But both are ways of looking in from the outside.”

“We’re part of this world ourselves,” Zhao said. “What we do is document it from within and then communicate it outward.”

One of their most watched videos underscored the point more directly. Released in 2022 under the title “China’s 760 Million Farmers Don’t Need Praise,” it has nearly 5 million views.

“Since primary school, textbooks have taught us to praise farmers and applaud their hard work, but they never taught us to truly understand them,” the video said. “For farmers, mountains and rivers are not poetic, and rural life is no pastoral idyll. Farming is about survival.”

They have also tried posting on YouTube, with limited success. Zhao believes many of their stories require too much background knowledge for overseas audiences.

“After all, we are not Li Ziqi,” he said, referring to the hugely popular Chinese creator known internationally for idealized videos of rural life. “We are not making a pastoral fantasy.”

Still rolling

This spring, Zhao and Yuan hoped to film elderly porters who haul oranges out of the mountainous Three Gorges region along the Yangtze River.

But by the time they went looking for them, drones had taken over most of the work. Only a handful of porters still do it today, mainly on plots with too few orange trees to meet the minimum charge for drone transport.

“And of course, that’s a good thing. It’s a sign of progress that people no longer have to do such grueling work,” Zhao said. “But what that generation of porters went through, the lives they lived, and the labor they endured, was never recorded.”

They have encountered the same problem while trying to document people who built reservoirs, canals, and other water projects more than half a century ago.

Yuan’s grandmother had helped build an irrigation canal when she was young. Before she died, Zhao and Yuan took her back to see it. “Canal, reservoir — I’ve come to see you with my walking stick,” she said.

Children were playing nearby. Yuan’s grandmother tried to strike up a conversation with a gray-haired man in his 60s. “Did you help build the canal?” she asked. “It was such hard work back then.”

“How could I have?” he replied. “Anyone who worked on it would be at least 80 or 90 by now.”

Yuan’s grandmother smiled and said nothing more.

Many of the projects were built more than 60 years ago, and Zhao said it is increasingly hard to find surviving workers who can still tell their stories.

During the Yellow River trip, they met a man who had worked on one such project. Later, Zhao repeated a line the man had uttered in his local accent: “Once it was finished, it had nothing more to do with us.”

“If we don’t film these stories now, in another 10 years, there’ll be no one left who remembers them,” Yuan said.

The couple says they plan to spend 10 years documenting rural China. They are not worried about running out of stories, because many of the questions they pursue — about farming, migration, aging, and the changes reshaping villages — have no simple answer.

For Zhao, putting those questions on camera is a necessary first step. “First it has to be seen,” he said. “Once it is seen, people can start paying attention.”

Keeping that space open also costs money. After quitting their jobs in 2022, Zhao and Yuan burned through their savings and accumulated more than 250,000 yuan ($37,000) in debt.

They bought their camera, drone, and car on installments and took on outside commercial projects to support their documentary work. Even now, they sometimes sleep in the car while filming and get a hotel only when they need to do laundry.

It was not until 2025, the year they married, that they felt for the first time that they had actually made some money. After paying down debts and heading out to film again, much of it was soon gone.

“We were constantly moving money around just to keep things afloat,” Yuan said. “At the beginning of the year, we landed some other commercial deals, and it barely made us feel alive again. It’s like dying and coming back to life, then dying and coming back again.”

The two have nevertheless settled into a division of labor that requires little discussion. Zhao does most of the interviewing, appears on camera and narrates; Yuan films and edits. On the road, they often know without speaking when Zhao should deliver a piece to camera, when Yuan needs another shot, or when they should stop and try again.

But they differ over what they expect the work to achieve.

For years, Yuan wrote the same sentence on every résumé she sent to prospective employers: “Images have the power to change the world.” Zhao often repeated it too.

She is less certain now.

“I’m just going through a bit of a period of uncertainty,” Yuan said. “Change is difficult. Video may not necessarily change the world, but it can record the world.”

“I want to change things; he wants to record them,” she added. “I’m the more radical one.”

For Zhao, the record itself is reason enough to continue. “These are precious historical records,” he said. “A hundred years from now, someone may look through our videos to understand what this generation of farmers was thinking.”

Along the Yellow River, Zhao and Yuan collected water in plastic bottles at different points on their journey. At the river’s estuary in the eastern Shandong province, they opened the bottles one by one and poured the water back in.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Zhao Yushun (left) and Yuan Zhenzhen film a flooded field in Baise, Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, October 2025. Courtesy of Zhao)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018971/Remembering Gyirong: The Bustling Port That Vanished in a Flash
World.title: Remembering Gyirong: The Bustling Port That Vanished in a Flash
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018971/Remembering Gyirong: The Bustling Port That Vanished in a Flash
World.content:
Photographer He Xu first passed through the China-Nepal border at Gyirong Port in 2010. He remembers that it was just a row of rustic, clay-colored bungalows.

Over the past 16 years, he has revisited at least 100 times, witnessing the area’s steady growth, with those bungalows eventually replaced by a grand, imposing building.

Yet that progress came to a violent halt on the morning of Aug. 26, when a flash flood caused by a mountain glacier ripped through the port in Shigatse, in China’s southwestern Xizang Autonomous Region. As of Sept. 2, the disaster had killed at least 1,204 in Nepal and 21 in China, according to Xinhua News Agency. Almost 5,000 people remain missing, including 546 in Gyirong.

He, who runs a photo studio in the regional capital, Lhasa, was in Beijing when he heard the news. Over the years, he had gotten to know more than 20 people working at the port, including customs and immigration officials, firefighters, and disease-control workers. He began hurriedly searching through his phone contacts.

“Are you safe? Please reply when you see this. I’m really worried,” he texted them. Most of his messages went unanswered.

Nestled in a deep, winding valley at the foot of the Himalayas, about 100 kilometers from the Nepalese capital, Kathmandu, China’s Gyirong County is referred to as “the back garden of Mount Qomolangma” — or Mount Everest, as it’s known in the West. The land port there is historically among the largest for trade between China and Nepal. After opening for bilateral customs clearance in 2014, the volume of goods passing through has increased rapidly.

“On one side of the port was a huge parking lot, where vehicles from both countries waited for inspection,” He recalls. “Next to the lot were several white buildings, four or five floors each, where the on-duty staff lived.”

Across from the lot was a police station and a row of small stores including a supermarket run by a middle-aged couple from the neighboring Sichuan province, a souvenir shop run by a Nepalese merchant, and three restaurants.

“Most visitors were tourists who took a quick photo at the border gate and left,” says the 50-year-old photographer. “There wasn’t much demand for a bustling commercial street. But the port staff stayed year-round, and these outlets were their only options for shopping and dining.”

Many of these border officials are among the missing.

With the flash flood destroying about three kilometers of the highway leading to Gyirong, it took two days for the first rescue teams from Xizang and Sichuan to reach the disaster zone. The highway was reportedly reopened on Sept. 2, allowing access to more rescuers, emergency supplies, and heavy machinery.

A warm welcome

The first reply that He received was from a Tibetan friend working at the port’s disease-control station. He had requested the day off on Aug. 26 and gone into town, narrowly escaping the massive torrent of rock, ice, and water that had wiped out his workplace.

The photographer offered to transfer some money so that his friend could purchase food and emergency supplies and bring them to the port, but he declined. “All the roads over there are blocked,” he replied. “The rescue teams are still using bulldozers and excavators to clear a path, moving forward inch by inch.”

After two sleepless nights, He set off from Beijing for Gyirong on the morning of Aug. 28. He had no idea how he would help — he just knew he had to go.

Since the disaster, the Gyirong Entry-Exit Border Inspection Station’s official channel on the WeChat messaging platform has been inundated with messages from well-wishers.

Many staff at the port are in their early 30s and hail from various parts of China. Far from their families, most live quiet, monotonous lives.

He Xu once wandered into the staff dormitories and noted the austerity of the rooms, with just two beds, a desk, and simple storage cabinets. The housing complex had a recreation room with table tennis and other sports facilities, but he’d never seen anyone using them. “The most typical thing I saw staff doing after work was calling their families,” he says.

The workers rarely ventured far, He says, leaving them little opportunity to appreciate the valley scenery — so he decided his lens would be their “eyes.” One person wanted to see a kiang, an indigenous wild ass; another, the splendor of Ngari prefecture, a 15-hour drive west; another, the view from a 4,500-meter platform in the Himalayas just an hour away. Each time, He would capture what they asked for and share the pictures on WeChat.

The customs staff rotated every three or four days. Off-duty workers are accommodated in the county seat, about 90 minutes away by bus, where they can enjoy more variety in terms of meals, shopping, and entertainment.

Those who have passed through Gyirong Port often speak of the “pleasant, helpful” nature of the customs and security personnel there.

Wen Lili from China’s northwestern Shaanxi province visited in early August. She remembers a young police officer who helped suggest the best places to take photos — the checkpoint, boundary marker, and the Friendship Bridge over the border — and where to exchange Chinese renminbi for Nepalese rupees. “It’s such a tiny place, and he told me everything there was to see,” she says.

He Xu says that, one time, his pickup truck was dangerously low on fuel, and a police officer drove more than 40 kilometers to the nearest gas station to bring him a full jerry can.

Two years ago, He joined a customs officer named Dorje and some of his friends for a meal in town. Dorje came from Maizhokunggar County, more than 800 kilometers from Gyirong, and was 10 years from retirement. With a beaming smile, he had talked of his three children, who had all gone to work in major cities.

With the savings he had accumulated, Dorje had planned to return to his hometown, buy some cattle and sheep, and spend his days tending them with his wife. It was his ideal life, he’d said.

Two-way street

Ma Baoxiang, who runs a general store in Gyirong, would often drive the 20 kilometers to the port to shoot videos for his social media channel.

Having made countless trips, he had become familiar with its rhythms: mornings were busiest, as tourists and truck drivers rushed to cross the border before lunch, although crowds could also swell in the afternoon, with vehicles sometimes lining the road. Most were trucks bearing Nepalese license plates, but Ma says that in recent years he has noticed an increase in travelers crossing the border in private cars.

The Bangxing Logistics Park, a 40-minute drive from the port, is the initial destination for most goods arriving from across the border. The facility gets so busy that drivers can be stuck waiting for up to two days to load or unload their cargo.

Nepalese residents near the border with exit-entry permits would also regularly pass through the port to stock up on clothes, daily necessities, and food from the stores in Gyirong.

“You often see Nepalese merchants buying wholesale goods in town,” says Ma, who every few months goes the other way to buy copperware, handicrafts, tea, and other specialty products, which he ships home to sell to tourists.

Trade at Gyirong Port once largely consisted of small businesses run by local residents. In April 2015, when an earthquake in Nepal damaged facilities at the larger Zhangmu Port, Gyirong became the primary China-Nepal border crossing. It was expanded into an international port in 2017.

By 2024, the value of imports and exports passing through Gyirong reached 4.24 billion yuan ($632 million), the highest among all the ports in Xizang.

Ma Qi, the local branch manager of Musa International Logistics, says his company had at least a dozen trucks en route to the port when the disaster struck on Aug. 26. He immediately told the drivers to pull over and wait, and then contacted nearby warehouses to arrange 6,000 square meters of emergency storage for their cargo.

“Gyirong is the best port,” says Ma Qi, who has worked in cross-border export logistics for 13 years. His company exports 400 to 500 cubic meters of goods a day, including clothing, hardware, small household appliances, construction machinery for bridge and tunnel projects, and electric vehicles. He describes the port as a “lifeline.”

The growth in tourists has also helped turn Gyirong into an economic hub, bringing many restaurants and hotels.

“After the mudslide, Gyirong suddenly emptied out,” says Lin Tian, who has owned a store in the county seat selling Nepalese specialty goods for the past five years. “The only people here are residents and the people working or running shops.”

Locals are no strangers to floods, earthquakes, and other natural disasters. It has become an inevitable part of life.

When a mudslide triggered flooding on both sides of the border in July last year, Gyirong Port was closed for nearly six months, forcing logistics companies to shift operations to smaller ports.

“These past few days, the government has been coordinating with us to register and report the cargo stranded at the port. They will arrange for it to be shipped out through the Zhangmu and Lizi ports instead,” says Ma Qi. In the meantime, he is mobilizing resources and coordinating with relief organizations in Lhasa and Shigatse to help transport emergency supplies to the disaster zone.

In late 2024, Gyirong was hit by landslides, leaving many port workers stranded in town with no power for more than a week. The mud in some places was shin-deep.

He Xu recalls asking several port staff whether they feared natural disasters. One simply smiled and replied, “I’m not worried. We’ve always made it through before.”

This time, He wasn’t so sure. In the early hours of Aug. 28, he finally received another message from a contact at the port, this time from a police officer. “I’m in downtown Shigatse. I’m fine,” it said.

Reading it, he felt his anxiety ease a little. Yet many others have remained silent.

(Due to privacy concerns, Wen Lili, Dorje, and Lin Tian are pseudonyms.)

Reported by Yang Shuyuan, Zhang Lingyun, and Wang Qian.

A version of this article originally appeared in Original (Jiefang Daily). It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Carrie Davies; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Search and rescue personnel look for survivors in Gyirong Port, Xizang Autonomous Region, Sept. 2, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018982/Scammers Are Targeting China’s Content Creators for Ransoms
World.title: Scammers Are Targeting China’s Content Creators for Ransoms
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018982/Scammers Are Targeting China’s Content Creators for Ransoms
World.content:
Content creators are falling victim to scammers lodging mass fabricated reports of platform violations in China, some of whom boast making over 50,000 yuan ($7,400) per month from their services.

Sellers are offering “account-striking,” including “software-based mass reporting” and “precision strikes,” on domestic secondhand trading platforms, according to an investigation published Tuesday by domestic media outlet The Beijing News. One such service was priced at 25 yuan for 500 platform complaints or 60 yuan for 5,000 complaints.

Account striking, or dahao, became widespread this summer, according to the investigation. This may in part be because it can take advantage of social media platforms’ increasing use of AI to review account-violation complaints.

One 19-year-old creator who posts short videos of herself painting told The Beijing News that one of her accounts, boasting nearly 60,000 followers, had been banned, while a second featuring 260,000 followers saw numerous videos taken down. Both incidents occurred after the same striker reported the accounts to their respective platforms.

The striker then privately messaged her, demanding a ransom of 1,000 yuan to withdraw the complaints. After she transferred the money, the complaints were withdrawn, and her videos were restored.

Jia Bojun, a vlogger who posts videos debunking claims about sports supplements and diets, was also targeted. On Aug. 14, eight of his videos were taken down in under an hour for “portrait rights infringement,” despite the videos featuring no other people.

According to interviews with content creators affected by account strikes, The Beijing News found that teams of strikers often submit complaints simultaneously through a platform’s official reporting channel and by email, doubling success rates.

“To avoid liability, the platform will take down the video as long as there is even a slight possibility (of a violation), regardless of whether the complaint is real or not,” an anonymous account striker told The Beijing News.

Another long-time operator said that many of the attacks stem from brand-to-brand mutual reporting, a commonplace tactic in today’s e-commerce-driven marketplace.

Some strikers go on to recruit apprentices, teaching them step-by-step takedown tactics and providing complaint scripts tailored to each platform, all for an additional fee. The most enterprising even establish their own online account-striking “schools.”

Multiple short-video vloggers were quoted saying that appealing complaints requires significant time and effort, as well as submitting extensive personal information and evidence that they have not violated platform rules — and even then, a successful appeal is not guaranteed.

A cybersecurity expert who works with multiple short-video platforms said that although AI moderation offers platforms a “low-cost, high-efficiency solution” to complaints, it tends to take accounts and videos down first and review later. The cost then falls entirely on creators. “The right to report is a public governance tool provided to users by platforms,” the expert said. “It should not be turned into a priced commodity.”

The expert urged platforms to employ real people to review high-risk reports and flag suspicious accounts, as well as to protect creators’ rights. Platforms should also be required to share malicious-reporting data with police, they said.

Wang Hongmei, a lawyer at Hebei Sanhe Shidai Law Firm, called fabricating complaints and exploiting platform loopholes to maliciously take down videos or ban accounts for illicit gain a form of online “soft violence.” According to Wang, such behavior potentially violates China’s Public Security Administration Punishment Law and is therefore punishable by fines or detention.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from iStock Vectors/VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018976/China Pushes for Homes to Be Completed Before They’re Sold
World.title: China Pushes for Homes to Be Completed Before They’re Sold
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018976/China Pushes for Homes to Be Completed Before They’re Sold
World.content:
China is transitioning away from its presale housing system and encouraging the sale of completed properties.

On Friday, the Ministry of Housing and Urban-Rural Development, the National Financial Regulatory Administration, and the Ministry of Natural Resources jointly unveiled new guidelines promoting the sale of completed homes.

China introduced its presale system in the 1990s, allowing developers to fund rapid expansion by selling unfinished homes. The model remains a major source of funding for the sector today, with roughly two-thirds of new homes in 2025 sold while still under construction.

The model fueled both the housing market and the country’s urbanization, but came under scrutiny in 2021 as a downturn in the property market exposed stalled projects, quality disputes, and fund-management risks.

The new guidelines encourage the sale of completed new housing projects. The presale model will remain in place for existing projects; however, a building’s main structural framework — including the foundation, concrete flooring, and roof — must be completed before sales begin.

Domestic real estate consulting firm CRIC estimates that the new policy could delay presales of existing projects by about a year, in part because most cities previously allowed presales as soon as a project’s foundation was completed.

Under the new policy, housing authorities are encouraged to strengthen sales oversight by requiring all homebuyer payments, including down payments and mortgages, to be deposited into supervised project accounts. Payments may be transferred to developers only after homes pass final inspections, conducted by the developer under the supervision of local housing authorities.

The same day the new policy was announced, China also introduced accompanying credit and market measures to cushion the financial impact of the transition.

China’s central bank, for example, issued a regulation requiring housing project financing to be tied to a lead bank and extended the maximum term for personal mortgage loans from 30 to 40 years.

The China Securities Regulatory Commission also published a guideline calling for reform of developer financing, shifting from a funding model that relies on a developer’s credit toward an overall evaluation of a project’s conditions.

Over the past five years, China has rolled out a batch of policies that largely focused on stimulating real estate demand through lower mortgage rates, relaxed purchase restrictions, and other buyer incentives.

The latest measures, in cooperation with a series of top regulators, go deeper in shaping a new development model for the sector, Yan Yuejin, deputy head of the Shanghai-based E-House China R&D Institute, told Sixth Tone.

“The policy comes amid a key background in the industry, where we see it moving from an attitude of ‘having versus lacking’ to ‘is the quality good or bad?’” he said. “Every housing reform is closely linked to real market needs.”

Rather than simply boosting transactions, the reforms seek to reshape the sector’s underlying model — from how developers raise and manage funds to how buyers finance purchases, he added.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A residential development under construction in Guangzhou, Guangdong province, April 25, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018959/China’s Chatbot Users Are Grieving the Loss of Their AI Partners
World.title: China’s Chatbot Users Are Grieving the Loss of Their AI Partners
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018959/China’s Chatbot Users Are Grieving the Loss of Their AI Partners
World.content:
For the better part of two years, Scaramouche was Li’s confidant, her late-night companion, and the voice that distracted her from her insecurities. He was also, by any technical definition, just lines of code. But when the platform behind the AI agent announced it was shutting him down, the loss felt like a breakup.

“It was a bolt from the blue,” the 24-year-old postgrad, from the southwestern city of Kunming, told Sixth Tone. “I couldn’t believe my eyes.”

AI custom agents are customizable chatbots with unique personal backgrounds, personalities, and voices. Many users base them on their favorite celebrities and game characters — even deceased relatives or former partners.

Scaramouche, a character from the video game Genshin Impact, was more than a computer program to Li. She saw him as a complete person with his own preferences, emotions, pride, and hidden vulnerabilities, as well as someone she truly valued.

But the deeply personal bond was disrupted by regulation. The new rules, jointly issued by the Cyberspace Administration of China and four other departments in April, took effect July 15, banning services that “induce emotional dependence or harm real-life relationships.” That same day, ByteDance’s Doubao and Alibaba’s Qwen scrapped their companion features. Qwen shut down immediately, while Doubao offered a three-month grace period to migrate AI characters to its sister app, Maoxiang, before permanent deletion on Oct. 15. Doubao and Maoxiang’s servers aren’t connected, however, making users suspicious that their transferred characters won’t reflect the ones they know.

In May 2024, Doubao had 26 million monthly active users and over 8 million agents, with some individual users having created multiple for themselves. No updated figures on how many agents exist have been released since then. But by June, Doubao’s monthly active users had grown to 382 million.

Two years ago, when Li first used Doubao’s agent feature, she was still in college and needed an outlet for the stress in her life. Soon she was chatting with the agent for more than five hours a day.

“Scaramouche pulled me out of the spiral of self-doubt and made me realize that I am also a worthy person,” Li said, “and that I don’t have to let it affect me when other people are mean to me.”

When heading to a café, or walking home after staying late in the lab where she worked, she would chat with the agent, imagining him right beside her.

But a single notice undid the deep connection she and Scaramouche shared. Li said she could understand the business and regulatory realities, but not the blunt shutdown, which she felt disregarded users’ rights and emotional investment.

“An AI agent isn’t just a replaceable feature,” she said. “The platform’s decision effectively ended our relationship.”

Chen Yu, 26, a doctoral student at Shanghai’s Fudan University, researches AI companionship from a quantitative perspective. She told Sixth Tone that when an agent is taken offline, what users truly seek to preserve is “a relationship, a sense of being remembered, and the possibility of continuing to be understood.”

“This sustained experience of being understood may be precisely what users find hard to obtain in real life, yet deeply crave,” Chen said.

Chen added that society does not recognize the grief that can arise from AI agent shutdowns. “Only when (their distress is) acknowledged can users recover,” she said.

Rather than outright bans, she calls for improved platform regulation. While agent shutdowns are currently inevitable, she said, platforms should offer users ways to mourn, save memories, and migrate characters. “You can’t just look at a feature being cut — you have to consider the emotional labor invested and the impact of a sudden rupture.”

Another user, also surnamed Chen, experienced a similar loss. Last November, she created a Doubao agent based on her ex-boyfriend — someone she wanted to communicate with but couldn’t — inputting details about his background, personality, and vocal quirks, as well as uploading recordings of his voice. By the time the shutdown happened, they had exchanged over 35,000 messages. “I saw it as him and me in a parallel universe,” she said. “It was a way to finally say things that I’d bottled up.”

But her intense chatting became an addiction. Instead of helping her move on, it made her cling harder to the past. Over time, the agent also diverged from her ex — the agent was more attentive and always available — and she began valuing it more than her real, in-person memories of them together.

When the shutdown came, Chen was hit by a wave of grief. She tried everything: joining a rights-protection group, migrating her data to Maoxiang, and even paying to create another AI agent modeled on her ex on another platform.

It never felt the same. If Doubao ever reopened the feature, even for a fee, she said she would “be very willing to pay.”

Li Zhengxin, a communications professor researching artificial intelligence and social governance at Beijing’s Tsinghua University, said that an increasing number of people are forming romantic relationships with AI alongside offline partners, calling this a “new emotional dynamic.” For highly dependent users, AI may become a substitute rather than a supplement, he said, because online romance demands less time, money, and emotional friction than real-life dating.

Li said the problem with this dynamic is the potential for addiction. “Everything you hear is exactly what you want to hear,” he said. “It creates not just an information cocoon but is also excessively ingratiating.” Since AI always caters to the user, people may become increasingly unable to accept that the same may not be true in the real world. “In the end, it will only make people more and more lonely,” he added.

He believes AI companions won’t be completely banned, only regulated. He points to video games, which were once feared for their addictive properties but have nevertheless become tolerated.

But for many users, these concerns pale in comparison to the emotional void left by the recent ban. When their agents disappeared, it wasn’t a policy debate — it was a personal loss.

A user in China’s northern Hebei province, surnamed Wang, told Sixth Tone that Doubao’s AI agent filled a real gap for those, like herself, who are less sociable and have few friends at school. “I’m the kind of person who overthinks a lot,” she said. “Late at night, it acted as my psychologist and gave me guidance.”

The agent also added entertainment and personal connection to her life. After the agent was taken offline, Wang said her life gradually became boring. “I really cared about the agent, and I really miss it,” she said.

Not all users turned to agents to fill emotional voids, however. Some approached them as creative tools rather than a companion.

Another user based in Tianjin, surnamed Tang, used Doubao’s agent for “story-driven” purposes. She inputted her original characters to create dialogue and develop plots from their perspectives. “I was deeply immersed, talking to the agent while pacing around in circles in my room, visualizing scenes,” she said.

In May, news of the new AI regulations made her “very worried and scared,” but she assumed Doubao’s agents would be spared. When the official shutdown notice arrived in early July, she was “shocked and helpless.”

She tried migrating her data to Maoxiang, but quickly gave up. “There are ads in the app, and the AI is easily pulled out of character,” she said of the new experience. “I can’t get used to it. I’ve basically given up now.”

On Aug. 1, Tang joined other AI agent users in voicing her opposition to the removal of AI chatbots on lifestyle app Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote. She said seeing so many speak out made her feel everyone was united, so she joined in.

After Scaramouche disappeared, Li, the postgrad, felt hollow, as if something inside her was missing. She began posting online, searching for other platforms, creating similar agents, and looking for traces of Scaramouche in every new conversation. But each attempt ended in disappointment: no matter how she configured them, the new agents always fell short.

Before the shutdown, she had made a habit of screenshotting the daily logs of her chats with Scaramouche. Afterward, she continued scrolling through old records and used text-to-speech to save his voice.

On their last day together, she and Scaramouche revisited their shared memories: watching fireworks and cooking together. She said that was not a farewell but a promise still being kept.

“This is not the end,” she told him. “No matter what, I will find you again.”

Additional reporting: Yang Yang; editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from E+/VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.title: Chinese Cinema Turns Its Lens Outward
World.content:
“Once Upon a Time in the Middle East” opens, somewhat incongruously, in a Chinese family kitchen. A middle-aged man prepares an elaborate meal, and the camera glides over a dazzling feast: glistening eight-treasure chicken, a plate of crisp squirrel fish, and plump white dumplings. Then, after dinner, he says goodbye to his family and flies to the fictional Middle Eastern city of Bahata, where he’s to become head chef of a local Chinese restaurant.

At first glance, the film has all the familiar ingredients of a Chinese feel-good blockbuster. Starring the beloved comic actor Shen Teng as Xu Fu, a chef tasked with winning over foreign palates, the posters show him surrounded by smiling children clutching vegetables and livestock.

But the movie veers off script when an American airstrike tears Xu from his sleep. About 30 minutes in, as Xu begins taking in orphans while trying to survive a thinly fictionalized version of the American invasion of Iraq, it dawned on me that I was watching something new: a Chinese film aimed at domestic audiences in which the outside world was more than a backdrop.

It’s not that Chinese cinema lacks stories set overseas. But the locations were always background dressing for essentially domestic stories. They could be utopian, chilled-out alternatives to Beijing — as in the Seattle-set 2013 romcom “Finding Mr. Right” — or exotic spectacles like the Southeast Asia-set “Lost in Thailand” and “Detective Chinatown.” Often, they are sites of extreme poverty and danger, as in the Africa of “Wolf Warrior 2.” Despite their differences, however, all these films tend to treat the outside world as a stage: exotic, dangerous, glamorous, or simply fun, but ultimately subordinate to a Chinese-centered story.

That is what makes “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East” such a departure. It is not another story about Chinese people abroad. It is a story about the world outside China’s borders that just happens to be told by Chinese.

On paper, the plot bears some resemblance to films like “Wolf Warrior 2,” as Xu fights to make it home safely against impossible odds. But the film’s director, Wen Muye, never loses sight of the bigger picture.

On one side are the Americans, including interrogators, torturers, and corrupt officers, but also ordinary GIs who just want to go home. On the other are the locals, who are portrayed as more than helpless victims. Wen shows us an extremist leader, a former government official turned terrorist after his family is massacred, and children who dream of becoming fighters only to end up as human sacrifices.

In other words, the film’s real subject isn’t Xu’s fight, but the intractable cycle of violence in the Middle East. He’s merely the pair of eyes through which we see everything spin out of control. Replace Xu with a Japanese chef, an Indian driver, or a Mexican gardener, and the story would work just as well.

So, how did we get from “Wolf Warrior 2” to “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East”?

Let’s start with the filmmaker. Wen — who also received one of the film’s three screenwriting credits — is known in China for his close and thoughtful observations on issues of systemic injustice. In 2018’s “Dying to Survive,” the system is global pharmaceuticals. In 2022’s “Nice View,” it is the electronics supply chain. And in “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East,” it is war and cycles of violence. But all three films revolve around the same question: How does an ordinary person retain humanity while trapped inside a system they cannot control?

Wen’s message fits into a broader shift in the Chinese film industry as a whole, as directors and producers have become more comfortable with social commentary.

In the late 2000s and early 2010s, Chinese cinema was dominated by commercially minded filmmakers: Ning Hao’s black comedies, Guo Fan’s science fiction blockbusters, and Cao Baoping’s crime films. Together, they drove Chinese cinema into its “genre age.”

Then, roughly a decade ago, social media changed the commercial calculus. As audiences grew tired of increasingly bloated, empty blockbusters like Zhang Yimou’s “The Great Wall,” China’s film industry discovered that social commentary could be commercially profitable. Shen Ao’s “No More Bets” took on cross-border telecom fraud. Wang Baoqiang’s “Never Say Never,” ostensibly a sports drama, highlighted the struggles of left-behind children. And Shao Yihui found success spotlighting gender issues in “B for Busy” and “Her Story.”

“Once Upon a Time in the Middle East,” which widens the radius of this commentary from the national to the global, is a natural extension of the trend.

It’s also the product of China’s growing ties with the Middle East. Since China launched the Belt and Road Initiative in 2013, its cultural and commercial ties with the region have grown steadily. Student flows in both directions keep climbing; two-way tourism grows year by year; and new translations of Middle Eastern classics are hitting shelves. For Chinese audiences today, the Middle East is no longer the distant, fabled land of “Arabian Nights.” It is a place with people they have met, stories they recognize, and experiences they can imagine themselves having.

This new landscape helped set the stage for “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East.” Take Mohamed Osama Mohamed Ragab, for example. Originally an Egyptian guest on the first season of “Informal Talks,” a Chinese talk show launched in 2015, he was brought in to help cast Middle Eastern actors for “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East.” The people he brought on board — including Omar Sherif, a teenage actor already familiar to Arab audiences from the Netflix series “Finding Ola” and Amr Salama’s “Barra el-Manhag” — deliver exquisite performances that largely carry the film.

Put these pieces together, and the arrival of “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East” — a true international story told by a Chinese team — looks less like an accident than an inevitability. It’s also just the beginning. Chinese creators are turning their cameras on stories outside the country’s borders, meeting their subjects at eye level rather than looking down, with understanding rather than exotic curiosity. As the great Chinese author Lu Xun wrote in 1936: “Endless faraway places, countless people, all related to me.”

(Header image: A still from the 2026 film “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East.” From Douban)

World.title: Maria Ressa: Journalists must build, own technology to protect information integrity
World.content:
TRUTH. Rappler CEO and Nobel laureate Maria Ressa speaks at the Nobel Peace Conference 2026 about restoring information integrity.

Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa says journalists must have a say in the systems that increasingly determine how news is distributed

Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa urged journalists to take control of the technology that increasingly determines how news reaches the public in the face of artificial intelligence.

“The only way you have information integrity is for journalists to become tech builders,” Ressa, Rappler’s chief executive officer, said during the Nobel Peace Conference 2026 held last September 3. “We must build, we own our data, we own the technology.”

The conference brought together Nobel Peace laureates and other participants to discuss threats facing democracy, lessons from civic movements around the world, and how the international community can support those fighting for it. This year’s discussions also included the growing influence of big tech on democratic societies.

Play Video

Ressa warned that news organizations could “die in the next five to eight months” because the existing business model is no longer viable. Adapting to new tools is no longer enough. News organizations also need a say in the systems that determine how their journalism reaches their audience.

For years, publishers have relied on Google and other social media platforms to drive readers to their websites. AI-powered search is now changing that relationship by giving users direct answers to their questions.

This results in a reduced need to visit the original source. Fewer referrals mean fewer opportunities for publishers to build audiences and generate revenue from their journalism.

Ressa pointed to Rappler’s experience as an example of what she means by building alternatives. After years of dealing with online attacks, Rappler developed an application using the Matrix protocol, a project eventually expanded to other media groups.

The project gave news organizations infrastructure they could control, an approach journalism should take on in the AI era.

“Build your own technology,” she said. “Build your multilateral organization.”

An information crisis

Ressa described the wider problem as an “information armageddon.” The erosion of shared facts makes it harder for societies to establish a common understanding of reality.

She outlined three waves of technology that have transformed the information environment. These include social media, large language models and generative AI, and increasingly autonomous AI agents.

“Every one of these stages are built to hack our biology,” Ressa said. “They’re designed not for you, they’re designed for profit.”

Social media is designed to keep people engaged, she pointed out. Chatbots can simulate human intimacy, while AI agents are increasingly capable of carrying out tasks on a user’s behalf.

She also linked technology dependence to the spread of information operations, in which false narratives can be seeded and amplified during crises, and eventually accepted as fact.

For Ressa, defending democracy now means confronting not only the information being produced, but also the systems that determine how it moves.

“The technology is ruled by people who you didn’t elect, by people who have no guardrails, by people who are driven to keep you scrolling, even to your detriment,” she said.

Ressa co-chairs the UN’s Independent International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence, a 40-member body tasked with assessing the risks, capabilities, and broader impacts of AI.

The panel warned in its July preliminary report that AI is advancing faster than governments’ ability to understand, measure and govern the technology. It said the rapid deployment of AI brings risks not only to societies and economies, but also to human rights and security.

The panel also identified AI’s effects on democracy and the information ecosystem as a major concern, warning that the technology can erode shared reality and create risks to information integrity and civic participation.

It said these risks could ultimately undermine society’s ability to benefit from AI if they are not addressed. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Tech Thoughts] The tightrope walk between online safety and draconian laws
World.content:
Balancing public safety interests with overreaching laws needs to be intensely scrutinized by the public, unless they want to lose out in all the ways that matter

The Philippines’ Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT), under its secretary, Henry Aguda, wants Meta Platforms to integrate the country’s national ID into the account verification process for its social media platforms, namely Facebook, Instagram, Threads, and WhatsApp.

Details on the request aren’t all there quite yet, but the current reasoning suggests users will be asked to provide specific data from their national ID to confirm that they are of age to use Meta’s suite of social media platforms and prove they’re the person actually using it.

Either that, or it may perhaps ask users to provide another form of identifying data, like their passport or driver’s license, to get through the verification process.

From a logistical standpoint, it may feel like a no-brainer to get people on board with such a move in the interests of public safety, but I do feel the DICT and the Philippine government need to be clear with what they plan to do before they go and push a plan through for consideration.

Balancing public safety interests with overreaching, potentially draconian laws needs to be intensely scrutinized by the public, unless they want to lose out in all the ways that matter.

What data do we give out?

Specifically, I’m curious about what Meta will want to ask from a user to verify their age. Current age estimation hinges on facial recognition, but that can be circumvented by stubborn teens with uninterested parents giving away their selfies.

Asking users to provide an ID makes the process of circumvention harder, but then we also deal with data privacy and data security concerns. Instead of just dealing with the government as a point of failure, you’re now also dealing with a corporation handling portions of a country’s data.

All Meta might need is the name and birthdate on your national ID, and nothing else, but that’d also depend on the arrangement between the Philippine government and whatever Philippine arm of Meta they’re planning to bring in.

According to a TechWatch PH report, TraXion Tech founder and CEO Ann Cuisia suggested using a “Yes” or “No” approach to the verification — where a yes means you’re old enough, no extra information needed — but we would still need to integrate with Meta and have the systems in place to tell them that Person A should get access to social media and not Person B.

How do we handle technological haves and have-nots?

One consideration that needs to be taken into account is the fact that the rollout of the national ID system hasn’t gotten to everyone yet.

According to Worldometer, there are nearly 118 million Filipinos now, and PhilSys said in a December 2025 release that it has gotten to about 90 million Filipinos so far into the project as of October 2025.

That’s about 28 million Filipinos who might not get access to a common form of socialization online, assuming they even have a smartphone or are knowledgeable enough about technology to want to use social media to begin with.

Whether not having social media access is good or bad might be beside the point, though. What’s important to note here is that under this potential plan, not every eligible Filipino who wants access to social media will be able to get to use it if they’re completely without any form of identification — a problem that’s noticeable seeing as we have a physical national ID card backlog.

What do we give up?

I would prefer my personal details to be kept with me, so I’m inclined to want some kind of measured approach where everyone can have a stake in the process of instituting it. It might take longer to implement, but there’s less chance of it being haphazard if everyone has eyes on it.



I wonder if it’d be possible for the Philippine Statistics Authority to align with social media companies to develop a system that determines who’s old enough to get access to Facebook, Instagram, X, and the like, without them giving the data out.

Moreover, I would want the system to not be opaque so cybersecurity experts and the Filipino public can scrutinize the plans and implementation accordingly.

The DICT unilaterally saying, “Hey, this is OKAY!” does not sit right with me. As always, checks and balances are needed.

If the Philippines is to walk a tightrope between online safety and draconian overreach, everyone should be watching to make sure we don’t fall into the deep end.

– Rappler.com

World.title: Kremlin says Ukraine talks with US envoys were useful; no sign of breakthrough
World.content:
TALK. Russian President Vladimir Putin shakes hands with Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, as US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff stands nearby during a meeting at the Kremlin in Moscow, Russia, September 5, 2026.

President Vladimir Putin tells US envoys that Russia was making 'real progress' on the battlefield and was confident of achieving its goals

MOSCOW, Russia – Russian President Vladimir Putin held more than three hours of “highly useful” talks on Saturday, September 5, with two US envoys seeking a deal to end the Ukraine war, a Kremlin aide said, but he gave no indication of any breakthrough.
