The aide, Yuri Ushakov, said Americans Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner “outlined a number of ideas regarding possible avenues for a settlement.” Ushakov did not say what these ideas were.

He said Putin had told the pair that Russia was making “real progress” on the battlefield and was confident of achieving its goals, while stressing the necessity of addressing “all the root causes of the conflict.”

These are statements that Moscow has made repeatedly since Putin launched the full-scale invasion of Russia’s smaller neighbor in February 2022. Both sides have intensified long-range air strikes in recent weeks while the front lines remain largely static.

Putin praises Trump’s efforts

A White House official told Reuters the talks had been “substantive” and that next steps would be announced in the coming weeks.

There was no comment from Witkoff and Kushner, who were visiting Moscow for the first time since January on behalf of President Donald Trump. They flew out of Moscow soon after the talks and are due to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy in Kyiv on Sunday, September 6.

“The talks went beyond a mere exchange of views on resolving the Ukrainian crisis. Economic issues and potential major, mutually beneficial Russian-American projects were discussed in some detail,” Ushakov said. “Overall, one can say that the negotiations were timely and highly useful for both sides.”

Putin’s investment envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, posted on X that the meeting had been an “important peacemaking visit.” He and Ushakov were both present at the meeting.

The Russian president praised Trump’s efforts to end the war.

“Understanding that he is entering a difficult situation, he nevertheless does not stop his efforts to help bring about a settlement and to make his contribution to resolving the Russian-Ukrainian conflict,” Putin said in televised remarks at the start of the talks.

Trump suggested on Friday, September 4, that the US had a fresh proposal aimed at ending the war but did not elaborate.

Putin promised to ensure the safety of the US negotiators. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said earlier that Putin had ordered the Russian military not to strike Kyiv for three days because of their trip.

A vast gulf in positions

Over the previous 10 days, Russia pounded the Ukrainian capital day and night with missiles and drones, including an attack on Friday on the headquarters of the SBU security service.

Ukraine has inflicted damaging hits throughout the summer on Russian refineries, oil terminals and warehouses of online retailer Wildberries, in an attempt to raise the cost to Moscow of continuing the war. Zelenskiy said Kyiv was prepared to refrain from strikes on Moscow through Monday.

Russia and Ukraine remain far apart on how to end the war, the deadliest in Europe since World War Two.

A person close to the Kremlin, speaking before reports emerged of the trip by Trump’s envoys, said Putin was still intent on capturing more territory.

“There is no chance of reaching an agreement regarding the front line until Putin finishes securing the remaining part of the Donetsk region,” this person told Reuters, adding that the Kremlin leader was confident — based on reports from his commanders — that this would happen by the end of the year.

Western military analysts see such a possibility as remote, given Moscow’s slow rate of progress. Ukraine has refused to surrender land it has successfully defended at huge cost, and rejects such terms as tantamount to surrender.

The Kremlin said on Friday the position that Putin set out in a speech two years ago — that Ukraine should cede the entire territory of four regions claimed by Russia and abandon its plan to join NATO — was “unshakeable.” – Rappler.com

World.title: When the lost Mindoro bleeding-heart was finally photographed
World.content:
SIGHTED. The Mindoro bleeding-heart recorded in one of nine camera traps deployed in the forests of Mindoro.

The detection of the elusive Mindoro bleeding-heart twenty years later inspires hope and forebodes changing habitats

MANILA, Philippines – The team set up nine camera traps in the forests of Mindoro last August. They determined the locations of the camera traps based on knowledge of the Mindoro bleeding-heart’s habitat, behavior, and as well as what the Iraya Mangyan knew about the endemic bird’s previous whereabouts.

“We combined historical data and then the biophysical and bioclimatic layers of Mindoro Island to create a [species distribution] model,” John Bibar, a researcher from the Center for Conservation Innovation (CCIPH) who was part of the field team, explained.

“When we got the result and zoomed in, the area was an ancestral domain in the northern part,” Bibar said.

Bibar and the rest of the team spent around two days scouring the forests of Mindoro to install the camera traps. They conducted transect walks and used bioacoustic devices.

On the last day of their week-long fieldwork, the team, composed of Manila-based conservationists and Iraya Mangyan patrollers, checked the recorded footage. They had moderate hopes. It was the first time they had deployed the camera traps.

Yet, there it was. In the footage from the last camera they checked. The Mindoro bleeding-heart, raising its right wing. A hello to the community of birders and conservationists it had inspired to wonder for 20 years.

“We said, ‘It looks like it’s saying hello to us,’” said Jennica Masigan, conservation program director of CCIPH. For Masigan, the search for the Mindoro bleeding-heart was personal.

FIELD. The expedition team at work in the forests of Mindoro last August. Photo courtesy of Center for Conservation Innovation

Masigan is a wildlife biologist whose curiosity about the bird began when she started doing field research. She would often hear from others how elusive and rare the Mindoro bleeding-heart was.

“But it wasn’t until I started leading field expeditions that I developed a passion for looking for this bird,” said Masigan.

The last confirmed sighting of the bird was in 2005, inside the Siburan Forest Reserve in Occidental Mindoro. The ground-dwelling pigeon is critically endangered. Its name comes from the distinct red patch on its chest.

Sightings of rare species are a cause for celebration for a community that has built a cause around them. More so among birders, a community of enthusiasts who travel long distances for the chance, however uncertain, to glimpse a rare bird. Birdwatchers help monitor the status of birds by sharing sightings within the community and documenting the species they spot.

CAPTURED. The endemic Mindoro bleeding-heart (right) photographed twenty years since its last documentation. It was detected upland which was unusual as it was more known to have resided in lower elevations. Photo courtesy of Center for Conservation Innovation

CAUGHT. Photos of the Mindoro bleeding-heart at the Sablayan Prison and Penal Farm in 2005, taken by Don Roberson. Courtesy of ebird

Conservationists have launched a global effort listing “lost” birds in a bid to find and document them.

The global initiative Search for Lost Birds defines a lost species as one “not confirmed alive by photographic, audio or genetic information for over 10 years in the wild and has no ex situ population under human care.”

Before CCIPH was able to record the Mindoro bleeding-heart last August, the bird was among those considered lost.

“Every year that passed without a trace of the Mindoro bleeding-heart pushed the conversation closer to that edge, whether continuing to search was still justified or whether it was time to let go,” the organization’s researchers wrote. “The bird, it turns out, was not ready to let go.”

LOST. A screenshot from Search for Lost Birds, a platform that lists down lost birds across the world. Listed among them are the Mindoro bleeding-heart (Gallicolumba platenae) and the Sulu bleeding-heart (Gallicolumba menagei).

Researchers say the pigeon’s reemergence should be understood in the context of changing habitats. The bird was traditionally known as a lowland species. But this particular Mindoro bleeding-heart appeared in front of a camera trap installed 900 meters above sea level.

CCIPH takes note of the “warning.” Species don’t leave their habitats, researchers said, “unless something about that habitat has stopped working for them.”

In 2020, CCIPH created the Mindoro Forest and Biodiversity Conservation Program. The conservation work involves the Indigenous Iraya Mangyan, as much of it covers their ancestral domain.

“The Mindoro bleeding-heart, it’s part of a forest that also supports people,” said Masigan. She mentioned that a protected forest is “shared value” between conservationists and the indigenous people who live in these lands.

“When we protect that bleeding heart, we are also protecting the ecological system that supports human well-being.”

– Rappler.com

Quotes translated to English for brevity.

World.title: Influencer boom at US Open tests boundaries of tennis etiquette
World.content:
SPORTS FASHION. Japan's Naomi Osaka enters the court before her second round match against Czech Republic's Katerina Siniakova at the US Open.

The growing love affair between influencers and the premier American tennis event has caused some growing pains

NEW YORK, USA – Influencers and content creators armed with smartphones and ring lights have featured prominently in the stands at this year’s US Open, as they try to grab the spotlight away from the on-court action at one of tennis’ marquee events.

Around 100 content creators were given credentials for the tournament, organizers said, with 20 of those dedicated to providing coverage of the food and beverage scene alone, where caviar-topped chicken nuggets and the famed “Honey Deuce” cocktail promise viral attention.

Thousands more amateur social media hounds can be found throughout the plaza and in the stands — after shelling out for their own tickets.

“I feel like every Slam kind of has their own identity and the US Open has kind of always been the ‘big-show Grand Slam,'” said the 2017 finalist Madison Keys.

‘A bit disrespectful’

Celebrities have long been ubiquitous in the stands — from A-list stars to US President Donald Trump — as the ultra-wealthy shell out thousands of dollars for seats at the see-and-be-seen event of New York’s summer sporting calendar.

But the growing love affair between influencers and the premier American tennis event has caused some growing pains.

A chair umpire was forced to reprimand a group of patrons for staging a disruptive photo shoot while two-time US Open champion Naomi Osaka was serving during her first-round win against Anastasia Zakharova on Monday.

This was one of the cringiest things I’ve ever seen live. The US Open used to be an actual tennis tournament https://t.co/1kAYND6VOe pic.twitter.com/c1jbi4lUlQ — Danny Singer (@michiganboy310) September 2, 2026

“Obviously if you come to a sporting event, you have to respect the sport,” Osaka told reporters on Thursday after her second-round win over Katerina Siniakova.

“It could be a good thing for people to make the sport of tennis popular to their specific audience, but I think it has to be managed a lot better, especially in the situation like first-round match.”

Another social media user attracted attention for all the wrong reasons when she posted a series of photos posing inside Arthur Ashe Stadium while Keys was in the middle of playing a point against Alina Korneeva, which breached basic tennis etiquette.

“I can appreciate the influencers coming and kind of showcasing the US Open experience,” said 2024 runner-up Jessica Pegula.

“But I do think that it’s tough when you see videos like that when they’re taking pictures and using the selfie lights. People are down there trying to perform, and it’s their career and their job. It seems like a bit disrespectful.

“I think it’s gotten a little maybe too much.”

The trend is a direct result of the tournament’s popularity, with surging attendance leading organizers to expand the main draw action to 15 days. The tournament was further expanded with the mixed doubles competition being held as a standalone event the week before singles action kicks off.

The men’s ATP tour expanded its partnership with TikTok earlier this year, citing a more than 25% increase in posts under #tennis during 2025.

“The more we try to raise awareness about tennis, the better it is, the more popular the sport is,” said 2021 champion Daniil Medvedev.

“For sure, if it disturbs during the play, like if you see the light or something, well, you always say to the referee, can be sometimes challenging, like if during the point this happens.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Alex Eala’s finest US Open run ends as skid vs friend Iva Jovic continues
World.content:
FRIENDS. Iva Jovic of the United States embraces the Philippines' Alexandra Eala after winning her third-round match in the 2026 US Open.

Alex Eala squanders a 4-2 lead in the deciding set as she falls short of a fourth-round berth at the US Open and remains winless against Iva Jovic

MANILA, Philippines – The third time, unfortunately, did not prove to be the charm for Alex Eala.

Eala remained winless against American world No. 14 Iva Jovic as she exited the US Open with a stinging 7-5, 3-6, 7-5 loss in the third round at the famed Arthur Ashe Stadium in Flushing Meadows, New York, on Saturday, September 5 (Sunday, September 6, Manila time).

Up 4-2 in the deciding set, the Filipina world No. 18 ran out of steam when it mattered most, sending her finest run in the final Grand Slam of the tennis calendar to a heartbreaking end at the hands of her close friend.

Eala fell to 0-3 against Jovic in their WTA Tour meetings after losing in straight sets in the opening round of the French Open in May and again in the second round of the Queen’s Club Championships in June.

But Eala, at one point, seemed poised for a breakthrough win over Jovic.

Playing in primetime at the world’s largest tennis stadium with a roaring crowd behind her, Eala finally took a set from Jovic and even grabbed a 4-2 lead in the decider.

Jovic, however, dug deep and won four of the last five games to come out triumphant in the 3-hour, 3-minute marathon and arrange a fourth-round clash with compatriot Coco Gauff.

Eala showed some resistance during that stretch as she saved a match point in the 10th game to knot the score at 5-5 before Jovic clinched the next two games.

Seeded 14th, Jovic moved to a second match point with a booming forehand winner, then sealed the victory when Eala dumped a shot into the net — the American falling flat on her back in tears after advancing to the US Open round of 16 for the first time in her career.

“I don’t even know what to say, that felt like a marathon and I felt like I lost my sanity five times over to win that match,” said Jovic.

“But it’s really worth it for this feeling. I’m usually not one to show that many emotions but this one really meant a lot to me so it’s everything to have another match here at the US Open.”

It was a painful exit for Eala as she came oh-so close to matching her best Grand Slam campaign, a fourth-round appearance in the Wimbledon Championships in July where she dethroned Poland’s Iga Swiatek in the third round.

Eala flashed a smile as she thanked the fans at Arthur Ashe Stadium, but the disappointment of the loss finally sank in as she fought back tears on her way to the dugout.

Still, it was a commendable run for Eala as she surpassed her showing last year, when she fell to Spain’s Cristina Bucsa in the second round after making history as the first Filipino to win a Grand Slam main draw match in the Open era following an upset of Denmark’s Clara Tauson.

This year, Eala swatted aside USA’s Mary Stoiana, 6-1, 6-2, to open her campaign, and then made quick work of Ukraine’s Oleksandra Oliynykova, 6-1, 6-4. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Two Pronged] Seasonal Affective Disorder hits, but my therapist’s dead. What now?
World.content:
'From the time I wake up to the time I go to sleep the rain never stops... I fear that, if my brain gets used to constantly feeling this down, it will consider this the “new normal” and I have to be on a higher medical regime forever after this.'

Rappler’s People section runs an advice column by couple Jeremy Baer and clinical psychologist Dr. Margarita Holmes.

Jeremy has a master’s degree in law from Oxford University. A banker of 37 years who worked in three continents, he has been training with Dr. Holmes for the last 10 years as co-lecturer and, occasionally, as co-therapist, especially with clients whose financial concerns intrude into their daily lives.

Together, they have written two books: Love Triangles: Understanding the Macho-Mistress Mentality and Imported Love: Filipino-Foreign Liaisons.

Dear Dr Holmes and Mr Baer,

I was 12 years old when I took my first antidepressants under the psychiatrist’s guidance. Before that, I was taking whatever my mother was, with her blessing.

By that time, my father could see that my mother was right: I was always sad. This sadness never seemed to leave. Sometimes it was worse than my ordinary sadness like when our kasambahays left without being told why or it rained very hard for several days.

My mother told my father she was the same when a child so he finally agreed to my seeing a psychiatrist too.

My psychiatrist, “Rebo,” was my mother’s psychiatrist and also became my younger brother’s. He saved my life many times.

With my particular depression, it took many years before we realized I was also bipolar. As soon as he prescribed a mood stabilizer, things seemed to make more sense.

We had to try many different mood stabilizers before we found a combination of medicines that finally worked for me day in, day out. Once we discovered what we called the “elixir” life became bearable. Sometimes even more than that.

My biggest success was not changing medication during the pandemic despite the isolation, the mistrust, and the constant loneliness.

Rebo promised I could increase my meds if I needed them increased. But he hoped I wouldn’t need to. He said that my brain might get used to this higher dosage that was really only needed for the pandemic.

I managed. I am still on the same meds I have been for the last 16 years. But this weather is worse than the pandemic.

From the time I wake up to the time I go to sleep the rain never stops. I wake up in a cold sweat every morning ever since this ceaseless rain began. I know sunny days appear, but they never last long enough to lift my depressions.

I see no end in sight.

I fear that, if my brain gets used to constantly feeling this down, it will consider this the “new normal” and I have to be on a higher medical regime forever after this.

What is wrong with me?

Should I look for another psychiatrist? Someone who can be my next Rebo? He is no longer (around). He died 2 years ago.

– Ana

Dear Ana,

As Dr Holmes has written an entire book on clinical depression I think it would be foolhardy of me to do other than to defer to her in this instance.

Best wishes,

– JAF Baer

Dear Ana,

Thank you very much for your letter. Let me answer your immediate question first: “Should I look for another psychiatrist?”

Yes.

Second question: “(Should I look for) someone who can be my next “Rebo”?

Absolutely not.

True, Rebo was extremely helpful to you; not just for weeks or months, but for more than 16 years, including the years you were both trying to find the cocktail of meds that could work for you. There is no doubt in my mind that your prognosis would not have been as good were he not your psychiatrist then.

However, sadly, Rebo is no longer around. To look for another Rebo would not make sense, although looking for someone with the qualities you found most helpful would be wise. Very wise.

I may be wrong (and if so, please correct me), but I feel Rebo had this rare gift and you were one of the ones blessed enough to have received it.

EXAMPLES: You were right alongside him in your joint quest of getting you better. He was not the one who always knew more than you and thus merely told you what to do. He actually listened to you, and took everything you said, felt, and feared into account. He was not focused on helping you merely with your immediate problem. He was aware that any decision you made now (like upping your meds) might affect the rest of your life.

But much more than that, he showed you the potential implications/ consequences of each action but left you to make the decision.

He treated you like a grown up.

Rebo may have been the best psychiatrist for you then, and may even have been one of the best psychiatrists for you now – if he were around (which sadly “he is no longer”) AND if he would have still been as responsive to this new you, with your new insights, new experiences, new fears, new achievements, new anxieties, etc.

Your job now is to find a psychiatrist whom you can work with smoothly – because you both have the same respect for truth, hard work, facts and wisdom.

Finally, the question which may have been asked merely rhetorically): What is wrong with me?!!?

Nothing that can’t be “fixed.” But this fixing is more of a change in perspective rather than an outside change.

SAD (seasonal affective disorder) is a type of depression linked to changes in seasons, usually starting late fall or winter. Some people suffer from a real depression, SAD, once or more times in their lives.

This can be due to several reasons, such as:

a disruption in our circadian rhythm. When things are out of sync, life gets harder… worse if it’s something as major as our biological clock!

a drop in serotonin. Heathcliff lovers may adore dark clouds and cold rain but us ordinary run of the mill lovers can get affected by the lower serotonin levels that we get this time of year;

a Vitamin D Deficiency due to less sunlight. Low vitamin D can negatively affect serotonin levels and worsen mood.

In my opinion, SAD is the West’s answer to our (the East’s) HAD (Habagat affective disorder) or to MAD (Monsoon affective disorder)

Research also shows that SAD is more common in women, young adults, people with a family history of depression, and those living far from the equator where winter days are much shorter. So you have been DOUBLE-WHAMMIED, Ana, by belonging to two risk groups!

Not the best state of affairs, but not the worst either…especially because you know that to be a fact. Thus, being depressed during cold, dark days does not mean something is wrong with you; it merely means you have SAD.

Might I also add that being double-whammied puts you in excellent company. We are now “double-whammied” classmates, Ana!!

All the best,

– MG Holmes

– Rappler.com

Life got complicated? Write to our Two Pronged duo at twopronged@rappler.com.

World.title: No cars, no condos: CHED sets limits on student-athlete perks
World.content:
While the Student-Athletes Protection Act features ‘detailed regulation against commercialization,’ enforcing it is another matter

READ: Part 1 | What CHED’s student-athletes protection memo means after Ateneo tragedy

Philippine collegiate leagues have long made decisions and rules with minimal government regulation. But in 2015, the government passed the Student-Athletes Protection Act (Republic Act No. 10676) that mandated “the protection and promotion of the rights and welfare of student-athletes.”

Although it took the Commission on Higher Education (CHED) a decade to operationalize this law, with the Memorandum Order No. 13 released only last June 1, it’s notable for its clear guidelines.

“The memorandum does not only pertain to protection of student-athletes from unsafe training and competition environment that might result in injury or even fatalities. It also protects the student-athletes from commercialization, from exploitation, from unfair residency rules, from mental health issues, and even academic neglect,” said Dr. Lorenzo Lorenzo, the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) representative who helped draft the memorandum.

“For instance, the section defining commercialization enumerates what items schools can extend to [student-athletes].”

Lavish gifts

For decades, there have been rumors that highly touted recruits in collegiate leagues get lavish offers beyond the standard scholarship and stipends, with cars, houses, condominiums, and excessive cash allowances among the alleged perks.

This time, the CHED Memorandum Order (CMO) lists specific benefits and incentives that student-athletes can receive, including:

Tuition

Board and lodging

School and athletic uniforms, equipment

Reasonable monthly living allowance

Medical services and insurance

Other benefits “to enhance academic and athletic performance”

“Anything beyond those items enumerated is defined as commercialization,” said Lorenzo.

“For example, if the financial incentives extend to the family, or extravagant gifts and gadgets were given, or a car and a condo were given — those are items that are beyond what is provided for by the Republic Act. So, this is defined as commercialization.“

The CMO also specifies what cannot be given to student-athletes, with Section 18 prohibiting the following:

Excessive cash allowances or stipends beyond what is reasonably necessary for educational, training, or living expenses

Lavish gifts or incentives such as high-value gadgets and luxury items

Luxury housing or accommodations, personal vehicles or similar privileges not ordinarily available to students

Unjustified academic exemptions, automatic passing grades, or unauthorized privileges inconsistent with academic standards or procedures

Preferential treatment such as priority access to resources or services creating inequity with the general student population

“Perhaps one of CMO No. 13’s strongest innovations is its detailed regulation against commercialization,” said NCAA basketball commissioner Rico Paolo Quicho said.

“Section 19 likewise regulates commercial endorsements involving a student-athlete’s name, image, or likeness by requiring written consent from both the student-athlete and, where applicable, the parents or legal guardians,” he added. “These provisions reinforce the amateur nature of collegiate athletics.”

League officials, however, admit that supervising each school will be a difficult task.

“It’s hard to monitor, so that’s the challenge with regard to policing the incentives. But we have actually already drafted [a rule] on maximum benefits that we parked because of this challenge,” said Rebo Saguisag, executive director of the University Athletic Association of the Philippines (UAAP).

“Suffice it to say, right now, for lack of enforcing power or monitoring power, or investigative body, in the meantime, we can start complying with CHED requirements insofar as the reportorial requirements are concerned.”

Quicho said documentation of the benefits, and communicating it “through official institutional policies or handbooks” can be a good start.

“This promotes transparency and prevents arbitrary or discriminatory distribution of benefit,” he said.

A student-athlete, as defined by law

According to Article 5 of the CMO, a student-athlete must have a minimum of 12 units per semester in a two-semester school year, or nine units in trimester setups.



The CHED also requires student-athletes to have an academic standing of at least 60% to be considered eligible.



A student-athlete’s status, however, will be terminated upon signing any contract to play professionally, as determined by the rules of the Games and Amusements Board (GAB).



During the 2020 pandemic when varsity action got shelved, GAB issued special guest licenses to collegiate athletes to allow them to play in pro sports leagues.

By 2024, however, the NCAA discontinued the practice, while the UAAP never adopted the policy.

“One of the most persistent issues confronting student-athletes is the tendency of some institutions to prioritize athletic success over academic achievement,” said Quicho.

“Student-athletes often miss classes due to training camps, tournaments, and travel schedules, resulting in learning gaps, delayed graduation, and academic underperformance.’

“In some instances, institutional pressure to maintain competitive sports programs may inadvertently encourage academic compromises,” he added. “This undermines the fundamental principle that participation in collegiate sports should complement, rather than replace, higher education.”

‘Incentives poison decisions’

Another issue top collegiate leagues deal with is “poaching,” or the sudden transfer of a student-athlete to another school within the league, which usually frustrates the alma mater that initially trained and honed the players’ skills.

Back in 2012, Jerie Pingoy, a former two-time UAAP juniors’ basketball MVP with the FEU Baby Tamaraws, spurned his high school and transferred to a stacked Ateneo Blue Eagles team for college.

Pingoy had already committed to play for the Tamaraws in the UAAP, but surprisingly left for the Blue Eagles. This led to bitter disputes, and eventually, the league crafted the so-called “Pingoy Rule,” which required high school transferees to sit out for two years before playing for their new college team.

The UAAP had since revised its rule on transferees.

“First and foremost, the freedom to transfer cannot be curtailed, especially if the student-athlete is after quality education. Another legitimate reason would be the sports program or the coach,” said Saguisag.



“Other than that, we want to address exploitation or commercialization, as incentives seem to poison the decisions of these young student-athletes.”

Another controversial transfer involved Mason Amos, who starred for Ateneo for one UAAP men’s basketball season before suddenly transferring to rival La Salle in 2024.

The move prompted the UAAP to again revise its transfer rule, where an athlete will have one year of eligibility deducted, on top of the existing one-year residency rule.

“If you sat out two years, we see how the skills of student-athletes have regressed, as well as physical fitness,” Saguisag said.



“I believe that the lawyers have studied [our rules], it’s permissible under current law, but the reason why we did that is when a person transfers, not for the legitimate reasons that I said, aside from commercialization, is to address the collegiality among member schools,” he added.



“The respect for other [schools]. Kung magkakasama tayo dito, sana wala namang ganyanan (We are all here together, let’s not do things like that)…because it leaves a bad taste in the mouth of each of the member schools.”

Report misconduct, exploitation

The CHED memorandum also gives student-athletes space to air grievances, as it requires schools to set up a complaints mechanism and policy.

In 2013, Mikee Bartolome, a decorated UAAP high school swimmer from the University of Santo Tomas, challenged a league rule after UST refused to allow her transfer despite passing the University of the Philippines’ college admission test.



With nowhere else to go, Bartolome sought a temporary restraining order and a Quezon City court granted it, allowing her to compete in UAAP Season 76.

But this time, student-athletes can now “report misconduct or exploitation.”

“An athlete’s grades, credentials, or academic documents cannot be withheld during a transfer, especially if they have no outstanding financial obligations to the school,” said Lorenzo.

Quicho added that CMO No. 13 subjects leagues and schools to “greater accountability.”

“They must register with the CHED, establish grievance mechanisms…investigate complaints, and comply with annual reporting requirements. These measures reinforce transparency and responsible governance throughout collegiate athletics,” he said.

CHED said student-athletes, parents or guardians, member schools or their alumni, and other stakeholders may file a complaint.

“Upon notice and hearing, CHED may impose the appropriate penalties under relevant laws, rules or regulations,” the memorandum states.

After an investigation, a school found guilty of violating the rules will merit a maximum fine of P1 million and/or a ban from participation in their respective leagues.



The leagues themselves may be fined a maximum of P1 million if found liable for any violation.

“There’s a continuous review of our policies. And again, it’s a matter of enforcing them, which is really a big challenge, but we have to start somewhere,” said Saguisag.

Quicho agreed that “the effectiveness of the memorandum will depend on consistent implementation, adequate institutional resources, meaningful enforcement, and ongoing monitoring to ensure that its protections translate into tangible improvements in the lives of student-athletes.”

CHED notes that the memorandum applies to all public and private schools, varsity leagues and inter-school competitions nationwide, off-campus activities, all persons involved in athletic programs, as well as foreign student-athletes.

Schools and athletic organizations have six months to comply with the required initial documentation after the memorandum rollout in June.

But as Saguisag reminded: “Legislating on that matter is one thing. Enforcing and policing it is another matter.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Iloilo City mayor: No quick fix to power woes
World.content:
INQUIRER FILES

ILOILO CITY — The Iloilo City government is working with energy-sector stakeholders on longer-term solutions to continuing power interruptions as residents demand clearer timelines and immediate measures, Mayor Raisa Treñas said.

In a statement on Sept. 4, Treñas said the city government understood how repeated outages were affecting households, businesses, workers, and everyday activities.

She clarified that the manual load shedding implemented by the National Grid Corp. of the Philippines (NGCP) was not directly under the control of the Iloilo City government.

Article continues after this 

She also said she recently met with Panay Energy Development Corp. during a meeting of the Iloilo City Business Development Council and learned of efforts to increase power generation capacity in the Visayas.

READ: Visayas power woes highlight need for gridwide upgrade

The mayor cited the expected entry into Iloilo City of LNGPH, described as an integrated liquefied natural gas terminal and power facility, as one development that could help address the region’s power requirements.

Treñas stressed that the supply problem extended beyond Iloilo City and affected the wider Visayas grid.

“There is no instant or overnight solution to this problem. But we are not taking this sitting down,” she said.

The mayor said the city would continue coordinating with power-sector stakeholders to better understand the situation and identify concrete measures to protect consumers. /mcm

World.title: Recto: 64% cut in Palace budget won’t hamper operations
World.content:
Executive Secretary Ralph Recto — Photo from the Facebook account of the Office of the Executive Secretary

MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the President (OP) will be able to maintain its operations despite a proposed 64-percent cut in its budget for 2027, Executive Secretary Ralph Recto said in a statement on Sunday.

The House appropriations committee earlier voted 37-5 to swiftly end debate on the OP’s P10.15-billion proposed budget, cutting short discussions after the panel deferred questioning over its spending plan due to parliamentary courtesy.

IRecto said the OP’s proposed budget was “enough for the center to oversee government operations, from responding to emergencies, delivering public services, monitoring economic plans, and protecting the national interests.”

Article continues after this 

“We are asking for less while remaining fully prepared to do more,” Recto said.

The OP’s 2027 proposed budget is significantly lower than its P28 billion budget this year, the bulk of which, at P17.55 billion, was earmarked for hosting the 2026 Asean Summits.

Recto said the OP’s budget cut was due to the “streamlining of the operations” of the OP’s 49 delivery units and the completion of activities related to the Philippines’ hosting of the 48th and 49th Asean Summits this year.

The funding will support Cabinet meetings, policy consultations, presidential engagements, and the daily operations of Malacañang as the nation’s principal center of executive decision-making and inter-agency coordination.

It will also help deliver timely assistance to vulnerable sectors and enable the government “to mount response to contingencies and challenges.”

Article continues after this 

READ: Budget watchdog flags ‘worrying’ House tradition on OP budget

“Every day, the president’s schedule is full because the demands of governing do not pause. But activity alone is not our measure of performance,” Recto said.

Article continues after this 

He assured that every policy, meeting, engagement, and official mission will produce a clear public dividend, whether through jobs and investments, stronger national security, better public services, or greater opportunities for Filipinos.

He likewise stressed that fiscal discipline and accountability remain at the core of the OP’s operations.

He also assured lawmakers that the proposed budget was crafted strictly within the parameters and processes established by the Department of Budget and Management (DBM).

“We sought no special treatment,” Recto said.

READ: Tinio questions OP’s secret funds, seeks fair transparency rules

Due to the parliamentary courtesy extended by the House to the OP, lawmakers were not able to scrutinize its P4.56 billion confidential and intelligence funds request for 2027, the same amount it had in the 2026 national budget.

The OP also did not need to explain the P1.014 billion it requested for its local and foreign missions and state visits budget for 2027 — slightly lower than its current budget of P1.018 billion for travel expenses.

The OP also has direct oversight authority over the Local Government Support Fund (LGSF), which the Marcos administration is proposing to allocate a record-high P58.32 billion in 2027. Critics warned this might become a tool for political patronage for the upcoming 2028 elections.

The same deference is also expected to be extended by the Senate finance committee once the OP’s 2027 proposed budget reaches the upper chamber.

World.title: 2 PWDs among 2026 Bar examinees
World.content:
INQUIRER FILE PHOTO

MANILA, Philippines — A blind person and an amputee were among the tens of thousands who took the Bar exam this year, Associate Justice Samuel Gaerlan said on Sunday.

READ: First day of 2026 Bar exams underway

Gaerlan, the Bar exam chairperson, said the two persons with disabilities were among those assigned an encoder to assist them in navigating the exam.

Article continues after this 

“We also have examinees who were allowed to take exams with the assistance of an encoder,” Gaerlan said in a press conference. “One lost sight to a rare form of meningitis … and one lost both arms.”

The Supreme Court (SC) justice also said one person deprived of liberty (PDL) took the Bar exam.

The male examinee, he said, was not required to take the exam behind bars.

“We allowed him to go to the local testing centers, but of course, with the implementation of security protocols,” he said.

Meanwhile, the Bar exam this year was conducted through laptops, but three examinees were allowed to take handwritten examinations.

Article continues after this 

Those granted the exemption were a 69-year-old “with a limited exposure to computers throughout their life,” a 64-year-old with a chronic eye condition, and a 49-year-old who “lost their laptop before their exam.”

As of Sunday morning, the SC logged a total of 11,900 exam applicants out of the 13,441 officially admitted to take the licensure test.

Article continues after this 

“There was an increase in the number of examinees this year as compared to other years,” Gaerlan said. “I think we have the highest number.”

The second and third days of the Bar exams will be held across 15 local testing centers nationwide on Sept. 9 and 13. /mcm

World.title: DBM to auto-release funds for gov’t salary deficiencies by Q4
World.content:
MANILA – Government employees who are promoted or whose positions are reclassified may soon receive salary adjustments faster as the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) moves to automatically release funds for personnel services (PS) deficiencies without requiring agencies to submit separate requests.

Acting Budget Secretary Kim Robert De Leon said the DBM is drafting a policy that would allow the department to identify salary funding gaps through updated agency plantilla records and release the necessary funds even without a formal request.

The policy is targeted for signing by the end of September, with live testing across government agencies scheduled in the fourth quarter of 2026.

Article continues after this 

Under the current system, agencies must inform the DBM of personnel who have been promoted or whose positions have been reclassified, including their new salary levels, before the department can determine and release additional funding.

“Hindi na kailangan pang i-request (There is no longer a need to request it),” De Leon said in a radio interview Saturday.

“Kailangan lang i-update ng ahensya yung master list na tinatawag namin ng kanilang plantilla, at ‘pag nakita namin na may kulang, kahit walang request, kailangan i-download namin sa kanila yung kakulangan nung pambayad ng pondo (The agency only needs to update its plantilla master list, and once we see that there is a deficiency, even without a request, we need to release the funds needed to pay for it),” he added.

De Leon said the reform will initially be tested in the fourth quarter, when agencies typically submit requests for PS deficiencies or additional funding to cover salaries and other personnel requirements.

The proposed mechanism could particularly benefit public school personnel whose positions are upgraded under the Department of Education’s (DepEd) Expanded Career Progression (ECP) System.

Article continues after this 

The DBM recently approved the release of PHP8.68 billion to cover salary differentials for 93,344 reclassified public school positions for fiscal years 2025 and 2026.

Under the proposed 2027 National Budget, PHP12.09 billion is also earmarked for the continued implementation of the ECP System.

Article continues after this 

The proposed DepEd budget for 2027 is PHP975.963 billion, including funding for salaries, the PHP10,000 annual teaching allowance, career progression, training, medical allowance, and other personnel benefits.

De Leon said the proposed automatic mechanism would apply not only to DepEd but also to other national government agencies with PS funding deficiencies.

World.title: Sara Duterte’s claim of fearing for her life ‘pure drama’ – Castro
World.content:
Vice President Sara Duterte arrives at the Quezon City Hall of Justice on Saturday, September 5, 2026, to post bail following an arrest warrant issued by Quezon City Regional Trial Court Branch 98. The warrant stems from three counts of grave threats filed against her. INQUIRER PHOTO / GRIG C. MONTEGRANDE

MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte’s remarks that she fears for her life were “pure drama,” former ACT Teachers Rep. France Castro said on Sunday.

Castro, a staunch critic of the Dutertes, said the vice president was in no position to cast herself as a victim after a warrant was issued for her arrest over charges that she threatened President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

She also said Duterte’s remarks on Saturday were an attempt to control the narrative and portray herself as a victim.

Article continues after this 

“This bratinella’s just full of drama,” Castro said, using the Filipino slang for a female brat.

“She only wants to flip the narrative and make herself the victim,” the former lawmaker added.

On Saturday, Duterte posted P360,000 bail for charges that she made grave threats against Marcos, First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and former Speaker Ferdinand Martin Romualdez. Before entering the Quezon City Hall of Justice, she said she did not trust the police or the court.

READ: Sara Duterte at QC Hall of Justice: ‘I don’t feel safe’

“I do not feel safe, I really do not feel safe. I don’t trust the court, I don’t trust the police,” she said.

Article continues after this 

Duterte said she had felt unsafe since 2023 due to harassment of her family by certain authorities, whom she did not name.

“The irony is striking: this is the same family that once threatened political opponents, those who exposed their misdeeds, and enforced tokhang and extrajudicial killings — now she claims to be the one under threat,” Castro said. /mcm

World.title: Adiong hits Sara Duterte’s safety fear remark: How ironic
World.content:
Vice President Sara Duterte arrives at the Quezon City Hall of Justic on eSeptember 5, 2026, to post bail following an arrest warrant issued by Quezon City Regional Trial Court Branch 98. The warrant stems from three counts of grave threats filed against her. (INQUIRER / GRIG C. MONTEGRANDE)

MANILA, Philippines — House prosecution panel spokesperson and Lanao del Sur Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong on Sunday criticized Vice President Sara Duterte who expressed fears for her safety, saying it was “ironic” as she was facing a grave threats case.

Duterte on Saturday posted a P360,000 bail for three counts of grave threats before a Quezon City court a day after an arrest warrant was issued against her.

Her cases stemmed from an online press conference in November 2023 where she said she had spoken to someone about having President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Marcos, and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez assassinated, if she herself is killed.

Article continues after this 

READ: Sara Duterte posts bail: ‘I don’t trust the court’

“How ironic na the reason why she was there ay para magpiyansa, mag-post bail on an allegation of a grave threat. Accused siya na siya yung nagbabanta,” Adiong said in an interview with dzRH.

(How ironic is that the reason why she was there to post bail was for an allegation of a grave threat. She was accused of making those threats.)

“So mukhang ito lang ata yung nakita natin na kung sino pa yung nagbanta, siya pa rin yung biktima,” Adiong added.

(So it seems that whoever made the threats was made to look like the victim.)

Article continues after this 

Before entering the QC Hall of Justice, Duterte said she does not trust the police and that she fears for her safety and that of her family.

She also said she had felt unsafe since 2023 as a result of harassment ther family was facing.

Adiong pointed out Duterte’s demeanor when she made the remarks on Saturday, saying that it was not the look of someone who seemed scared for her life, noting that “it’s the other way around.”

“Pero if you’re looking at the way, the demeanor and the manner by which she was telling this to her lawyers, hindi yun yung nakikita natin na takot na takot. Palaban pa rin siya. Mas matapang pa nga siya doon kaysa doon sa mga pulis,” Adiong said.

(But if you’re looking at that way, the demeanor and the manner by which she was telling this to her lawyers, it does not show fear. She is still feisty. She is braver than the police officers there.)

Adiong, however, said the supposed threats against Duterte should still be investigated.

The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Saturday said it has not received any information regarding any threats against Duterte and her family.

PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. (left) and Vice President Sara Duterte (right) (Photos from Office of the Chief PNP/Facebook and INQUIRER FILE)

World.title: Butuan City water crisis sparks calls for accountability, solutions
World.content:
The Butuan City Water District’s Pump Station 1 in Barangay Baan, Butuan City. (Photo from Butuan City Public Information Office)

SAN FRANCISCO, Agusan del Sur — Criticism of the Butuan City Water District (BCWD) and the city government has intensified as residents endure another round of water supply interruption, prompting calls for greater accountability and a long-term plan to secure the city’s water supply.

Posts on social media stated the recurring shortages could no longer be treated solely as an emergency caused by dry weather.

Consumers urged the BCWD and local officials to disclose what measures had been completed and how they intended to prevent similar crises.

Article continues after this 

The criticism followed the return of BCWD’s “Oplan Sag-Ob,” an emergency measure that allows concessionaires to fetch water from designated distribution stations when regular service is inadequate.

While residents acknowledged the importance of water rationing during emergencies, they said the program should not become a substitute for reliable infrastructure and long-term preparation.

“Emergency measures should remain emergency measures. They cannot become institutionalized substitutes for infrastructure,” Luna Kaisog stated.

Kaisog called on the BCWD to publicly present a comprehensive water security and drought resilience plan containing measurable targets, project costs and completion timelines.

The proposed plan should include projections of Butuan’s water demand, the condition of existing pumping stations, reservoirs and wells, possible alternative sources, additional storage requirements, watershed protection measures and targets for reducing water lost through leaks and other causes, she said.

Article continues after this 

Butuan City Mayor Lawrence Lemuel “Law” Fortun raised the water shortage issue during his State of the City Address on Aug. 5.

Fortun said water supply remained the responsibility of the BCWD, but disclosed that the city government had purchased three submersible pumps to help improve water pressure, particularly during dry periods.

Article continues after this 

He, however, acknowledged that these interventions would not be enough to solve the city’s water problems.

On Aug. 24, BCWD reported that the Taguibo watershed had experienced 23 days without sufficient rainfall. Streamflow had declined to about 42 million to 43 million liters a day, while the dam level had dropped to 3.58 meters—below the four-meter critical threshold.

The deterioration prompted the water district to resume “Oplan Sag-Ob (Fetch Water)”

Resident Allen Kenneth Pacis questioned why stronger contingency measures had not been put in place despite earlier indications of a potentially severe dry period.

Pacis said the water shortage affected not only households and businesses but also hospitals and patients, including those undergoing dialysis who depend on a reliable water supply for treatment.

“This is not simply an inconvenience,” he said, warning that disruptions in essential services could have serious consequences for patients.

Netizens called on the city government and the water district to publish project timelines, expected additional capacity and contingency measures that could be activated before water levels reach critical thresholds.
