In today’s AFL briefing: Gryan Miers advocates for Jake Koldjashnij’s return to football.

Luke McDonald says Kangaroos players loved Alastair Clarkson. Geelong forward Gryan Miers wants the AFL Players’ Association to find a way for key defender Jake Kolodjashnij to resume his football career before the year is out. Jake Kolodjashnij, pictured in 2024, signed an agreement acknowledging the risks he was taking if he continued playing after an ambigious concussion panel finding AFL Photos The 31-year-old has not played since the revelation he signed an agreement with the club in February 2024 to mitigate the Cats’ exposure to risk following an ambiguous finding from the AFL’s concussion panel. The agreement was not lodged with the AFL and the Cats received a $140,000 fine for the breach, which they accepted.



It also included a contentious clause which was removed after drawing condemnation from the Players’ Association, despite players’ representatives being aware of a similar clause being signed off by a VFL player with a history of concussion earlier in the decade. Miers, who has been playing with what he described as a non-functioning ACL throughout the season, told 3AW on Saturday that he was advocating with the AFLPA for Kolodjashnij’s return. Gryan Miers and Jake Kolodjashnij with their coach Chris Scott (centre) after Geelong’s win in the 2022 grand final. AFL Photos “I am the AFLPA delegate [for Geelong] as well, so I am putting some serious pressure on them because I want ‘Kola’ [Jake Kolodjashnij] to be back out there,” Miers said. “Not only are we in a really good finals campaign but our VFL is in a prelim’ final as well.” Miers said he was disappointed that Kolodjashnij had been forced out of the game due to the controversy. The Players’ Association said players and clubs cannot enter into a contract which is outside the purview of the collective bargaining agreement, even though Kolodjashnij’s career might end without the agreement in place.



“I feel really bad for the situation ‘Kola’ is in and I really hope, which doesn’t seem likely at the moment, we can figure something out to get him out there … to hopefully continue his career but, if not, finish it off in the right way,” Miers said. Kolodjashnij has not spoken publicly since revealing himself on August 7 as the player who signed the agreement, which the club considered an acknowledgment of risk but was also designed to mitigate the club’s risk if a future legal claim relating to concussion occurred. Gryan Miers has kept playing with an unstable ACL which will require surgery at season’s end. Getty Images He entered into the agreement willingly and had played with it for nearly three seasons before the agreement was revealed. His teammates are offering him support as he continues to train. Both the Cats AFL and VFL teams will play finals this weekend. Miers said he was determined to ensure Kolodjashnij was not forgotten after the Cats’ penalty. He said it was now up to the AFL and Players’ Association’s vow to address issues which had been allowed to drift since Kolodjashnij received his finding from the concussion panel.



“[It’s] in the hands of people that I am not involved in, but I am putting some pressure on whoever I can to make sure the questions are being asked for ‘Kola’ because I don’t feel like he should be in the position he is in right now from it,” Miers said. “I guess it is a really confusing and tough situation for all involved, and for the future of the game as well, so I understand why things are happening but, where I can, I am trying to help him out.” ‘We loved Clarko’: North veteran reacts to ruthless coach sacking Kangaroos’ veteran Luke McDonald says the players loved their former coach Alastair Clarkson as intrigue around North Melbourne’s decision to sack the four-time premiership coach continues to bubble. North Melbourne veteran Luke McDonald spoke about the club’s decision to cut coach Alastair Clarkson. Chris Hopkins McDonald, who has played under four coaches during his 236-match career, said he felt as though the team was about to launch and described the vacant coaching job as an “enviable job” because of the talent on the list.



He said Clarkson – a four-time premiership coach at Hawthorn – took the North Melbourne job when the club was “at a pretty low ebb”, bringing stability to Arden Street. “We loved ‘Clarko’ [Alastair Clarkson],” McDonald said. “We got on really well with Clarko. He had a big impact on a number of our players, but in saying that we also support the club’s decision because we are not where we want to be right now. We want to still be playing. We want to be playing finals.” Sacked North Melbourne coach Alastair Clarkson. Getty Images Despite all that, McDonald said he supported the board’s decision to end Clarkson’s tenure with one year remaining on his contract. He also excused football manager Todd Viney’s brutally frank remarks about Clarkson’s performance in the post-sacking press conference on Wednesday. “It’s an emotional decision ... we support the club’s decision and we want to be playing September footy,” McDonald said.



Viney and president Sonja Hood told Clarkson his time was up on Tuesday night following a unanimous board decision. He said the coach didn’t see the decision coming, but it was based on feedback from key people within the club that indicated they had lost their belief that Clarkson was the right man for the job. Viney said there were “gaping” holes in the gameplan when providing reasons for the decision at the post-sacking press conference. Clarkson hit back in an interview with this masthead saying he felt as though the club had “danced on my grave” with their comments. Loading McDonald – who was co-captain of the Kangaroos under Clarkson in 2023 and 2024 – refused to comment on whether the coach’s communication of the gameplan was confusing for the players. “I am not going to get into the nitty-gritty on the reasons because, at the end of the day, there is a lot of information the board have that we don’t as players,” McDonald said.



“We are not where we want to be as a footy club. We want to keep improving and keep getting better. That comes from the playing group. Obviously, we are going to bring in a new coach who is going to help that, but it’s going to come from our leaders, our young guys getting better and that is what we can control.” North Melbourne have not played finals since 2016, and Clarkson was the fourth coach to lead the team since Brad Scott – who took them to two preliminary finals. McDonald has played under Clarkson, Scott, Rhyce Shaw and David Noble. Loading “When a decision like that is made, the first thing you do as players is reflect on yourself,” McDonald said. “We have got to be better and play better footy and put ourselves in better positions that don’t lead to these decisions. The first thing we do as players is look at ourselves.



“We support the club’s decision, but it doesn’t make it any easier.” Related Article Exclusive

AFL 2026 ‘I feel like my life’s shot’: Alastair Clarkson’s first interview after his brutal North Melbourne sacking He said he didn’t know what type of coach the team needed but he was confident the board would make the right call despite the past three coaches now failing to lead the team to finals. “I would have thought it would be an enviable job,” McDonald said. Teammate Jackson Archer said he did not have a bad word to say about Clarkson, but the decision showed that the AFL is a cut-throat industry. World.title: Clancy faces years of confinement, no matter what comes next
World.content:
Analysis WorldNorth AmericaCourts Clancy faces years of confinement, no matter what comes next Mark Arsenault and Christina Morales September 6, 2026 — 4:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Plymouth: Whatever happens next in the murder case against Lindsay Clancy after a Massachusetts jury failed on Friday (US time) to reach a verdict, it is certain that she will remain institutionalised for many months, if not years. Even if she is not ultimately convicted, medical and legal experts have said that her future will be one of confinement. Clancy does not deny strangling her three children with exercise bands in 2023. Her symptoms of postpartum psychosis in the months before she killed them were at the centre of her defence. Her lawyers argued that she was not legally responsible for the deaths. Lindsay Clancy does not deny strangling her three children with exercise bands in 2023. Her symptoms of postpartum psychosis in the months before she killed them were at the centre of her defence. Mark Chavous/Pool The Enterprise via AP That view apparently convinced most of the jury members in the month-long trial. Notes from the jury suggested that 11 of the 12 jurors seemed ready to acquit Clancy. But one lone juror declined to join the rest, even after apparently expressing doubts about her guilt.



A similar debate has captivated and divided the American public for weeks. At its core is a fundamental disagreement about how Clancy should spend the rest of her life. Should she be labelled a criminal and imprisoned? Or should she be regarded as a victim of a sort, who should be provided treatment? In neither case would she go free. But to what end should her confinement serve? Related Article Updated

Courts Judge declares mistrial in Lindsay Clancy murder case that gripped America Michelle Oberman, a law professor at Santa Clara University who studies legal issues around pregnancy and motherhood, said it felt like a “watershed moment” that most jurors seemed inclined to support the idea that Clancy should be helped, not punished. Eleven of 12 jurors apparently agreed, she said, that “postpartum mental illness is real, and that postpartum psychosis can cause someone to do something they’d never otherwise do”. The murder charges against Clancy remain intact after the mistrial and will keep her locked up in a local psychiatric hospital for now, while the state decides whether to try her again, according to her lawyer, Kevin Reddington.



In remarks after the judge declared the mistrial, Reddington said Clancy would be returning to Tewksbury Hospital, where she was held during the trial. It is a state-run psychiatric facility about an hour’s drive from where Clancy was tried in Plymouth, Massachusetts. The judge set a September 29 status hearing in the case. Loading Timothy Cruz, the Plymouth County district attorney, did not immediately pledge to retry Clancy, saying on Friday that the decision would come later. But he strenuously defended his decision to charge her with first-degree murder and said the case was about seeking justice for her three dead children. The forceful tone of his remarks signalled that he was not likely to walk away from seeking accountability for Clancy, though it is possible the case could end with a negotiated plea bargain that forgoes the need for another lengthy and gut-wrenching trial.



Cruz dismissed the suggestion that the case was about mental health issues after the mistrial was announced, saying the trial was “about getting justice for those three little babies”. Related Article Analysis

Courts The Lindsay Clancy army, from mums in pink to right-wing podcasters If Clancy is ultimately found not responsible for the crimes, experts say she may be sent to a high-security forensic psychiatric hospital – a centre to treat people who have stood criminal trial – for long-term mental healthcare. Several psychiatrists said for many women, symptoms of postpartum psychosis were treated and resolved within a year. But even if she is found not guilty because of that diagnosis, Clancy will most likely be treated for other ongoing issues, such as suicidal thoughts and a potential diagnosis of bipolar disorder, which can be a risk factor for postpartum psychosis. Dr Katrina Furey, a reproductive psychiatrist, has treated patients with postpartum psychosis for about a decade. She said treatment could be conducted through a combination of drugs, and sometimes with electroconvulsive therapy, in which electricity is used to trigger a short seizure that can help “reset the brain”.



The treatment had a bad reputation from Hollywood movies, Furey said, but was routine and often effective. “The endgame of treatment is for mum to feel like her normal self again,” she added. Clancy “grieves the loss of those three children”, her lawyer, Kevin Reddington, said on Friday. Charles Krupa “Many of these women have no significant past psychiatric history, and then get very ill very quickly,” said Dr Nicole H. Cirino, a psychiatrist who serves on the Postpartum Psychosis Task Force at Postpartum Support International, a non-profit. She continued: “Reconciling that and thinking about how to move forward, particularly if they have legal involvement, is really something that is quite complicated and takes some time.”



Patients often worked with a team of psychiatrists, psychologists, social workers, nurses, peer advisers and other therapists while they were hospitalised, said Dr Susan Hatters-Friedman, a forensic and reproductive psychiatrist at Case Western Reserve University and the former president of the American Academy of Psychiatry and the Law. Related Article Opinion

Women's health It’s the terrifying case that’s gripping America. But is this mother a murderer or a victim? Julia Baird Journalist, broadcaster, historian and author The goal of forensic hospitalisation is not just to manage patients’ mental illness, but to prepare them to heal and possibly return to society. The treatment plan for patients such as Clancy very likely also includes helping them cope with the killings of their children. Clancy “grieves the loss of those three children”, Reddington said on Friday. In many states, including Massachusetts, people found not guilty by reason of insanity often spent more time hospitalised than they would have in prison, said Dr Renée Sorrentino, a forensic psychiatrist who is licensed in Massachusetts.



In Massachusetts, she said, Clancy would be reviewed for discharge on an annual basis. Doctors could recommend that she be discharged from the hospital if they believed her symptoms had improved and if they determined that she was not a danger to others. The Plymouth County district attorney’s office would then be notified. If it disagreed with the medical team’s assessment, it could obtain its own experts or argue in court that Clancy should remain hospitalised. A judge would then decide whether she could be released, Sorrentino said. “Humane mental health treatment is really important for her, and for us to think about as a society,” said Dr Nirmaljit Dhami, the medical director of an inpatient psychiatric ward in California focused on perinatal mental health and preventive care. In 2012, Deanna Laney, a Texas woman who was found not guilty by reason of insanity for killing two of her children and seriously injuring a third in 2003, was released from a psychiatric hospital after treatment. Several conditions were placed on her release. An Illinois woman, Paula Sims, was granted parole in 2021, after serving 30 years in prison for killing her infant daughter. Her lawyer said the decision to grant her parole was a recognition that “postpartum psychosis is real”.



Some women, however – like Andrea Yates, a Texas woman who in 2006 was found not guilty by reason of insanity in the killings of her five children – choose to waive their right to a review and remain hospitalised instead. World.title: Good sex feels increasingly rare. We need to change that
World.content:
September 6, 2026 — 4:23pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Last week at the park with our kids, my husband and I passed a car with towels covering the windows. Weird, but ok. My husband said the car’s occupants must’ve been having sex, which made sense, later, of the flushed faces of the young man and woman hovering near the car as they hugged. The prude in me was shocked, it being broad daylight and all. Today, consensual, legal, enjoyable sex counts as a win. Getty Images Then, a second thought. If no one was getting choked (even consensually) during sex, or allegedly pack raped by private school boys, or allegedly having their boundaries crossed by drunk footballers, then today, consensual, legal, enjoyable sex counts as a win. Good sex feels increasingly rare. Recent terrible headlines represent one distortion of sex. But there are other forces arrayed against us that are driving the sexes apart. We shouldn’t take this lying down. The reported Gen Z sex recession, our phone addiction, the substitution effect of online porn: all culprits here. There’s more.





When Dozer of RecipeTin Eats fame died, we mourned for Nagi Maehashi’s devoted companion. Nagi’s recipes are on high rotation at my house, but what I really eat up is the single-lady-porn she serves up: the fantasy of independent, successful womanhood, complete with dog and giant kitchen island. If this is modern spinsterhood – emphasis on “if”; Maehashi is coy about her private life – it looks so good. We’re so heteropessimistic that last year, Vogue asked, “is having a boyfriend embarrassing now?” Actually, it’s been ick for years. Barbie and Ken, and Peter Quill and Gamora, parted ways in 2023’s biggest blockbusters Barbie and Guardians of the Galaxy. No one would blink if Barbie or Gamora described themselves as “boysober” or “self-partnered”. Or if the guys consoled themselves that they’re “kenough”. Related Article Opinion

Sex & relationships Are men or women to blame for ‘heterofatalism’? I have a theory Julia Baird Journalist, broadcaster, historian and author We’ve apparently found a third way between the tragedy (everyone dies) and the comedy (everyone gets married): marriage carks it and everyone lives their best fake single lives online. Freya India is blunt in GIRLS®, her account of the inner online lives of Gen Z women: our culture is increasingly one where “marriage and families [are seen] only as traps instead of something to be treasured”. No one (except Nagi, perhaps) looks that happy, though. Maybe our dilemma is mythic? Susan Faludi just wrote in The New York Times that we’re in “a zero-sum struggle over which gender gets to own the hero’s journey”, convinced that “whoever owns the myth owns the culture”. But the idea that one sex has to end up “on top” is a failure of imagination. What if the real prize is each other?



2026 has given us two pro-marriage moments: Taylor Swift’s fairytale wedding to Travis Kelce and the ending of Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey. Maybe Taylor and Odysseus are the ones with main character energy in their relationships. But one person revolving around the other isn’t the ideal of marriage, or shouldn’t be. Rather, two people might face in the same direction, together. As Odysseus says in Homer’s epic, “There is nothing more admirable than when two people who see eye to eye keep house as man and wife, confounding their enemies and delighting their friends”. Not that marriage should outstrip all else. But we’re so downbeat about romantic love, we’d benefit from more pro-sex, pro-marriage material. How did we start with that couple’s carpark sexcapades and end with marriage? Treating sex and marriage interchangeably is a quirk of my Christian sexual ethics – not everyone’s thing, clearly, and admittedly, traditional relationships frequently fall short of the ideal of lifelong love, sex, fidelity. Still, the extremes haunting our cultural imagination of sex and relationships are worse. Online, the sexes seem mutually hostile, while sex in the news feels soiled by abuse, entitlement, indifference. Freed from the shackles of religion and tradition, the future was supposed to be extremely sex positive. It can’t be if the sexes retreat from each other instead.



That young couple had public sex. But even sex that takes place in private is public because sex always has spillover effects for our common life. These days, good sex resists the growing divide between men and women and our habit of looking at a screen rather than another human face. Sex like that isn’t just good, but great. Justine Toh is Senior Research Fellow at the Centre for Public Christianity.

World.title: Cheerleading fever sweeps Melbourne in record-breaking fan dance
World.content:
It’s a site that’s drawn huge crowds for countless legendary Australian sporting moments – from AFL grand finals to Matildas fever and the Australian Open. But on Sunday afternoon, Federation Square bore witness to something rather un-Australian. Thousands packed into the square waving shimmery golden pom-poms to welcome the San Francisco 49ers Gold Rush Cheerleaders, the official cheer squad for the National Football League (NFL) team. Staying cheerful: Fans at Federation Square on Sunday. Chris Hopkins Ahead of Australia’s first local NFL game, in which the San Francisco 49ers will take on the Los Angeles Rams at the MCG on Friday, the Gold Rush cheerleaders have already made history, setting a world record for the largest cheerleading dance, one which had 1424 people taking part. The dancers led an ecstatic crowd in a simple choreographed routine, set to a soundtrack of David Bowie’s Let’s Dance and Lady Gaga’s Just Dance.



The previous world record was held by Wing Dance Promotion, a cheerleading school in Japan, which staged its event with 1371 people in August 2015. Editor's pick Exclusive

NFL 2026 ‘Here to stay’: The numbers behind the NFL’s major Australian gamble Cheerleading, a distinctly American sport, has grown rapidly in Australia over the past few decades: more than 60,000 competitors are now registered with the Australian All Star Cheerleading Federation. The Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders has one Australian dancer, Faith Ward, who is the third-ever Aussie to have made the team. Zara, 12, and Quinn, 11, from Southern Cross Cheer, said on Sunday that it was inspirational to see such talented cheerleaders on our shores.



“It’s so fun to be here today. The energy is just amazing, and the NFL cheerleaders are so good,” Zara said. “They’re all so in sync; it’s amazing to watch them.” Some passionate Melbourne dancers arrived as early as 7am, hoping to get a front-row spot to see their cheer heroes from the 49ers perform onstage. Penny Tropman, 5, sat atop dad Aaron’s shoulders to participate in the record-breaking cheer dance. Chris Hopkins Penny Tropman, 5, and her father, Aaron, made the journey to Federation Square from Armadale to be part of the world record. Hoisted on her dad’s shoulders, Penny was enraptured and slightly overwhelmed as thousands of pom-poms shimmered high in the air. “I think as a young kid, it’s pretty cool to say you got to be part of a world record,” Aaron Tropman said. “This record is an opportunity to try and show off as much of this great city as we can.”



The 49ers, whose signature gold and red colours swept Federation Square, are the league’s most popular team in Australia, according to the NFL. The San Francisco 49ers cheerleaders on stage at Federation Square. Chris Hopkins “I think that comes from being one of the top teams in the ’80s, when a lot of people here consumed the NFL,” the league’s Australia and New Zealand general manager, Charlotte Offord, told The New York Times. Indeed, despite not having won a Super Bowl since 1995, the 49ers have maintained a devoted fan base. Friday’s match will be the first in a multi-year contract the NFL has signed with the Victorian government. Tickets, which went on sale in April, sold out almost immediately. Stefanie Shackelford (left) from California and Tricia Escamilla from Texas met on Sunday in Federation Square and bonded over their shared love of the San Francisco 49ers. Chris Hopkins



Californian Stefanie Shackelford, 61, and Texan Tricia Escamilla, 54, are both lifelong 49ers fans and travelled from the US to Melbourne for their team. They met in Federation Square and became fast friends. Editor's pick Streaming Guilt, ambition and a ponytail: Australian dancer makes the Dallas Cowboys Cheerleader squad “Our fans truly support our players, and I think that’s one of the best things when you’re at a game – the camaraderie between the fans and the players and the vibe. All of that, it’s just amazing,” says Shackelford. Adds Escamilla of seeing love for her team sweep Melbourne: “It’s just so impressive to have 49ers fans all across the globe, so that was exciting.” Melbourne reportedly beat multiple other cities to host the event, and the partnership is expected to boost the visitor economy.



Early tourism numbers, according to hotel analytics company STR, show hotel bookings for September 10 and 11 have quadrupled compared to the same dates last year, while American flight searches for Melbourne in early September have been up 149 per cent. Fans from more than 35 countries have bought tickets. Kyra, a member of the 49ers Gold Rush cheer squad (the NFL does not disclose cheerleaders’ surnames or ages), is visiting Australia for the first time. “It’s been super-exciting and amazing to be here. I’m just really grateful,” she says. “It’s really special to see faithful fans come out here and really represent Australia just as much as we represent them in America.”



Like most NFL cheerleaders, Kyra dances part-time, practising for five hours every weekend with her squad. She makes a living as an executive assistant in the venture capital world. “We do this because we love it, so we get together on weekends and share that amongst everyone that loves the sport of it,” she says. World.title: Indonesian volcano eruption halts flights at country’s busiest airport
World.content:
Updated WorldAsiaVolcanoes Indonesian volcano eruption halts flights at country’s busiest airport Tatan Syuflana , Niniek Karmini and and Elias Visontay Updated September 6, 2026 — 4:07pm ,first published 2:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Jakarta: Indonesia’s Anak Krakatau volcano erupted early on Sunday, prompting the cancellation of all flights at Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta International Airport as volcanic ash drifted across parts of western Indonesia. Indonesia’s Geological Agency said the volcanic island in Indonesia’s Sunda Strait, between the main Java and Sumatra islands, had shown signs of activity since Friday before erupting briefly at 3.53am (Jakarta time) on Sunday. The agency’s closed-circuit camera showed lava flares at the mountain. Volcanic ash spread across parts of the capital, Jakarta, and Lampung province on the southern tip of Sumatra island, Indonesia’s Centre for Volcanology and Geological Hazard Mitigation said. Flight operations were suspended until 1.30pm (4.30pm AEST) due to the ash, Soekarno-Hatta International Airport posted on Instagram, stranding hundreds of passengers at the country’s busiest airport.



Passengers sought refunds and reclaimed checked baggage as departure boards displayed a growing list of cancelled flights. The suspension had affected 301 flights, including 58 international flights, airport operator Angkasa Pura said in a statement. Singapore Airlines said it had cancelled flights to and from Jakarta for the rest of the day. Four Qantas flights – the arriving and departing non-stop services between Sydney and Jakarta and Melbourne and Jakarta – were cancelled on Sunday. Flight paths for other Qantas services traversing the region were disrupted. Qantas said its meteorologists and operations teams were closely monitoring conditions in and around Jakarta and thanked affected customers for their patience.



A Garuda Indonesia service from Sydney to Jakarta scheduled for Sunday morning was also delayed as airlines waited for the volcanic ash disruption to pass. Related Article Volcanoes Three hikers feared dead in volcanic eruption Other international flight disruptions, including cancellations, delays and rescheduled services, involved Hong Kong and Amsterdam, as well as Seoul, South Korea, Doha, Qatar, and Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. Domestic flights to Lampung, Bali and Surabaya were also cancelled or diverted. Indonesia’s Directorate General of Civil Aviation said it was closely monitoring the eruption’s impact on air travel and co-ordinating with airlines, airport operators, air navigation services and the meteorology agency. It said 170 aircraft parked overnight at Soekarno-Hatta remained on airport aprons. “Safety remains our top priority in every operational decision,” Lukman F. Laisa, Ministry of Transportation director general of civil aviation, said in a statement.



He warned that flight schedules could face cascading disruptions affecting aircraft rotations, fleet availability and terminal capacity as airlines work to restore operations. Authorities urged travellers to check with airlines for the latest flight information and advised passengers to temporarily avoid the airport unless necessary. Indonesia’s volcanology agency and the Darwin Volcanic Ash Advisory Centre in Australia identified two ash clouds using satellite imagery. One plume rose to an altitude of 6100 metres while drifting north-east, affecting parts of Jakarta, Banten, West Java and surrounding waters. A second cloud reached 15,200 metres and was moving westward and north-westward, covering parts of Banten, Lampung and Bengkulu provinces, the southern Sunda Strait and sections of the Indian Ocean west of Sumatra.



No casualties were reported, and no evacuation order was issued. The nearest settlement is more than 16 kilometres away. But residents and visitors were warned to stay at least three kilometres from the volcano’s active crater. Related Article Volcanoes 'There is a huge range in activity': Indonesia's erupting volcanoes Anak Krakatau, which means “child of Krakatau”, is the offspring of the famous Krakatau, whose monumental 1883 eruption triggered a period of global cooling. The eruption caused a tsunami in 2018 that killed at least 430 people in Sumatra and Java. Researchers believe volcanic activity triggered an underwater landslide and caused a large chunk of Anak Krakatau’s south-west slope to collapse and displace a large volume of water. Since then, the volcano has been rated at the second-highest alert status on a scale of four. Scientists said Anak Krakatau island was now only about a quarter of its original size.

World.title: Hidden cameras, no script: Oasis documentary goes inside the Gallagher brothers’ split
World.content:
CultureMoviesFilm Festivals Hidden cameras, no script: Oasis documentary goes inside the Gallagher brothers’ split Stephanie Bunbury September 6, 2026 — 4:02pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“I wasn’t prepared for the outpouring of joy and tears, and the sense of what it meant to people,” says Noel Gallagher. He is interviewed somewhere in the middle of the mighty Oasis reunion tour of 2025, chronicled in a new documentary, Don’t Look Back in Anger, that screened at the Venice Film Festival. “The gravity of it took me by surprise. It knocked me back.” Noel and Liam Gallagher attend the Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger screening at the Venice Film Festival. Getty Images The film, scripted by Peaky Blinders writer Stephen Knight and directed by Dylan Southern and Will Lovelace, is full of rolling tides of people in bucket hats and parka jackets surging into stadiums, weeping as they hear their favourites or simply laughing with glee.



A Catholic bishop in Manchester gives a sermon comparing the streams of people heading for the concert to a pilgrimage. It isn’t just about the music, as one fan says. It’s the reconciliation of two of Manchester’s favourite sons that has moved the crowds across the world. Related Article Melbourne live reviews Oasis bring Wonderwall magic to Melbourne – and the crowd goes wild Fifteen years after a final fight between the Gallagher brothers broke up the band, Noel tells the directors that touring with his estranged brother is “a chance to change the narrative of the band”. Famously, they hadn’t spoken since their blazing row in a Los Angeles dressing room, right before they were due on stage, leaving fans hanging. Liam, in a separate interview to camera, predicts simply – and true to form – that their first comeback show in Cardiff will be “f---ing carnage”. Both turn out to be right. The Gallaghers were in Venice for their premiere but – also true to form – didn’t come to the press conference. There was some speculation that they didn’t want to be pinned down on the prospects of another tour; more likely, it was just the Gallaghers being Gallaghers.



Meanwhile, Knight, Southern and Lovelace fielded questions. Stephen Knight says how surprised he was to be asked by Liam Gallagher’s team “to create a documentary with a plot” around the tour, given he had previously written only fiction. He jumped at it. “Of course, who wouldn’t? I’m a big fan.” Meanwhile, he says, everyone connected to Oasis was surprised by the huge response to news that they would tour again, playing songs from their first two albums. The shows sold out immediately. “There was such a demand for tickets – not only from the generation that grew up with them, but the next generation who had a strong attachment to the music. The question was why had that happened? Why did this music endure?” The Gallagher brothers arrive in Venice. Getty Images The rise and rise of Oasis, the battle of the brothers and the split is despatched quickly at the start of the film. “It’s called Don’t Look Back in Anger for a reason,” says Knight. “We’re not looking back at what happened. The spirit of this was intentionally, at a time of spite and social media meanness, about reconciliation.”



The aim of the film, says Lovelace, was to capture that as it happened. “I think the whole world was interested in that 15 years apart, would it work and what was it going to be like.” Editor's pick Live music This Aussie busker has gone viral for his Oasis set. But he’s been playing this spot for years At the beginning of Don’t Look Back in Anger, the filmmakers used 12 hidden cameras to record their rehearsals; the brothers speak where necessary, but barely look at each other. At least the music still works: the Gallaghers are both in their late 50s, but their voices are still true and Liam still attacks the microphone, as he says, “like I want to bite its head off”. On tour, the directors asked local cinematographers at stadium shows in several cities – Seoul, Manchester, Sao Paulo, Buenos Aires, with just a brief glimpse of Melbourne – to film what they wanted, on the stage or in front of it.



Feud? What feud? Liam and Noel Gallagher embrace on stage during the Melbourne leg of their reunion tour last year. Richard Clifford The performances are there – Oasis fans get plenty of bang for their bucks – but so are people trying to answer Knight’s initial questions. “As a writer of fiction, you get humbled by reality,” he says. Editor's pick Gallery icon 25 images Red carpet Venice Film Festival 2026: All the action on and off the red carpet “You hear why people are connected to a particular song, and it’s so eloquent. In South Korea, one woman said that when you fall down, some music picks you up but with Oasis, when you fall down, they fall down with you and then pick you up from the ground. I could never have written that.” Southern says: “On tour, it became as much about the crowd and how that influenced their relationship.” Fans cry – one man even falls to his knees and prays – but so do the band.



Towards the end of the tour, Noel admits that he often had to turn his back on the audience. The film culminates in their first joint interview in decades, ribbing each other about how early they need to go to bed at their age. “It’s not scripted, so we didn’t know what was going to happen,” says Knight. Editor's pick Floods She was given up for dead, then a faint cry came from the depths of the mud “The relationship develops on tour, their kids become friends, and once again, it’s family. We were very fortunate because that’s exactly what we hoped would happen, because from the beginning we wanted to make this a film about reconciliation and forgiveness.” The brothers have seen it and, according to Knight, are “beyond satisfied”. No further fights are expected, says Lovelace. “They appear to be getting on pretty well.” Find out the next TV, streaming series and movies to add to your must-sees. World.title: Defiant Dockers vow to block out naysayers
World.content:
NationalWAAFL 2026 Defiant Dockers vow to block out naysayers Justin Chadwick September 6, 2026 — 3:47pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Fremantle have vowed to avoid the outside “catastrophising” as they attempt to get their premiership assault back on track. The Dockers were widely tipped to cruise through to the grand final after snaring the minor premiership in stunning fashion. Two-time All-Australian Jordan Clark of the Dockers. AFL Photos But Thursday night’s 32-point qualifying final loss to Hawthorn means Fremantle will now have to do things the hard way to reach the decider. The Dockers will host Geelong in a semi-final at Optus Stadium on Friday night, with the winner to face the Swans in Sydney in a preliminary final.



Fremantle defender Jordan Clark was a rare shining light against the Hawks, racking up a game-high 38 disposals to go with 549m gained in what was his 150th AFL match. The 25-year-old had a simple method for Dockers players looking to avoid getting down in the dumps by their poor display. “You don’t read the media. You don’t buy into all the bullshit in the outside world,” Clark told AAP. “Everyone outside of us probably thinks it’s game over and catastrophising. But inside the four walls, we’re so confident in what we can do. “The world’s not over, and the sun comes up tomorrow, and we get to have another crack at it, so it’s all good.”



View post on X Fremantle won a club-record 14 consecutive games this season, but have now lost three of their past four matches, with Clark conceding Fremantle aren’t “humming” at the moment. “But we always know that it’s never far away,” he said. “We’ve seen that across this year - it doesn’t take much for us to turn it around and get on our bikes. “I’ve got full belief in this group. We’re such a good footy team when we get it right, and we’re not far off.



“So as far as it was a disappointing result, I’m actually so excited about the rest of the year.” Fremantle now need to win back-to-back games in order to reach the grand final - something that doesn’t scare Clark. “It’s been done before. It depends who you ask whether it is the hard way or the easy way,” Clark said. “It means we don’t get back-to-back weeks off or anything like that, but if you want to look at the positives, we get to keep playing. “We love playing footy, and that’s what we’re here to do. It’s not the hard way for us. It’s just another chapter in the story this year.”



Geelong secured a spot in the semi-final with a 33-point elimination final win over Carlton in front of 96,680 fans at the MCG on Friday night. Patrick Dangerfield wound back the clock with five goals from 21 disposals, while Max Holmes tallied 16 disposals and three clearances on restricted game time in his return from a broken ankle.

World.title: AFLW round four: Freo’s injury blow; Kangas smash to 31st straight win
World.content:
Injured AFLW powerhouse Mim Strom was forced to play ruck coach on the bench as the Dockers steamrolled a Monique Conti-less Richmond by 25 points on the road.

Two-time All-Australian ruck Strom was in agony at Ikon Park after a tackle from Tigers midfielder Emelia Yassir in the first quarter of Sunday’s clash.

Recruit Eden Zanker was first cab off the rank in the ruck, while Gabby O’Sullivan kicked three goals to help lift the Dockers to a 9.6 (60) to 5.5 (35) win in Indigenous Round.

Lisa Webb’s Dockers (2-2) can finish the fourth week of the 12-fixture competition in the top eight, but are bracing to lose Strom for part of their finals push.

Before Sunday, Strom had played 78 consecutive matches since making her debut in 2020.

“She’s been on the bench with a big smile so she’s hard to get a read on, but I’ll get a medical update,” coach Webb told Seven Plus at three-quarter time.

“She’s been a ruck coach on the side. She’s been a warrior for us, and we’ll look after her.”

World.title: Dental bills lead surge in requests to Christchurch charity fund
World.content:
Christchurch's Mayor's Welfare Fund has paid more than $200,000 to assist people with dental and electricity payments as the cost of living bites.

Those numbers have nearly doubled from the year prior.

Councillor Yani Johanson, the chair of the advisory fund committee, said the fund has paid out $122,474 for dental work so far in 2026, with a maximum of $2000 given out to any individual.

Dental expenses were previously counted as part of the medical category, but this year the fund had dental as a separate category due to the high number of requests.

"There is a huge need - the tragedy is of course that the more people don't go to the dentist, the longer they leave it, the higher the cost for treatment," Johanson said.

Poor dental health had a huge impact on a person's quality of life, self-esteem and health, he said.

"It's a damning indictment on our society and country that we have such huge need because it has become completely unaffordable for so many people and that's why we are seeing such an increase in demand," Johanson said.

The medical category accounted for $55,702 last year, including dental.

Requests for help with electricity bills had also jumped, with the fund paying out $109,599 so far this year, compared with $58,000 last year and $38,000 in 2024.

"Power prices are just going up and up and up, and people's income is just not meeting the cost of living. So we are seeing a significant increase in requests for help," Johanson said.

The Christchurch City Council's Mayor's Welfare Fund started as the Mayor's Coal and Blanket Fund in 1897 and was renamed in 1973.

In 1992 the Mayor's Welfare Fund Charitable Trust was created to administer the fund.

Johanson said the city has a proud tradition of helping those most in need.

"It's a fund of last resort to help people when there is no other option for funding to meet the basics that are needed to provide for their well-being."

The fund covers specific categories, and applications are assessed by an administrator on a case-by-case basis.

Items covered include electricity and rent arrears, firewood, medical costs, childcare arrears and funeral costs.

In the past year requests for help with child and adult learning assessments were added to the eligible criteria.

The fund gave out $54,876 for adult assessments and $39,936 for child assessments so far in 2026.

In the past year the fund received 702 applications with 447 approved, 98 declined, 129 withdrawn and 28 yet to be decided.

Johanson said the number of applications to the fund had increased hugely, as had the amount of money given out.

The fund is likely to pay $700,000 in grants by the end of this year compared with $371,000 last year.

Councillors had agreed to pay their directors' fees to the fund.

World.title: Election 2026: Political parties target supermarkets, NZ Super and more with fresh policy announcements
World.content:
The election campaign is heating up, with parties announcing a raft of new policies on Sunday, less than nine weeks out from the general election.

Politicians targeted superannuation, supermarkets, climate change and the housing market in their latest announcements throughout the day.

Here's everything you need to know about politicians' latest pledges.

Greens announce 'KiwiMart' plan

The Green Party has revealed its plan to establish a publicly-owned supermarket chain to break up the duopoly and drive down food prices.

The initiative is part of its 'Affordable Kai' policy, which would cost more than $6 billion over four years.

"We're not short of supermarkets, we're short of competition," co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick said.

"As experts have noted, divestment - that is, buying already existing stores - is key to breaking up the duopoly."

Plans to lure an existing chain to NZ had failed, she said, and further action was needed.

Foodstuffs and Woolworths would be forced to sell 120 stores and two distribution centres into public ownership, Swarbrick said.

That would require new legislation, she added.

Winston Peters says the cost of NZ Super for migrants is a "ticking timebomb" for the country. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

NZ First promises citizens-only superannuation

New Zealand First will restrict superannuation to citizens from 2029.

Leader Winston Peters said the cost of NZ super for migrants was a "ticking timebomb" for the country.

"How is it fair that the tax burden of supporting seniors now goes to paying for the full retirement of someone who has migrated to our country and only lived and paid taxes for sometimes less than half of the time compared to those who have worked their whole lives here?" he said on Sunday.

"If you want to get NZ Super then you need to sign up, be proud enough of New Zealand, and show full commitment to our country and become a citizen."

The party does not support other changes to entitlements or eligibility, or raising the retirement age to 67.

ACT vows to end 'political virtue signalling' over climate change

ACT leader David Seymour said the country's approach to dealing with climate change was broken and sending the country broke.

On Sunday he announced the party's plan to change that by ditching the net zero emissions target, repealing the Zero Carbon Act and cutting carbon tax if elected.

"A small trading nation can't ignore climate policy, but overdoing it backfires and puts unnecessary costs on Kiwi businesses and households," he said on Sunday.

The party's climate change spokesperson Simon Court said ACT would also seek a "better deal" for New Zealand under the Paris Agreement, regarding treatment of methane and CO2.

"If they're not prepared to be reasonable, maybe we should look at pulling out," he said.

National eyes easier path to homeownership

National has vowed to help more people buy their first home by expanding access to the First Home Loan scheme run by Kāinga Ora

It allows buyers to purchase their first home with a 5 percent deposit, rather than 20 percent which most banks require.

If re-elected, National said it would increase the income threshold so anyone earning less than $300,000 combined could access it - whether that was single or combined income.

"Right now, a junior doctor on $100,000 can't access the scheme," housing spokesperson Chris Bishop said.

World.title: Weather: Rain and snow warnings issued as trough crosses central NZ
World.content:
Heavy rain is causing flooding, slips and fallen trees across parts of Canterbury and the West Coast.

State Highway 6 between Punakaiki and Fox River has been closed because of a slip at Meybille Bay.

NZTA Waka Kotahi said flooding was also occurring on several highways between Greymouth, Reefton and Murchison.

Snow was also affecting higher parts of the South Island, including Lindis Pass, with people urged to take extra care on the roads.

MetService's website shows locations covered by warnings and watches at 11am Sunday. MetService / Screenshot

Up to 200 millimetres of rain was expected in the ranges today.

MetService said a large trough is crossing central New Zealand on Sunday and early Monday, bringing heavy rain and potentially snow to mountain passes.

An orange-level warning is in place for Grey and Buller Districts, and Nelson Lakes, from 9am Sunday until 1am Monday.

The MetService warning issued at 9:17am said residents should expect "a further 100 to 140 mm of rain about the ranges on top of what has already fallen," and 50-70 mm elsewhere.

It said peak intensities of up to 25mm/h were expected this afternoon and early evening.

At the same time, it issued a heavy rain warning for the Tararua Range, effective from 5pm Sunday until 3pm Monday, with up to 150 millimetres expected overnight.

It said there was a "minimal chance" of the either warning being upgraded, but urged people to avoid low-lying areas.

"Streams and rivers may rise rapidly. Surface flooding, slips, and difficult driving conditions possible."

Rain watches were in place for the Westland ranges north of Mt Cook until 10pm, Tasman west of Takaka until 3am Monday, and the Canterbury High Country north of Mt Cook and southwestern Marlborough until 4am Monday.

Watches will come into force for northern Taranaki at 6pm, southern and eastern Wellington and Wairarapa away from the ranges at 11pm, and the Ruahine Range at 3am Monday.

Road snowfall warnings

By 10am Sunday, MetService had issued road snowfall warnings for five mountain passes in the South Island.

Further north, rain is expected to turn to snow about the summits of Arthur's Pass and Porters Pass (both SH73) from 9pm Sunday until early Monday morning.

World.title: Tenancy Tribunal orders tenant to clean his room after old takeaway and fizzy drink rubbish causes odour
World.content:
It's a common sight in many homes across the country - a boy's messy, smelly room.

But unable to send their tenant to time out after repeatedly asking him to clean his room, a landlord instead turned to the Tenancy Tribunal.

According to a recently released decision, the tenant had let rubbish pile up so badly in his room it made the home smell bad.

Photos provided to the tribunal showed rubbish in the bedroom, including takeaway food packaging, empty containers and fizzy drink bottles.

The rubbish had marked and stained the walls and likely damaged and caused deterioration to the carpet.

Tribunal adjudicator Theo Baker ordered the tenant to get rid of the rubbish, vacuum his room and clean all surfaces.

The tenant was also ordered to pay the $28 filing fee to the landlord.

The tenant and landlord were granted name suppression.

The landlord initially served the tenant with a 14-day remedy notice, with an extension granted over a weekend to allow the work to be completed.

But when the room was still unclean, the landlord applied to the tribunal claiming the tenant was in breach of the tenancy agreement and the Residential Tenancies Act because of the rubbish.

The room-by-room tenancy was in a three-bedroom apartment, and the landlord told the tribunal the condition and smell of the tenant's room were making it harder to get a new tenant.

The smell from the room had spread into the flat's common areas and the foyer area of the level.

The rubbish blocked the floor, creating a potential fire hazard.

The tenant told the tribunal he was finding it difficult to clear the rubbish and was experiencing a mental block.

A landlord took their tenant to the Tenancy Tribunal after struggling to get them to clean their room (file photo). Flickr

"It is strongly recommended that the tenant gets some help with cleaning his room," Baker said.

"There are organisations who can provide a non-judgmental service."

If the tribunal finds the tenant has failed to comply with an obligation under the Residential Tenancies Act, it can make an order for the landlord to do the work.

If a work order was not made by consent of both parties, the tribunal must also make a monetary order as an alternative to compliance with the work order.

The landlord did not seek a monetary order alternative.

The tenant agreed he must clean his room, so Baker treated the claim as a consent order and did not impose a monetary amount.

Tenant risks losing tenancy

A work order may also authorise the landlord to undertake the work and charge the tenant the costs, if the tenant fails to comply with the work order and alternative monetary order.

A monetary limit must be imposed by the tribunal on the costs that can be charged, however, the landlord was reluctant for this to happen.

Baker also considered whether a conditional termination order should be made, but the landlord did not seek termination in their application.

"Termination was not mentioned in the notice of hearing that went to the parties. Therefore, I do not have the power to order a conditional termination at present," Baker said.

"I also record that the tenant is in serious danger of losing his tenancy.

"If he does not meet his obligations, and the landlord follows the correct steps, it is not certain, but very likely that the tribunal would terminate on an application for termination.

"I encourage the tenant to seek help."

* This story originally appeared in the New Zealand Herald.

World.title: New Zealand First pledges to restrict Superannuation to citizens from 2029
World.content:
New Zealand First has pledged to restrict Superannuation to citizens only from 2029 if elected.

Leader Winston Peters, announcing the policy at a public meeting in Hamilton on Sunday, said many had raised concerns about the affordability of Superannuation.

"With our growing older population and the increasing costs of Super on taxpayers, how is it fair that the tax burden of supporting seniors now goes to paying for the full retirement of someone who has migrated to our country and only lived and paid taxes for sometimes less than half of the time compared to those who have worked their whole lives here?" he said.

"New Zealand First believes we need to instil some meaning and value back into being a Kiwi, and back into being a New Zealand Citizen."

The establishment of New Zealand Super in 1977 did not account for current immigration levels, Peters said.

He described the cost of Superannuation for migrants as a "ticking timebomb".

"If you want to get NZ Super then you need to sign up, be proud enough of New Zealand, and show full commitment to our country and become a citizen.

"Our taxpayers should no longer continue to be used as a bottomless pit by some migrants to our country," Peters said.

"This is about economic fairness, and it is about putting New Zealanders first."

New Zealand First was not supporting other changes to entitlement or eligibility for New Zealand Superannuation, nor raising the age to 67.

World.title: ACT unveils election climate policy, vows to scrap net zero target and repeal Zero Carbon Act
World.content:
The ACT party has vowed to get rid of the net zero emissions target, repeal the Zero Carbon Act and cut carbon tax if elected.

Its climate policy is largely a repeat of what it brought to the 2023 election campaign, and promises not to "kneecap New Zealand's prosperity for the sake of political virtue signalling".

ACT leader David Seymour said the country's approach to dealing with climate change was broken and sending the country broke.

"A small trading nation can't ignore climate policy, but overdoing it backfires and puts unnecessary costs on Kiwi businesses and households," he said.

ACT's policy was "grounded in economic reality" and would reduce emissions without imposing costs on New Zealanders that trading partners were unwilling to bear, Seymour said.

The policy includes:

repealing the Zero Carbon Act and scrapping the target of net zero emissions by 2050, instead benchmarking New Zealand's emissions cap against major trading partners

cutting the Carbon Tax by removing the Government's minimum price for Emissions Trading Scheme auctions

introducing a carbon tax refund, returning 100 per cent of net carbon auction revenue to New Zealanders

opposing new climate taxes, including a tax on agricultural emissions

discouraging productive farms being converted into carbon forests and requiring forest owners to carry long-term costs and risks of their forests

offering "carbon assistance" to businesses that can demonstrate a competitive disadvantage against overseas producers if those competitors have lower or no carbon costs

ACT leader David Seymour said the government was not making money through carbon actions because it refused to sell units for less than $70.

"If we remove that artificial price floor, we can start selling New Zealand units back into the ETS," he said.

"The taxpayer will get the revenue from that as a carbon dividend for each household."

Seymour said households paid nearly $500 annually in carbon tax which was built in to things like petrol and power.

"We would have the government start selling units again at whatever the market price is and return that money to households."

Inland Revenue could issue it as a refund against taxes, he said.

ACT Climate Change spokesperson Simon Court said ACT would also seek a "better deal" for New Zealand under the Paris Agreement.

New Zealand has pledged to halve its emissions by 2030.

"New Zealand produces a tiny share of global emissions," Court said.

"We should play our part, but there is no virtue in sacrificing jobs, household incomes and productive land so politicians can boast about being more ambitious than everyone else."

Seymour added the Paris Agreement did not reflect New Zealand's status as an agricultural nation, viewing methane and carbon dioxide as having the same impact.

"That's unfair on an agriculturally-based economy like New Zealand," he said.

"So we say, Paris needs to change and reflect the true science that methane is different from CO2. If they're not prepared to be reasonable, maybe we should look at pulling out."

Court said ACT's climate policy would reward efficient local businesses, rather than push production offshore.

"If a New Zealand business can produce steel, cement, aluminium or food more efficiently than its overseas competitors, closing that business is an economic own goal and an environmental one too," he said.

"ACT will cut unnecessary costs, protect Kiwi jobs, give carbon revenue back to households and let innovation deliver cleaner solutions."

World.title: Leopard seal draws crowds at Lower Hutt beach
World.content:
A leopard seal lying on Petone Beach in Lower Hutt has been attracting dozens of curious spectators.

The Department of Conservation (DOC) estimates more than 150 people have come to see the sea mammal since it came ashore on Saturday afternoon.

"It's so awesome to have animals like this come and visit us around New Zealand," says DOC ranger Melody McLaughlin

"I really have to give a shoutout to people because they've been awesome. They've been really respectful, keeping space, giving the animal plenty of space.

"This part of Petone Beach is a off-leash dog walking area. And everybody yesterday and today that we have seen have had their dogs on leads."

DOC thanked dog owners for keeping their pets on leads. DOC / Supplied

McLaughlin said that's wise because leopard seals can severely injure or kill dogs that get too close, particularly smaller breeds.

"I think people just have to be aware these animals are apex predators. They are not afraid of moving objects coming in front of them."

At the same time, she said people need to be mindful that leopard seals are a protected species, so need to be given their space.

DOC says about 150 people have come to see the leopard seal. DOC / Supplied

McLaughlin said the sight of them on New Zealand beaches is rare but becoming more common.

"[In] the last few years, this is probably the third one that I've seen. We had a massive, huge leopard seal in Oriental Parade by the boat sheds for a time."

She said DOC staff have not been trying to get this one back into the water.

World.title: Greens vow to break up supermarket duopoly, set up publicly owned 'KiwiMart'
World.content:
The Green Party is campaigning on establishing a publicly owned supermarket chain to break up the duopoly and drive down food prices.

The initiative is part of its 'Affordable Kai' policy which would cost more than $6 billion over four years, and included expanding the school lunch programme.

Co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick said successive governments had failed to lure an existing chain to New Zealand to introduce competition in the sector, which is dominated by Foodstuffs and Woolworths.

"That's why today we are announcing the real solution: a supermarket owned by all New Zealanders, for all New Zealanders," she said.

"We're not short of supermarkets, we're short of competition. As experts have noted, divestment - that is, buying already existing stores - is key to breaking up the duopoly."

The publicly owned chain, KiwiMart, would be mandated to prioritise affordability.

Co-leader Marama Davidson said it was unacceptable that people were going without food because they could not afford it, given New Zealand produces enough to feed 40 million people.

"Government has abdicated its responsibilities and left it to the market, in fact literally, the supermarket," she said.

Foodstuffs and Woolworths would be forced to sell 120 stores and two distribution centres into public ownership which would require new legislation, Swarbrick said.

The party said its plan would cost about $2.8b.

Parliamentary Library modelling estimated it would cost $1.3b to buy the stores and distribution centres, and $1.5b to establish KiwiMart, it said.

Swarbrick said KiwiMart would start with 15 percent market share.

A publicly owned supermarket was not a new idea, Swarbrick said.

"This is something that has been identified by experts and economists, the likes of Consumer New Zealand as a consumer advocacy group, who have identified that as a small country at the bottom of the world, that it does make sense to have a publicly owned supermarket as a third competitor," she said.

"We are proud to say it's something that the Greens are taking to the election to actually increase affordability for New Zealanders. "

The Greens' full Affordable Kai policy also includes:

restoring and permanently funding the school lunch programme Ka Ora, Ka Ako and expanding it to 150,000 more children ($2.2b)

increasing food bank funding from $8 million to $25m ($72m) doubling the cap on Work and Income food grants ($388m)

a $150m annual Fair Food Fund for community-led food security initiatives ($600m)

increasing funding, penalties and powers for the Commerce Commission, including a mandatory pricing accuracy code with automatic compensation when shoppers are overcharged ($104m)

banning supermarket price gouging and extending that to include other "uncompetitive" sectors like energy and fuel

a National Food Strategy, including legislating the right to adequate and nutritious food.

Davidson said the policy would rebuild parts of the food system the current government had "run down".

World.title: Ex-Eagle says 'conservative and vanilla' AFL club's main focus is money
World.content:
Former West Coast midfielder Sharrod Wellingham says the Eagles have become "conservative and vanilla", with a focus on money rather than on-field success, following another poor AFL season.

West Coast finished 16th with four wins in 2026, which took their total victories to 15 since the beginning of the 2022 campaign.

"I feel like West Coast have become so complacent because they've got a lot of off-field success as a business and they've got a lot of things that they're doing right when it comes to making money," Wellingham said on 102.5 ABC Perth's SportsTalk program.

"I feel like that's where their focus is.

" They're not aggressive, they're not ruthless and the invisible board is definitely a factor. "

Wellingham, who was part of Collingwood's 2010 premiership side under Mick Malthouse before joining the Eagles in 2013, warned West Coast was in danger of going down the same path as other historically successful clubs that have drifted into irrelevance.

"There's the potential for West Coast to develop into an Essendon," he said.

Wellingham played 79 games for West Coast after winning a premiership with Collingwood. (Paul Kane, file photo: Getty Images)

West Coast has made several high profile changes in recent years, with the appointment of Don Pyke as chief executive, Andrew McQualter as coach, and Elizabeth Gaines as chair of the board.

But Wellingham said he didn't feel like much had changed at the club, which had struggled on the field in recent years.

He pointed to the decision to trade away pick three in 2024 to secure the services of now co-captain Liam Baker from Richmond, a decision which ultimately cost the Eagles access to the AFL Rising Star Jagga Smith.

If the Eagles had decided to draft Smith, they would have a midfield boasting Harley Reid, Elijah Hewett, Willem Duursma and Smith.

Jagga Smith was drafted by Carlton. (Getty Images: Russell Freeman)

"It was a terrible decision," Wellingham said.

"There is zero swag that comes out of West Coast ... they're conservative and vanilla.

"I don't know where the change is going to come from. Yes, you want to have good people and be of sound culture, but you've got to have some ruthlessness.

"I feel like there's nothing that sounds like that and feels like that that's coming from the footy club at the moment."

Eagles CEO Don Pyke hinted at the club's determination to return to the AFL summit during West Coast's end of season awards, when he said "September is for finals, not functions".

World.title: Aussie Patterson claims Diamond League Final title with 'insane' win
World.content:
Australia's Eleanor Patterson has continued her outstanding season by winning the women's high jump at the Diamond League Final in Brussels.

Patterson was joined on the podium by fellow Australian and reigning world champion, Nicola Olyslagers, who finished third.

The result gave Australia two victories across the weekend at the King Baudouin Stadium, following Cameron Myers's triumph in the men's 1,500m on the opening night.

Myers wins Diamond League Final Cameron Myers has beaten a star-studded field at the Diamond League Final in Brussels.

Patterson successfully cleared 2.01 metres with her final attempt at the height, edging out Ukrainian Olympic champion and world-record holder, Yaroslava Mahuchikh (1.99m).

Mahuchikh failed with her three attempts at 2.01m.

Olyslagers cleared 1.95m to round out the top-three placings.

Patterson attempted 2.03m, which is the same height as Mahuchikh's 2026 world lead, but could not manage a successful clearance.

She added the Diamond League Final title to her second Commonwealth Games gold, which she won in Glasgow in late July.

Her win came a week after she equalled her personal best (PB) of 2.02m in Germany.

"It's amazing," Patterson said.

"I've only won a Diamond League meet once before in 2023, so to win the final is insane. I knew I was in good shape after jumping 2.02m a few days ago.

"It was chilly, but I just went out to have fun and I'm super happy with how today turned out."

Eleanor Patterson celebrates her win in Brussels. (Getty Images: Tim Clayton)

Patterson said ignoring the performances of her rivals was the key to victory.

"Today, I stayed clinical and stuck to my own process, which really paid off," she said.

Australia's Olympic silver medallist Jessica Hull was third in the women's 1,500m, producing a season-best time of 3:54.73.

"It's nice to run the fastest I have all year in September, I think that shows my training works when you want to peak this time of the year," Hull said.

Poland's Klaudia Kazimierska saluted with a world-leading time and meet record of 3:54.05, which was also a PB.

Kenyan Dorcus Ewoi was second in a PB of 3:54.73, while Hull's Australian teammate Abbey Caldwell (3:57.19) finished seventh.

Meanwhile, Australia's Sarah Billings was fifth in the women's 800m with a time of 1.59.99.

Swiss star Audrey Werro claimed the meet record in winning with 1:54.75.

World.title: Sweeny exits US Open to end Australia's singles chances
World.content:
Dane Sweeny's gallant US Open campaign has come to a frustrating end with a tough third-round loss to 21st-seeded Italian Luciano Darderi.

Sweeny complained of a hip injury during a 6-4, 6-3, 6-3 defeat to the world number 22 that left Australia without a second-week singles hope in New York for the first time in five years.

Alex de Minaur's shock second-round loss to Botic van de Zandschulp meant Sweeny was Australia's last player standing at Flushing Meadows.

"It's been an amazing week, a career-changing week, but I can't help but feel a bit disappointed just with today's performance," Sweeny said.

"I just wasn't really feeling it, just not really feeling the timing and the rhythm as I have been. I just made a lot of cheap errors and that was quite frustrating.

"I was OK to lose a match, but I really wanted to test him more and bring a good level so I could make an absolute fight out of it.

"Win or lose, I wanted to really make him work for the victory at least and I wasn't able to do that."

The world number 123 only gained a last-minute entry to the US Open after two late withdrawals allowed Tennis Australia to grant Sweeny the reciprocal wildcard it initially handed to Alexei Popyrin.

Dane Sweeny reached the last 32 for the first time at a major. (Getty images/USTA: Dustin Satloff)

Despite his disappointment, Sweeny cashed in on his good fortune.

The 25-year-old turned his first US Open main-draw appearance into a watershed run to the last 32 of a major for the first time.

The Queenslander will walk away with a life-changing cheque for $402,500 and a fresh career-high ranking.

"The financial side of things, that will help with coaching and people you travel with," Sweeny said.

Sweeny is provisionally slated to climb to number 109 in the world.

If he can crack the top 100 by season's end, Sweeny will earn direct entry to the Australian Open for the first time.

"That's exciting too. But that will take care of itself," Sweeny said.

"It's hard not to worry about that because we're indoctrinated to want that low number next to our name, but I can just focus on working hard, focus on improving.

"Particularly just staying really kind to myself and trying to enjoy the journey."

American tilt takes a hit

Past US Open finalists Taylor Fritz, Madison Keys and Amanda Anisimova all crashed out in the third round, dealing a stinging blow to home fans.

Men's ninth seed ​Fritz had yet to drop a set in New York and looked well on his way to another routine victory before Argentina's Francisco Cerundolo found his best tennis to flip the script and win 3-6, 4-6, 6-3, 6-4, 6-4.

It was the earliest exit in four years for the 2024 runner-up, as Cerundolo reached the ​fourth round for the first time.

The American ‌women fared no better as China's Zheng Qinwen fought back from a 5-0 deficit in the decider to beat 2017 runner-up Keys 1-6, 7-6 (7/3), 7-5, collapsing on the court in utter joy as she fights back from a career slump.

Zheng Qinwen celebrates her win over Madison Keys. (Getty Images: Al Bello)

Zheng will next face 2022 champion and former world number one, Iga Świątek, who got past Czech Marie Bouzková 7-6 (7/3), 7-6 (7/3).

Tenth-seeded Anisimova, last ​year's runner-up, was unable to reverse ‌her fortunes in a frustrating year at the majors, with a 6-2, 7-5 defeat by Anastasia Potapova.

Coco Gauff, the 2023 US Open winner, provided the lone bright spot for the Americans when she beat Spain's Cristina Bucșa 6-3, 6-4 in the third round.

AAP/Reuters

World.title: How the Panthers and Warriors can win the NRL minor premiership
World.content:
The NRL minor premiership is still up for grabs heading into the final day of the home-and-away season, with the New Zealand Warriors on top and the Penrith Panthers ready to pounce.

The Warriors moved to outright first with a narrow win in Auckland on Saturday, but the Panthers only need a slender win on Sunday afternoon to reclaim top spot, where they have spent much of the 2026 season.

The Warriors and Panthers will finish in the top two, and in practical terms there is little different between the two spots entering the finals series.

Both sides will host two matches in the finals, including qualifying finals next week.

But the minor premier does get a monetary prize, and confidence heading into finals footy, knowing they finished on top of the pile after 27 gruelling rounds of rugby league.

Here is how the Warriors and Panthers can win the minor premiership, and what happens when first and second are level on points, and point differential.

NRL top two

1st: New Zealand Warriors — 42, points for 728, points against 418, point differential +310

2nd: Penrith Panthers — 40, points for 645, points against 337, point differential +308

How the Warriors can become minor premiers

Panthers fail to beat Wests Tigers

Panthers defeat Tigers by one point

With a nail-biting one-point win over Manly yesterday in Auckland, the New Zealand Warriors put themselves in outright first on the NRL ladder.

ABC NRL Daily podcast Andrew Moore and the ABC NRL team bring you your daily dose of NRL conversation. The team give you the context and depth beyond the headlines.

But their fate is out of their hands.

If the Tigers cause an upset and defeat the Panthers this afternoon, then the Warriors will win the minor premiership.

If the Panthers beat the Tigers, they will draw level on points with the Warriors, and then the minor premiership will be decided by point differential.

The Warriors hold a very narrow two-point advantage over the Panthers in the points differential — Warriors +310, Panthers +308.

That means if the Panthers can only manage a one-point win over the Tigers at Western Sydney Stadium, then the Warriors would finish first by having a superior points differential +310-+309.

How the Panthers can become minor premiers

Defeat Wests Tigers by two or more points

The first thing the Panthers must do is beat Wests Tigers.

Then, how much they beat the Tigers by will decide who finishes first and second on the NRL ladder.

The Panthers will finish as minor premiers if they beat the Warriors by two or more points.

If two teams finish on the same points and have the same points differential, the NRL splits the two sides based on a tiebreaker: points for divided by points against, then multiplied by 100 (Points for / points against x 100).

If this tiebreaker is needed, then the Panthers will finish higher as their defence this year has conceded much less than the Warriors, greatly assisting that tiebreaker maths equation.

Who will the Panthers and Warriors face in the first week of finals?

By finishing in the top two, the Warriors and Panthers have earned the right to host two matches in the finals.

Each will host qualifying finals in week one. If they win, they will host a preliminary final in week three.

If the Panthers or Warriors lose in week one, they then host a cut-throat semifinal in week two against a side that was victorious in week one elimination finals played between the teams that finished fifth-eighth.

In week one, whoever finishes first will host the Sydney Roosters (4th) and the team that finishes second will host the Dolphins (3rd).

The NRL will announce dates and times for week one of the final once all matches in round 27 finish.

World.title: Wallabies escape with draw against Pumas after late penalty try
World.content:
The Wallabies have snatched a 28-28 draw with Argentina in Mendoza after they were awarded a penalty try with 10 minutes remaining in the Test.

Trailing 28-21, the Wallabies were on the attack inside the Pumas' 22 when the home side's fullback Santiago Carreras deliberately knocked the ball on in defence.

Referee James Doleman felt he had no other option but to award the Wallabies a penalty try.

Carreras was shown a yellow card for his infringement only a minute after teammate Lucio Cinti committed the same offence and was sent from the field for 10 minutes.

The Pumas were reduced to 13 players but the Wallabies failed to take advantage.

They could not break the deadlock in the shadows of full-time, but still secured a history-making 1-0 series win.

The Wallabies had previously never won a multi-Test series on Argentine soil.

The result also left new coach Les Kiss with an unbeaten record (three wins and a draw) since taking over from Joe Schmidt.

Kiss will be sweating on Carter Gordon's scan results after the Wallabies' replacement fly half left the field in the second half with an ankle injury.

It was an unconvincing performance from the Wallabies, who had led 14-0 following converted tries to captain Harry Wilson and Max Jorgensen in the first half.

The Pumas responded before the half-time break with tries to skipper Pablo Matera and Ignacio Mendy, both of which were converted by Carreras.

The Wallabies and Pumas could not be split on the scoreboard in Mendoza. (Getty Images: Alejandro Pagni)

It was 14-14 at half-time, before the Wallabies broke the deadlock with Fraser McReight's try from close range in the 47th minute.

Ryan Lonergan added the extras but it was a short-lived lead after the Pumas responded through converted tries to Ignacio Ruiz and Matera.

The Pumas held their advantage until Carreras's indiscretion late in the match.

The Wallabies, who won the opening Test 27-21 in Jujuy last week, now have three weeks to prepare for their next clash.

They face world champions South Africa in Perth on September 27.

Look back at how the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Piastri hit with grid penalty at Italian Grand Prix
World.content:
Australia's Oscar Piastri has been hit with a three-place grid penalty at the Italian Grand Prix after he was found guilty of impeding another driver in qualifying.

Piastri finished third in qualifying but will start from sixth on the grid at Monza.

Stewards decided on the grid drop after finding the McLaren driver had impeded Red Bull's Liam Lawson.

Piastri, seventh on the drivers' standings, is on the third row alongside Red Bull's four-time world champion Max Verstappen.

The decision means Ferrari holds down the second row with Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton, behind surprise pole sitter Pierre Gasly and George Russell.

Gasly, who won at Monza in 2020, upset the favourites to grab a stunning career-first pole position with Renault-owned Alpine.

He seized pole from Mercedes's George Russell with a lap of one minute and 21.786 seconds.

Pierre Gasly will start from pole for the first time in his career. (Getty Images/Formula 1: Dom Gibbons)

His effort was 0.060 quicker than the Briton.

"It's been nine years trying to chase the opportunity to get ‌a pole," said Gasly, who was the last of the pole contenders to complete his final ⁠flying lap.

"I won my first race in Monza and got my first ‌pole at this track. It's something special ​around here."

Gasly had already hinted ‌at something special in the earlier phases, leading Q1 and fourth fastest in Q2.

His mechanics erupted in jubilation as the pole was confirmed, a day after he had been stripped of third place at last June's Monaco Grand Prix.

Russell, ​a ‌title contender, hailed an incredible performance by the 30-year-old Frenchman.

"We were finishing a game of chess about 15 minutes before qualifying and he beat me there and I went, 'Well, I ⁠think I will beat you in qualifying,' and here ‌we are, he's ahead of me ‌again," Russell said.
